SQL Mastery

The relational model and the query language, then the system underneath them: how the planner turns a declarative query into a plan and how to read the plan back, what an index actually costs, why MVCC makes a rollback cheap, and every isolation anomaly produced by two real sessions. Then the operational material — vacuum and bloat, WAL and durability, partitioning, row-level security, and the migrations you can run while the site is up.

How to use this course

  • This course is where the data lives. It assumes the Foundations course, or equivalent programming experience; it does not assume you have used a database. §1 starts with the relational model, the server as a separate process, and psql.
  • It teaches PostgreSQL, not a lowest common denominator. Where behaviour is standard SQL the course says so, and where it is specific to PostgreSQL the course says that too — but the examples use PostgreSQL's real features rather than avoiding them, because a practitioner works with one database, not with the intersection of all of them.
  • Everything here was run against a real server. Every code block was executed against PostgreSQL 18.6 through psql, and every printed result is what that server returned. The concurrency sections were produced by two live sessions, not described — including the write skew that REPEATABLE READ permits and SERIALIZABLE refuses. In about a dozen places the installed server and the documentation disagree, and the course reports what the server did: in 18, for example, generated columns default to VIRTUAL, and a virtual column cannot be indexed.
  • The authority is the PostgreSQL 18 documentation and the server. The syllabus was derived from the complete tutorial and SQL-language parts of the PostgreSQL 18 documentation, fetched on 2026-09-02, plus the chapters on roles, maintenance, backup, reliability and the WAL, triggers, the rule system and PL/pgSQL.
  • The course goes from the model down to the machine. §1–§5 are the model, syntax, data types, schema and schema design. §6–§11 are the query language: joins, grouping, set operations and pagination, subqueries and CTEs, window functions, and modifying data. §12–§13 are indexes and the planner. §14–§16 are transactions and MVCC, locking, and vacuum and the WAL. §17–§20 cover JSON, arrays, ranges and full-text search; views, functions and triggers; partitioning; and security and operations. §21 builds a system and makes it hold up.
  • Each section has numbered subsections, queries with their real output, and exercises with worked solutions. Plan costs and timings are properties of the machine they ran on, so yours will differ. The plan shapes — which node, which index, which estimate is wrong — are the claims, and those should match.

You need a PostgreSQL 18 server and a database you are willing to break. Check the client version and create a scratch database before starting:

psql --version          # psql (PostgreSQL) 18.x
createdb scratch        # a database to experiment in; drop it with dropdb scratch

Versions every example in this course was produced against: PostgreSQL 18.6, through its own psql.

What you are actually learning

Not a list of clauses. Five mechanisms, each of which explains a large class of behaviour:

  1. Declarative queries become plans. You describe the result and the planner chooses how to produce it. EXPLAIN prints that choice as a tree, and comparing estimated rows against actual rows from the top down finds the wrong decision every time (§13).
  2. An index is a cost you pay on every write. Selectivity decides whether one helps at all, column order is equality, then range, then sort, and a condition in Filter rather than Index Cond narrowed nothing (§12).
  3. Every row has versions. MVCC is why a reader never blocks a writer, why a rollback costs almost nothing, and why a lost update needs no exotic isolation level — read 100, another session adds 50, write 70, and the 50 is gone without an error (§14).
  4. Integrity belongs in the database. A partial unique index or an exclusion constraint makes a double booking impossible under concurrency, where the application-side check always has a race. Every such rule survives the second code path; the application versions do not (§4, §17).
  5. A database is operated, not just queried. Dead rows accumulate and vacuum reclaims them, one idle transaction holds back cleanup for every table in the cluster, and a schema can be migrated live only if you know which ALTER rewrites the table (§16, §20).

By the end you should be able to design a schema that protects itself, write a query and then read the plan that proves it is fast, predict what two concurrent transactions will do to each other, and change a production schema without taking the site down — without looking anything up.

SECTION 1

The Relational Model, the Server and psql

Start with a puzzle. A table holds two rows. Each row has a column called note. You ask the database for every row where note equals 'set', or where note does not equal 'set'. How many rows come back?

Every value is either equal to 'set' or not, so the answer must be two. Guess before reading on.

The answer is one. Exercise 5 at the end of this section builds exactly that table, runs exactly that query, and the server prints 1. The missing row has no value in note at all, and SQL treats "no value" in a way that surprises almost everyone the first time. §1.12 explains it, and by then the answer will look obvious.

That puzzle is a good first taste of SQL. SQL (usually said "sequel" or "S-Q-L") is the language you use to store data in a database and ask questions about it. It looks like simple English, and most of the time it does what the English says. The places where it does not are what this course is for.

SQL is the only programming language in wide use that is declarative about data: you describe the result you want, and something else decides how to get it. You do not say "go through the rows one by one"; you say "the rows where the country is Brazil". That single property explains almost everything else about the language:

  • why it is strange to read at first;
  • why the same query can be fast on Monday and slow on Tuesday;
  • and why §13 on the planner is as important as any section about syntax.

Here is a picture to keep in mind for the whole section: an archive of index cards, run by an archivist.

  • Each box holds cards of one kind, all with the same printed fields: a box of customer cards, a box of order cards.
  • You never walk among the boxes yourself. You hand the archivist a written request saying what you want, and the archivist decides how to find it.
  • The archive keeps a register of its own boxes, written on the same kind of cards.

Every idea in this section has a place in that archive:

In the archive In PostgreSQL Section
A box of cards, all with the same fields a table, which the theory calls a relation §1.1
One card a row §1.1
"Find the cards for Brazil", with no instructions on how a declarative query §1.2
The archivist who decides how to search the query planner §1.2
The archive building, holding several separate archives a database cluster holding databases §1.3
The receptionist who assigns each visitor a personal archivist the postmaster and its backend processes §1.3
The guest list at the gate pg_hba.conf §1.4
Your own assistant at the desk, who carries requests and writes down answers psql §1.5
An instruction to your assistant, not to the archivist a backslash meta-command §1.5
The archive's register of its own boxes the system catalogs §1.9
A blank field on a card NULL §1.12
A request slip handed back with an arrow under the word the archivist could not read an error with a caret and a hint §1.13

This course is written against PostgreSQL 18, a free database server and one of the most widely used. It teaches PostgreSQL rather than a lowest common denominator of every database. Where behaviour is standard SQL you will be told; where it is PostgreSQL-specific you will also be told, because knowing which is which is what makes knowledge portable. Averaging across five database engines produces a course that teaches none of them well enough to work with.

Every code block in this course was executed against a real PostgreSQL 18.6 server, and every printed result is what that server actually returned.

1.1 What "Relational" Means

PostgreSQL is a relational database, and the word names an idea from 1970. The relational model, formulated by E. F. Codd in 1970, rests on one idea: all data is held in relations, and all access is through operations that take relations and return relations.

A relation is what you will usually call a table: a set of rows, where each row holds the same named, typed values. A customers table is a relation. Each customer is a row, and each row has an email, a name and a country. In the archive, a relation is one box of cards, all printed with the same fields.

Four consequences follow, and each is something people get wrong when they arrive from other ways of storing data, such as spreadsheets or lists in a program.

A table has no order
Rows are a set. Without ORDER BY you have no guarantee about sequence, however consistent the answer looks in testing (§8.7). This is the most commonly violated rule in the whole language.
A row has no position
There is no "third row" and no pointer to a row. Rows are identified by their values — which is what a key is (§5.7).
Every operation returns a relation
This is the closure property, and it is why a SELECT can appear anywhere a table can: in FROM, in WHERE, as the source of an INSERT. One rule, composed.
Relationships are values, not links
An order does not contain a customer; it carries a customer's key, and the join reconstitutes the relationship at query time. Nothing is nested and nothing is pre-joined.

In the archive: cards in a box have no reliable order, because they get pulled out and put back. There is no "third card", only the card whose number is 42. And an order card does not have the customer's card stapled to it; it has the customer's number written on it.

SQL is not a perfect copy of Codd's model, and it differs in two ways:

  • a SQL table is a bag rather than a set, because it permits duplicate rows unless a key forbids them;
  • NULL (§5.7), SQL's marker for a missing value, has no place in Codd's algebra at all.

Both departures are practical rather than accidental, and both cause real surprises, which is why they get their own treatment later. The opening puzzle is one of those surprises.

The operations underneath the syntax are relational algebra: selection (WHERE, which keeps some rows), projection (the select list, which keeps some columns), join, union, intersection, difference, and rename. Every query you write is a composition of those. And because the algebra says the answer is the same either way, the planner is free to re-arrange them however it likes.

Two terms to keep, because the rest of the course leans on them: relational model and relational algebra.

1.2 Declarative, and What It Buys

A declarative query says what, not how. Look at what you do not write in SQL:

  • no loop over rows;
  • no choice of index, the lookup structure that finds rows fast (§12);
  • no decision about whether to sort now or later;
  • no join algorithm.

You write the what, and the query planner (§13) constructs the how fresh on every execution, from statistics about the data as it is today. In the archive, you write "all customer cards from Brazil" on the slip. The archivist decides whether to flip through every card or to use the tabbed divider for countries, and may decide differently next week, when the box is fuller.

The benefit is that a query written in 2015 gets faster when you add an index in 2026, without being touched. The cost is that performance is not evident from the text. Two queries that return identical results can differ by four orders of magnitude, ten thousand times, and nothing in the SQL says which is which. That is the trade the language makes, and learning to read EXPLAIN is how you stop being at its mercy.

The corollary is a habit worth adopting now: think in sets, not in rows.

  • "For each customer, look up their orders" is procedural thinking, step-by-step instructions. It produces a query per customer.
  • "Join customers to orders" is one statement the planner can execute a dozen different ways.

Almost every performance disaster in an application's data layer is a loop that should have been a join.

The term to keep from this subsection: query planner.

And the one before it: declarative query.

1.3 The Server

PostgreSQL is a client/server system. The server is a program that owns the data and runs queries. A client is any program that connects to it and sends queries: the psql terminal program, a Python application, a reporting tool. Several clients can connect at once.

PostgreSQL runs one process per connection: each connected client gets its own copy of the server program, working only for it. The parts have names, and the names appear in documentation and error messages:

database cluster
One data directory, one server, and several databases inside it. "Cluster" here means a collection of databases sharing one server — nothing to do with a cluster of machines. Created by initdb.
postmaster
The supervisor process. It listens for connections and forks a child for each; it never executes your queries itself.
backend process
One OS process per connection, running your statements. A process, not a thread — which is why max_connections is a real limit and why connection pooling (§20.3) matters so much.
shared buffers
The shared memory cache of table and index pages that every backend reads and writes through. BUFFERS in EXPLAIN (§13.4) counts hits in it.

In the archive picture: the cluster is the archive building. The postmaster is the receptionist, who never fetches a card but assigns each visitor a personal archivist. That archivist is the backend process. Shared buffers are the big reading-room table where pulled drawers sit, so that the next archivist who needs the same drawer finds it already out.

A database inside a cluster is a hard boundary. One connection can address exactly one database, and a query cannot join across two of them without an extension, an add-on package for the server. To organise one application's tables, use schemas (§4.14), which are named folders inside one database, not separate databases.

createdb and dropdb are small command-line programs that create and remove a database. They are thin wrappers over the SQL statements CREATE DATABASE and DROP DATABASE. New databases are copies of the template1 template. So anything you install there appears in every database you create afterwards: occasionally useful, occasionally a surprise.

Each of these is referred to later, so here they are once more: database cluster, initdb, createdb, dropdb, postmaster and backend process.

1.4 Connecting

A client connects over the network (TCP) or over a Unix socket, a connection between two programs on the same machine. It speaks the libpq protocol, PostgreSQL's set of rules for the conversation. Every PostgreSQL driver in every language is either libpq itself or a reimplementation of that protocol.

What a client needs is a connection string, the address of the database plus who you are. It comes in either of two forms, a URL or a list of key=value pairs. Both lines below say the same kind of thing: user, host, port 5432 (PostgreSQL's standard port), database name, and whether to require encryption:

postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname?sslmode=require
host=localhost port=5432 dbname=shop user=app sslmode=require

Whether the server accepts you is decided by pg_hba.conf, host-based authentication. It is the archive's guest list at the gate: a file of rules, read from top to bottom, and the first rule that matches decides.

  • Each rule matches on connection type, database, user and client address.
  • Each rule names an authentication method: scram-sha-256 for passwords, peer for matching the operating-system user on a local socket, cert, ldap, and in PostgreSQL 18 oauth.

A connection refused with "no pg_hba.conf entry for host" means no rule matched, not that your password was wrong.

1.5 psql

psql is PostgreSQL's terminal client: a program you type SQL into, which sends it to the server and prints the answer. This course uses it throughout, and for a reason that is not habit: it is a real part of the system.

  • Its meta-commands look inside the database's own records, run scripts, format output and drive migrations.
  • Every result printed in this course is psql's own output. A driver in another language would show you that language's way of printing values instead, and none of §1.6 would exist.

In the archive, psql is your own assistant at the desk. Most of what you say, the assistant passes to the archivist. But some instructions are for the assistant alone: "show me the list of boxes", "write the answers in a wider format". Those are meta-commands.

Meta-commands begin with a backslash, are interpreted by psql rather than sent to the server, and need no semicolon. The first one to learn asks "where am I connected?":

\conninfo

The output names the database, user, host and port of the current session. The values below are from this course's own server, and yours will differ:

You are connected to database "course_main" as user "course" on host "127.0.0.1" at port "55432".

Read it as one sentence: database course_main, user course, on the local machine at port 55432.

\conninfo prints the connection you are actually on. \conninfo is worth running on any unfamiliar prompt, because being connected to the wrong database is a mistake that only announces itself later. A few more to know from day one:

  • \q quits.
  • \? lists every meta-command.
  • \h SELECT prints the syntax summary for a SQL command, which is faster than opening a browser.

The meta-command to keep from this subsection: \q.

1.6 Inspecting a Database

This family of meta-commands is the reason to keep psql open beside your editor. They answer "what is in this database?" without you writing a single query.

First, something to inspect: the demonstration schema this course uses from §5 onward. A schema in this sense is the design of the tables: their names, columns and rules. Four tables describe a small shop:

  • customers, one row per customer;
  • products, one row per thing for sale;
  • orders, one row per order, carrying the number of the customer who placed it;
  • order_items, one row per product in an order.

You do not need to understand every word of the statements yet; §4 teaches them. Read them as four box labels with the fields printed on each card. The first line sets the time zone to UTC, so that every date and time in the course prints the same on every machine. psql answers each statement with its name: SET, then CREATE TABLE four times, which is the server reporting that each one succeeded:

SET timezone = 'UTC';

CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  full_name    text NOT NULL,
  country      text NOT NULL,
  signed_up_at date NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  product_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku         text    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        text    NOT NULL,
  category    text    NOT NULL,
  price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers,
  placed_on   date   NOT NULL,
  status      text   NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped','cancelled'))
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES orders ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES products,
  quantity   integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_cents integer NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

SET
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE

\dt, "describe tables", lists the tables:

\dt

            List of tables
 Schema |    Name     | Type  | Owner  
--------+-------------+-------+--------
 public | customers   | table | course
 public | order_items | table | course
 public | orders      | table | course
 public | products    | table | course
(4 rows)

Four tables, all in the public schema, all owned by the user course. That is the list of boxes.

\d on a name describes the object, and describing a table is the single most useful thing psql does:

\d customers

                                   Table "public.customers"
    Column    |           Type           | Collation | Nullable |           Default            
--------------+--------------------------+-----------+----------+------------------------------
 customer_id  | bigint                   |           | not null | generated always as identity
 email        | text                     |           | not null | 
 full_name    | text                     |           | not null | 
 country      | text                     |           | not null | 
 signed_up_at | date                     |           | not null | 
Indexes:
    "customers_pkey" PRIMARY KEY, btree (customer_id)
    "customers_email_key" UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, btree (email)
Referenced by:
    TABLE "orders" CONSTRAINT "orders_customer_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id)

Read it from the top.

  • Columns: the five fields on every customer card, with each one's type (bigint, a whole number; text; date).
  • Nullable: not null on every column means no card may leave that field blank.
  • Default: customer_id is numbered automatically, generated always as identity.
  • Indexes: two lookup structures, one for the key and one that keeps every email unique.
  • Referenced by: the orders table points at this one.

That gives columns, types, nullability, defaults, indexes, and what references this table. The last is how you discover, before writing a DELETE, what else depends on these rows.

The rest of the family follows one pattern: \d plus a letter for the object kind, and a trailing + for more detail.

\dt
tables
\di
indexes
\dv
views
\df
functions
\dn
schemas
\du
roles (§20.1)
\dp
privileges (§20.6)
\dx
installed extensions
\d+
the same with sizes, storage and descriptions
\l
databases in this cluster
\sf
the source of a function

\connect (or \c) switches database or user without leaving psql. That is the only way to move between databases in a session, since a connection is bound to one.

\dn lists schemas, the named folders inside a database. A fresh database has one, public:

\dn

      List of schemas
  Name  |       Owner       
--------+-------------------
 public | pg_database_owner
(1 row)

What to carry forward from this subsection: \l, \connect, \d+, \di, \dn, \df, \dv, \du, \dp, \dx and \sf.

1.7 Controlling Output

psql prints results as a table, one row per line. A row wider than the terminal wraps around and becomes unreadable. \x switches to \x expanded output, which turns each row on its side. The block below switches it on, runs a query, and switches it off again:

\x
SELECT current_user, current_database();
\x

Expanded display is on.
-[ RECORD 1 ]----+------------
current_user     | course
current_database | course_main

Expanded display is off.

Each record becomes a block of column | value lines, one line per column. -[ RECORD 1 ] marks where each row starts. \x auto picks per result, expanded only when the row is too wide, and it is the setting to put in ~/.psqlrc, the file psql reads every time it starts.

\pset controls formatting in detail:

  • \pset format csv prints comma-separated values, ready for a spreadsheet;
  • \pset null '(null)' prints a visible word for a missing value. It is worth setting permanently, so that an empty string and a NULL stop looking identical;
  • \pset pager off stops psql from opening long results in a page-by-page viewer.

\timing on reports how long each statement took:

\timing on
SELECT count(*) FROM customers;
\timing off

Timing lands on its own line after the result, and the value naturally differs on every run:

Timing is on.
 count 
-------
     0
(1 row)

Time: 0.412 ms
Timing is off.

The count is 0 because no customers have been added yet. The line that matters is Time:.

That is client-side round-trip time, not server execution time. It is the time from psql sending the request to psql finishing the printing of the answer. It includes network latency and result formatting. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (§13.4) is what measures the server.

The terms above, gathered: \x expanded output, \timing, EXPLAIN ANALYZE and execution time.

1.8 Scripting with psql

Four meta-commands turn psql from a prompt you type into into a scripting tool, a program that runs a file of steps.

\set defines a variable, substituted with a leading colon. Here threshold is set to 10000, and :threshold in the query is replaced by it:

\set threshold 10000
SELECT count(*) AS above_threshold FROM products WHERE price_cents > :threshold;

 above_threshold 
-----------------
               0
(1 row)

The count is 0 because the products table is still empty; what matters is that :threshold was accepted.

Substitution is textual, done by psql before the server sees anything. psql pastes the text 10000 where :threshold was, like find-and-replace. Two consequences:

  • :var inside a quoted string is not substituted, and :'var' and :"var" exist to quote a value as a literal or an identifier;
  • it is not a bind parameter, the safe way a program hands values to the server separately from the SQL, and it is not protection against injection (§20.5).

\gexec runs the result of a query as SQL. The query produces statement text; psql executes each row. Below, a query builds one SELECT count(*) statement for each of two tables, and \gexec runs both:

SELECT 'SELECT count(*) AS ' || tablename || ' FROM ' || tablename || ';' AS stmt
FROM pg_tables WHERE schemaname = 'public' AND tablename IN ('customers','products')
ORDER BY tablename
\gexec

 customers 
-----------
         0
(1 row)

 products 
----------
        0
(1 row)

Two little results, one per generated statement, each labelled with its table name.

That is generated SQL, run in one round trip. It is the standard way to say "do this to every table matching a pattern" (dropping a set of indexes, granting on a schema, vacuuming a list) without writing a shell loop.

A few more scripting meta-commands:

  • \gset captures a single-row result into psql variables.
  • \include, usually written \i, reads a file of SQL and runs it, which is how a schema is loaded from a script. \i file.sql includes a script.
  • \watch 5 re-runs the last query every five seconds, which is how you observe pg_stat_activity during an incident.
  • \copy streams a file in or out through the client. The difference from server-side COPY (§11.9) is that \copy reads a file on your machine and needs no server file permissions.

ON_ERROR_STOP is the one setting that belongs in every script:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP on
SELECT 1 AS this_script_will_stop_at_the_first_error;

 this_script_will_stop_at_the_first_error 
------------------------------------------
                                        1
(1 row)

The query ran normally and printed 1. The setting shows its value only when something fails.

Without it, psql reports an error and carries on to the next statement. For a migration script, a script that changes a database's structure, that means the failure scrolls past and half your changes are applied. Every example in this course runs with it on, and §14.4 is the one deliberate exception.

\if, \elif, \else and \endif give conditional execution, usually driven by a variable set with \gset.

One line each, for reference: psql variable, \watch, \include, \if and bind parameter.

1.9 The System Catalogs

PostgreSQL stores its own metadata, the data about your data (which tables exist, their columns, their indexes), in ordinary tables, in the pg_catalog schema. You can query them like anything else. This is the archive's register of its own boxes, written on the same kind of cards as everything else.

That is not a curiosity. Every \d command is a query against these tables, and psql -E will show you exactly which. The query below asks pg_class about three objects:

SELECT relname, relkind, relnatts AS columns
FROM pg_class
WHERE relname IN ('customers','orders','customers_pkey')
ORDER BY relname;

     relname     | relkind | columns 
-----------------+---------+---------
 customers       | r       |       5
 customers_pkey  | i       |       1
 orders          | r       |       4
(3 rows)

Read the three rows:

  • customers has relkind r, a table, with 5 columns;
  • customers_pkey has relkind i, an index, built on 1 column;
  • orders is a table with 4 columns.

pg_class holds every relation, and "relation" here includes tables (relkind = 'r'), indexes ('i'), views ('v'), materialized views ('m'), sequences ('S') and partitioned tables ('p'). They share one catalog because they share one namespace: you cannot have a table and a view with the same name.

Three more to know by name:

  • pg_index holds what makes an index an index: its columns, whether it is unique, whether it is valid (§12.11).
  • pg_attribute holds columns.
  • pg_stat_activity is not a catalog but a view of live sessions, and it is the first place to look when something is wrong (§15.7).

Every catalog row has an object identifier type: an oid, a 4-byte unsigned integer that is the real name of everything inside PostgreSQL. Inside the archive, every box has a number, and the label is only for people.

The regclass type is an oid that displays and parses as a relation name, which makes it far more pleasant to use. The query below turns the name customers into its oid, and checks that it is the same oid the catalog holds:

SELECT 'customers'::regclass AS name_to_oid,
       'customers'::regclass::oid = (SELECT oid FROM pg_class WHERE relname='customers') AS same;

 name_to_oid | same 
-------------+------
 customers   | t
(1 row)

same is t, true: the name and the catalog agree.

'customers'::regclass resolves the name through the current search_path (§4.14), the list of schemas PostgreSQL searches for a name, and errors if it does not exist. That makes it a safer way to write a table name into a query than a bare string. regtype, regproc and regnamespace do the same for types, functions and schemas.

The term to keep: object identifier type.

1.10 information_schema

information_schema is the SQL-standard alternative: a set of views over the same metadata, defined by the standard and therefore portable across engines. A view is a saved query you can read like a table (§18). The query below lists the columns of products, in the order they were defined:

SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'products'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

 column_name | data_type | is_nullable 
-------------+-----------+-------------
 product_id  | bigint    | NO
 sku         | text      | NO
 name        | text      | NO
 category    | text      | NO
 price_cents | integer   | NO
(5 rows)

Five columns, their types, and NO for "nullable?" on every one.

Which one should you use?

  • Use information_schema when the query must run on more than one engine.
  • Use pg_catalog when you need something the standard does not describe, which is most PostgreSQL-specific detail, including index methods, table sizes, planner statistics and extensions.

information_schema is also slower, because its views do more work to present a standard shape.

The term to keep: planner statistics.

1.11 The Shape of the Language

SQL statements fall into groups, and the names are worth knowing because error messages and documentation use them.

Data definition language
CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE — structure. §4. In PostgreSQL these are transactional (§14.6), which is unusual and valuable.
Data manipulation language
INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE — contents. §11. SELECT is often counted here and sometimes split off as "query language"; nothing depends on the distinction.
Transaction control
BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT. §14.
Data control
GRANT, REVOKE. §20.

The SQL standard, currently ISO/IEC 9075:2023, defines a core plus a large set of optional features, and no implementation supports all of it. PostgreSQL supports the core plus a substantial share of the optional features, and adds a great deal that is not in the standard at all.

Two facts about the standard matter in practice:

  • it is not freely available, so "the standard says" is rarely checkable;
  • conformance is a spectrum rather than a badge, so portability is always a question about specific features rather than about engines.

To have in hand before moving on: data definition language and data manipulation language.

1.12 Three-Valued Logic, in Advance

This is where the opening puzzle is answered. One thing must be said before you write a single WHERE clause, because it causes wrong answers rather than errors.

SQL's logic has three values: true, false, and unknown. NULL means "no value here": a blank field on the card. Any comparison with it yields unknown rather than true or false. Is a blank equal to 'set'? Nobody knows. Is it different from 'set'? Nobody knows either.

The query below compares NULL with itself, in four ways:

SELECT NULL = NULL           AS null_equals_null,
       NULL <> NULL          AS null_differs,
       (NULL = NULL) IS NULL AS the_result_is_unknown,
       NULL IS NULL          AS the_right_way;

 null_equals_null | null_differs | the_result_is_unknown | the_right_way 
------------------+--------------+-----------------------+---------------
                  |              | t                     | t
(1 row)

Read the four columns:

  • null_equals_null is blank. That is psql printing NULL, which is to say unknown. NULL = NULL is not true, and it is not false either.
  • null_differs is blank too, for the same reason.
  • the_result_is_unknown is t: the result of NULL = NULL really is NULL.
  • the_right_way is t: IS NULL asks "is this blank?", and that question has a real answer.

Now the puzzle. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. So a row whose condition evaluates to unknown is discarded exactly as if it were false. But NOT unknown is still unknown, so the row is discarded by the negation too.

A row can fail both WHERE x = 1 and WHERE x <> 1. In the puzzle, the row with a blank note failed note = 'set', failed note <> 'set', and so failed their OR as well. Only one row came back. That is not a bug, and it is the single most common source of quietly missing rows in a report.

IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the operators that return a real boolean, a true-or-false value. §5.7 develops this properly; the point of raising it here is that you will meet it in your first hour.

1.13 Reading an Error

PostgreSQL's errors are unusually informative, and reading them properly saves a great deal of time. Here is one, provoked on purpose by misspelling customers. (ON_ERROR_STOP off lets the example carry on after the error.) The query:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT * FROM custmers;

ERROR:  relation "custmers" does not exist
LINE 1: SELECT * FROM custmers;
                      ^

The archivist handed the slip back with an arrow under the word it could not read. An error has three parts:

  • the message, here relation "custmers" does not exist;
  • the line and a caret pointing at the offending token, the ^ under custmers;
  • and, often, a DETAIL and a HINT.

The hint is frequently the whole answer. Misspell a column instead:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT contry FROM customers;

ERROR:  column "contry" does not exist
LINE 1: SELECT contry FROM customers;
               ^
HINT:  Perhaps you meant to reference the column "customers.country".

The HINT names the column you meant, customers.country. PostgreSQL compared your misspelling with the real column names and suggested the nearest.

Every error also carries a five-character SQLSTATE code, which is what programs should match on rather than the message text. Messages are translated into the server's language, and they change between releases; the codes do not. A few you will meet:

  • 23505 is a unique violation;
  • 23503 a foreign-key violation;
  • 40001 a serialization failure (§14.15);
  • 40P01 a deadlock (§15.6).

\errverbose after an error prints the code and the server source location.

What This Section Established

The picture: an archive of index cards, run by an archivist. Each box is a table of cards with the same fields; you hand the archivist a request saying what you want, and the archivist decides how to find it. Your assistant at the desk is psql, the guest list at the gate is pg_hba.conf, the archive's register of its own boxes is the catalogs, and a blank field on a card is NULL.

The relational model: unordered sets of typed rows, identified by value rather than position, with every operation returning another relation. A table has no order, so ORDER BY is the only guarantee you have.

SQL is declarative. You write what, the planner decides how, on every execution, from current statistics. That is why an index added later speeds up a query written years earlier, and why performance is invisible in the text. Think in sets, not rows.

A cluster is one server holding several databases; the postmaster forks one backend process per connection; shared buffers is the page cache they share. A connection addresses exactly one database, so schemas rather than databases organise an application.

pg_hba.conf decides who may connect and how.

psql is part of the system, not a convenience. \d and its family describe every object and reveal what references a table; \x transposes wide rows; \pset null stops NULL and the empty string looking alike; \timing measures the round trip, not the server; \set, \gexec, \gset, \watch, \i and \copy make it a scripting tool; \set ON_ERROR_STOP on belongs in every script, because without it a failed migration keeps going.

Metadata lives in ordinary tables. pg_catalog (pg_class, pg_index, pg_attribute) is complete and PostgreSQL-specific; information_schema is standard and portable. oid is the real identity of everything, and regclass is an oid that reads as a name.

Three-valued logic: NULL = NULL is unknown, not true. A row can fail both x = 1 and x <> 1. IS NULL is the operator that returns a boolean.

Errors carry a message, a caret, often a HINT naming the column you meant, and always a SQLSTATE: match on the code, never the text.

Exercises

1. Find the catalog behind a meta-command. Start psql with -E and run \dt. Capture the query psql issued. Explain what each join in it is for, then write your own simpler version that lists table names and row-count estimates.

2. Prove a table has no order. Create a table, insert rows, and select them without ORDER BY — repeatedly, and after an UPDATE to one row. Report what you observe and explain it in terms of §14.7. Then state why observing a stable order is not evidence of a guarantee.

3. Generate SQL with \gexec. Write one query that generates and runs a SELECT count(*) for every table in public, labelled by table name. Then adapt it to generate ANALYZE statements for every table over a given size.

4. Compare the two metadata sources. Answer "which columns of orders are nullable" from information_schema and from pg_catalog. Then answer "which index method does each index on orders use" from both, and report what happens.

5. Break three-valued logic on purpose. Build a table where one row has a NULL in a column. Write a WHERE clause and its negation, and show that the row appears in neither result. Then write the version that includes it, and state the rule in one sentence.

6. Read three errors. Provoke a syntax error, a missing-column error and a unique-violation error. For each, record the message, the SQLSTATE, and which part of the output told you the most. Say which one you would match on in application code and why.

Solution

1. The catalog behind \dt.

psql -E echoes the internal query, which joins pg_catalog.pg_class to pg_catalog.pg_namespace on relnamespace, filters relkind to the table kinds, excludes the system schemas with pg_catalog.pg_table_is_visible(c.oid), and formats the owner through pg_catalog.pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner).

A simpler version:

SELECT relname, reltuples::bigint AS estimated_rows
FROM pg_class WHERE relkind = 'r' AND relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
ORDER BY relname;

   relname   | estimated_rows 
-------------+----------------
 customers   |             -1
 order_items |             -1
 orders      |             -1
 products    |             -1
(4 rows)

reltuples is the planner's estimate from the last ANALYZE (§13.10), not a count, which is why it is instant on a table with a billion rows. -1 is not a row count: it is the sentinel for "never analysed". That distinction was introduced in PostgreSQL 14 precisely because the previous sentinel was 0, and a never-analysed table was indistinguishable from an empty one — a difference that matters enormously to the planner.

2. A table has no order.

Selecting without ORDER BY typically returns rows in physical order, which is insertion order on a freshly loaded table — so it looks stable. Update one row and it moves: as §14.7 measures, an UPDATE writes a new row version at a new ctid, so the updated row jumps to the end.

Observing a stable order proves only that this plan, on this data size, on this machine, happened to produce it. The moment the table grows enough for a parallel sequential scan (§13.12), or the planner chooses a HashAggregate (§13.9), or a Bitmap Heap Scan visits pages in physical rather than index order, the sequence changes — with no change to your query.

3. \gexec.

§1.8 has the counting version. The ANALYZE variant:

SELECT 'ANALYZE ' || quote_ident(relname) || ';' AS stmt
FROM pg_class WHERE relkind = 'r' AND relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
  AND pg_relation_size(oid) > 8192
ORDER BY relname
\gexec

ANALYZE
ANALYZE

quote_ident is not optional. A table named order or My Table produces invalid SQL without it, and generated SQL built by string concatenation is precisely where injection lives (§20.5) — even when the strings come from your own catalog.

4. Two metadata sources.

Nullability is available from both: information_schema.columns.is_nullable and pg_attribute.attnotnull.

The index method is available only from pg_catalog — joining pg_index to pg_class to pg_am. information_schema has no view for indexes at all, because indexes are not in the SQL standard: they are a physical implementation detail the standard deliberately does not describe.

That is the general rule in one example. Anything the standard treats as physical — indexes, storage, statistics, extensions, sizes — is absent from information_schema and present in pg_catalog.

5. Three-valued logic.

CREATE TABLE tvl (id int, note text);
INSERT INTO tvl VALUES (1, 'set'), (2, NULL);
SELECT count(*) AS matches_equal    FROM tvl WHERE note = 'set';
SELECT count(*) AS matches_not_equal FROM tvl WHERE note <> 'set';
SELECT count(*) AS matches_either   FROM tvl WHERE note = 'set' OR note <> 'set';
SELECT count(*) AS with_is_distinct FROM tvl WHERE note IS DISTINCT FROM 'set';

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
 matches_equal 
---------------
             1
(1 row)

 matches_not_equal 
-------------------
                 0
(1 row)

 matches_either 
----------------
              1
(1 row)

 with_is_distinct 
------------------
                1
(1 row)

Two rows in the table, and note = 'set' OR note <> 'set' finds one of them. The rule: WHERE keeps rows where the condition is true, and a comparison involving NULL is unknown rather than false — so negating it does not rescue the row. IS DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe comparison and returns the row.

6. Three errors.

A syntax error gives 42601 and a caret at the token. A missing column gives 42703 and — as §1.13 shows — a HINT naming the intended column, which is PostgreSQL's own similarity check and better than any guess you would make. A unique violation gives 23505 with a DETAIL naming the constraint and the conflicting key value.

Match on SQLSTATE. 23505 is stable across versions and locales; "duplicate key value violates unique constraint" is translated into the server's configured language and has been reworded before. The DETAIL line is the most useful to a human and the least safe to parse — it contains the offending data, which also means it should not be logged anywhere the data is sensitive.

SECTION 2

SQL Syntax, Expressions and Type Conversion

Start with a puzzle. A shop has six orders, and three of them are over $100. You want the share of orders that are over $100. So you count the big orders, divide by the count of all orders, and ask the server for the answer.

Three out of six is one half. Guess what the server prints before reading on.

It prints 0. Not an error, not a warning: a plain zero, looking perfectly reasonable. Exercise 2 at the end of this section runs exactly that query, and the server's real output is printed there. §2.6 explains why it happens, and the fix is a few characters long.

That puzzle is what this section is about. §1 showed what a database holds and how to talk to it. This section looks one level down, at the text of a statement itself:

  • how PostgreSQL reads the characters you type and splits them into pieces;
  • what the pieces of an expression are (an expression is anything that works out to a value, like 1 + 2 or price * 2);
  • and, the part that produces the real surprises, how PostgreSQL decides what type each value is: whole number, decimal, text, date, and so on.

Why types get so much attention here: a SQL query never declares them. Nowhere do you write "this '2026-01-01' is a date". PostgreSQL infers each value's type, which means it works the type out from where the value sits. It also picks each operator, such as + or >, by looking at the types on both sides. Usually it lands on what you meant. When it lands somewhere else, you do not get an error. You get a different answer, like the 0 above, or a query that quietly stops using an index (a lookup structure that makes searches fast, taught in §12) and becomes slow.

The archive from §1 still works as the picture. This section is about how the archivist reads your request slip:

  • The slip is read word by word, and the archivist copies every name in small letters unless you put it in quotes.
  • A value you write on the slip, like '2026-01-01', carries no label saying what kind of thing it is. The archivist labels it by looking at the field you compare it with.
  • To compare or combine two things, the archivist picks a tool that fits both labels: a ruler for numbers, a calendar for dates. If two tools fit equally well, the archivist refuses to guess and hands the slip back.

Every idea in this section has a place in that picture:

At the archivist's desk In PostgreSQL Section
The words on the slip, read one at a time tokens, the lexical structure §2.1
Names copied in small letters unless in quotes identifiers fold to lower case §2.2
The printed words of the request form, the same on every slip key words §2.3
Text copied exactly, between quote marks string constants §2.4
A value written with no label a constant of type unknown §2.5
Writing the label yourself a cast, x::t §2.5
The counting tool that only knows whole numbers integer division §2.6
Two conditions the archivist may check in either order undefined evaluation order §2.7
A numbered checklist, checked from the top CASE §2.8
Labels added without asking, only when filing, or only on request implicit, assignment and explicit casts §2.10
Picking the tool that fits both labels operator resolution §2.11
Which alphabetical filing rule to follow collation §2.12

2.1 What a Statement Is Made Of

A statement is one complete instruction to the server, such as a SELECT. Before PostgreSQL can run it, it has to read it, and it reads it the way you read a sentence: as a row of separate words. Each word is called a token.

A statement's lexical structure — the level at which PostgreSQL reads the characters — is a sequence of tokens. There are six kinds:

  • key words, the fixed words of the language, like SELECT and AS;
  • identifiers, the names you choose, like a table or column name;
  • quoted identifiers, names written inside double quotes;
  • constants, values written straight into the statement, like 42 or 'hello';
  • operators, symbols like + and =;
  • special characters, like commas, parentheses and the semicolon.

Whitespace (spaces, tabs, line breaks) separates tokens and is otherwise insignificant, so a statement may be spread over any number of lines. A semicolon terminates it. Here is one statement spread over four lines, with two comments inside it:

SELECT 'hello'  AS greeting,     -- a line comment
       42       AS answer        /* a block comment,
                                    which may span lines */
;

 greeting | answer 
----------+--------
 hello    |     42
(1 row)

Reading the output: one row, with two columns called greeting and answer. Everything after --, and everything between /* and */, is gone. The server skipped it.

A SQL comment is a note for human readers that the server ignores. It runs to the end of the line with --, or between /* and */. Block comments nest, unlike C's (C being the programming language whose comment style SQL borrowed). So you can comment out a region that already contains a block comment, and the inner */ does not end the outer comment early.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: lexical structure and sql comment.

2.2 Identifiers Fold to Lower Case

An identifier is a name you choose: the name of a table, a column or a function. Here is the first rule that catches people. An unquoted SQL identifier is folded to lower case. "Folded" means converted: whatever case you type, PostgreSQL turns the name into small letters before it looks the name up. That is the archivist copying every name in small letters.

This is the single most consequential lexical rule in PostgreSQL, and it differs from the SQL standard (the official rulebook that SQL databases are meant to follow), which folds to upper case.

To see it, create a table whose name is in double quotes. Double quotes tell PostgreSQL "keep this name exactly as written". Then ask information_schema (one of the catalogs from §1.9, where the database lists its own tables) what was stored:

CREATE TABLE "MixedCase" ("Col" int);
SELECT table_name, column_name FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'MixedCase';

CREATE TABLE
 table_name | column_name 
------------+-------------
 MixedCase  | Col
(1 row)

Reading the output: CREATE TABLE means the table was made, and the catalog lists it as MixedCase with a column Col, capitals intact. The quoted name preserved its case exactly. Now try to reach it without quotes:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT * FROM MixedCase;

ERROR:  relation "mixedcase" does not exist
LINE 1: SELECT * FROM MixedCase;
                      ^

Reading the error: the server looked for a table called mixedcase, in small letters, and found none. The caret ^ points at the word it could not find.

MixedCase folded to mixedcase, which does not exist. Every reference to a quoted identifier must itself be quoted, forever. Once a name has a capital letter in it, the only way to reach it is to write it in double quotes, spelled exactly, every time.

That is why the convention in PostgreSQL is lower_snake_case without quotes: small letters, with words joined by underscores, like order_items. It is the only spelling that survives being written in any case anywhere, because ORDER_ITEMS, Order_Items and order_items all fold to the same name.

The rule catches people arriving from tools that quote everything. Some ORMs (libraries that write SQL for a program, so the programmer does not have to) and GUI designers (programs for drawing tables with the mouse) create a column called "userId". From then on, every hand-written query against it needs the quotes too. Leave them out and userId folds to userid, and the query fails with column "userid" does not exist.

What a name may contain:

  • An unquoted identifier may contain letters, digits, underscores and $, and may not start with a digit.
  • A quoted one may contain anything except a null byte (the character whose code is zero), including spaces, punctuation and key words.

In summary, the vocabulary here is sql identifier.

2.3 Key Words

Key words are the fixed words of the language: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, CREATE. They are the printed words on the request form, the same on every slip. Key words are case-insensitive: select, SELECT and SeLeCt are the same token.

The convention in this course, and in most SQL, is upper case for key words and lower case for identifiers. The reason is readability: the capitals stand out, so the shape of a statement is visible at a glance.

Can a key word be used as a name? It depends on the word. PostgreSQL sorts its key words into groups:

  • reserved words cannot be an identifier without quoting. SELECT and FROM are reserved.
  • unreserved words can. name, value, type, year and several hundred others are unreserved.
  • two in-between categories hold words that are allowed as some kinds of name but not others.

Relying on a word being unreserved is fragile. A word unreserved today can become reserved in a later major version, and then every query that uses it as a name breaks. So a column called end or order should be renamed rather than quoted.

You do not need to memorise the list. pg_get_keywords() lists them all with their category, which is the authoritative answer rather than a remembered list.

2.4 String Constants

A constant, also called a literal, is a value written straight into the statement. A string constant is a piece of text, and its plain form is text between single quotes, like 'hello'.

What if the text itself contains a single quote, or a tab? PostgreSQL has four spellings for those cases. Here they are side by side:

SELECT 'it''s'                                     AS doubled_quote,
       E'tab\there'                                AS escape_string,
       U&'\0041\0042'                              AS unicode_escape,
       $$a string with 'quotes' and \backslashes$$ AS dollar_quoted;

 doubled_quote | escape_string | unicode_escape |              dollar_quoted              
---------------+---------------+----------------+-----------------------------------------
 it's          | tab     here  | AB             | a string with 'quotes' and \backslashes
(1 row)

Reading the output, column by column:

  • doubled_quote: two single quotes in a row, '', came out as one, giving it's.
  • escape_string: the E in front switched on backslash codes, so \t became a real tab character, which psql shows as a wide gap.
  • unicode_escape: \0041 and \0042 are the Unicode code points for A and B. (A code point is the number the Unicode table gives each character.)
  • dollar_quoted: everything between the $$ marks came out exactly as written, quotes and backslashes included.

The four forms, and what each is for:

'...'
The standard form. A single quote inside is written twice. A backslash is an ordinary character — standard_conforming_strings has been on since PostgreSQL 9.1.
E'...'
C-style escapes: \t, \n, \\, \x41. PostgreSQL-specific, and the only way to write a control character inline.
U&'...'
Unicode escapes by code point.
$$...$$
Dollar quoting. A dollar-quoted string has nothing special inside it — no escaping at all. A tag may be added ($sql$...$sql$) so that nested bodies can be distinguished.

Dollar quoting is what makes function bodies bearable (§18.12). A function body is a small program stored in the database, and it is written as one long string. A PL/pgSQL body (PL/pgSQL is PostgreSQL's built-in language for writing such programs) is full of single-quoted strings of its own. Inside an ordinary '...' string, every one of those quotes would need doubling, and a body inside that body doubled again. Inside $$...$$, nothing needs escaping at all.

One more trick: two adjacent string constants separated by a newline are concatenated (joined into one). That is how a long literal is wrapped over several lines.

What to carry forward from this subsection: dollar-quoted.

2.5 Numeric Constants and Typed Literals

Every value in PostgreSQL has a type: integer for whole numbers, numeric for exact decimals, text for strings, date for dates, and many more. A numeric constant gets its type from how it is written:

  • with no decimal point and within range, it is integer, then bigint when it is too big for an integer;
  • with a decimal point or an exponent (like 1e3, meaning 1 times 10 to the 3rd), it is numeric.

The function pg_typeof() tells you the type of any value, so you can watch this happen:

SELECT pg_typeof(1)          AS int_literal,
       pg_typeof(1.5)        AS decimal_literal,
       pg_typeof('x')        AS string_literal,
       pg_typeof('x'::text)  AS cast_text,
       pg_typeof(1 + 1.5)    AS mixed,
       pg_typeof(now())      AS now_type;

 int_literal | decimal_literal | string_literal | cast_text |  mixed  |         now_type         
-------------+-----------------+----------------+-----------+---------+--------------------------
 integer     | numeric         | unknown        | text      | numeric | timestamp with time zone
(1 row)

Reading the output, column by column:

  • 1 is integer and 1.5 is numeric, as the rules said.
  • 'x' on its own is unknown. That is the surprise, and the next paragraph explains it.
  • 'x'::text is text, because ::text labelled it.
  • 1 + 1.5 is numeric: a whole number mixed with a decimal gives a decimal.
  • now() returns a timestamp with time zone, a date and time that knows its time zone.

A bare string constant has the type unknown. It is not text — it is a placeholder, and PostgreSQL resolves it from context. This is the value with no label from the archive. Compared to a date column it becomes a date; passed to a function expecting inet (the type for network addresses) it becomes an inet.

That deferred decision is what makes WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01' work without a cast. It is also why an unknown in a position with no context (a bare SELECT 'x') defaults to text: with nothing to compare against, text is the safest guess.

Note 1.5 is numeric, not double precision. Double precision is the fast, approximate kind of decimal that most programming languages use by default, where a value like 0.1 is stored only approximately. PostgreSQL prefers exactness for a written decimal, which is the opposite of most programming languages.

A typed literal is a constant with its type written beside it, so PostgreSQL does not have to work the type out. Converting a value to a type you name is called a cast: you write the label yourself. A typed literal can be written three ways, and they are equivalent:

SELECT CAST('42' AS integer) AS sql_standard,
       '42'::integer         AS postgres_cast,
       integer '42'          AS typed_literal;

 sql_standard | postgres_cast | typed_literal 
--------------+---------------+---------------
           42 |            42 |            42
(1 row)

All three printed 42. They differ only in where you can use them:

  • CAST(x AS t) is the standard and portable: it works in every SQL database.
  • x::t uses the cast operator, which is PostgreSQL's and is what you will read everywhere.
  • t 'literal' works only on a literal, never on a column or a calculation.

The terms above, gathered: cast operator and double precision.

2.6 Operators and Precedence

An operator is a symbol that combines values, like +, *, /, or ||, which joins two strings. The values on each side are its operands. Precedence is the rule for which operator runs first when there are several, the same as in school arithmetic, where multiplication comes before addition.

Here are the common operators, including the one behind this section's puzzle:

SELECT 1 + 2 * 3       AS precedence,
       (1 + 2) * 3     AS with_parens,
       'a' || 'b'      AS concatenation,
       5 / 2           AS integer_division,
       5.0 / 2         AS numeric_division,
       5 % 2           AS modulo,
       2 ^ 10          AS power;

 precedence | with_parens | concatenation | integer_division |  numeric_division  | modulo | power 
------------+-------------+---------------+------------------+--------------------+--------+-------
          7 |           9 | ab            |                2 | 2.5000000000000000 |      1 |  1024
(1 row)

Reading the output, column by column:

  • precedence is 7: 2 * 3 ran first, then 1 +.
  • with_parens is 9: the parentheses forced the addition first.
  • concatenation is ab: || joined the two strings.
  • integer_division is 2. Hold on to that one.
  • numeric_division is 2.5000000000000000.
  • modulo is 1: % gives the remainder, and 5 divided by 2 leaves 1.
  • power is 1024: ^ raises to a power, and 2 to the 10th is 1024.

5 / 2 is 2. This is the puzzle's answer. Division between two integers is integer division and truncates toward zero: it throws the fraction away, with no rounding and no error. It is the archivist's counting tool that only knows whole numbers. 5.0 / 2 is 2.5 because one operand is numeric, so the whole expression is.

The puzzle's query divided one count by another, and a count is always a whole number, so 3 divided by 6 came out as 0. This is the most common arithmetic surprise in SQL, and the fix is to make one operand non-integer: 5::numeric / 2, or 5 * 1.0 / 2.

Operator precedence is the full order, loosest to tightest (the tightest runs first): OR, AND, NOT, comparison, IS/BETWEEN/IN/LIKE, addition, multiplication, exponentiation, casts, subscripts. Two practical consequences:

  • a AND b OR c means (a AND b) OR c, because AND binds tighter than OR.
  • :: binds tighter than everything arithmetic, so 1 + 2::text is a type error rather than '3'. The cast applies to the 2 alone, and PostgreSQL is then asked to add a number to a piece of text, which it has no operator for.

PostgreSQL lets you define new operators with CREATE OPERATOR, which is why extensions (add-on packages you install into PostgreSQL) can add @>, <-> and ->>. An operator is resolved by looking at the types on both sides, which is §2.11.

One line each, for reference: operator precedence.

2.7 Value Expressions

A value expression is anything that produces a value. You have already used several: a constant, a column name, an operator with its operands. The full list is worth having in one place, because it shows everywhere a value may appear, including where a subquery (a SELECT written inside another statement) may appear:

column reference
col, t.col, schema.t.col.
positional parameter
$1 — in a prepared statement (§13.13) or a function body.
array subscript
An array subscript — arr[2], arr[1:3] — and since PostgreSQL 14 the same syntax on jsonb['key'] (§17.3).
field selection
(composite).field — the parentheses are required.
operator / function
Including an aggregate expression and a window function call (§7, §10).
scalar subquery
(SELECT ...) returning one row and one column (§9.2).
array constructor
ARRAY[1,2,3], or ARRAY(SELECT ...).
row constructor
ROW(1,'a') or just (1,'a') — the basis of §8.9's keyset comparison.

A few words in that list are new, and each is taught where the list points:

  • a positional parameter is a numbered placeholder, filled in with a real value later;
  • an aggregate is a function such as count() or sum() that turns many rows into one value;
  • a composite value is a row-shaped value with named fields;
  • scalar means a single value, one row and one column.

Now a rule that is easy to get wrong. When a condition has several parts, which part does PostgreSQL work out first?

The expression evaluation order — the order in which parts of an expression are computed — is not defined, and this is a documented absence of a guarantee rather than an observed behaviour. WHERE x <> 0 AND 10 / x > 1 is not promised to evaluate the guard first, so it is not promised to avoid a division by zero. On the slip you wrote two conditions, and the archivist is free to check them in either order.

Worth being precise about, because it is easy to over-claim: on PostgreSQL 18 this course could not provoke that failure. Six variants of a guarded division were tried: with and without an index, with ORDER BY, with GROUP BY, and across a join. All of them applied the filter before the division and returned the right answer.

The hazard is real in the sense that nothing forbids the other order. A future plan, a different version or a LEAKPROOF-related rewrite may take it. (LEAKPROOF is a label on a function promising that it reveals nothing about its inputs, and it lets the planner run that function earlier than it otherwise would.) So write it correctly rather than relying on the observation.

CASE does guarantee that a WHEN is evaluated before its THEN, and that no later branch runs once one matches. It is the numbered checklist, checked from the top. That is the construct to reach for when a guard is load-bearing, meaning the query is only correct if the guard runs first. §2.8 introduces CASE itself.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: column reference, positional parameter, aggregate expression, array constructor, row constructor and expression evaluation order.

2.8 Conditional Expressions

A conditional expression picks a value depending on a test, like "if this, then that" in everyday speech. SQL's main one is CASE. Here it sorts three order amounts, in cents, into price tiers:

SELECT cents,
       CASE WHEN cents > 30000 THEN 'premium'
            WHEN cents > 5000  THEN 'standard'
            ELSE 'budget' END AS tier
FROM (VALUES (900), (6400), (31900)) AS t(cents)
ORDER BY cents;

 cents |   tier   
-------+----------
   900 | budget
  6400 | standard
 31900 | premium
(3 rows)

Reading the output: 900 matched no WHEN, so it fell through to the ELSE and became budget. 6400 failed the first test and passed the second. 31900 passed the first test and stopped there, which is the "checked from the top" guarantee at work.

CASE comes in two forms:

  • the searched form above, where each WHEN has its own test;
  • the simple form CASE expr WHEN v1 THEN ... END, which compares one value against a list of values with =, and therefore never matches NULL (§1.12 showed that comparing with NULL never gives true).

Without an ELSE, an unmatched CASE yields NULL.

Four short functions cover jobs you would otherwise write a whole CASE for, and they are worth knowing by name:

SELECT coalesce(NULL, NULL, 'third') AS coalesce,
       nullif('n/a', 'n/a')          AS nullif,
       greatest(3, 7, 5)             AS greatest,
       least(3, 7, 5)                AS least;

 coalesce | nullif | greatest | least 
----------+--------+----------+-------
 third    |        |        7 |     3
(1 row)

Reading the output, column by column:

  • coalesce returned third, the first argument that is not NULL.
  • nullif returned NULL, shown as an empty space, because its two arguments were equal.
  • greatest and least returned the largest and the smallest of their arguments.

coalesce returns the first non-null argument and evaluates lazily: it stops at the first non-null one and never computes the rest. nullif(a, b) returns NULL when they are equal, and that has two standard uses:

  • turning a sentinel like '' or 'n/a' into a proper null. A sentinel is a made-up value standing in for "no value".
  • avoiding division by zero: x / nullif(y, 0) yields NULL rather than raising an error.

The greatest( and least( functions ignore nulls, unlike almost everything else in SQL, where one NULL makes the whole result NULL. greatest(1, NULL) is 1, not NULL, and least( behaves the same way. Other databases disagree here (some return NULL as soon as any argument is NULL), and PostgreSQL's choice is occasionally exactly what you want.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: greatest(.

2.9 Calling Functions

A function takes some inputs, called arguments, and returns a value: upper('hi') returns 'HI'. Function call syntax allows arguments to be passed three ways:

  • positional, matched by their order;
  • named, matched by name, as in make_interval(days => 3);
  • a mixture of the two.

Named notation makes a call with several optional arguments readable, because each value says what it is for. Here are four calls, each in a different style:

SELECT format('%s-%s', 'a', 'b')                     AS positional,
       overlay('Txxxxas' placing 'hom' from 2 for 4) AS keyword_syntax,
       substring('PostgreSQL' from 5 for 3)          AS substring,
       concat_ws('-', 'a', NULL, 'c')                AS variadic_skipping_nulls;

 positional | keyword_syntax | substring | variadic_skipping_nulls 
------------+----------------+-----------+-------------------------
 a-b        | Thomas         | gre       | a-c
(1 row)

Reading the output, column by column:

  • positional: format filled each %s with the next argument in order, giving a-b.
  • keyword_syntax: overlay replaced 4 characters starting at position 2 with hom, turning Txxxxas into Thomas.
  • substring: the 3 characters starting at position 5 of PostgreSQL, which are gre.
  • variadic_skipping_nulls: concat_ws joined its arguments with - and left the NULL out.

Several standard functions use key words rather than commas — substring(x FROM y FOR z), overlay, trim(BOTH ' ' FROM x), extract(YEAR FROM d) — which is the SQL standard's syntax. PostgreSQL also accepts a plain comma form for some of them (substring('PostgreSQL', 5, 3) returns the same gre), but not for extract, where a comma is a syntax error. The key-word form is the one that works everywhere.

A variadic function takes any number of trailing arguments. concat_ws above joined 'a' and 'c' and skipped the NULL, where plain || would have made the whole thing NULL.

Mixed notation — positional first, then named — is allowed; named before positional is not.

To have in hand before moving on: function call syntax, named notation, variadic function and as keyword.

2.10 Casts, and the Three Kinds

§2.5 showed how to write a cast yourself. Most of the time you do not have to, because PostgreSQL converts or combines values for you when that is safe. Each of these three expressions mixes two different types, and none of them has a cast:

SELECT 1::int8 = 1::int4                              AS cross_type_equality,
       date '2026-01-01' + 30                         AS date_plus_integer,
       timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00+00' + interval '1 month' AS timestamp_plus_interval;

 cross_type_equality | date_plus_integer |  timestamp_plus_interval  
---------------------+-------------------+---------------------------
 t                   | 2026-01-31        | 2026-02-01 00:00:00+00
(1 row)

Reading the output:

  • cross_type_equality is t, for true: an 8-byte integer (int8) and a 4-byte integer (int4) compared without complaint.
  • date_plus_integer is 2026-01-31: adding 30 to a date adds 30 days.
  • timestamp_plus_interval is exactly one month later. An interval is a length of time, like '1 month'.

None of those needed an explicit cast, because PostgreSQL's cast catalogue records, for each pair of types, whether the conversion may be applied automatically. There are three levels:

implicit
Applied anywhere, silently. Reserved for conversions that cannot lose information — int4 to int8, int to numeric.
assignment
Applied when storing into a column, but not in an expression. INSERTing an int into a text column works; 1 || 'x' does not.
explicit
Only when you write :: or CAST. Anything lossy or potentially failing.

In the archive, those are three kinds of label: one the archivist adds without asking, one added only when filing a card into a box, and one added only when you write it yourself.

Type conversion between two types is therefore not one thing but three, and which one applies decides whether you must write the cast yourself. A cast that cannot succeed on the data raises at run time, not plan time. The server accepts the statement, starts running it, and fails only when it meets a value it cannot convert:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT 'abc'::integer;

ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "abc"
LINE 1: SELECT 'abc'::integer;
               ^

Reading the error: abc is not a number, so the conversion to integer failed, and the caret points at the value.

The reason implicit casts are so restricted is that they interact with operator resolution. Operator resolution is the process §2.11 describes for choosing which operator to run. PostgreSQL used to have many more implicit casts, and removed most of them in version 8.3 because they made expressions resolve in surprising ways. The classic was that date = 'literal' might silently compare as text. The current conservatism is a deliberate correction.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: implicit cast and explicit cast.

In summary, the vocabulary here is type conversion.

2.11 How an Operator Is Chosen

When you write a + b, PostgreSQL has to choose which + to run. There is not one + but dozens: one for two integers, one for two decimals, one for a date and a number, and so on. Choosing among them is the archivist picking the tool that fits both labels.

Type resolution is the process by which PostgreSQL decides what everything in an expression is. For a + b, it searches for an operator named + whose argument types match. The algorithm, simplified to what matters:

  1. Exact type match wins.
  2. Otherwise, candidates reachable by implicit casts are considered.
  3. Among those, one is chosen using preferred types within each type category — text among strings, timestamptz among dates and times, and float8 among numbers. Note that int4 is not preferred, even though it is the everyday integer type.
  4. An unknown argument is assumed to be whatever the other side needs.
  5. If no single candidate wins, it is an error rather than a guess.

That last point is the important one, and it produces messages like "operator is not unique": two tools fit equally, and the archivist hands the slip back. The remedy is always the same: add an explicit cast so that one candidate matches exactly.

Rule 4 is why WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01' works: '2026-01-01' is unknown, the other side is timestamptz, so the literal becomes a timestamptz. And it is why the opposite order of operations is a performance trap. WHERE created_at::date = '2026-01-01' puts the cast on the column, which, as §12.14 explains, stops the index being usable. Exercise 6 shows both plans side by side.

What to carry forward from this subsection: preferred type.

The terms above, gathered: type resolution.

2.12 Collation in Expressions

Is a before B? It depends on the rules you sort by. In plain byte order (the order of the characters' codes, where every capital letter comes before every small one) it is not. In a dictionary it is.

Text comparison and ordering are decided by a collation (§17.20): a set of rules for which character comes before which. It is the alphabetical filing rule the archivist follows. A collation propagates through an expression, travelling with the values. When two inputs have different explicit collations the result is an error; when they have different implicit collations from their columns, one wins by a defined set of rules.

Here is the same comparison under two different collations:

SELECT 'a' < 'B' COLLATE "C"           AS byte_order,
       'a' < 'B' COLLATE "en-US-x-icu" AS dictionary_order;

 byte_order | dictionary_order 
------------+------------------
 f          | t
(1 row)

The same comparison, opposite answers. Under "C", which is byte order, 'a' < 'B' is f (false), because capital B has a smaller code than small a. Under "en-US-x-icu", an English dictionary order, it is t (true).

A COLLATE clause makes a collation expression, attaching to any expression and can be written in a WHERE, an ORDER BY, or a column definition. It matters most in three places:

  • ORDER BY on text;
  • the LIKE prefix optimisation of §12.10;
  • unique constraints on case-varying text.

One line each, for reference: collation expression.

What This Section Established

The picture: the archivist reads your slip word by word, copies unquoted names in small letters, labels each unlabelled value from the field it is compared with, and picks the tool that fits both labels, refusing to guess when two fit equally. Most surprises in this section, the puzzle's 0 among them, come from a label you did not know was there.

Statements are token streams; whitespace is insignificant; block comments nest.

Unquoted identifiers fold to lower case, quoted ones do not — measured, "MixedCase" is unreachable as MixedCase. Which is why the convention is unquoted lower_snake_case, forever.

Key words are case-insensitive. Reserved words need quoting; the reserved list grows between versions, so rename rather than quote.

Strings: '' doubles a quote, backslashes are literal, E'...' gives C escapes, and dollar quoting suspends all escaping — which is what makes function bodies readable.

1 is integer, 1.5 is numeric, and a bare string constant is unknown until context resolves it. CAST(x AS t), x::t and t 'lit' are the three spellings.

5 / 2 is 2 — integer division truncates. Precedence puts AND above OR and :: above arithmetic. Evaluation order within an expression is undefined, so use CASE when a guard must short-circuit.

CASE has searched and simple forms; the simple form never matches NULL. coalesce is lazy, nullif(y, 0) prevents division by zero, and greatest/least ignore nulls where nearly everything else propagates them.

Functions take positional, named and mixed notation; several standard ones use key words instead of commas; variadic functions like concat_ws skip nulls.

Casts are implicit, assignment or explicit. Implicit ones are deliberately rare because they distort operator resolution — most were removed in 8.3 for exactly that reason.

Operator resolution prefers an exact match, then implicit casts, then preferred types, and errors rather than guessing. An unknown literal becomes whatever the other operand is — which is why col > 'literal' works and col::date = 'literal' is the version that loses the index.

Collation propagates through expressions and changes comparison results, not just display order.

Exercises

1. Make an identifier unreachable. Create a table with a quoted mixed-case name and a quoted mixed-case column. Then try five ways to select from it without quotes and report each error. State the naming rule you would put in a style guide and why.

2. Divide wrongly. Write a query computing a percentage from two integer columns that returns 0 for every row. Fix it three ways and say which you would use. Then make the same query fail on a zero denominator, and fix that too.

3. Watch a literal resolve. Use pg_typeof to show a string constant becoming three different types in three different contexts. Then find a context with no context, and report what it becomes.
