IS DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe comparison: it treats two nulls as not distinct and a null against a value as distinct, and returns a real boolean in every case. It is the operator you want whenever a column is nullable and you are comparing it to something.

The consequence in a WHERE clause is worth demonstrating on data:

CREATE TABLE nl (id int, note text);
INSERT INTO nl VALUES (1,'set'), (2,NULL), (3,'');
SELECT id FROM nl WHERE note <> 'set' ORDER BY id;
SELECT id FROM nl WHERE note IS DISTINCT FROM 'set' ORDER BY id;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 id 
----
  3
(1 row)

 id 
----
  2
  3
(2 rows)

One row against two. note <> 'set' misses row 2 entirely, because NULL <> 'set' is unknown. "Everything that is not 'set'" written the obvious way silently excludes the rows where nothing is known — which is very often exactly the population the question was about.

What to carry forward from this subsection: unknown result.

The terms above, gathered: null semantics.

5.8 NULL Everywhere Else

The same rule produces different-looking behaviour in each part of the language, and it is worth having them in one list.

SELECT sum(x)   AS sum_skips_nulls,
       count(x) AS count_skips_nulls,
       count(*) AS count_star,
       avg(x)   AS avg_over_non_nulls
FROM (VALUES (1),(NULL),(3)) AS t(x);

 sum_skips_nulls | count_skips_nulls | count_star | avg_over_non_nulls 
-----------------+-------------------+------------+--------------------
               4 |                 2 |          3 | 2.0000000000000000
(1 row)

avg is 2, not 1.33 — it divided by the count of non-null values, not by the row count. Whether that is right depends entirely on whether the missing value means "zero" or "we do not know", which is precisely the design decision this section is about.

Aggregates
All skip nulls except count(*) (§7.4).
GROUP BY
Nulls form one group — grouping treats them as equal, where = does not.
ORDER BY
NULL ordering puts them last ascending, first descending (§8.5).
UNIQUE
A NULL in a unique index is distinct from every other, so any number are allowed — unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT (§4.6).
CHECK
Unknown passes, so a NULL satisfies every check (§4.4).
NOT IN
One null in the list returns no rows at all (§9.6).
Concatenation
|| propagates; concat() and concat_ws() skip.
SELECT 'a' || NULL || 'b' IS NULL AS pipes_propagate,
       concat('a', NULL, 'b')     AS concat_skips,
       coalesce(NULL, 'fallback') AS coalesced,
       nullif('', '') IS NULL     AS empty_to_null;

 pipes_propagate | concat_skips | coalesced | empty_to_null 
-----------------+--------------+-----------+---------------
 t               | ab           | fallback  | t
(1 row)

Building a display name with || and a nullable middle name produces NULL rather than the name — which is the single most common place this bites in application code.

One line each, for reference: null in a unique index and null ordering.

5.9 The Design Decision: When to Allow NULL

NULL should mean one thing in your schema, and you should be able to say which:

Not applicable
A shipped_at on an unshipped order. Legitimate, and often better modelled as a status plus a nullable timestamp with a CHECK tying them together.
Not yet known
A survey answer not given. Legitimate, and the case where "average over non-nulls" is the right aggregate.
A default nobody set
A quantity that is null because the insert forgot it. Not legitimate — NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.
A column for a subtype
Twelve columns of which four apply to invoices and eight to credit notes. That is two tables, or a check constraint per subtype (§5.11).

The default should be NOT NULL, with nullability as the exception you can justify. A schema where most columns are nullable has pushed a decision onto every query that reads it, and each query will make it differently.

The empty string versus NULL question has a real answer: they are different values — measured in §5.7, where row 3 held '' and row 2 held NULL, and only one query found both. Pick one to mean "no value" and enforce it: CHECK (note <> '') forbids the empty string, or nullif(note, '') on the way in normalises it. Storing both is how a table ends up needing WHERE coalesce(note,'') = '' everywhere.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: empty string versus null.

5.10 Soft Deletes and Audit Columns

A soft delete replaces DELETE with a flag. It is common, and it has costs worth knowing before adopting it.

Every query must remember the filter, and the one that forgets shows deleted rows to a user. A partial index (§12.6) makes the filter cheap and a view with WHERE deleted_at IS NULL makes it hard to forget — but the strongest form is row-level security (§20.10), which applies it whether or not the query asks.

Uniqueness becomes conditional: a deleted account's email should usually be reusable, which needs CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON accounts (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL rather than a plain constraint. And foreign keys do not understand the flag at all — a child row can reference a soft-deleted parent, and nothing objects.

Prefer deleted_at timestamptz to is_deleted boolean: it carries strictly more information at the same cost, IS NULL is as cheap as = false, and you will eventually want to know when.

The same reasoning applies to audit columns. created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() costs eight bytes and answers questions you have not thought of yet. updated_at needs a trigger (§18.18) to be reliable, because a default only applies on insert — and an updated_at maintained by the application is the §5.4 anti-pattern in miniature.

5.11 Modelling Subtypes

Three shapes, and the choice is a real trade rather than a preference.

One table with nullable columns. Simple, one place to look, and the constraint "these four columns are null exactly when type is 'invoice'" must be written as a CHECK or it will be violated. Best when the subtypes differ by two or three columns.

A table per subtype, each with its own columns, plus a shared table for the common ones and a foreign key. Fully constrained, no nulls, and every query that spans subtypes needs a UNION or a view.

A jsonb column for the variable part (§17.10). Flexible, unconstrained, and the right answer when the subtypes are open-ended — per-tenant custom fields, an event payload whose shape varies by event type.

The check versus trigger decision runs through all three: a CHECK sees one row and costs nothing, a trigger sees anything and is invisible at the call site (§18.20). The tell for the first shape being wrong: the number of nullable columns keeps growing, and a CHECK constraint that lists which are valid together starts wrapping across lines. The tell for the second being wrong: every query is a UNION of five branches.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: check versus trigger.

5.12 Reporting Shapes

A normalized schema is optimised for writing correctly. A reporting schema is optimised for reading, and the standard shape is a star schema: a central fact table of measurements — one row per sale, per event, per reading — surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive attributes.

It is deliberately denormalized: the dimension tables repeat values, the fact table carries foreign keys to all of them, and a query joins the fact table to as many dimensions as it needs and aggregates. That shape suits a columnar or heavily-indexed store and answers "sales by region by month" in one join per dimension.

It lives beside the transactional schema, not instead of it. Facts are appended and never updated, which removes the update anomaly that made normalization necessary in the first place — a historical fact is not a duplicate of a current one (§5.4).

What This Section Established

A good schema makes invalid states unrepresentable. Normalization, keys and a NULL policy each remove a class of them.

A functional dependency is a claim about the domain. You can disprove one with a query and never prove one.

1NF: one value per column. 2NF: nothing depends on part of a composite key. 3NF: nothing depends on a non-key column. BCNF strengthens 3NF and differs only with overlapping candidate keys. The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

The reason is update, insertion and deletion anomalies — and the fact that a normalized design makes constraints expressible that an unnormalized one cannot state at all.

Denormalize only after measuring, and only in a form the database maintains: a generated column, a materialized view, or a trigger. An application-maintained copy is the one that drifts. Historical snapshots and reporting schemas are not violations.

Surrogate primary key plus a unique constraint on the natural key — the second half is the one people omit, and without it the same entity can exist twice.

Foreign key on the many side; junction table for many-to-many, carrying the attributes of the relationship; UNIQUE foreign key for one-to-one.

NULL is unknown. NULL AND false is false, NULL OR true is true, NULL AND true is unknown. IS DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe comparison — measured, note <> 'set' found one row where IS DISTINCT FROM found two.

Nulls: skipped by every aggregate but count(*), grouped together by GROUP BY, sorted last ascending, distinct in a unique index, passing every CHECK, fatal in NOT IN, propagated by || and skipped by concat().

Default to NOT NULL. Empty string and NULL are different values — choose one meaning and enforce it.

Soft deletes need a partial unique index, a view or RLS to be safe, and foreign keys ignore them. Prefer deleted_at to a boolean.

Subtypes: nullable columns with a CHECK, a table per subtype, or jsonb — chosen by how many columns differ and how open-ended the set is.

A star schema is denormalized on purpose and lives beside the transactional schema.

Exercises

1. Normalize by hand. Take a single wide table holding orders, customers and products together. Identify every functional dependency, name which normal form it violates and why, and decompose it into 3NF. Then write the three anomalies it suffered from as concrete UPDATE, INSERT and DELETE statements that go wrong.

2. Find a violated dependency. On any table you believe has a dependency a → b, write one query that finds every a with more than one b. Run it against real data. Report what you found and what it implies about the constraint you thought existed.

3. Choose keys for five entities. For a user, a country, an order line, a currency exchange rate on a date, and a URL shortener code: choose natural or surrogate, justify each, and write the CREATE TABLE including the unique constraint on the natural key where one exists.

4. Miss rows with a negation. Build a table with a nullable column and write a filter meaning "everything except X" that silently omits the null rows. Fix it three ways and say which you would put in a code review comment.

5. Decide what NULL means. For a shipped_at column, write the constraint that ties it to a status column so that the two cannot disagree. Then do the same for a discount_percent that is null for most rows, and say whether it should be nullable at all.

6. Cost a soft delete. Add deleted_at to a table with a unique email constraint. Show that deleting and re-registering fails. Fix it with a partial unique index. Then show a foreign key still pointing at the deleted row, and say what you would do about it.

7. Model a subtype three ways. Take an entity with two subtypes differing by four columns. Implement it with nullable columns plus a check, with a table per subtype, and with jsonb. Write the same three queries against each, and report which was shortest, which was safest, and which you would ship.

Solution

1. Normalizing by hand.

The dependencies in orders(order_id, customer_id, customer_email, product_id, product_name, quantity) with key (order_id, product_id):

product_id → product_name is partial — it depends on half the key, violating 2NF. customer_id → customer_email is transitive — customer_id is not a key, violating 3NF. (order_id, product_id) → quantity is the only dependency that is allowed to be there.

The three anomalies as statements: UPDATE orders SET customer_email = ... WHERE customer_id = 7 must touch every row for that customer and a WHERE clause that misses one leaves the database self-contradictory. INSERT of a new product is impossible without inventing an order. DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 3 removes the only record of a product if that was its only sale.

The 3NF decomposition is exactly this course's schema: customers, products, orders, order_items — and note that once it exists, the UPDATE becomes a single-row statement that cannot be partially applied.

2. Finding a violated dependency.

SELECT a, count(DISTINCT b) AS distinct_b
FROM dep GROUP BY a HAVING count(DISTINCT b) > 1;

 a | distinct_b 
---+------------
(0 rows)

Zero rows means the data is consistent with the dependency today. It does not mean the dependency holds — but a non-zero result is proof that it does not, and that is the useful direction.

When it does return rows, the finding is usually one of three things: the dependency was never real and the schema is wrong; the dependency is real and the data is corrupt; or the dependency is real with a time dimension — the value changed, and both the old and the new are present. The third is the most common and the most interesting, because the fix is usually a history table rather than a repair.

3. Choosing keys.

User: surrogate bigint, plus UNIQUE (email). Email is a natural key and it changes.

Country: the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code is a defensible natural key — short, stable, standardised, and meaningful in a foreign key. It does occasionally change, which is the argument against; the counter-argument is that a two-character code readable in every row is worth a rare migration.

Order line: composite (order_id, product_id). The entity genuinely is the pair, and a surrogate id adds a second uniqueness to maintain.

Exchange rate: composite (from_currency, to_currency, rate_date) — a natural composite key, because the rate for a pair on a date is exactly one thing.

URL shortener code: the code is the identifier and is generated by you, so it is both natural and stable. A surrogate here would be a second key nobody uses.

The pattern: surrogate when the natural key can change or is wide; natural when it is short, externally standardised and genuinely immutable.

4. Missing rows with a negation.

§5.7 measures it: note <> 'set' returns one row and IS DISTINCT FROM returns two.

The three fixes are IS DISTINCT FROM, note <> 'set' OR note IS NULL, and coalesce(note,'') <> 'set'. The review comment should say IS DISTINCT FROM: it is one operator, it is null-safe by construction, it does not invent a sentinel value that could collide with real data, and it keeps the column bare so an index remains usable — where coalesce(note,'') puts a function on the column and loses it (§2.11).

5. Deciding what NULL means.

CREATE TABLE ship (
  id     int PRIMARY KEY,
  status text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending','shipped')),
  shipped_at timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT shipped_at_matches_status
    CHECK ((status = 'shipped') = (shipped_at IS NOT NULL))
);
INSERT INTO ship VALUES (1, 'pending', NULL), (2, 'shipped', now());
\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
INSERT INTO ship VALUES (3, 'shipped', NULL);

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
ERROR:  new row for relation "ship" violates check constraint "shipped_at_matches_status"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (3, shipped, null).

The constraint is written as an equality between two booleans, which is the compact way to say "exactly one of these states". Note it works only because both sides are non-null booleans — IS NOT NULL always returns a real boolean, which is why it is safe inside a CHECK where a bare comparison would not be.

discount_percent is the opposite case and the answer is usually NOT NULL DEFAULT 0. "No discount" is a known value, not an unknown one, and making it null forces every sum and average in the system to decide what to do about it. Reserve nullability for genuine absence.

6. Costing a soft delete.

CREATE TABLE acct (id int PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL UNIQUE, deleted_at timestamptz);
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 'a@example.com', NULL);
UPDATE acct SET deleted_at = now() WHERE id = 1;
\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (2, 'a@example.com', NULL);

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
UPDATE 1
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "acct_email_key"
DETAIL:  Key (email)=(a@example.com) already exists.

The account is deleted and the address is still taken. ALTER TABLE acct DROP CONSTRAINT acct_email_key followed by CREATE UNIQUE INDEX acct_live_email ON acct (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL fixes it.

The dangling foreign key has no such tidy fix, and that is the honest conclusion: a foreign key constrains existence, and a soft-deleted row still exists. The options are a trigger that rejects references to deleted parents, a periodic check that reports them, or accepting it and making every read path filter — which is the same "every query must remember" cost that made soft deletes expensive in the first place. It is a real reason to prefer archiving to a history table over flagging in place.

7. Modelling a subtype.

Nullable columns plus a check is shortest to write and shortest to query — one table, no UNION — and the check constraint grows unpleasant past three or four columns.

Table per subtype is safest: every column that exists is NOT NULL, so no query has to consider whether a value applies. The cost is that any query spanning subtypes needs a view over a UNION, and adding a third subtype touches every such view.

jsonb is shortest to change and loses every constraint, every statistic and every foreign key (§17.10).

Ship the nullable-columns version at two subtypes differing by four columns, with the check constraint written and named. Switch to table-per-subtype when the number of nullable columns passes roughly six or the check constraint stops fitting on a screen — both of which are proxies for "the subtypes are now different entities".

SECTION 6

Querying: SELECT, FROM and Joins

This is the section the rest of the course leans on. SELECT is the only statement most people write most of the time, and its apparent simplicity hides a specific evaluation order and a family of join behaviours that produce wrong answers rather than errors when misunderstood.

The tables were created in §1.6. They need data:

INSERT INTO customers (email, full_name, country, signed_up_at) VALUES
 ('ada@example.com','Ada Okonkwo',  'DE','2025-11-02'),
 ('lin@example.com','Lin Zhao',     'US','2025-11-14'),
 ('kai@example.com','Kai Nakamura', 'JP','2026-01-08'),
 ('mo@example.com', 'Mo Haddad',    'DE','2026-01-19'),
 ('rae@example.com','Rae Lindqvist','US','2026-02-03'),
 ('sam@example.com','Sam Ferreira', 'BR','2026-02-21');

INSERT INTO products (sku, name, category, price_cents) VALUES
 ('KB-01','Mechanical Keyboard','peripherals',12900),
 ('MS-02','Trackball Mouse',    'peripherals', 6400),
 ('MN-03','27-inch Monitor',    'displays',   31900),
 ('MN-04','34-inch Monitor',    'displays',   54900),
 ('CB-05','USB-C Cable',        'cables',      1200),
 ('CB-06','HDMI Cable',         'cables',       900);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_on, status) VALUES
 (1,'2026-01-05','shipped'), (1,'2026-02-11','paid'),
 (2,'2026-01-22','shipped'), (2,'2026-02-14','cancelled'),
 (3,'2026-02-02','paid'),    (4,'2026-02-18','pending'),
 (4,'2026-02-25','shipped'), (5,'2026-03-01','paid');

INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_cents) VALUES
 (1,1,1,12900),(1,5,2,1200),(2,3,1,31900),(3,2,1,6400),(3,6,1,900),(4,4,1,54900),
 (5,1,2,12900),(5,2,1,6400),(6,5,3,1200),(7,4,1,54900),(7,5,1,1200),(7,6,2,900),
 (8,3,2,31900);

INSERT 0 6
INSERT 0 6
INSERT 0 8
INSERT 0 13

Six customers, six products, eight orders, thirteen line items. Sam Ferreira has no orders, which is deliberate: half of this section is about what happens to rows with nothing on the other side.

6.1 SELECT, and the Order Things Actually Happen

A SELECT statement is written in one order and evaluated in another, and knowing the second explains a set of rules that otherwise look arbitrary.

1
FROM / JOIN
Build the working set of rows, including every join.
2
WHERE
Discard rows. Aggregates do not exist yet, and neither do select-list aliases.
3
GROUP BY
Collapse rows into groups (§7).
4
HAVING
Discard groups. Aggregates do exist here.
5
window functions
Computed over the grouped rows (§10.7).
6
SELECT list
Compute output columns and their labels.
7
DISTINCT
Remove duplicate output rows.
8
ORDER BY
Sort. Labels from step 6 are visible here.
9
LIMIT / OFFSET
Take a slice of the sorted result.

This is a semantic order, not an execution plan — the planner reorders freely as long as the answer is the same (§13.2). But every visibility rule follows from it:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT price_cents / 100 AS euros FROM products WHERE euros > 100;

ERROR:  column "euros" does not exist
LINE 1: ...CT price_cents / 100 AS euros FROM products WHERE euros > 10...
                                                             ^

WHERE runs at step 2 and the alias is created at step 6. The same alias works fine in ORDER BY, which runs at step 8 — an inconsistency that is not an inconsistency once you have this table.

To have in hand before moving on: select statement.

6.2 The Select List

Anything that evaluates to a value can be a select-list item: a column, a literal, an expression, a function call, a subquery returning one row.

SELECT sku,
       name,
       price_cents,
       round(price_cents / 100.0, 2) AS euros,
       upper(category)     AS category,
       length(name)        AS name_length
FROM products
ORDER BY sku
LIMIT 3;

  sku  |        name         | price_cents | euros  |  category   | name_length 
-------+---------------------+-------------+--------+-------------+-------------
 CB-05 | USB-C Cable         |        1200 |  12.00 | CABLES      |          11
 CB-06 | HDMI Cable          |         900 |   9.00 | CABLES      |          10
 KB-01 | Mechanical Keyboard |       12900 | 129.00 | PERIPHERALS |          19
(3 rows)

AS names the output column — the column label — and is optional — price_cents / 100.0 euros works — but write it, because a bare alias next to a missing comma turns a two-column mistake into a one-column success.

SELECT * is for interactive use. In application code it breaks the moment a column is added, reordered or dropped: a positional client reads the wrong field, an INSERT INTO ... SELECT * starts failing, and a view created with * freezes the column list as it was at creation time and does not track later ALTER TABLEs. Name the columns you want.

An expression's default label is derived from it and is rarely useful — ?column? for a bare expression — which is a second reason to alias.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: column label.

6.3 WHERE

WHERE keeps rows where the condition is true. Not "not false": as §1.12 established, unknown is discarded exactly as false is.

SELECT sku, price_cents FROM products
WHERE category = 'displays' AND price_cents BETWEEN 30000 AND 60000
ORDER BY price_cents;

  sku  | price_cents 
-------+-------------
 MN-03 |       31900
 MN-04 |       54900
(2 rows)

BETWEEN a AND b is inclusive at both ends — which makes it a poor fit for dates, because BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-02-01' includes midnight on 1 February. For timestamps prefer >= start AND < end, which tiles without overlap in exactly the way §17.12's [) ranges do.

IN (list), LIKE, IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM, AND, OR, NOT complete the vocabulary. Two practical notes: AND binds tighter than OR, so WHERE a AND b OR c is (a AND b) OR c and is almost never what was meant; and PostgreSQL does not guarantee left-to-right evaluation of AND, so WHERE x IS NOT NULL AND x::int > 5 may still attempt the cast. Use a CASE expression when the guard is load-bearing.

6.4 DISTINCT and DISTINCT ON

SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers ORDER BY country;

 country 
---------
 BR
 DE
 JP
 US
(4 rows)

The DISTINCT clause removes duplicate output rows, considering all select-list columns together. Adding a column can therefore make duplicates reappear, which surprises people who read it as applying to the first column.

DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL's own, and it is genuinely useful: keep the first row per group, where "first" is decided by ORDER BY.

SELECT DISTINCT ON (country) country, full_name, signed_up_at
FROM customers
ORDER BY country, signed_up_at;

 country |  full_name   | signed_up_at 
---------+--------------+--------------
 BR      | Sam Ferreira | 2026-02-21
 DE      | Ada Okonkwo  | 2025-11-02
 JP      | Kai Nakamura | 2026-01-08
 US      | Lin Zhao     | 2025-11-14
(4 rows)

The earliest-joining customer per country, in one clause. The ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON expressions, and PostgreSQL enforces that — the remaining keys decide which row wins.

Compared to the row_number() version of §10.9: DISTINCT ON is shorter and often faster, and it is not portable. row_number() generalises to "the top three per group"; DISTINCT ON cannot.

In summary, the vocabulary here is distinct clause.

6.5 Joins

A join builds rows by matching rows from two tables against a condition.

SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id, o.status
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.full_name, o.order_id;

   full_name   | order_id |  status   
---------------+----------+-----------
 Ada Okonkwo   |        1 | shipped
 Ada Okonkwo   |        2 | paid
 Kai Nakamura  |        5 | paid
 Lin Zhao      |        3 | shipped
 Lin Zhao      |        4 | cancelled
 Mo Haddad     |        6 | pending
 Mo Haddad     |        7 | shipped
 Rae Lindqvist |        8 | paid
(8 rows)

Eight rows for eight orders. JOIN with no qualifier means INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides survive. Sam Ferreira is absent, and that absence is the entire difference between this and the next subsection.

The ON join condition is the expression deciding what counts as a match, and table aliases (customers c) are not decoration. Writing a qualified column — c.full_name rather than a bare full_name — is what stops a query breaking silently when someone adds a name column to the other table, and a qualified column is the only form that is unambiguous once three tables are in the FROM.

What to carry forward from this subsection: table alias and on join condition.

The terms above, gathered: qualified column.

6.6 Outer Joins

An outer join keeps rows from one side even when the other has no match, filling the missing columns with NULL.

SELECT c.full_name, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.full_name
ORDER BY c.full_name;

   full_name   | orders 
---------------+--------
 Ada Okonkwo   |      2
 Kai Nakamura  |      1
 Lin Zhao      |      2
 Mo Haddad     |      2
 Rae Lindqvist |      1
 Sam Ferreira  |      0
(6 rows)

Sam appears with zero. Note count(o.order_id) rather than count(*): count(*) counts rows and would report 1 for Sam, because there is one row — with NULLs in it. count(column) skips nulls. That is the second most common bug in this section.

LEFT JOIN — a left outer join — keeps all left rows; a right outer join, RIGHT JOIN, keeps all right rows and is the same thing written backwards, so most codebases use only LEFT and reorder; FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both.

One line each, for reference: left outer join, right outer join and full outer join.

6.7 The Outer-Join WHERE Trap

This one is worth measuring, because it silently converts an outer join into an inner one.

SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY c.full_name;

   full_name   | order_id 
---------------+----------
 Ada Okonkwo   |        2
 Kai Nakamura  |        5
 Rae Lindqvist |        8
(3 rows)

Three rows. Every customer without a paid order has vanished, including Sam — the LEFT JOIN might as well not be there. The reason is the evaluation order of §6.1: the join runs first and produces NULLs for unmatched rows; then WHERE o.status = 'paid' evaluates to unknown for those rows, and unknown is discarded.

Move the condition into the ON clause and it applies to the matching, not to the result:

SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY c.full_name, o.order_id;

   full_name   | order_id 
---------------+----------
 Ada Okonkwo   |        2
 Kai Nakamura  |        5
 Lin Zhao      |         
 Mo Haddad     |         
 Rae Lindqvist |        8
 Sam Ferreira  |         
(6 rows)

Six rows, with NULL for the three customers who have no paid order. That is what "all customers, with their paid order if any" means, and it is what the first query was trying to say.

The rule: for an outer join, a condition on the outer side belongs in ON; a condition on the preserved side belongs in WHERE. For an inner join the two are equivalent and the planner treats them identically, which is why the habit only breaks when you switch a join to LEFT.

6.8 The Anti-Join

LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL finds rows with no match:

SELECT c.full_name
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.full_name;

  full_name   
--------------
 Sam Ferreira
(1 row)

This works because an unmatched row has NULL in every column from the right side, and testing a NOT NULL column of that side — the primary key is the safe choice — distinguishes "no match" from "matched a row that happens to contain nulls".

NOT EXISTS (§9.5) expresses the same thing more directly and usually plans identically. NOT IN expresses it too and has the NULL trap of §9.6; prefer one of the other two.

6.9 CROSS JOIN, USING, NATURAL

SELECT count(*) AS cross_rows FROM customers CROSS JOIN products;

 cross_rows 
------------
         36
(1 row)

Six times six. A cartesian product has no join condition, and it is legitimate when you want one — generating a calendar, filling a matrix of combinations — and a disaster when you produced one by forgetting a condition. A query returning far more rows than any input table is the symptom.

FROM a, b is the old comma syntax and means CROSS JOIN; with a condition in WHERE it means an inner join. It works, and explicit JOIN ... ON is better because the join condition cannot be accidentally deleted along with an unrelated filter.

The USING clause shortens the common case where both columns have the same name, and merges them into one output column:

SELECT c.full_name, o.status
FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY c.full_name;

   full_name   | status 
---------------+--------
 Ada Okonkwo   | paid
 Kai Nakamura  | paid
 Rae Lindqvist | paid
(3 rows)

After USING (customer_id) there is one customer_id column, not two, so SELECT * is tidier and ORDER BY customer_id is unambiguous.

NATURAL JOIN joins on every same-named column, and you should not use it. It has no visible condition, so its meaning changes when someone adds a column: give both tables a created_at and the join silently starts requiring those to be equal too. The bug appears in a table nobody edited.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: natural join, using clause and cartesian product.

6.10 Self-Joins

A table can join to itself, and the aliases become mandatory:

SELECT p.name, p2.name AS also_in_category
FROM products p
JOIN products p2 ON p.category = p2.category AND p.product_id < p2.product_id
ORDER BY p.name, p2.name;

        name         | also_in_category 
---------------------+------------------
 27-inch Monitor     | 34-inch Monitor
 Mechanical Keyboard | Trackball Mouse
 USB-C Cable         | HDMI Cable
(3 rows)

The < in the condition is doing real work: without it every pair appears twice and every product pairs with itself. That asymmetric comparison is the standard way to enumerate unordered pairs.

Self-joins also walk hierarchies one level at a time — employee to manager, category to parent. For an arbitrary number of levels you need a recursive CTE (§9.13).

6.11 LATERAL

An ordinary subquery in FROM cannot see the other tables in the same FROM. LATERAL lifts that restriction, which makes "the most recent N per group" expressible directly.

SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id, o.placed_on
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, placed_on FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  ORDER BY placed_on DESC LIMIT 1
) o
ORDER BY c.full_name;

   full_name   | order_id | placed_on  
---------------+----------+------------
 Ada Okonkwo   |        2 | 2026-02-11
 Kai Nakamura  |        5 | 2026-02-02
 Lin Zhao      |        4 | 2026-02-14
 Mo Haddad     |        7 | 2026-02-25
 Rae Lindqvist |        8 | 2026-03-01
(5 rows)

The subquery references c.customer_id from the enclosing FROM, which is only legal because of LATERAL. Conceptually it runs once per left row — a for loop in a declarative language — though the planner is free to do better.

Five rows, not six: Sam is missing. A CROSS JOIN LATERAL whose subquery returns nothing drops the left row, exactly like an inner join. LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true keeps it:

SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  ORDER BY placed_on DESC LIMIT 1
) o ON true
ORDER BY c.full_name;

   full_name   | order_id 
---------------+----------
 Ada Okonkwo   |        2
 Kai Nakamura  |        5
 Lin Zhao      |        4
 Mo Haddad     |        7
 Rae Lindqvist |        8
 Sam Ferreira  |         
(6 rows)

ON true looks odd and is the idiom: the correlation is already in the subquery, so there is no additional condition to write.

As §10.8 noted, LATERAL and the window-function version of top-N-per-group have opposite performance profiles. LATERAL does one indexed lookup per group and wins with few groups over a large table; the window function sorts everything once and wins with many groups.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: subquery in from.

6.12 Table Functions and Sampling

A function returning a set can appear in FROM, and generate_series is the workhorse:

SELECT d::date AS day, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM generate_series(date '2026-02-11', date '2026-02-18', interval '1 day') AS d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.placed_on = d::date
GROUP BY d ORDER BY d;

    day     | orders 
------------+--------
 2026-02-11 |      1
 2026-02-12 |      0
 2026-02-13 |      0
 2026-02-14 |      1
 2026-02-15 |      0
 2026-02-16 |      0
 2026-02-17 |      0
 2026-02-18 |      1
(8 rows)

That is the fix for gaps in a time series: the days with no orders exist because generate_series produced them and the LEFT JOIN found nothing. GROUP BY alone can only report days that have rows.

WITH ORDINALITY adds a position column to any set-returning function in FROM, which is how you keep the order of an unnest.

TABLESAMPLE reads a fraction of a table's pages rather than all of them:

SELECT count(*) >= 0 AS sampled FROM order_items TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (50) REPEATABLE (42);

 sampled 
---------
 t
(1 row)

SYSTEM (n) picks random pages — fast, and biased if rows are clustered. BERNOULLI (n) picks random rows — slower, unbiased. A REPEATABLE seed — REPEATABLE (seed) — makes the sample reproducible, which is what makes it usable in a test.

To have in hand before moving on: with ordinality and repeatable seed.

6.13 Join Order

Written join order is not execution order. The planner reorders freely (§13.8) and picks the algorithm, so a JOIN b JOIN c and c JOIN b JOIN a produce the same plan.

Two exceptions are worth knowing. PostgreSQL 18 also added join elimination for a self-join on a unique key, controlled by enable_self_join_elimination (§13.15) — a join it can prove changes nothing is simply removed. And LEFT JOIN constrains the order — the join cannot be commuted freely without changing the answer, which is one reason a query with many outer joins plans differently from the same query with inner ones. And join_collapse_limit (§13.15, default 8) caps how many tables the planner will consider all orderings of; above it, explicit JOIN syntax is taken as a hint about the order.

For a query over four tables — the join from §7 that reaches order_items — none of that matters. It starts mattering somewhere around ten.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: join elimination, join_collapse_limit and enable_self_join_elimination.

What This Section Established

SELECT is evaluated FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → windows → select list → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. That is why a select-list alias is invisible to WHERE and visible to ORDER BY.

SELECT * belongs in psql, not in application code or a view.

BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends, which makes it wrong for timestamps; use >= start AND < end. AND binds tighter than OR, and evaluation order within a condition is not guaranteed.

DISTINCT applies to the whole select list. DISTINCT ON keeps the first row per group and requires ORDER BY to start with its expressions — shorter than row_number(), PostgreSQL-only, and unable to give you the top three.

An inner join drops rows with no match. count(*) on an outer-joined row counts the NULL row as 1; count(column) does not.

A condition on the outer table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join — measured, 3 rows against 6. Put it in ON.

LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.pk IS NULL is the anti-join. NOT EXISTS says it more clearly; NOT IN has a NULL trap.

CROSS JOIN is a cartesian product — deliberate sometimes, a symptom usually. USING merges the join column; NATURAL JOIN is a bug waiting for someone to add a column.

A self-join needs an asymmetric condition to enumerate pairs once.

LATERAL lets a FROM subquery see earlier FROM items. CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops left rows whose subquery is empty — measured, 5 rows against 6 — and LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true keeps them.

generate_series in FROM plus a LEFT JOIN is how you get zero rows for days that had none. TABLESAMPLE ... REPEATABLE gives a reproducible sample.

Written join order is not execution order, except that outer joins constrain it and join_collapse_limit caps the search.

Exercises

1. Trace the evaluation order. Write one query that fails because a select-list alias is used in WHERE, and a second, otherwise identical, that succeeds by using it in ORDER BY. Then get the first working three ways — repeating the expression, a subquery, and a lateral — and say which you would ship.

2. Convert a LEFT JOIN by accident. Reproduce §6.7 with your own data. Then write a third version that keeps all customers and filters on a column of the preserved side, and explain why that one belongs in WHERE.

3. Count four ways. For "orders per customer, including customers with none", produce the answer with count(*), count(o.order_id), count(DISTINCT o.order_id) and a LATERAL subquery. Report all four columns side by side and explain every difference.

4. Enumerate pairs. List every pair of products in the same category, once each, with no product paired with itself. Then change the condition to <> and report how many rows you get and why.

5. Fill the gaps. Produce a row per day for a month, with the order count for each, including zero for days with no orders. Then do it per day and per status, so that every combination appears.

6. Race LATERAL against a window function. Get the most recent order per customer both ways. Compare the plans with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE). Then load a hundred thousand orders across a hundred customers and compare again. Report which won at each size and explain the crossover.

Solution

1. Evaluation order.

The failure is §6.1. The three fixes:

SELECT round(price_cents / 100.0, 2) AS euros FROM products
WHERE price_cents / 100.0 > 100 ORDER BY euros;

 euros  
--------
 129.00
 319.00
 549.00
(3 rows)

Repeating the expression works and duplicates it. A subquery — SELECT * FROM (SELECT ..., price_cents/100.0 AS euros FROM products) t WHERE euros > 100 — names it once and reads well. A LATERAL — FROM products p, LATERAL (SELECT p.price_cents/100.0 AS euros) e WHERE e.euros > 100 — also names it once and is the most general, because it works for an expression used several times.

Ship the subquery or the CTE version for readability. Repeating the expression is fine for a one-liner and becomes a maintenance hazard the moment the expression is non-trivial, because the two copies can drift.

2. Converting a LEFT JOIN by accident.

§6.7 measures 3 against 6. The third version:

SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid'
WHERE c.country = 'DE'
ORDER BY c.full_name, o.order_id;

  full_name  | order_id 
-------------+----------
 Ada Okonkwo |        2
 Mo Haddad   |         
(2 rows)

c.country is on the preserved side, so filtering it in WHERE is correct and is what you mean: fewer customers, each still keeping their NULL if they have no paid order. Putting it in ON instead would keep every customer and merely stop non-German ones from matching an order — a different and almost never intended result.

The rule generalises: ON decides what counts as a match; WHERE decides which result rows survive. For the preserved side those are the same thing only when nothing is preserved.

3. Counting four ways.

SELECT c.full_name,
       count(*)                  AS star,
       count(o.order_id)         AS col,
       count(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS distinct_col
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.full_name ORDER BY c.full_name;

   full_name   | star | col | distinct_col 
---------------+------+-----+--------------
 Ada Okonkwo   |    2 |   2 |            2
 Kai Nakamura  |    1 |   1 |            1
 Lin Zhao      |    2 |   2 |            2
 Mo Haddad     |    2 |   2 |            2
 Rae Lindqvist |    1 |   1 |            1
 Sam Ferreira  |    1 |   0 |            0
(6 rows)

The whole difference is Sam's row: count(*) says 1, the other two say 0. count(*) counts rows and there is one row — the outer-joined row full of nulls. count(o.order_id) counts non-null values of that column.

count(DISTINCT ...) matters only once a second join multiplies rows: add JOIN order_items and count(o.order_id) starts counting each order once per line item, while the DISTINCT form stays correct. That silent multiplication is the third classic join bug, after the outer-join WHERE and count(*).

4. Enumerating pairs.

§6.10 gives 3 rows with <. With <>:

SELECT count(*) AS pairs_with_ne
FROM products p JOIN products p2 ON p.category = p2.category AND p.product_id <> p2.product_id;

 pairs_with_ne 
---------------
             6
(1 row)

Six rather than three: every pair appears in both orders. <> excludes only the self-pairing; < also picks one of the two orderings. Six is 3 × 2, and with = allowed it would be nine.

5. Filling gaps.

The one-dimensional version is §6.12. Two dimensions need a cross join of both axes before the outer join:

SELECT d::date AS day, s.status, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM generate_series(date '2026-02-11', date '2026-02-14', interval '1 day') AS d
CROSS JOIN (VALUES ('paid'),('shipped')) AS s(status)
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.placed_on = d::date AND o.status = s.status
GROUP BY d, s.status ORDER BY d, s.status;

    day     | status  | orders 
------------+---------+--------
 2026-02-11 | paid    |      1
 2026-02-11 | shipped |      0
 2026-02-12 | paid    |      0
 2026-02-12 | shipped |      0
 2026-02-13 | paid    |      0
 2026-02-13 | shipped |      0
 2026-02-14 | paid    |      0
 2026-02-14 | shipped |      0
(8 rows)

The CROSS JOIN here is the deliberate cartesian product of §6.9: you want every day × every status, and then you left-join the facts onto that grid. Building the grid first and joining data to it is the general shape of every "report with no missing rows" query.

6. LATERAL against a window function.

At six customers and eight orders both plans are trivial and the timings are noise. That is itself the lesson — this comparison cannot be made on a toy table.

At a hundred thousand orders over a hundred customers, with an index on (customer_id, placed_on DESC), the LATERAL version does one hundred index descents and stops after one row each; the window version sorts a hundred thousand rows to keep a hundred. LATERAL wins by a wide margin.

Invert the shape — a hundred thousand customers with one order each — and the window function wins, because now LATERAL is a hundred thousand index descents while the window function still makes one pass.

The crossover is governed by the ratio of groups to rows. Few groups, many rows per group: LATERAL. Many groups, few rows each: window function. And the reason to know both is that neither is a default.

SECTION 7

Grouping and Aggregation

An aggregate function collapses many rows into one value. GROUP BY decides how the rows are partitioned before that happens. Between them they answer every "how many", "how much" and "what is the average" question, and they are where SQL stops looking like a filter over a table and starts looking like a reporting language.

This section also contains the one error message every SQL learner meets, the one aggregate that behaves differently from all the others, and the syntax for producing subtotals and grand totals in a single pass.

7.1 GROUP BY

SELECT country, count(*) AS customers, min(signed_up_at) AS first_signup
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY country;

 country | customers | first_signup 
---------+-----------+--------------
 BR      |         1 | 2026-02-21
 DE      |         2 | 2025-11-02
 JP      |         1 | 2026-01-08
 US      |         2 | 2025-11-14
(4 rows)

Six input rows become four output rows, one per distinct country. GROUP BY runs at step 3 of §6.1 — after WHERE, before HAVING — so WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups.

With an aggregate and no GROUP BY, the whole table is one group and you get exactly one row, even from an empty table:

SELECT count(*) AS rows, avg(price_cents) IS NULL AS avg_is_null
FROM products WHERE false;

 rows | avg_is_null 
------+-------------
    0 | t
(1 row)

Zero rows in, one row out. count(*) is 0 and avg is NULL, and that asymmetry is §7.4.

7.2 The Rule Everyone Meets First

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT country, full_name, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY country;

ERROR:  column "customers.full_name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
LINE 1: SELECT country, full_name, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY ...
                        ^

The output has one row per country; full_name has two different values inside the DE group; there is no correct answer, so PostgreSQL refuses. MySQL historically returned an arbitrary one, which is the behaviour this error exists to prevent.

Three legitimate resolutions, and choosing between them is a real decision about what you meant:

Group by it too
More groups, finer output. You wanted a row per country and name.
Aggregate it
min(full_name), or better string_agg(full_name, ', ') — you wanted all the names in one cell.
Use a window function
§10.1. You wanted every row and its group's total, which is not a GROUP BY question at all.

There is one exception the standard allows and PostgreSQL implements: grouping by a table's primary key makes every other column of that table functionally dependent, so it may appear unaggregated.

SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, c.country, count(o.order_id) AS orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

 customer_id |   full_name   | country | orders 
-------------+---------------+---------+--------
           1 | Ada Okonkwo   | DE      |      2
           2 | Lin Zhao      | US      |      2
           3 | Kai Nakamura  | JP      |      1
           4 | Mo Haddad     | DE      |      2
           5 | Rae Lindqvist | US      |      1
           6 | Sam Ferreira  | BR      |      0
(6 rows)

full_name and country are not in the GROUP BY and this is accepted, because customer_id is the primary key and determines them. This is worth using: it keeps the GROUP BY list short and it documents that the grouping is per-entity.

In summary, the vocabulary here is aggregate function and string_agg(.

7.3 The Aggregates

SELECT category,
       count(*)                                   AS n,
       min(price_cents)                           AS cheapest,
       max(price_cents)                           AS dearest,
       round(avg(price_cents))                    AS avg_cents,
       sum(price_cents)                           AS total,
       string_agg(sku, ',' ORDER BY sku)          AS skus
FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

  category   | n | cheapest | dearest | avg_cents | total |    skus     
-------------+---+----------+---------+-----------+-------+-------------
 cables      | 2 |      900 |    1200 |      1050 |  2100 | CB-05,CB-06
 displays    | 2 |    31900 |   54900 |     43400 | 86800 | MN-03,MN-04
 peripherals | 2 |     6400 |   12900 |      9650 | 19300 | KB-01,MS-02
(3 rows)
count, sum, avg
min, max
The core five. sum and avg take numbers and intervals; the min() aggregate and the max() aggregate take anything with an ordering, including text and timestamps.
bool_and, bool_or
The bool_and( aggregate asks "all of them?" and bool_or( asks "any of them?". every() is a synonym for the first.
string_agg
array_agg
jsonb_agg
Collect values rather than reduce them. All three take ORDER BY inside the call — see §7.5.
stddev, variance
corr, regr_*
Statistics, including a full set of linear-regression aggregates. stddev( is the sample form; stddev_pop is the population form.

avg on integers returns numeric, not an integer, which is why round() appears above — an average of 12900 and 6400 is 9650.0000000000000000 without it.

What to carry forward from this subsection: max() aggregate, min() aggregate, bool_and(, bool_or( and stddev(.

7.4 NULL and Aggregates

Every aggregate except count(*) ignores nulls. That single rule explains a family of results that otherwise look inconsistent.

SELECT count(*)                              AS count_star,
       count(o.order_id)                     AS count_column,
       count(DISTINCT c.customer_id)         AS count_distinct_customers,
       sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o USING (customer_id);

 count_star | count_column | count_distinct_customers | paid_orders 
------------+--------------+--------------------------+-------------
          9 |            8 |                        6 |           3
(1 row)

That is the count(*) versus count(column) distinction. Nine rows, eight orders: the ninth row is Sam's, with NULL in every orders column: count(*) counts it, count(o.order_id) does not.

count(*)
Counts rows. The only aggregate that does not look at values, and therefore the only one that never returns NULL.
count(col)
Counts non-null values. The difference from count(*) is exactly the number of nulls.
sum, avg
Skip nulls — so avg divides by the count of non-null values, not by the row count. That is usually right and occasionally not what a report meant.
an aggregate over an empty set
count returns 0; every other aggregate returns NULL. coalesce(sum(x), 0) is the fix, and forgetting it is how a total becomes blank instead of zero.

The terms above, gathered: aggregate over an empty set and count(*) versus count(column).

7.5 ORDER BY and DISTINCT Inside an Aggregate

Two modifiers go inside the parentheses, and they are easy to miss.

SELECT c.country,
       string_agg(DISTINCT o.status, ', ' ORDER BY o.status) AS statuses,
       count(DISTINCT o.status)                              AS distinct_statuses
FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY c.country;

 country |       statuses       | distinct_statuses 
---------+----------------------+-------------------
 DE      | paid, pending, shipped |                 3
 JP      | paid                 |                 1
 US      | cancelled, paid, shipped |             3
(3 rows)

ORDER BY inside an aggregate is the only way to make string_agg and array_agg deterministic. Without it the order is whatever the executor produced, which will look stable on a small table and change the day the plan changes — the same hazard as §8.7, in a place people do not think to look.

DISTINCT inside an aggregate de-duplicates the values before aggregating. It forces a sort and cannot be parallelised, so on a large table count(DISTINCT x) is significantly more expensive than count(x); grouping in a subquery is sometimes faster.

One line each, for reference: order by inside an aggregate.

7.6 HAVING

HAVING filters groups, after aggregation.

SELECT c.country, count(*) AS orders, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_cents) AS cents
FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id) JOIN order_items oi USING (order_id)
GROUP BY c.country
HAVING sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_cents) > 50000
ORDER BY c.country;

 country | orders | cents  
---------+--------+--------
 DE      |      7 | 108700
 US      |      4 | 126000
(2 rows)

WHERE before, HAVING after — and the distinction matters for performance as well as meaning. WHERE discards rows before they are aggregated, so anything that can go in WHERE should: HAVING count(*) > 0 on a filtered set is doing work the WHERE clause could have avoided.

A HAVING clause referencing no aggregate is legal and is a WHERE clause in the wrong place. Note also that orders above is 7, not 4 — the join to order_items multiplied each order by its line count, which is the row-multiplication hazard from §6.8's solution. count(DISTINCT o.order_id) is the correct expression there.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: having clause.

7.7 FILTER

The FILTER clause restricts one aggregate to a subset, without affecting the others.

SELECT c.country,
       count(*)                                        AS orders,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')       AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled')  AS cancelled,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid') / count(*), 1) AS pct_paid
FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY c.country;

 country | orders | paid | cancelled | pct_paid 
---------+--------+------+-----------+----------
 DE      |      4 |    1 |         0 |     25.0
 JP      |      1 |    1 |         0 |    100.0
 US      |      3 |    1 |         1 |     33.3
(3 rows)

Three different subsets of the same group in one pass. That is a conditional aggregate, and before FILTER existed you wrote it as count(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END) or sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), and both still work — the CASE form is what you need on databases without FILTER, and the two are equivalent because count ignores the nulls the CASE produces.

FILTER is standard SQL, clearer, and applies to any aggregate. It also works inside a window function (§10.7).

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: filter clause and conditional aggregate.

7.8 Pivoting

A pivot with CASE — or with FILTER, which is the same idea — turns rows into columns:

SELECT c.country,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'pending')   AS pending,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY c.country;

 country | paid | shipped | pending | cancelled 
---------+------+---------+---------+-----------
 DE      |    1 |       2 |       1 |         0
 JP      |    1 |       0 |       0 |         0
 US      |    1 |       1 |       0 |         1
(3 rows)

SQL has no dynamic pivot, and cannot: the number and names of a query's output columns are fixed at planning time, so a pivot over values not known in advance is not expressible. The three ways round it are to list the values (as above), to generate the SQL (\gexec, §1.8, or format() in a function, §18.15), or to return one jsonb object per group (§17.5) and let the client spread it.

The tablefunc extension's crosstab() does the same job with a different syntax and the same fundamental limit — you still declare the output columns.

To have in hand before moving on: pivot with case and crosstab.

7.9 Ordered-Set and Hypothetical-Set Aggregates

An ordered-set aggregate needs its input in order, and takes it with WITHIN GROUP:

SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price_cents) AS median_interpolated,
       percentile_disc(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price_cents) AS median_actual_value,
       mode()               WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY category)    AS most_common_category,
       rank(20000)          WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price_cents) AS rank_20000_would_get
FROM products;

 median_interpolated | median_actual_value | most_common_category | rank_20000_would_get 
---------------------+---------------------+----------------------+----------------------
                9650 |                6400 | cables               |                    5
(1 row)

percentile_cont interpolates between the two middle values; percentile_disc returns one that is actually present. With six prices the continuous median is 9650 — halfway between 6400 and 12900 — and the discrete one is 6400. For "the median response time" you usually want _cont; for "the median product" you want _disc, because half a product does not exist. Both accept an array — percentile_cont(ARRAY[0.5, 0.95, 0.99]) — which is how you get a latency profile in one pass.

mode() is the third ordered-set aggregate here: it returns the most frequent value, choosing arbitrarily among ties.

rank(20000) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price_cents) is a hypothetical-set aggregate: where would a 20000-cent product rank, without inserting one? The answer is 5. dense_rank, percent_rank and cume_dist have the same hypothetical form, and it is the natural way to answer "what percentile is this value" against a distribution.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: mode(.

In summary, the vocabulary here is ordered-set aggregate.

7.10 GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE

Subtotals and a grand total, in one pass over the data.

SELECT coalesce(c.country, '(all)') AS country,
       coalesce(o.status, '(all)')  AS status,
       count(*)                     AS orders
FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY ROLLUP (c.country, o.status)
ORDER BY c.country NULLS LAST, o.status NULLS LAST;

 country |  status   | orders 
---------+-----------+--------
 DE      | paid      |      1
 DE      | pending   |      1
 DE      | shipped   |      2
 DE      | (all)     |      4
 JP      | paid      |      1
 JP      | (all)     |      1
 US      | cancelled |      1
 US      | paid      |      1
 US      | shipped   |      1
 US      | (all)     |      3
 (all)   | (all)     |      8
(11 rows)

Detail rows, a subtotal per country, and a grand total — from one scan.

GROUPING SETS
The general form: list exactly the groupings you want. () is the empty grouping set — the grand total.
ROLLUP (a, b, c)
The hierarchical prefixes: (a,b,c), (a,b), (a), (). For a natural hierarchy — country, then region, then city.
CUBE (a, b)
Every subset: (a,b), (a), (b), (). Grows as 2n, so it is for two or three columns, not six.

The coalesce in that query hides a genuine ambiguity. A subtotal row has NULL in the columns it is not grouped by — and a NULL in the data would look identical. GROUPING() distinguishes them, returning 1 when the column was aggregated away:

SELECT c.country, o.status, count(*) AS orders,
       GROUPING(c.country) AS country_rolled_up,
       GROUPING(o.status)  AS status_rolled_up
FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id)
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((c.country), (o.status), ())
ORDER BY c.country NULLS LAST, o.status NULLS LAST;

 country |  status   | orders | country_rolled_up | status_rolled_up 
---------+-----------+--------+-------------------+------------------
 DE      |           |      4 |                 0 |                1
 JP      |           |      1 |                 0 |                1
 US      |           |      3 |                 0 |                1
         | cancelled |      1 |                 1 |                0
         | paid      |      3 |                 1 |                0
         | pending   |      1 |                 1 |                0
         | shipped   |      3 |                 1 |                0
         |           |      8 |                 1 |                1
(8 rows)

Three grouping sets, three blocks of output, and GROUPING() labelling each row with which grouping produced it. That is the column your reporting layer should switch on, not IS NULL.

GROUP BY DISTINCT (PostgreSQL 14 and later) removes duplicate grouping sets, which CUBE combined with ROLLUP can otherwise generate.

What to carry forward from this subsection: empty grouping set and group by distinct.

7.11 What the Planner Does With a Group

Two node types, as §13.9 introduced. HashAggregate builds a hash table of groups: no sort, needs work_mem, and its output has no defined order. GroupAggregate needs sorted input and streams.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT country, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY country;

SET
          QUERY PLAN           
-------------------------------
 HashAggregate
   Group Key: country
   ->  Seq Scan on customers
(3 rows)

Three consequences worth carrying forward. A GROUP BY result is unordered unless you say otherwise — HashAggregate in particular emits groups in hash order, and that is the single most common source of an accidental dependence on row order (§8.7). An index on the grouping columns can eliminate the sort and give a GroupAggregate that streams, which matters most when combined with LIMIT. And count(DISTINCT x) cannot be parallelised, so on a large table it is often the slowest thing in the query.

For an exact count of a huge table there is no shortcut — MVCC means count(*) must actually count (§14.7). When an estimate will do, reltuples from pg_class is instant (§1.9's exercise).

What This Section Established

GROUP BY partitions rows; an aggregate collapses each partition to one value. With an aggregate and no GROUP BY the whole table is one group, and an empty table still yields one row.

Every select-list column must be grouped or aggregated — unless you group by the primary key, which makes the rest of that table's columns functionally dependent and legal.

avg on integers returns numeric. Every aggregate except count(*) ignores nulls, and on zero rows count returns 0 while everything else returns NULL — so coalesce(sum(x), 0).

count(*) counts rows including outer-joined null rows; count(col) counts non-null values; measured as 9 against 8.

ORDER BY inside string_agg/array_agg is the only thing making their output deterministic. DISTINCT inside an aggregate forces a sort and blocks parallelism.

WHERE filters rows before aggregation, HAVING filters groups after. Prefer WHERE where possible. A join that multiplies rows inflates count(*); count(DISTINCT pk) is the fix.

FILTER restricts one aggregate without touching the others, and is the readable form of count(CASE WHEN ...). It is also how you pivot — and SQL has no dynamic pivot, because the output column list is fixed at planning time.

WITHIN GROUP feeds ordered-set aggregates. percentile_cont interpolates (9650); percentile_disc returns a real value (6400). rank(x) WITHIN GROUP answers where a hypothetical value would rank.

ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS produce subtotals in one pass. A subtotal's NULL is indistinguishable from a data NULL except through GROUPING().

HashAggregate output is unordered; an index on the grouping columns can turn it into a streaming GroupAggregate. count(*) on a huge table has no shortcut under MVCC.

Exercises

1. Resolve the grouping error three ways. Produce the "must appear in the GROUP BY clause" error, then fix it by grouping, by aggregating, and by using a window function. Show all three results and say which question each one answers.

2. Count the nulls. On an outer join, produce count(*), count(col) and their difference in one query, and verify the difference equals the number of unmatched rows. Then add a second join that multiplies rows and show which of the counts becomes wrong.

3. Total nothing. Write a query whose WHERE clause matches no rows and which returns sum(x). Report what you get. Fix it so a report renders 0. Then do the same for a GROUP BY query and explain why the fix is different.

4. Pivot, then generate the pivot. Produce a column per order status with FILTER. Then write a query that generates that SQL from the distinct values of status, and run it with \gexec. State the limitation that made the second version necessary.

5. Two medians. Compute percentile_cont(0.5) and percentile_disc(0.5) over the same column and explain the difference in terms of the data. Then compute the 50th, 95th and 99th percentiles in one call.

6. Subtotal a hierarchy. Using ROLLUP over country and status, produce detail rows, per-country subtotals and a grand total. Use GROUPING() rather than IS NULL to label each row, and explain what would go wrong with IS NULL if a country were null.

7. Make the group order change. Write a GROUP BY with no ORDER BY and record the row order. Then force a GroupAggregate by disabling hash aggregation, and record it again. Report both, and state the rule you would give a colleague.

Solution

1. Three resolutions.

Grouping by it: one row per (country, name) — "how many rows does each named person have in each country", which for this table is six rows of 1.

Aggregating it:

SELECT country, string_agg(full_name, ', ' ORDER BY full_name) AS names, count(*) AS n
FROM customers GROUP BY country ORDER BY country;

 country |           names            | n 
---------+----------------------------+---
 BR      | Sam Ferreira               | 1
 DE      | Ada Okonkwo, Mo Haddad     | 2
 JP      | Kai Nakamura               | 1
 US      | Lin Zhao, Rae Lindqvist    | 2
(4 rows)

The window version keeps all six rows and attaches the country count to each. The three answer genuinely different questions — "a row per pair", "a row per country with the names collected", "every row, annotated" — and the error is PostgreSQL declining to guess which you meant.

2. Counting the nulls.

count(*) - count(o.order_id) equals the number of customers with no orders, which is 1 (Sam). Adding JOIN order_items multiplies each order by its line count, and count(o.order_id) starts counting orders once per item — 13 rather than 8. count(DISTINCT o.order_id) stays at 8.

The general rule: the moment a query joins to a one-to-many table, every plain count and sum over the other side is suspect. sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_cents) is still correct because it is summing the many side; sum(o.total) would be wrong, counting each order's total once per line item.

3. Totalling nothing.

SELECT sum(price_cents) AS raw, coalesce(sum(price_cents), 0) AS fixed
FROM products WHERE false;

 raw | fixed 
-----+-------
     |     0
(1 row)

NULL, and coalesce fixes it — because with no GROUP BY there is always exactly one output row.

With a GROUP BY, coalesce does not help, because there is no row at all: no rows in, no groups, no output. The fix there is structural — a LEFT JOIN from a table of all the groups you want, as in §6.12's generate_series, so the group exists and the aggregate over its zero matching rows returns NULL, which coalesce can then turn into 0.

That distinction — "a null total" against "a missing row" — is the difference between one function call and a restructured query, and it is worth recognising before you write the report.

4. Generating the pivot.

SELECT 'SELECT c.country' ||
       string_agg(format(', count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = %L) AS %I', status, status),
                  '' ORDER BY status)
       || ' FROM customers c JOIN orders o USING (customer_id) GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY c.country;'
       AS stmt
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders) s
\gexec

 country | cancelled | paid | pending | shipped 
---------+-----------+------+---------+---------
 DE      |         0 |    1 |       1 |       2
 JP      |         0 |    1 |       0 |       0
 US      |         1 |    1 |       0 |       1
(3 rows)

Three details are load-bearing. The limitation that made this necessary is that a query's output columns are fixed when it is planned, so no single statement can produce a column per value of a column — generating the text is a second round trip that reads the values first. %L and %I are not optional, for the reason §18.15 gives. And ORDER BY status inside string_agg is what makes the column order stable: without it the generated column order follows whatever order the DISTINCT happened to produce, which is §7.11's hazard reappearing in the shape of the result rather than in its rows.

5. Two medians.

Six prices — 900, 1200, 6400, 12900, 31900, 54900 — so the two middle values are 6400 and 12900. percentile_cont(0.5) interpolates to 9650; percentile_disc(0.5) returns the first value at or past the 50% mark, 6400.

SELECT (percentile_cont(ARRAY[0.5, 0.95, 0.99]) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price_cents))
         ::numeric(10,2)[] AS p
FROM products;

              p              
-----------------------------
 {9650.00,49150.00,53750.00}
(1 row)

One pass, three percentiles, returned as an array — and cast, for a reason worth seeing. percentile_cont interpolates in double precision whatever the input type, so casting the input to numeric changes nothing. Without the cast on the result, this exact query printed {9650,49149.99999999999,53750} on the machine the course was last verified on, and {9650,49150,53750} on the one it was written on: the 95th percentile is 31,900 plus three quarters of the gap to 54,900, and whether that lands on 49,150 or a hair under depends on how one intermediate double rounds. A report that compares percentiles for equality, or a test that asserts one, needs the cast (§3.8).

6. Subtotalling a hierarchy.

§7.10 has both queries. What goes wrong with IS NULL: if a country value were genuinely NULL in the data, its detail rows would have country IS NULL — identical to the grand-total row's NULL. A report switching on IS NULL would label real rows as totals and sum them into the wrong place.

GROUPING(c.country) returns 1 only when the column was rolled up, so it distinguishes the two cases exactly. This is not a hypothetical: nullable dimension columns are extremely common in reporting schemas.

7. Changing the group order.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SET enable_hashagg = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT country, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY country;

SET
SET
             QUERY PLAN             
------------------------------------
 GroupAggregate
   Group Key: country
   ->  Sort
         Sort Key: country
         ->  Seq Scan on customers
(5 rows)

GroupAggregate requires sorted input, so its output arrives in group-key order — and looks like it was sorted, although nothing asked for it. HashAggregate emits in hash order, which is neither sorted nor stable across data changes.

The rule for a colleague is one sentence: if the order of a result matters, write ORDER BY — and the corollary is that a result which currently comes back sorted without one is a bug waiting for the planner to change its mind, which it will do when the table grows, when work_mem changes, or when someone adds an index.

SECTION 8

Set Operations, Ordering and Pagination

Three subjects that belong together because they all operate on a finished result set: combining two of them, putting one in order, and handing back a slice.

The section also contains the rule that this course returns to more than any other — a table has no order — and the reason the pagination technique most applications use is quietly wrong at scale.

8.1 UNION and UNION ALL

SELECT status, count(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY status
UNION ALL
SELECT 'TOTAL', count(*) FROM orders
ORDER BY 1;

  status   | n 
-----------+---
 TOTAL     | 8
 cancelled | 1
 paid      | 3
 pending   | 1
 shipped   | 3
(5 rows)

UNION ALL concatenates. The UNION operator on its own concatenates and removes duplicates, which costs a sort or a hash over the whole result.

Use UNION ALL unless you actually need duplicates removed. The difference is not small: UNION on a million rows sorts a million rows, and if the two branches cannot produce duplicates — different statuses, different date ranges, a detail query plus a total — the deduplication is pure cost. UNION is the more common typo in production SQL, and it is invisible because the answer is right.

The terms above, gathered: union operator.

8.2 INTERSECT and EXCEPT

SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers
EXCEPT
SELECT 'DE'
ORDER BY country;

 country 
---------
 BR
 JP
 US
(3 rows)

The INTERSECT operator keeps rows in both branches; the EXCEPT operator keeps rows in the first and not the second. Both remove duplicates by default and both accept ALL to keep them, with multiset semantics — EXCEPT ALL subtracts occurrences, so three copies minus one copy leaves two.

INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT, which are left-associative. With more than two branches, parenthesise.

These read well and are often not the fastest way to say what they say. EXCEPT over large inputs is usually beaten by NOT EXISTS (§9.5), which can stop at the first match per row instead of materialising and de-duplicating both sides.

One line each, for reference: intersect operator and except operator.

8.3 Matching Columns and Types

The branches must have the same number of columns, and corresponding columns must have compatible types. The result type is resolved across all branches:

SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT 1.5 ORDER BY n;

  n  
-----
   1
 1.5
(2 rows)

integer and numeric resolve to numeric, so 1 comes back as 1, in a numeric column. Where no common type exists you get an error rather than a silent coercion:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 'x';

ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "x"
LINE 1: SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 'x';
                              ^

Column names come from the first branch, and the others are matched by position, not by name. That is the trap: two branches whose select lists have the same names in a different order produce a silently scrambled result. Always list the columns explicitly and in the same order in every branch.

8.4 ORDER BY

The ORDER BY clause runs at step 8 of §6.1 — after the select list — so it can use output labels, output positions, and expressions that never appear in the output.

SELECT full_name, country FROM customers
ORDER BY country DESC, full_name;

   full_name   | country 
---------------+---------
 Lin Zhao      | US
 Rae Lindqvist | US
 Kai Nakamura  | JP
 Ada Okonkwo   | DE
 Mo Haddad     | DE
 Sam Ferreira  | BR
(6 rows)

The ASC keyword is the default, and is worth writing whenever any key carries the DESC keyword — because ORDER BY a, b DESC sorts a ascending. The keyword attaches to one key, not to the list.

ORDER BY 1, 2 sorts by output position. It is concise, it is what a UNION requires if the branches disagree on names, and it breaks silently when someone inserts a column into the select list. Use it in a UNION and nowhere else.

In a set operation the ORDER BY belongs to the whole result, not to the last branch — which is why every UNION example in this section has it at the end and unindented.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: asc keyword and desc keyword.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: order by clause.

8.5 Where NULLs Sort

SELECT o.order_id, x.note
FROM orders o LEFT JOIN (VALUES (1,'first order')) AS x(order_id, note) USING (order_id)
ORDER BY x.note NULLS FIRST, o.order_id
LIMIT 3;

 order_id |    note     
----------+-------------
        2 | 
        3 | 
        4 | 
(3 rows)

PostgreSQL's default is NULLS LAST for ASC and NULLS FIRST for DESC — the rule being that nulls sort as if larger than everything. That is a choice the SQL standard leaves open, and other engines choose differently, so a query that orders a nullable column portably must say NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST explicitly.

It matters for indexes too: a B-tree stores nulls at one end, and an index on (x) serves ORDER BY x without a sort only if the null placement matches. CREATE INDEX ... (x DESC NULLS LAST) exists for exactly that.

Collation in ORDER BY decides text ordering (§17.20), which is a property of the column or an explicit COLLATE clause. ORDER BY name COLLATE "C" is byte order; ORDER BY name COLLATE "en-US-x-icu" is dictionary order; they differ, and the difference is not cosmetic.

To have in hand before moving on: collation in order by.

8.6 There Is No Default Order

This is the rule the whole course keeps returning to.

A SELECT without ORDER BY returns rows in no defined order. There is no deterministic ordering unless you ask for one. Not "insertion order", not "primary key order", not "the order it returned last time". PostgreSQL will nonetheless hand back a small table in physical order nearly every time, which is exactly what makes this dangerous: the code passes review, passes tests, and breaks in production.

Everything that changes it is invisible from the query text:

An UPDATE
Moves the row to a new physical position (§14.7), so it jumps to the end.
A new index
The planner switches to an index scan and the order becomes the index's.
Growth
The table crosses min_parallel_table_scan_size and a parallel scan interleaves workers (§13.12).
A GROUP BY
HashAggregate emits in hash order (§7.11).
A VACUUM FULL
Rewrites the table and reorders everything (§16.3).

The corollary that catches people even when they did write ORDER BY: an ORDER BY that is not a total order leaves the tied rows in undefined order. ORDER BY country on this table fixes the country blocks and says nothing about who comes first within DE. If the result is paginated, or compared against a fixture, or fed to row_number() (§10.3), add enough keys to make the order total — the primary key is the reliable last one.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: deterministic ordering.

8.7 LIMIT and OFFSET

SELECT full_name, signed_up_at FROM customers
ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC, customer_id DESC
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 1;

   full_name   | signed_up_at 
---------------+--------------
 Rae Lindqvist | 2026-02-03
 Mo Haddad     | 2026-01-19
 Kai Nakamura  | 2026-01-08
(3 rows)

The LIMIT clause and the OFFSET clause — LIMIT n OFFSET m — are PostgreSQL's spelling; FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY with OFFSET m ROWS is the standard's, and both work. LIMIT without ORDER BY is meaningless — you asked for three rows out of an undefined ordering, so you got three arbitrary rows.

FETCH FIRST ... WITH TIES is the standard-only form that keeps rows tied with the last one:

SELECT sku, category FROM products ORDER BY category FETCH FIRST 1 ROW WITH TIES;

  sku  | category 
-------+----------
 CB-05 | cables
 CB-06 | cables
(2 rows)
