One row requested, two returned, because both are in the cables category and the ORDER BY cannot separate them. That is a genuinely useful answer for "the top scorers" — and note it works only with FETCH FIRST, not with LIMIT.

LIMIT also changes the plan: the planner will prefer a strategy with a low startup cost when it knows you want few rows, which is why an index that removes the sort is worth far more with a LIMIT than without one (§13.9).

In summary, the vocabulary here is limit clause and offset clause.

8.8 Why OFFSET Pagination Breaks

OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20 looks like it fetches twenty rows. It does not: the server produces the first 10,020 rows and discards 10,000 of them. Page one is instant, page five hundred is a table scan, and the cost grows linearly with the page number.

The correctness problem is worse than the performance one. Between page 3 and page 4 the underlying data changes; a row inserted before your position shifts everything by one, so a row you have already seen appears again on the next page, and a deletion makes a row disappear without ever being shown. There is no OFFSET value that fixes this, because the offset is counted against a result set that no longer exists.

8.9 Keyset Pagination

The fix is to remember where you were rather than how many you skipped.

SELECT full_name, signed_up_at, customer_id FROM customers
WHERE (signed_up_at, customer_id) < (DATE '2026-01-19', 4)
ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC, customer_id DESC
LIMIT 2;

  full_name   | signed_up_at | customer_id 
--------------+--------------+-------------
 Kai Nakamura | 2026-01-08   |           3
 Lin Zhao     | 2025-11-14   |           2
(2 rows)

This is the seek method: the client sends back the sort key of the last row it saw — here (2026-01-19, 4) — and the query resumes from there. Three properties follow:

Constant time
An index on (signed_up_at, customer_id) seeks straight to the position. Page five hundred costs what page one costs.
Stable
Rows inserted above your position do not shift it, so nothing is skipped or repeated.
No page numbers
You can go forward and back, not jump to page 47. That is the real cost, and it is why "load more" interfaces are more common than numbered pages on large datasets.

(a, b) < (x, y) is a row constructor comparison, and using it rather than a < x OR (a = x AND b < y) is not merely tidier: the row form is what a B-tree on (a, b) can turn into a single index seek, while the expanded OR form usually cannot. That is the whole technique in one line of syntax.

The tie-break column is what makes it a stable sort key and the order total — §8.6 — or two rows with the same timestamp will bracket the boundary and one of them will be lost.

What to carry forward from this subsection: seek method, stable sort key and row constructor comparison.

8.10 VALUES

VALUES is a statement in its own right, producing a table:

SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,'one'), (2,'two'), (3,'three')) AS t(n, word) ORDER BY n DESC;

 n |  word  
---+--------
 3 | three
 2 | two
 1 | one
(3 rows)

It needs an alias with column names to be useful in FROM. Three places it earns its keep: as the source of a multi-row INSERT (§11.3), as a small lookup table joined into a query without creating one, and as the grid in a report that must show every combination (§6.12's solution) — a VALUES list of the statuses you want, cross-joined to the dates you want, left-joined to the facts.

Its types are inferred from the first row, so VALUES (1), (2.5) resolves to numeric and VALUES (NULL), (1) needs a cast on the first — VALUES (NULL::int), (1) — or you get "column has unknown type".

The terms above, gathered: values list.

What This Section Established

UNION ALL concatenates; UNION also de-duplicates at the cost of a sort over the whole result. Prefer UNION ALL unless duplicates are actually possible — the wrong one is invisible because the answer is right.

INTERSECT and EXCEPT de-duplicate too, take ALL for multiset semantics, and are often beaten by EXISTS/NOT EXISTS on large inputs.

Branches are matched by position, not by name, and the result's column names come from the first branch. Types are resolved across all branches.

ORDER BY sees output labels and positions. ASC/DESC attach to one key, not to the list. In a set operation it belongs to the whole result.

PostgreSQL sorts nulls last ascending, first descending; the standard does not require it, so say NULLS FIRST/NULLS LAST when it matters. Text order is collation-dependent.

There is no default row order, and an UPDATE, a new index, table growth, a HashAggregate or a VACUUM FULL will each change it without changing your query. An ORDER BY that is not a total order leaves ties undefined — add the primary key.

LIMIT without ORDER BY returns arbitrary rows. FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES keeps rows tied with the last, and only exists in that spelling — measured, one row requested and two returned.

OFFSET n produces and discards n rows, so paging cost grows with page number, and concurrent inserts make rows repeat or vanish between pages.

Keyset pagination compares a row constructor against the last row seen: constant time, stable under concurrent writes, no page numbers. (a, b) < (x, y) is what a (a, b) index can seek on; the expanded OR form usually is not.

VALUES in FROM needs a column alias, infers types from the first row, and is how you build the grid a gap-free report joins onto.

Exercises

1. Measure the cost of UNION. Build two large result sets that cannot overlap. Time UNION and UNION ALL over them and compare the plans. Report what UNION added, and say how you would spot the mistake in a code review.

2. Scramble a UNION. Write two branches whose select lists have the same column names in different orders. Show the result and explain why no error was raised. Then state the discipline that prevents it.

3. Prove there is no default order. Take a table, select without ORDER BY, and record the sequence. Change it three ways — update a row, add an index the planner will use, and force a parallel scan — recording the sequence each time. Then write the one-sentence rule.

4. Break OFFSET pagination. Page through a table twenty rows at a time with OFFSET. Between page 2 and page 3, insert a row that sorts before your position. Show a row appearing twice. Then do the same with keyset pagination and show it does not.

5. Compare the two page-500 costs. With a table of a million rows, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) both OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20 and the keyset equivalent. Report both plans and both timings, and explain the difference in terms of what each has to produce.

6. Sort ties on purpose. Order a result by a non-unique column and paginate it. Demonstrate a row being lost at a page boundary. Fix it by making the sort total, and explain why the primary key is the right last key.

Solution

1. The cost of UNION.

UNION adds a HashAggregate or Unique-over-Sort node above the Append; UNION ALL is an Append alone. On large inputs the deduplication dominates, and it also needs work_mem — a UNION that spills to disk is a common and unexplained slowdown.

In review, the tell is a UNION whose branches provably cannot produce a common row: different tables, disjoint filters, or a detail query plus an aggregate. Each of those is UNION ALL written wrongly. The reason it survives review is that the result is identical, so nothing ever fails.

2. Scrambling a UNION.

SELECT full_name AS a, country AS b FROM customers WHERE country = 'JP'
UNION ALL
SELECT country AS b, full_name AS a FROM customers WHERE country = 'BR'
ORDER BY 1;

      a       |      b       
--------------+--------------
 BR           | Sam Ferreira
 Kai Nakamura | JP
(2 rows)

No error, because both branches are (text, text) and that is all the type system checks. The names on the second branch are ignored entirely — they exist only to confuse the reader.

The discipline: write the columns explicitly and in the same order in every branch, and never use SELECT * in one. Where the branches genuinely come from different tables, aliasing every column identically in both makes a mismatch visible on the page.

3. No default order.

The three changes each produce a different sequence, and §8.6 lists why. The rule in one sentence: if the order of a result matters to anything — a user, a test, a page boundary, a row_number() — write ORDER BY, and make it total.

The stronger version, worth internalising: a result that comes back correctly ordered without ORDER BY is not evidence of anything except that today's plan happens to produce it.

4. Breaking OFFSET pagination.

With ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC and 20 rows a page, inserting a row that sorts into page 1 pushes every subsequent row down by one position. Page 3 (OFFSET 40) then starts one row earlier than it would have, so the last row of page 2 appears again as the first row of page 3. A deletion does the mirror image and skips a row entirely.

Keyset pagination is immune because the boundary is a value, not a count: the client asks for "rows after (2026-01-19, 4)", and inserting a row elsewhere does not move that boundary.

5. Page 500.

OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20 shows Limit over a scan whose actual rows is 10,020 — the executor produced them all and threw 10,000 away. The keyset version shows an Index Scan with actual rows=20 and an Index Cond on the row constructor.

The timing difference is roughly the ratio of those row counts, and it grows with the page number: page 5,000 produces 100,020 rows for the offset version and still 20 for the keyset one.

6. Ties at a page boundary.

With ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC and two customers signed up on the same day, the two rows can appear in either order. If the boundary falls between them, page 1 may end with one of them and page 2 may begin with the same one — or with neither.

Making the order total fixes it: ORDER BY signed_up_at DESC, customer_id DESC. The primary key is the right last key because it is unique and never null, which is exactly what "total order" requires. A created_at timestamp is not a substitute: two rows can share one, and then you are back where you started.

SECTION 9

Subqueries and Common Table Expressions

The closure property from §1.1 — every operation returns a relation — is what makes a SELECT legal anywhere a value or a table is legal. This section is the catalogue of those places, plus WITH, which gives a subquery a name, and recursion, which is the one thing plain SQL cannot express without it.

The practical theme is that several of these constructs say the same thing with very different performance, and one of them has a NULL trap that silently returns nothing.

9.1 Where a Subquery Can Go

Select list
A scalar subquery — must return at most one row and one column, and yields NULL if it returns none.
FROM
A derived table. Needs an alias. With LATERAL (§6.11) it may reference earlier FROM items.
WHERE / HAVING
As a scalar, or with EXISTS, IN, ANY, ALL.
WITH
A named subquery, usable more than once, and the only place recursion is possible.

A subquery that mentions a column from the enclosing query is correlated; one that does not is uncorrelated. That distinction decides almost everything about how it performs.

9.2 Scalar Subqueries

An uncorrelated scalar subquery is evaluated once and used as a constant:

SELECT name, price_cents FROM products
WHERE price_cents > (SELECT avg(price_cents) FROM products)
ORDER BY price_cents;

      name       | price_cents 
-----------------+-------------
 27-inch Monitor |       31900
 34-inch Monitor |       54900
(2 rows)

That is a query you cannot write without a subquery, because WHERE price_cents > avg(price_cents) is illegal — an aggregate over the rows you are filtering does not exist yet at step 2 of §6.1.

Returning more than one row is a runtime error, not a compile-time one:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT (SELECT country FROM customers) AS one_country;

ERROR:  more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression

Which means a scalar subquery that is correct today can fail on tomorrow's data. Where the subquery is not provably single-row, add LIMIT 1 and an ORDER BY that makes the choice deliberate — or restructure as a join.

One line each, for reference: avg(.

9.3 Correlated Subqueries

A correlated subquery references the outer row, and is conceptually evaluated once per outer row:

SELECT c.full_name,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS orders,
       (SELECT max(o.placed_on) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS latest
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.full_name;

   full_name   | orders |   latest   
---------------+--------+------------
 Ada Okonkwo   |      2 | 2026-02-11
 Kai Nakamura  |      1 | 2026-02-02
 Lin Zhao      |      2 | 2026-02-14
 Mo Haddad     |      2 | 2026-02-25
 Rae Lindqvist |      1 | 2026-03-01
 Sam Ferreira  |      0 | 
(6 rows)

Note Sam: count(*) over no rows is 0, and max over no rows is NULL (§7.4). A LEFT JOIN with GROUP BY gives the same answer.

This shape is where §13.6's loops trap lives. Two correlated subqueries means two lookups per outer row; a hundred thousand customers means two hundred thousand index descents, and the plan reports them per-loop so the total is not visible unless you multiply. The join form gives the planner the option of a hash join, which the subquery form does not.

That flattening has a name — subquery flattening — and for one aggregate the planner will often do it anyway. For several, or for anything with a LIMIT, it usually cannot — which is when LATERAL (§6.11) is the better tool, because one lateral subquery can return several columns at once where each scalar subquery is a separate pass.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: correlated subquery and subquery flattening.

9.4 Derived Tables

A subquery in FROM is a table, and it needs a name:

SELECT category, n FROM (
  SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM products GROUP BY category
) AS by_category
WHERE n > 1
ORDER BY category;

  category   | n 
-------------+---
 cables      | 2
 displays    | 2
 peripherals | 2
(3 rows)

That particular query is HAVING written the long way. Derived tables earn their place when you need to filter or join on something computed at a different level — a window function's output (§10.8), a rank, a running total — because those cannot appear in WHERE.

A CTE (§9.8) does the same job with the name at the top instead of buried in the middle, which is why most people reach for one now.

9.5 EXISTS and NOT EXISTS

An EXISTS subquery asks whether it returns any row. It does not care what the row contains, which is why SELECT 1 is the convention:

SELECT full_name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'shipped')
ORDER BY full_name;

  full_name  
-------------
 Ada Okonkwo
 Lin Zhao
 Mo Haddad
(3 rows)

EXISTS can stop at the first matching row, which is the reason it is usually the fastest of the four ways to say this. The planner turns it into a semi-join: like an inner join, but emitting each left row at most once regardless of how many matches it has — so it never multiplies rows the way §6.8's solution warns about.

NOT EXISTS is the anti-join, and it is the safe one:

SELECT full_name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY full_name;

  full_name   
--------------
 Sam Ferreira
(1 row)

Same answer as the LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL form of §6.8, usually the same plan, and considerably easier to read correctly — there is no "which column do I test for null" question.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: semi-join and exists subquery.

9.6 IN, and the NOT IN Trap

The IN predicate is comfortable and the NOT IN operator has a sharp edge.

SELECT count(*) AS matched FROM products WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items);
SELECT count(*) AS not_matched FROM products WHERE product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items);

 matched 
---------
       6
(1 row)

 not_matched 
-------------
           0
(1 row)

Both correct — because order_items.product_id is NOT NULL. Make it nullable and the second query silently returns nothing:

SELECT 1 AS row_returned WHERE 3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL);

 row_returned 
--------------
(0 rows)

Zero rows, and 3 is obviously not 1, 2 or NULL. That is the NOT IN NULL trap. The reason is §1.12's three-valued logic. x NOT IN (a, b, c) means x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> c; 3 <> NULL is unknown; true AND true AND unknown is unknown; and WHERE discards unknown. A single NULL anywhere in the list makes NOT IN return no rows at all.

This is not a corner case. WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT parent_id FROM child) is an extremely common query, and parent_id is nullable in an extremely common schema. The query returns nothing, the application shows an empty list, and nothing errors.

Use NOT EXISTS
Null-safe by construction, and usually the better plan. This is the fix.
or exclude the nulls
NOT IN (SELECT x FROM t WHERE x IS NOT NULL). Correct, and it requires you to remember, every time.

IN itself is safe — a NULL in the list can only produce unknown for rows that were not going to match anyway.

For a literal list rather than a subquery, = ANY(ARRAY[...]) (§17.11) is the better form: one bind parameter instead of N, so the query text is stable and its plan is cached.

To have in hand before moving on: in predicate, not in operator and the not in null trap.

9.7 ANY, ALL and Row Comparisons

IN is shorthand for = ANY, and the general forms take any comparison operator:

SELECT name, price_cents FROM products
WHERE price_cents > ALL (SELECT price_cents FROM products WHERE category = 'cables')
ORDER BY price_cents;

        name         | price_cents 
---------------------+-------------
 Trackball Mouse     |        6400
 Mechanical Keyboard |       12900
 27-inch Monitor     |       31900
 34-inch Monitor     |       54900
(4 rows)

The ALL operator — > ALL — means greater than every one; > ANY (also spelled SOME) means greater than at least one. ALL over an empty subquery is true and ANY over an empty subquery is false, which follows from the logic and surprises people the first time an empty set makes a filter match everything.

ALL carries the same NULL hazard as NOT IN, for the same reason.

Row constructor comparison compares tuples lexicographically:

SELECT (1, 'b') > (1, 'a')     AS row_compare,
       (1, NULL) IS NOT NULL   AS row_is_not_null,
       (1, NULL) IS NULL       AS row_is_null;

 row_compare | row_is_not_null | row_is_null 
-------------+-----------------+-------------
 t           | f               | f
(1 row)

(1, NULL) is neither IS NULL nor IS NOT NULL — for a row, IS NULL means every field is null and IS NOT NULL means every field is not null, so a partially-null row is neither. That is a genuine oddity in the standard, and the reason to test the individual columns.

The useful application of row comparison is the keyset pagination of §8.9, where (a, b) < (x, y) becomes a single index seek.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: all operator.

9.8 Common Table Expressions

The WITH clause names a subquery before the main query, which turns nesting into sequence:

WITH recent AS (
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, placed_on FROM orders WHERE placed_on >= '2026-02-01'
), totals AS (
  SELECT r.order_id, sum(oi.quantity * oi.unit_cents) AS cents
  FROM recent r JOIN order_items oi USING (order_id)
  GROUP BY r.order_id
)
SELECT r.order_id, c.full_name, t.cents
FROM recent r JOIN customers c USING (customer_id) JOIN totals t USING (order_id)
ORDER BY r.order_id;

 order_id |   full_name   | cents 
----------+---------------+-------
        2 | Ada Okonkwo   | 31900
        4 | Lin Zhao      | 54900
        5 | Kai Nakamura  | 32200
        6 | Mo Haddad     |  3600
        7 | Mo Haddad     | 57900
        8 | Rae Lindqvist | 63800
(6 rows)

A CTE can reference earlier CTEs — totals uses recent — and the main query can use any of them, more than once. That is the readability argument, and it is a strong one: a three-level nested subquery reads inside-out, and the same logic as three CTEs reads top to bottom.

In summary, the vocabulary here is with clause.

9.9 MATERIALIZED and the Optimisation Fence

Here is the part that has changed, and where old advice is now wrong.

Before PostgreSQL 12, every CTE was an optimization fence: it was executed on its own, its result materialised, and no predicate could be pushed into it. That made WITH a performance trap — moving a subquery into a CTE could make a query dramatically slower — and it also made it a deliberate tool, because sometimes forcing materialisation is what you want.

From PostgreSQL 12, a CTE that is used exactly once, is not recursive and has no side effects is inlined, exactly like a derived table. The fence is gone by default, and two keywords control it explicitly:

WITH cheap AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT product_id, price_cents FROM products WHERE price_cents < 10000
)
SELECT count(*) AS n FROM cheap;

WITH cheap AS NOT MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT product_id, price_cents FROM products WHERE price_cents < 10000
)
SELECT count(*) AS n FROM cheap;

 n 
---
 3
(1 row)

 n 
---
 3
(1 row)

Same answer, different plans. Use a MATERIALIZED CTE when it is expensive and referenced several times — computing it once beats computing it three times — or when you deliberately want to freeze a result before modifying the underlying table. Use NOT MATERIALIZED to force inlining of a CTE that is referenced more than once but is cheap and would benefit from having the outer WHERE pushed into it.

The practical guidance: write CTEs for readability, and reach for the keywords only when EXPLAIN says you need to.

What to carry forward from this subsection: materialized cte and optimization fence.

9.10 Data-Modifying CTEs

A CTE can be an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE with RETURNING, which makes "move rows from one table to another, atomically" a single statement:

CREATE TABLE archive_orders (order_id bigint, status text);
WITH removed AS (
  DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled' RETURNING order_id, status
)
INSERT INTO archive_orders SELECT order_id, status FROM removed;
SELECT order_id, status FROM archive_orders ORDER BY order_id;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
 order_id |  status   
----------+-----------
        4 | cancelled
(1 row)

One statement, so the delete and the insert cannot be separated by a crash or by another transaction. Three rules govern the semantics and each is a real hazard:

All statements see the same snapshot, which settles the question of CTE visibility of changes: a data-modifying CTE's changes are not visible to the other parts of the same statement. A SELECT alongside a DELETE CTE sees the rows as they were.

Execution order between CTEs is not defined. Two CTEs modifying the same rows have unpredictable interaction; do not write that.

A data-modifying CTE runs even if nothing references it — the reverse of the ordinary rule, and it is how you write "delete these, and return that" in one statement.

The terms above, gathered: cte visibility of changes.

9.11 Recursive CTEs

WITH RECURSIVE is the one construct that lets SQL follow a chain of arbitrary length. It has a fixed shape: a base term, UNION ALL, and a recursive term that references the CTE itself.

WITH RECURSIVE countdown(n) AS (
  SELECT 5
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n - 1 FROM countdown WHERE n > 1
)
SELECT n FROM countdown ORDER BY n DESC;

 n 
---
 5
 4
 3
 2
 1
(5 rows)

The evaluation is iterative rather than truly recursive. PostgreSQL keeps a working table: the base term fills it; the recursive term runs against only what the last iteration produced, and its output becomes the new working table; the process stops when an iteration produces nothing. Everything produced along the way is the result.

That "only the last iteration" detail is why the recursive term cannot use an aggregate, ORDER BY, LIMIT or an outer join on the recursive reference — none of them make sense against a partial working table, and PostgreSQL rejects them.

UNION instead of UNION ALL de-duplicates against everything produced so far, which stops some cycles at the cost of a comparison per row.

9.12 Walking a Hierarchy

The real use is a hierarchical query over a tree — a graph traversal that computes the transitive closure of a parent link.

CREATE TABLE org (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text, manager_id int REFERENCES org);
INSERT INTO org VALUES (1,'ceo',NULL), (2,'vp-eng',1), (3,'vp-ops',1), (4,'lead',2), (5,'dev',4);

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth, name::text AS path
  FROM org WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT o.id, o.name, o.manager_id, c.depth + 1, c.path || ' > ' || o.name
  FROM org o JOIN chain c ON o.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT depth, path FROM chain ORDER BY path;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 5
 depth |           path            
-------+---------------------------
     1 | ceo
     2 | ceo > vp-eng
     3 | ceo > vp-eng > lead
     4 | ceo > vp-eng > lead > dev
     2 | ceo > vp-ops
(5 rows)

Two things carried through the recursion make this useful: depth, incremented each level, which gives you indentation and a depth limit; and path, accumulated as text, which gives you a sortable representation of the tree — ordering by it produces exactly the pre-order traversal shown.

Start from a leaf and follow manager_id upward instead, and the same shape answers "who is this person's whole management chain".

One line each, for reference: transitive closure, graph traversal and hierarchical query.

9.13 Cycles

A cycle in the data makes a naive recursive query run forever. Since PostgreSQL 14 the CYCLE clause does cycle detection for you:

CREATE TABLE cyc (a int, b int);
INSERT INTO cyc VALUES (1,2), (2,3), (3,1);

WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT a, b FROM cyc WHERE a = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.a, c.b FROM cyc c JOIN walk w ON c.a = w.b
) CYCLE a SET is_cycle USING trail
SELECT a, b, is_cycle FROM walk ORDER BY a, b, is_cycle;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 a | b | is_cycle 
---+---+----------
 1 | 2 | f
 1 | 2 | t
 2 | 3 | f
 3 | 1 | f
(4 rows)

CYCLE a SET is_cycle USING trail says: track column a, set is_cycle to true when a value repeats, and keep the visited list in trail. The row that closes the cycle is returned with is_cycle = true and the recursion stops there rather than looping.

Before 14 you did it by hand — carry an array of visited keys, append to it each level, and stop when the next key is already in it. That still works and is worth knowing, because it lets you decide what counts as a repeat.

The SEARCH clause is the companion: SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord or SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY id SET ord adds a column you can ORDER BY to get the traversal order you want, without the string-path trick of §9.12.

Always bound a recursive query in production. A depth < 50 condition in the recursive term costs nothing and turns a runaway query into a wrong answer you will notice, which is strictly better than a session that never returns.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: cycle detection, search breadth first and search depth first.

9.14 Choosing Between Them

Four ways to say "customers who have an order", and they are not equivalent:

EXISTS
Semi-join. Stops at the first match, never multiplies rows, null-safe. The default choice.
IN (subquery)
Usually planned identically to EXISTS. Reads well for a short list of values; its negation is the trap of §9.6.
JOIN
Multiplies rows when the right side has several matches — so it needs DISTINCT, which then costs a sort. Correct when you actually want columns from the other table.
Correlated scalar
Readable for one derived value per row, and one lookup per row if the planner cannot flatten it (§13.6).

The rule that covers most cases: if you need columns from the other table, join; if you only need to know whether a row exists, use EXISTS. Using a join for the second gives you a DISTINCT you did not need and a row multiplication you might not notice.

What This Section Established

A subquery is legal in the select list (scalar), in FROM (derived table, LATERAL to correlate), in WHERE/HAVING, and in WITH.

An uncorrelated scalar subquery runs once. Returning more than one row is a runtime error, so a scalar subquery that is not provably single-row needs ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 or a restructure.

A correlated subquery is one lookup per outer row, and §13.6's per-loop reporting hides the total. LATERAL returns several columns in one pass where several scalar subqueries are several passes.

EXISTS is a semi-join: first match wins, no row multiplication, null-safe. NOT EXISTS is the anti-join and is the safe way to say it.

NOT IN with a single NULL in the list returns no rows at all — measured, 3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) matched nothing. Use NOT EXISTS.

ANY/ALL generalise IN to any operator. ALL over an empty set is true. A row IS NULL only if every field is null and IS NOT NULL only if none is, so (1, NULL) is neither.

WITH turns nesting into sequence. Since PostgreSQL 12 a single-use CTE is inlined, so the pre-12 "CTEs are an optimisation fence" advice is obsolete; MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED control it explicitly.

A data-modifying CTE moves rows atomically in one statement. All parts see the same snapshot, order between CTEs is undefined, and a data-modifying CTE runs whether or not anything references it.

WITH RECURSIVE is base term, UNION ALL, recursive term. The recursive term sees only the previous iteration's output, which is why it cannot aggregate, sort or limit. Carry depth and path to get a limit and a sortable traversal.

The CYCLE clause detects repeats and stops; SEARCH gives a depth-first or breadth-first ordering column. Bound the depth in production regardless.

Join when you need the other table's columns; EXISTS when you only need to know it is there.

Exercises

1. Make a scalar subquery fail. Write one that works today and breaks when a second row is added. Then fix it three ways — LIMIT 1 with an explicit ORDER BY, an aggregate, and a LATERAL join — and say which you would ship.

2. Reproduce the NOT IN trap. Build a parent and child table where the child's foreign key is nullable, insert one null, and show NOT IN returning nothing. Then show NOT EXISTS returning the right answer and compare the two plans.

3. Count the lookups. Write "each customer with their order count and latest order date" as two correlated scalar subqueries, as a LEFT JOIN with GROUP BY, and as one LATERAL. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) all three and report the loops on the inner nodes.

4. Test the fence. Write a query with a CTE referenced once, and compare its plan against the same logic as a derived table. Then add MATERIALIZED and compare again. State what the keyword changed and when you would want it.

5. Move rows atomically. Write a single statement that deletes rows from one table and inserts them into another. Then prove that the SELECT half of a similar statement does not see the deletion, and explain why in terms of snapshots.

6. Walk a tree both ways. With a self-referencing table, write one recursive query that lists everyone under a given manager with their depth, and another that lists a given person's whole chain of managers upward. Add a depth bound to both.

7. Survive a cycle. Introduce a cycle into your hierarchy. Show a naive recursive query failing to terminate — bound it so you can observe it — then fix it with the CYCLE clause and again with a manually carried array. Say what the manual version can do that CYCLE cannot.

Solution

1. Breaking a scalar subquery.

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT full_name, (SELECT status FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS status
FROM customers c ORDER BY full_name;

ERROR:  more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression

It would have worked while every customer had at most one order. The three fixes:

LIMIT 1 with ORDER BY placed_on DESC — correct and documents which one you meant. LIMIT 1 without an ORDER BY is the version to avoid: it works, and it picks arbitrarily.

An aggregate — max(o.status) — is honest only when the aggregate is the answer you want, which for a status it is not.

LATERAL is what to ship when you need more than one column from that row, because the other two need one subquery per column and LATERAL needs one for all of them.

2. The NOT IN trap.

CREATE TABLE nn_parent (id int PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE nn_child (id int PRIMARY KEY, parent_id int);
INSERT INTO nn_parent VALUES (1), (2), (3);
INSERT INTO nn_child VALUES (10, 1), (11, NULL);
SELECT count(*) AS with_not_in     FROM nn_parent WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT parent_id FROM nn_child);
SELECT count(*) AS with_not_exists FROM nn_parent p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM nn_child c WHERE c.parent_id = p.id);

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
INSERT 0 2
 with_not_in 
-------------
           0
(1 row)

 with_not_exists 
-----------------
               2
(1 row)

Zero against two. Parents 2 and 3 have no children and NOT IN found neither, because the NULL in nn_child.parent_id makes every comparison unknown.

The plans differ as well: NOT EXISTS becomes an anti-join, while NOT IN over a nullable column cannot — the planner must keep the null semantics, which blocks the anti-join transformation entirely. So the null-safe form is also the faster one, and there is no case for NOT IN over a nullable column.

3. Counting the lookups.

The two-scalar-subquery version shows two SubPlan nodes, each with loops equal to the customer count — two lookups per row.

The LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY version shows one join and one aggregate: one pass over each table.

The LATERAL version shows one nested loop with loops equal to the customer count, but one inner scan producing both columns.

So the ranking by lookups is join < lateral < scalar subqueries. The ranking by speed depends on the data: with few customers and an index on orders(customer_id), the lateral version wins because it never touches most of orders; with many customers it loses to the hash join, exactly as §6.13's exercise found.

4. Testing the fence.

Single-use CTE and derived table produce identical plans on PostgreSQL 12 and later — the CTE is inlined and does not appear as a separate node.

MATERIALIZED reintroduces a CTE Scan node over a materialised result, and the outer WHERE is no longer pushed inside. That is a loss when the outer filter is selective, and a win when the CTE is expensive and used more than once, because the alternative is computing it twice.

The case for MATERIALIZED that has nothing to do with performance: freezing a result before the same statement modifies the underlying rows, so that the CTE and the modification cannot interact.

5. Moving rows atomically.

§9.10 has the working statement. The snapshot proof:

CREATE TABLE snap_demo (id int);
INSERT INTO snap_demo VALUES (1), (2), (3);
WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM snap_demo WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM snap_demo) AS visible_to_select,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM gone)      AS deleted_by_cte;
SELECT count(*) AS after_statement FROM snap_demo;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 visible_to_select | deleted_by_cte 
-------------------+----------------
                 3 |              1
(1 row)

 after_statement 
-----------------
               2
(1 row)

The SELECT inside the same statement saw 3, the delete removed one, and afterwards there are 2. Every part of a statement reads from the snapshot taken at the start of that statement, so the SELECT cannot see a change the same statement is making. This is the same rule as §14.10's — one snapshot per statement — applied within a statement rather than across two.

6. Walking a tree both ways.

Downward is §9.12 with a WHERE id = <root> base term and AND c.depth < 20 in the recursive term.

Upward inverts the join condition:

WITH RECURSIVE up AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth FROM org WHERE name = 'dev'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT o.id, o.name, o.manager_id, u.depth + 1
  FROM org o JOIN up u ON o.id = u.manager_id
  WHERE u.depth < 20
)
SELECT depth, name FROM up ORDER BY depth;

 depth | name   
-------+--------
     1 | dev
     2 | lead
     3 | vp-eng
     4 | ceo
(4 rows)

The only change is which side of the join carries the recursive reference: o.manager_id = c.id walks down, o.id = u.manager_id walks up.

7. Surviving a cycle.

The naive version never terminates, and bounding it with depth < 10 is what lets you see that it is producing the same rows repeatedly rather than making progress.

The CYCLE clause version is §9.13. The manual version carries an array:

WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT a, b, ARRAY[a] AS visited, false AS looped FROM cyc WHERE a = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.a, c.b, w.visited || c.a, c.a = ANY(w.visited)
  FROM cyc c JOIN walk w ON c.a = w.b
  WHERE NOT w.looped AND array_length(w.visited, 1) < 20
)
SELECT a, b, visited, looped FROM walk ORDER BY array_length(visited, 1);

 a | b |  visited  | looped 
---+---+-----------+--------
 1 | 2 | {1}       | f
 2 | 3 | {1,2}     | f
 3 | 1 | {1,2,3}   | f
 1 | 2 | {1,2,3,1} | t
(4 rows)

Same result. What the manual version can do that CYCLE cannot: choose what counts as a repeat. CYCLE tracks equality on the columns you name. The manual array can hold a derived value — a normalised key, a pair, a hash — so you can say "a cycle is returning to the same node in the same state", which is what you need when the same node may legitimately be visited twice by different paths.

SECTION 10

Window Functions

A window function computes a value across a set of rows related to the current row, and — this is the whole point — returns one result per input row rather than collapsing them. GROUP BY gives you one row per group; a window function gives you every row, with the group's answer attached.

That single difference makes a large class of queries expressible that otherwise need a self-join or a correlated subquery: running totals, ranks, "each row's share of its group's total", "the gap since the previous row", "the top three per category". If you have ever written a query that joins a table to an aggregate of itself, this section replaces it.

Everything below runs against one small table, deliberately small enough that you can check every number by hand.

CREATE TABLE sales (region text, seller text, month int, amount int);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES
 ('north','ada',1,100),('north','ada',2,120),('north','ada',3, 90),
 ('north','lin',1,200),('north','lin',2, 80),('north','lin',3,300),
 ('south','kai',1,150),('south','kai',2,150),('south','kai',3, 50),
 ('south','mo', 1, 60),('south','mo', 2,240),('south','mo', 3,180);

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 12

10.1 OVER: The Aggregate That Does Not Collapse

sum(amount) is an aggregate. sum(amount) OVER (...) is a window function. Same function, different call, completely different result shape.

SELECT region, seller, amount,
       sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS region_total,
       round(100.0 * amount / sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region), 1) AS pct
FROM sales WHERE month = 1
ORDER BY region, seller;

 region | seller | amount | region_total | pct  
--------+--------+--------+--------------+------
 north  | ada    |    100 |          300 | 33.3
 north  | lin    |    200 |          300 | 66.7
 south  | kai    |    150 |          210 | 71.4
 south  | mo     |     60 |          210 | 28.6
(4 rows)

Four input rows, four output rows, each carrying its region's total and its own share of it. With GROUP BY region you would have two rows and no way to see ada and lin separately.

OVER () — empty parentheses — means the whole result set is one window. Adding PARTITION BY divides it into independent groups, and the function restarts in each. There is no GROUP BY anywhere in that query, and there does not need to be: window functions do not group, they annotate.

10.2 The Three Parts of a Window Definition

Everything inside OVER (...) is one of three clauses, and they are always in this order.

PARTITION BY
Divides rows into groups. The function is computed independently in each, and never sees across the boundary. Omit it and there is one partition containing everything.
ORDER BY
Orders rows within the partition. Required by rank(), lag() and anything else whose answer depends on sequence. Adding it also changes the default frame, which is §10.4 and the source of the most common bug in this section.
frame clause
ROWS, RANGE or GROUPS — which subset of the ordered partition this row's computation actually covers. Almost always omitted, which is why its default matters so much.

The window ORDER BY is not the query's ORDER BY. They are independent: one decides what the function computes, the other decides how the result is printed. A query can have both, with different keys, and often should.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: window order by.

10.3 The Ranking Functions

Six functions answer "where does this row sit in the order?", and the differences between the first three show up only when there are ties.

SELECT seller, month, amount,
       row_number()   OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, month) AS rn,
       rank()         OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)        AS rnk,
       dense_rank()   OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)        AS drnk,
       round(percent_rank() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)::numeric, 2) AS prnk,
       round(cume_dist()    OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC)::numeric, 2) AS cd
FROM sales WHERE region = 'south'
ORDER BY amount DESC, month;

 seller | month | amount | rn | rnk | drnk | prnk |  cd  
--------+-------+--------+----+-----+------+------+------
 mo     |     2 |    240 |  1 |   1 |    1 | 0.00 | 0.17
 mo     |     3 |    180 |  2 |   2 |    2 | 0.20 | 0.33
 kai    |     1 |    150 |  3 |   3 |    3 | 0.40 | 0.67
 kai    |     2 |    150 |  4 |   3 |    3 | 0.40 | 0.67
 mo     |     1 |     60 |  5 |   5 |    4 | 0.80 | 0.83
 kai    |     3 |     50 |  6 |   6 |    5 | 1.00 | 1.00
(6 rows)

The two 150s are peers — a peer row is one the window's ORDER BY cannot distinguish from another — and the three functions treat them differently.

row_number()
3 and 4. Always a distinct integer per row, so it must break the tie somehow — and if the ordering does not determine which, the choice is arbitrary and may differ between runs. That is why the window above orders by amount DESC, month: to make the result reproducible.
rank()
3 and 3, then the next row is 5. Peers share a rank and the following rank skips — "joint third, then fifth", as a race result is written.
dense_rank()
3 and 3, then 4. No gaps. Counts distinct values rather than rows.
percent_rank()
(rank - 1) / (total - 1). Always starts at 0 and ends at 1.
cume_dist()
The fraction of rows at or before this one, peers included. Never 0; always ends at 1.
ntile(n)
Divides the partition into n buckets as evenly as it can, earlier buckets taking the remainder. Order-sensitive in the same way row_number() is.

row_number() with an ambiguous order is a latent bug. It will look right in testing, because a small table comes back in physical order every time. Always give the window enough columns to make the order total.

To have in hand before moving on: peer row, dense_rank(, percent_rank(, cume_dist( and ntile(.

10.4 The Frame, and the Running-Total Trap

This is the subsection to read twice.

Without a frame clause, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — and RANGE treats all peers of the current row as part of the frame. So a "running total" over a column with duplicate values does not run one row at a time.

SELECT seller, month, amount,
       sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)                        AS default_frame,
       sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_frame
FROM sales WHERE region = 'north'
ORDER BY month, seller;

 seller | month | amount | default_frame | rows_frame 
--------+-------+--------+---------------+------------
 ada    |     1 |    100 |           300 |        100
 lin    |     1 |    200 |           300 |        300
 ada    |     2 |    120 |           500 |        420
 lin    |     2 |     80 |           500 |        500
 ada    |     3 |     90 |           890 |        590
 lin    |     3 |    300 |           890 |        890
(6 rows)

The first row's "running total" is 300, not 100. Both month-1 rows are peers under ORDER BY month, so both frames already include both rows. The column headed rows_frame is what people mean by a running total: 100, 300, 420, 500, 590, 890.

The rule is short: if the window's ORDER BY is not unique, RANGE and ROWS give different answers, and you almost certainly want ROWS. Either write ROWS explicitly, or order by something unique.

The frame clause takes three unit types and two bounds:

ROWS
Counts physical rows. 1 PRECEDING means one row back, peers or not. Predictable, and what you want for moving windows.
RANGE
Counts by value of the ordering column. Peers move together. With a numeric or interval offset — RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — it becomes genuinely useful: a true time window regardless of how many rows fall in it.
GROUPS
Counts peer groups. 1 PRECEDING means the whole preceding group of equal values, however many rows that is.

Bounds are UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, n PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW, n FOLLOWING, UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, and the start must not be after the end. Frame exclusion — EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW, EXCLUDE GROUP, EXCLUDE TIES and EXCLUDE NO OTHERS — removes rows from a frame that would otherwise contain them:

SELECT month, amount,
       count(*) OVER (ORDER BY month GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) AS grp_frame,
       count(*) OVER (ORDER BY month GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING
                      EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW) AS excl_current,
       count(*) OVER (ORDER BY month RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
                      EXCLUDE TIES) AS excl_ties
FROM sales ORDER BY month, amount;

 month | amount | grp_frame | excl_current | excl_ties 
-------+--------+-----------+--------------+-----------
     1 |     60 |         8 |            7 |         1
     1 |    100 |         8 |            7 |         1
     1 |    150 |         8 |            7 |         1
     1 |    200 |         8 |            7 |         1
     2 |     80 |        12 |           11 |         5
     2 |    120 |        12 |           11 |         5
     2 |    150 |        12 |           11 |         5
     2 |    240 |        12 |           11 |         5
     3 |     50 |         8 |            7 |         9
     3 |     90 |         8 |            7 |         9
     3 |    180 |         8 |            7 |         9
     3 |    300 |         8 |            7 |         9
(12 rows)

GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING on month 2 covers all three months — twelve rows — because each month is one peer group of four. EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW drops exactly the one row. EXCLUDE TIES keeps the current row but drops its peers, which is why month 3's cumulative count is 9 rather than 12.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: frame exclusion.

10.5 Running Totals and Moving Averages

With ROWS, the two most common shapes are one line each.

SELECT seller, month, amount,
       sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running,
       round(avg(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month
                         ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING), 1) AS moving3,
       lag(amount)  OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month) AS prev,
       lead(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month) AS next
FROM sales WHERE region = 'north'
ORDER BY seller, month;

 seller | month | amount | running | moving3 | prev | next 
--------+-------+--------+---------+---------+------+------
 ada    |     1 |    100 |     100 |   110.0 |      |  120
 ada    |     2 |    120 |     220 |   103.3 |  100 |   90
 ada    |     3 |     90 |     310 |   105.0 |  120 |     
 lin    |     1 |    200 |     200 |   140.0 |      |   80
 lin    |     2 |     80 |     280 |   193.3 |  200 |  300
 lin    |     3 |    300 |     580 |   190.0 |   80 |     
(6 rows)

Both counters restart at lin, because PARTITION BY seller makes them independent.

lag() and lead() are NULL at the partition edges, which is correct and is a thing your calling code must handle. Both take optional second and third arguments — lag(amount, 2, 0) looks two rows back and substitutes 0 rather than NULL. Note the moving average at the edges is over two rows, not three, because the frame is clipped at the partition boundary; avg divides by what is actually in the frame.

The difference from the previous row is the idiom worth memorising: amount - lag(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month).

In summary, the vocabulary here is lead( and partition bound.

10.6 first_value, last_value and the Frame Again

SELECT seller, month, amount,
       first_value(amount) OVER w AS first_v,
       last_value(amount)  OVER w AS last_v_default,
       last_value(amount)  OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month
                                 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
                                                     AS last_v_full,
       nth_value(amount, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month
                                 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
                                                     AS second_v
FROM sales WHERE region = 'north'
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month)
ORDER BY seller, month;

 seller | month | amount | first_v | last_v_default | last_v_full | second_v 
--------+-------+--------+---------+----------------+-------------+----------
 ada    |     1 |    100 |     100 |            100 |          90 |      120
 ada    |     2 |    120 |     100 |            120 |          90 |      120
 ada    |     3 |     90 |     100 |             90 |          90 |      120
 lin    |     1 |    200 |     200 |            200 |         300 |       80
 lin    |     2 |     80 |     200 |             80 |         300 |       80
 lin    |     3 |    300 |     200 |            300 |         300 |       80
(6 rows)

last_value with the default frame returns the current row. Look at last_v_default: 100, 120, 90 — it is just amount again. This is the single most reported "bug" in window functions and it is not one: the default frame ends at CURRENT ROW, so the last row of the frame is the current row.

The fix is ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, shown as last_v_full — and nth_value( needs the same frame for the same reason. first_value( needs no such care because the default frame already starts at the partition's beginning — which is exactly why the asymmetry surprises people.

This block also introduces the WINDOW clause: define a window once, name it, and reference it with OVER w. When three columns share a definition, this is the difference between a readable query and a wall of repetition. A named window can also be extended: OVER (w ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING).

What to carry forward from this subsection: window clause and named window.

10.7 Where Window Functions Happen

The window function processing order puts them after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, and before ORDER BY, DISTINCT and LIMIT. Two consequences follow, and both are constantly hit.

You cannot filter on a window function in WHERE.

SELECT seller, amount, rank() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS r
FROM sales WHERE rank() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) <= 3;

ERROR:  window functions are not allowed in WHERE
LINE 2: FROM sales WHERE rank() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) <= 3;
                         ^

The WHERE clause runs first, so the rank does not exist yet. Wrap the query in a subquery or a CTE and filter outside — which is exactly the top-N pattern in §10.8.

A window function sees post-aggregation rows. So you can put an aggregate inside a window function, and the double nesting is legal and useful:

SELECT region, sum(amount) AS region_total,
       round(100.0 * sum(amount) / sum(sum(amount)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_all
FROM sales GROUP BY region ORDER BY region;

 region | region_total | pct_of_all 
--------+--------------+------------
 north  |          890 |       51.7
 south  |          830 |       48.3
(2 rows)

sum(sum(amount)) OVER () reads as "the total of the group totals". The inner sum is the aggregate that produced the grouped rows; the outer one is a window over those rows. There is no third pass and no subquery.

FILTER (§7.7) works inside a window aggregate too:

SELECT seller, month, amount,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE amount > 100) OVER (PARTITION BY seller) AS big_months
FROM sales WHERE region = 'north' ORDER BY seller, month;

 seller | month | amount | big_months 
--------+-------+--------+------------
 ada    |     1 |    100 |          1
 ada    |     2 |    120 |          1
 ada    |     3 |     90 |          1
 lin    |     1 |    200 |          2
 lin    |     2 |     80 |          2
 lin    |     3 |    300 |          2
(6 rows)

The terms above, gathered: rank() OVER and window function processing order.

10.8 Top-N Per Group

The query everybody needs and nobody writes correctly the first time: the two best months per region.

SELECT region, seller, month, amount FROM (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC, month) AS rn
  FROM sales
) t
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY region, amount DESC, month;

 region | seller | month | amount 
--------+--------+-------+--------
 north  | lin    |     3 |    300
 north  | lin    |     1 |    200
 south  | mo     |     2 |    240
 south  | mo     |     3 |    180
(4 rows)

The subquery exists only because of §10.7 — the filter cannot go in WHERE. Three details decide whether this is right:

row_number versus rank. row_number gives exactly N rows per group; rank gives at least N, including everything tied at the boundary. Pick deliberately: "the top 2" and "everyone tied for the top 2" are different requirements.

The tiebreak in the window's ORDER BY. amount DESC, month rather than amount DESC, so that two equal amounts produce a defined answer.

It scales badly at large N over large tables, because it ranks every row before discarding most of them. When the group count is small and the table is large, a LATERAL join (§6.11) that fetches the top few per group through an index is far cheaper — and §13 is how you tell which you have.

10.9 Deduplication

Deduplication with row_number is the same shape with rn = 1: keep the newest row per key.

CREATE TABLE dupes (email text, created date, note text);
INSERT INTO dupes VALUES ('a@x','2026-01-01','first'), ('a@x','2026-01-03','latest'),
                         ('b@x','2026-01-02','only');

SELECT email, created, note FROM (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created DESC) AS rn FROM dupes
) t
WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY email;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 email |  created   |  note  
-------+------------+--------
 a@x   | 2026-01-03 | latest
 b@x   | 2026-01-02 | only
(2 rows)

To actually delete the duplicates rather than hide them, the same subquery drives a DELETE:

DELETE FROM dupes WHERE ctid IN (
  SELECT ctid FROM (
    SELECT ctid, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created DESC) AS rn
    FROM dupes) t
  WHERE rn > 1);
SELECT count(*) AS rows_left FROM dupes;

DELETE 1
 rows_left 
-----------
         2
(1 row)

ctid (§14.7) is used here because the table has no primary key — which is exactly the situation that produced the duplicates. It is safe within one statement and is not something to store; if the table has a key, use it.

Compare DISTINCT ON (§6.11), which does the same job in one clause when you want the whole row and PostgreSQL is your only target. row_number() is the portable form and the one that generalises to rn <= 3.

One line each, for reference: deduplication with row_number.

10.10 Gaps and Islands

A classic that looks impossible until you see the trick: collapse consecutive runs of equal values into one row each.

CREATE TABLE readings (id int, day date, ok boolean);
INSERT INTO readings VALUES
 (1,'2026-01-01',true),(2,'2026-01-02',true),(3,'2026-01-03',false),
 (4,'2026-01-04',true),(5,'2026-01-05',true),(6,'2026-01-06',true),
 (7,'2026-01-07',false),(8,'2026-01-08',true);

SELECT ok, min(day) AS island_start, max(day) AS island_end, count(*) AS days
FROM (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)
               - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ok ORDER BY day) AS grp
      FROM readings) t
GROUP BY ok, grp
ORDER BY island_start;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 8
 ok | island_start | island_end | days 
----+--------------+------------+------
 t  | 2026-01-01   | 2026-01-02 |    2
 f  | 2026-01-03   | 2026-01-03 |    1
 t  | 2026-01-04   | 2026-01-06 |    3
 f  | 2026-01-07   | 2026-01-07 |    1
 t  | 2026-01-08   | 2026-01-08 |    1
(5 rows)

The trick is the difference of two row numbers. One counts rows in overall order; the other counts rows within each value's own sequence. While a run continues, both increase by one, so their difference is constant — and the moment the value changes, the difference jumps. That constant is a group id you can GROUP BY, and it was computed by nothing but two window functions.

This shape solves a whole family of problems: consecutive days of a streak, uninterrupted periods of downtime, contiguous ranges of ids, sessionising an event log by a gap threshold (use lag() to detect gaps larger than the threshold, then a running sum() over the resulting flags to number the sessions).

10.11 Performance

A window function needs its partition sorted, so the plan usually contains a WindowAgg over a Sort — and if an index already provides that order, the sort disappears. (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC) is served by an index on (region, amount DESC).

Three practical notes:

Reuse the window definition. Two functions with identical OVER clauses share one WindowAgg node and one sort. Two functions with different clauses need two sorts. The WINDOW clause makes sharing visible and is the reason to use it beyond brevity.

Order the windows compatibly. (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) and (PARTITION BY a, b ORDER BY c) can share a sort; unrelated orderings cannot.

A window function is usually cheaper than the self-join it replaces. The join reads the table twice; the window reads it once and sorts. On large tables the difference is substantial, and it is the main practical argument for learning this section.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: over clause.

What This Section Established

A window function returns one row per input row, with a value computed across related rows. GROUP BY collapses; OVER annotates.

OVER () is the whole result. PARTITION BY splits it. The window's ORDER BY is independent of the query's.

Ranking: row_number() always distinct — arbitrary among peers unless the order is total; rank() shares and skips (3, 3, 5); dense_rank() shares without skipping (3, 3, 4); percent_rank(), cume_dist(), ntile().

The default frame is RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, which includes peers. Measured: a "running total" over a non-unique ORDER BY reported 300 on its first row instead of 100. Write ROWS unless you specifically want value-based framing.

ROWS counts rows, RANGE counts by value (and takes offsets, including intervals), GROUPS counts peer groups. EXCLUDE removes the current row, its group, or its ties.

last_value with the default frame is the current row — measured as 100, 120, 90, which is just the column back again. Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

lag() and lead() are NULL at partition edges and take default arguments. Frames clip at partition boundaries, so edge averages divide by fewer rows.

Window functions run after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and before ORDER BY/LIMIT. So WHERE rank() OVER ... <= 3 is an error, and you wrap in a subquery — which is the top-N pattern. And sum(sum(x)) OVER () is legal: a window over aggregated rows.

row_number() = 1 deduplicates; <= N gives top-N per group; the difference of two row_number()s is a group id for consecutive runs.

Reusing one WINDOW definition means one sort; an index matching (partition, order) removes it altogether.

Exercises

1. Break a running total. Build a table with duplicate values in the ordering column, compute a running total with no frame clause, and show that it jumps by the whole peer group. Fix it two ways — with ROWS, and by making the order unique — and say which you would prefer in a report and why.

2. Rank three ways. On data with ties, produce row_number, rank and dense_rank side by side. Then answer two different business questions with them: "who are the top three sellers" and "what are the top three sales figures". State which function each needs.

3. Retrieve the partition's last row. Show last_value returning the current row with the default frame. Fix it with an explicit frame. Then get the same answer without a frame clause, using first_value and a reversed order, and say which you find more readable.

4. Compare to the alternative. Write "each row's share of its group total" twice — once with a window function, once with a GROUP BY subquery joined back. Compare the plans with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE), and report how many times each reads the table.

5. Sessionise an event log. Given events with timestamps and a user id, group each user's events into sessions where a gap of more than 30 minutes starts a new one. Number the sessions per user and report each one's start, end and event count.

6. Filter on a rank. Show the error from putting a window function in WHERE. Then get the result three ways: a subquery, a CTE, and a LATERAL join. Compare the plans and say when each is the right choice.

Solution

1. Breaking a running total.

§10.4 is the measured version: 300 where 100 was wanted, because both month-1 rows are peers under ORDER BY month.

Both fixes give the same numbers. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING is the one to prefer in a report, because it states the intent locally — anyone reading the query sees "row by row" without having to check whether the ordering column happens to be unique. Making the order unique fixes this query and leaves the next person to rediscover the hazard.

2. Ranking three ways.

"Top three sellers" means three rows, so row_number() with a documented tiebreak — someone has to be third, and the query should decide rather than the storage layer.

"Top three sales figures" means three distinct values, so dense_rank() <= 3, which returns however many rows share those three figures.

rank() answers a third question, the one a sports table asks: joint third, and nobody is fourth. It is rarely what a business question means, which is why it is the one most often chosen by mistake.

3. The partition's last row.

§10.6 measures both. The third way:

SELECT seller, month, amount,
       first_value(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY seller ORDER BY month DESC) AS last_in_partition
FROM sales WHERE region = 'north' ORDER BY seller, month;

 seller | month | amount | last_in_partition 
--------+-------+--------+-------------------
 ada    |     1 |    100 |                90
 ada    |     2 |    120 |                90
 ada    |     3 |     90 |                90
 lin    |     1 |    200 |               300
 lin    |     2 |     80 |               300
 lin    |     3 |    300 |               300
(6 rows)

Reversing the order and taking first_value works because the default frame starts at the partition boundary, which is the well-behaved end. Which is more readable is a genuine judgement call: the explicit frame says what it does, while the reversed order is shorter and needs a comment. The explicit frame is safer, because the reversed-order trick silently breaks if someone later adds a frame clause.

4. Window against self-join.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
SELECT region, seller, amount, sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) FROM sales;

SET
                          QUERY PLAN                           
---------------------------------------------------------------
 WindowAgg (actual rows=12.00 loops=1)
   Window: w1 AS (PARTITION BY region)
   ->  Sort (actual rows=12.00 loops=1)
         Sort Key: region
         Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 25kB
         ->  Seq Scan on sales (actual rows=12.00 loops=1)
(6 rows)

One Seq Scan. The join version contains two, one for the detail rows and one under the aggregate, plus a join node. On twelve rows the difference is noise; on ten million it is a second scan of the whole table, and that is the argument.

5. Sessionising.

CREATE TABLE session_events (user_id int, at timestamptz);
INSERT INTO session_events VALUES
 (1,'2026-01-01 10:00+00'),(1,'2026-01-01 10:05+00'),(1,'2026-01-01 11:30+00'),
 (2,'2026-01-01 10:00+00'),(2,'2026-01-01 10:20+00');

SELECT user_id, session_no, min(at) AS started, max(at) AS ended, count(*) AS events
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, at,
         sum(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY at) AS session_no
  FROM (
    SELECT user_id, at,
           CASE WHEN at - lag(at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY at)
                     > interval '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
    FROM session_events) a) b
GROUP BY user_id, session_no
ORDER BY user_id, session_no;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 5
 user_id | session_no |        started         |         ended          | events 
---------+------------+------------------------+------------------------+--------
       1 |          0 | 2026-01-01 10:00:00+00 | 2026-01-01 10:05:00+00 |      2
       1 |          1 | 2026-01-01 11:30:00+00 | 2026-01-01 11:30:00+00 |      1
       2 |          0 | 2026-01-01 10:00:00+00 | 2026-01-01 10:20:00+00 |      2
(3 rows)

Three window passes: lag finds the gap, a CASE turns "gap too big" into a 1, and a running sum of those flags numbers the sessions. The first row of each partition has a NULL lag, so its CASE yields 0 and every user's first session is numbered 0 — which is correct and worth noticing rather than patching.

This is §10.10's idea in a different costume: a running aggregate over a change-flag turns "consecutive things" into a group key.

6. Filtering on a rank.

The error is in §10.7. The subquery form is §10.8. The CTE form is identical in plan — PostgreSQL does not materialise a CTE unless told to (§9.11) — and is more readable when there are several stages.

The LATERAL form is different in kind:

SELECT r.region, t.seller, t.amount
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT region FROM sales) r
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT seller, amount FROM sales s
                    WHERE s.region = r.region ORDER BY amount DESC, month LIMIT 2) t
ORDER BY r.region, t.amount DESC;

 region | seller | amount 
--------+--------+--------
 north  | lin    |    300
 north  | lin    |    200
 south  | mo     |    240
 south  | mo     |    180
(4 rows)

Choose by shape. The window version sorts the whole table once and is the right choice when the groups are many or N is large relative to the group. The LATERAL version does one small indexed lookup per group and wins decisively when there are few groups and a large table — the classic "latest row per customer over ten million orders", where the window form sorts ten million rows to keep a few thousand.

SECTION 11

Modifying Data

Four statements write rows — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE — plus COPY for bulk and TRUNCATE for emptying. This section is about all of them, about RETURNING, which turns a write into a query, and about ON CONFLICT, which is how you write a row that may already exist without a race.

The recurring theme is concurrency. Almost every writing statement has a naive form that works alone and is wrong under load, and a correct form that is barely longer. §14 and §15 explained why; this section is where the shapes live.

CREATE TABLE inv (
  sku        text PRIMARY KEY,
  qty        integer NOT NULL,
  updated_at date    NOT NULL DEFAULT '2026-01-01'
);

CREATE TABLE

11.1 INSERT

INSERT INTO inv (sku, qty) VALUES ('A', 5), ('B', 3)
RETURNING sku, qty, updated_at;

 sku | qty | updated_at 
-----+-----+------------
 A   |   5 | 2026-01-01
 B   |   3 | 2026-01-01
(2 rows)

INSERT 0 2

An INSERT statement should always name its columns. INSERT INTO inv VALUES ('A', 5, ...) depends on column order, which means an ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN in the middle of the table silently changes what your statement means. The column list is two seconds of typing and removes a whole class of failure.

Columns you omit get their DEFAULT, or NULL if there is none. DEFAULT VALUES inserts a row that is entirely defaults, and the keyword DEFAULT may appear in a VALUES list for one column.

A multi-row VALUES is one statement, and that matters: one round trip, one WAL flush, one set of constraint checks. Inserting a thousand rows in a thousand statements is roughly an order of magnitude slower than one statement with a thousand rows — and both are slower than COPY (§11.10).

INSERT SELECT — INSERT INTO ... SELECT — is the other source, and it is how you populate one table from another without the data leaving the server.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: insert statement, insert select and multi-row values.

11.2 RETURNING

RETURNING makes a write return rows, in the same round trip:

INSERT INTO inv (sku, qty) VALUES ('D', 1) RETURNING sku, qty, updated_at;

 sku | qty | updated_at 
-----+-----+------------
 D   |   1 | 2026-01-01
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1

This is how you get a generated key, a computed default, or a trigger's modification (§18.18) without a second query — and unlike a second query it cannot race, because it reports what this statement did.

It works on all four writing statements, takes any expression, and feeds a data-modifying CTE (§9.10).

PostgreSQL 18 added OLD and NEW qualifiers, so one UPDATE can report both sides of the change:

UPDATE inv SET qty = 0 WHERE sku = 'B'
RETURNING sku, old.qty AS was, new.qty AS now;

 sku | was | now 
-----+-----+-----
 B   |   3 |   0
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

Before 18 the unqualified names meant the new row and the old values were simply unavailable — you fetched them first, in a separate statement, with a race in between. RETURNING old.*, new.* now writes an audit record in one statement.

To have in hand before moving on: returning old.

11.3 ON CONFLICT: Upsert Without a Race

"Insert this row, or update it if it exists" written as SELECT then branch is a race: two sessions can both find nothing and both insert. ON CONFLICT makes the database arbitrate.

INSERT INTO inv (sku, qty) VALUES ('A', 10)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = inv.qty + EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = '2026-02-01'
RETURNING sku, qty, updated_at;

 sku | qty | updated_at 
-----+-----+------------
 A   |  15 | 2026-02-01
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1

Three pieces of vocabulary, all of them load-bearing.

conflict target
(sku) — which uniqueness violation you are handling. It must correspond to a unique index, called the arbiter index. A violation of any other constraint still raises an error, which is what you want.
the EXCLUDED pseudo-table
The row that would have been inserted. inv.qty is the existing value, EXCLUDED.qty the proposed one, so inv.qty + EXCLUDED.qty accumulates.
the tag says INSERT
INSERT 0 1 even though a row was updated. The command tag does not distinguish, so an application that needs to know which happened must use RETURNING and compare — or a MERGE (§11.9), which does report it.

DO NOTHING is the other action, and it skips silently:

INSERT INTO inv (sku, qty) VALUES ('A', 99) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING sku;
SELECT sku, qty FROM inv ORDER BY sku;

 sku 
-----
(0 rows)

INSERT 0 0
 sku | qty 
-----+-----
 A   |  15
 B   |   0
 D   |   1
(3 rows)

RETURNING returned nothing, because DO NOTHING produced no row — which is how you distinguish "inserted" from "skipped". Note that DO NOTHING without a conflict target ignores every uniqueness violation, including ones you did not anticipate; naming the target is safer.

Two limits worth knowing. ON CONFLICT cannot handle a conflict against a row inserted by the same statement — VALUES ('A',1),('A',2) with ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE raises "cannot affect row a second time"; de-duplicate the input first. And DO UPDATE takes a WHERE clause, so you can update conditionally: DO UPDATE SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty WHERE inv.updated_at < EXCLUDED.updated_at implements last-write-wins by timestamp rather than by arrival.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, excluded pseudo-table and arbiter index.

11.4 UPDATE

UPDATE inv SET qty = qty + 1, updated_at = '2026-03-01'
WHERE sku = 'D'
RETURNING sku, qty;

 sku | qty 
-----+-----
 D   |   2
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

An UPDATE statement that computes the new value from the old in SQL is safe under concurrency — §14.11 measured the alternative losing an update. SET qty = qty + 1 re-reads the row after waiting for any concurrent writer; SET qty = 2 computed in the application does not.

An UPDATE with no WHERE updates every row, and PostgreSQL will not stop you. In psql, \set ON_ERROR_STOP on does not help here — nothing errored. The habit that does: write the SELECT first, check the count, then convert it to an UPDATE by editing the front of the line.

In summary, the vocabulary here is update statement.

11.5 UPDATE FROM and DELETE USING

To update rows using values from another table, PostgreSQL's UPDATE ... FROM is the readable form:

CREATE TABLE deliveries (sku text, delta int);
INSERT INTO deliveries VALUES ('A', 4), ('B', 7), ('C', 2);

UPDATE inv SET qty = inv.qty + d.delta
FROM deliveries d WHERE d.sku = inv.sku
RETURNING inv.sku, old.qty AS before, new.qty AS after;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 sku | before | after 
-----+--------+-------
 A   |     15 |    19
 B   |      0 |     7
(2 rows)

UPDATE 2

'C' is not in inv, so it updated nothing — UPDATE ... FROM is an inner join, not an upsert. That is §11.9's job.

A multi-column assignment — SET (a, b) = (expr, expr), or = (sub-SELECT) — updates several columns from one source in one clause.

The trap in UPDATE ... FROM is duplicates on the other side. If deliveries held two rows for 'A', the target row is updated once, with values from an arbitrarily chosen one of them — no error, no warning. Aggregate the source first (FROM (SELECT sku, sum(delta) AS delta FROM deliveries GROUP BY sku) d) whenever the join is not provably one-to-one.

DELETE ... USING is the same idea:

DELETE FROM inv USING deliveries d
WHERE d.sku = inv.sku AND d.delta = 2
RETURNING inv.sku;

 sku 
-----
(0 rows)

DELETE 0

Nothing, because 'C' was never inserted into inv. The RETURNING count is how you confirm that a delete matched what you expected — a DELETE that hits zero rows is silent otherwise.

What to carry forward from this subsection: multi-column assignment.

11.6 DELETE and TRUNCATE

A DELETE statement removes rows one MVCC version at a time: it writes a new row version marking each as dead (§14.7), fires row triggers, respects foreign keys, and leaves the space for vacuum to reclaim.

A TRUNCATE statement empties a table by discarding its files:

CREATE TABLE t_demo (id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, v int);
INSERT INTO t_demo (v) VALUES (1), (2);
TRUNCATE t_demo RESTART IDENTITY;
INSERT INTO t_demo (v) VALUES (9) RETURNING id, v;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
TRUNCATE TABLE
 id | v 
----+---
  1 | 9
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1
DELETE
TRUNCATE
Speed
proportional to rows
constant
Lock
ROW EXCLUSIVE
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE — blocks readers
Row triggers
fire
do not fire
Space
reclaimed by vacuum
returned immediately
WHERE
yes
no

Both are transactional — a TRUNCATE inside a rolled-back transaction leaves the table intact, which is not true in MySQL. RESTART IDENTITY resets the sequences, and CASCADE truncates tables that reference this one, which is the only way to truncate a table with incoming foreign keys and is worth pausing over before typing.

The terms above, gathered: truncate statement.

One line each, for reference: delete statement.

11.7 Deleting a Lot of Rows

A DELETE of ten million rows is one transaction: it holds locks for its whole duration, generates a large WAL burst, blocks vacuum for its whole duration (§16.5), and either finishes or rolls back the lot.

The standard remedy is a batched loop in a procedure (§18.16), committing every few thousand rows:

CREATE PROCEDURE purge_inv() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE n int;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    DELETE FROM inv WHERE sku IN (SELECT sku FROM inv WHERE qty = 0 LIMIT 1000);
    GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT;
    EXIT WHEN n = 0;
    COMMIT;
  END LOOP;
END $$;
CALL purge_inv();
SELECT count(*) AS rows_with_zero_qty FROM inv WHERE qty = 0;

CREATE PROCEDURE
CALL
 rows_with_zero_qty 
--------------------
                  0
(1 row)

Each batch is a short transaction, so vacuum can keep up and locks are released between batches. The trade is that the operation is no longer atomic — an interruption leaves it half done — which is acceptable precisely because deleting rows that already qualify is idempotent.

When you are deleting most of a large table, the faster shape is different: create a new table with the rows you want to keep, then swap. That is one write of the survivors rather than one write per deleted row, and it leaves no bloat.

11.8 MERGE

A MERGE statement (standard SQL, PostgreSQL 15 and later) applies several actions from one source in one statement:

MERGE INTO inv AS t USING deliveries AS s ON t.sku = s.sku
WHEN MATCHED AND s.delta > 5 THEN UPDATE SET qty = t.qty + s.delta
WHEN MATCHED THEN DO NOTHING
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (sku, qty) VALUES (s.sku, s.delta)
RETURNING merge_action(), t.sku, t.qty;

 merge_action | sku | qty 
--------------+-----+-----
 UPDATE       | B   |  14
 INSERT       | C   |   2
(2 rows)

MERGE 2

merge_action() reports what happened to each row — INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE — which is the thing ON CONFLICT cannot tell you. PostgreSQL 17 added WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, which fires for target rows the source does not contain, making a full three-way synchronisation expressible in one statement.

MERGE is not an upsert replacement, and this is the important distinction. ON CONFLICT is built on a unique index and is atomic against concurrent inserters: the index arbitrates. MERGE evaluates its ON condition against a snapshot, so two concurrent MERGEs can both decide NOT MATCHED and both insert — and if there is a unique constraint, one gets a duplicate-key error rather than merging.

ON CONFLICT
Concurrent upsert on a unique key. PostgreSQL-specific. Use this for "insert or update this row".
MERGE
Standard SQL, several actions including DELETE, reports what it did. Best for a batch synchronisation you control the concurrency of — at SERIALIZABLE, or with the target locked.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: merge statement, when not matched by source and merge_action(.

11.9 COPY

COPY FROM is the bulk path, and it is far faster than INSERT because it bypasses per-statement overhead entirely.

CREATE TABLE bulk (id int, name text);
COPY bulk (id, name) FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT csv);
1,alpha
2,beta
3,gamma
\.
SELECT id, name FROM bulk ORDER BY id;

CREATE TABLE
COPY 3
 id | name  
----+-------
  1 | alpha
  2 | beta
  3 | gamma
(3 rows)
