COPY ... FROM '/path' reads a file on the server, which needs superuser or the pg_read_server_files role. \copy is the psql meta-command that does the same through the client connection, reading a file on your machine with your permissions — which is what you want nine times in ten.

COPY TO goes the other way, writing a result set out. Options: CSV format and the others — FORMAT csv|text|binary, HEADER, DELIMITER, NULL, QUOTE, FORCE_NOT_NULL, and FREEZE to mark rows frozen immediately (§16.7) when loading into a table created in the same transaction.

HEADER MATCH (PostgreSQL 16) validates that the file's header matches the column list, rather than merely skipping a line — which turns "the columns moved" from silent corruption into an error.

And the newest addition, which changes how a messy import is done:

CREATE TABLE bad (id int, name text);
COPY bad (id, name) FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT csv, ON_ERROR ignore, LOG_VERBOSITY verbose);
1,alpha
oops,beta
3,gamma
\.
SELECT id, name FROM bad ORDER BY id;

CREATE TABLE
NOTICE:  skipping row due to data type incompatibility at line 2 for column "id": "oops"
NOTICE:  1 row was skipped due to data type incompatibility
COPY 2
 id | name  
----+-------
  1 | alpha
  3 | gamma
(2 rows)

ON_ERROR ignore skips malformed rows instead of aborting the whole load, and LOG_VERBOSITY verbose names each one. PostgreSQL 18 adds REJECT_LIMIT to cap how many may be skipped before the load fails anyway, and a silent verbosity level. Before this existed, one bad row in a million-row file meant the entire load rolled back and you found the row by bisection.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: copy from, copy to and csv format.

11.10 Loading Fast

For a large load, the statement is only part of the cost. The rest is indexes, constraints and WAL.

Use COPY
Not a loop of INSERTs. If you must use INSERT, batching writes into multi-row VALUES in one transaction is the next best thing.
Drop indexes first
Building an index once over the finished table is much cheaper than maintaining it row by row (§12.18). Same for foreign keys.
Raise maintenance_work_mem
It governs the index build that follows.
Raise max_wal_size
Fewer checkpoints, fewer full-page writes (§16.11).
ANALYZE afterwards
Not optional. A freshly loaded table has statistics saying it is empty (§13.10), and every plan against it is wrong until autovacuum catches up.

Two stronger options when the table is created in the same transaction as the load: CREATE TABLE ... ; COPY ... WITH (FREEZE) avoids a later freeze pass, and — if wal_level = minimal — the load can skip WAL entirely, because a crash would discard the whole table anyway. UNLOGGED (§4.4) does the same at any WAL level, at the cost of the table being emptied by a crash.

To have in hand before moving on: batching writes.

11.11 The Write Cost of a Row

Three mechanisms decide what a write actually costs, and all three were established earlier:

Every index is another write (§12.18). An insert into a table with five indexes is six writes.

An update that changes no indexed column and fits on its page is a HOT update (§14.7) — no index maintenance at all. fillfactor reserves free space on each page precisely to make that more likely: ALTER TABLE t SET (fillfactor = 85) leaves 15% free, which is worth it on a heavily updated table and wasteful on an append-only one.

Every update leaves a dead tuple (§16.2), so write volume drives vacuum load. A row updated a hundred times a second is a hundred dead versions a second for autovacuum to collect.

Which yields one design rule worth stating plainly: updating a narrow, unindexed column is cheap; updating an indexed one is not. Splitting a hot counter or a last_seen_at into its own narrow table is a standard fix, and it works because it removes those updates from the wide table's indexes entirely.

11.12 Writes That Are Safe to Repeat

An idempotent write is one that may run twice without changing the result. A retryable transaction (§14.15) may do exactly that. So may a job whose worker died after committing but before acknowledging (§15.5). Idempotence is what makes that harmless, and there are three reliable shapes:

A unique key plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The second attempt inserts nothing. This is the workhorse — for consuming a message with an id, recording a payment with a reference, or importing a file twice.

An absolute rather than relative update. SET status = 'paid' is idempotent; SET attempts = attempts + 1 is not. Where a counter must be exact, count rows in another table instead of incrementing.

A conditional update. UPDATE ... SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'pending' succeeds once and then matches nothing, and RETURNING tells you which happened. That is optimistic concurrency without a version column.

The version-column form is the explicit one: UPDATE t SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2, where a row count of zero means someone else got there first. It costs a column and gives the application a chance to merge rather than retry blindly.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: optimistic concurrency.

In summary, the vocabulary here is idempotent write.

What This Section Established

Name the columns in every INSERT. A multi-row VALUES is one statement, one round trip, one WAL flush — and COPY beats it.

RETURNING reports what the statement did, in the same round trip and without a race. PostgreSQL 18 adds old. and new. qualifiers, measured returning 3 and 0 from one UPDATE.

ON CONFLICT (target) DO UPDATE is the race-free upsert: the conflict target must match a unique arbiter index, EXCLUDED is the proposed row, and the command tag says INSERT even when it updated. DO NOTHING returns no row from RETURNING, which is how you tell them apart. It cannot resolve a conflict against a row the same statement inserted.

UPDATE ... SET qty = qty + 1 is concurrency-safe; the same arithmetic in the application is the lost update of §14.11.

UPDATE ... FROM with duplicates on the source side updates the target once, arbitrarily, with no warning. Aggregate the source unless the join is provably one-to-one.

TRUNCATE is constant-time, takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, skips row triggers, returns space immediately, takes no WHERE — and is transactional, unlike MySQL's.

Delete large volumes in committed batches from a procedure; when deleting most of a table, write the survivors to a new table and swap.

MERGE reports merge_action() and handles several actions including DELETE, but it is not atomic against concurrent inserters — ON CONFLICT is, because a unique index arbitrates.

COPY ... FROM reads a server-side file; \copy reads a client-side one and is usually what you want. HEADER MATCH validates the header. ON_ERROR ignore skips malformed rows — measured, two rows loaded and one skipped with a NOTICE naming it — and REJECT_LIMIT caps how many.

For a fast load: COPY, indexes and foreign keys built afterwards, raised maintenance_work_mem and max_wal_size, and ANALYZE at the end, which is not optional.

Write cost: one write per index, HOT updates avoid index maintenance entirely, fillfactor makes them likelier, and every update feeds vacuum.

Idempotent writes: a unique key with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, absolute rather than relative updates, or a conditional UPDATE whose row count tells you whether you were first.

Exercises

1. Break an unnamed INSERT. Write an INSERT with no column list, then ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN in a position that changes its meaning, and show the resulting failure or — worse — the resulting silent misplacement. State the rule.

2. Upsert under concurrency. Implement "insert or increment a counter" with SELECT then branch, and with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. Run both from two sessions and show the first losing an increment. Then explain what the unique index is doing in the second.

3. Tell insert from update. With ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, write a statement that reports which of the two happened for each row. Then do the same with MERGE and compare the amount of work.

4. Multiply an UPDATE FROM. Build a source table with two rows for the same key and run UPDATE ... FROM. Report what the target holds. Then fix it by aggregating and explain why PostgreSQL did not raise an error.

5. Delete a million rows three ways. Compare a single DELETE, a batched procedure, and create-new-table-and-swap. Report elapsed time, WAL volume, peak lock duration, and resulting table size. Say which you would use at 10% and at 90% of the table.

6. Load a messy file. Build a CSV with three malformed rows out of a thousand. Load it with plain COPY, then with ON_ERROR ignore, then with REJECT_LIMIT 2. Report what each does, and describe the pre-17 procedure you have just replaced.

7. Make a write idempotent. Take a job that inserts a payment and increments a balance. Make the whole thing safe to run twice, and prove it by running it twice. State which of the three shapes you used for each half and why.

Solution

1. The unnamed INSERT.

CREATE TABLE unnamed (a int, b int);
INSERT INTO unnamed VALUES (1, 2);
ALTER TABLE unnamed ADD COLUMN c int;
\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
INSERT INTO unnamed VALUES (3, 4);
SELECT a, b, c FROM unnamed ORDER BY a;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
ALTER TABLE
INSERT 0 1
 a | b | c 
---+---+---
 1 | 2 |  
 3 | 4 |  
(2 rows)

ADD COLUMN appends, so the statement still works and c is null. That is the benign case, and it is why the habit survives.

The damaging case is a column dropped and re-added, or a table rebuilt with a different order — then VALUES (3, 4) lands in different columns with no error, because both are int. The rule: name the columns, and the reason is that positional matching binds your statement to a table shape that is not part of any contract.

2. Upsert under concurrency.

The SELECT-then-branch version loses increments exactly as §14.11 measured: both sessions read the same value, both compute the same new one, and one write overwrites the other.

ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = inv.qty + EXCLUDED.qty cannot lose one. The unique index is doing two things: it detects the conflict, and — because index insertion is serialised on the index page — it makes the detection atomic. The second session's insert attempt blocks on the index entry the first is creating, and when it unblocks it takes the DO UPDATE path against the committed row.

That is why the conflict target must be a unique index. Without one there is nothing to serialise on, and there is no upsert.

3. Telling insert from update.

With ON CONFLICT, the trick is a column that only one path sets:

CREATE TABLE which (k int PRIMARY KEY, v int, touched text);
INSERT INTO which (k, v, touched) VALUES (1, 10, 'inserted')
ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET v = EXCLUDED.v, touched = 'updated'
RETURNING k, touched;
INSERT INTO which (k, v, touched) VALUES (1, 20, 'inserted')
ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET v = EXCLUDED.v, touched = 'updated'
RETURNING k, touched;

CREATE TABLE
 k | touched  
---+----------
 1 | inserted
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1
 k | touched  
---+----------
 1 | updated
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1

Both report INSERT 0 1; only the touched column distinguishes them. xmax = 0 is the other common trick — an inserted row has no xmax, an updated one does — and it is more fragile.

MERGE needs no trick: merge_action() says INSERT or UPDATE directly. That is the honest advantage of MERGE, set against its concurrency weakness.

4. Multiplying an UPDATE FROM.

CREATE TABLE dupsrc (sku text, delta int);
INSERT INTO dupsrc VALUES ('A', 10), ('A', 100);
UPDATE inv SET qty = inv.qty + d.delta FROM dupsrc d WHERE d.sku = inv.sku
RETURNING inv.sku, new.qty;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
 sku | qty 
-----+-----
 A   |  29
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

One row updated, and qty went from 19 to 29 — it applied +10 and discarded the +100 entirely. Which of the two it used is arbitrary.

PostgreSQL does not error because the semantics are defined: an UPDATE produces at most one new version per target row per statement, and when the join offers several source rows one is chosen. It is a documented behaviour rather than a bug, and it is exactly the kind of documented behaviour that produces wrong numbers in production. The fix is to make the join one-to-one:

UPDATE inv SET qty = inv.qty + d.delta
FROM (SELECT sku, sum(delta) AS delta FROM dupsrc GROUP BY sku) d
WHERE d.sku = inv.sku RETURNING inv.sku, new.qty;

 sku | qty 
-----+-----
 A   | 139
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

139 — both deliveries applied.

5. Deleting a million rows.

The single DELETE is fastest in raw elapsed time and worst in every other respect: one long transaction, locks held throughout, one large WAL burst, vacuum blocked for the duration, and a table left as bloated as the rows removed.

The batched procedure is slower in total and better behaved: short transactions, vacuum keeps up, locks released between batches, and it can be stopped and resumed.

Create-and-swap writes only the survivors, so at 90% deleted it is by far the cheapest — one write of 10% of the rows instead of a dead version for each of the 90% — and it leaves a compact table needing no vacuum. Its cost is an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the rename and the need to recreate indexes, constraints and privileges on the new table.

At 10%: batched delete. At 90%: create-and-swap. The crossover is roughly where the survivors are cheaper to write than the victims are to mark dead, which is somewhere around half.

6. Loading a messy file.

Plain COPY aborts on the first bad row and rolls back the entire load — with a message naming the line, which is the only thing that made the pre-17 procedure possible.

ON_ERROR ignore loads 997 rows and reports three skipped. REJECT_LIMIT 2 fails, because three exceeds two — which is the setting you want when "a few bad rows" is acceptable and "the file is the wrong format" is not.

The procedure this replaces: load into a staging table with every column as text, so nothing can fail; then INSERT INTO real SELECT ... WHERE <every column casts cleanly>; then inspect the remainder. That still has a place when you want to keep the bad rows for inspection rather than discard them — ON_ERROR ignore discards them.

7. Making a write idempotent.

CREATE TABLE payments (ref text PRIMARY KEY, cents int NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE balances (account text PRIMARY KEY, cents int NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO balances VALUES ('acct', 0);

WITH ins AS (
  INSERT INTO payments (ref, cents) VALUES ('pay-001', 500)
  ON CONFLICT (ref) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING cents
)
UPDATE balances SET cents = cents + (SELECT coalesce(sum(cents), 0) FROM ins)
WHERE account = 'acct'
RETURNING cents;

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
 cents 
-------
   500
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

Run the identical statement again:

WITH ins AS (
  INSERT INTO payments (ref, cents) VALUES ('pay-001', 500)
  ON CONFLICT (ref) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING cents
)
UPDATE balances SET cents = cents + (SELECT coalesce(sum(cents), 0) FROM ins)
WHERE account = 'acct'
RETURNING cents;

 cents 
-------
   500
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

Still 500. The insert half uses the unique-key shape: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on the payment reference. The increment half is relative and therefore not idempotent on its own — so it is made conditional on the insert having happened, by driving it from the RETURNING of the CTE. Second time round the CTE returns no rows, the sum is coalesce(NULL, 0), and the balance does not move.

Both halves are in one statement, so they cannot be separated by a crash — which is the third requirement and the reason this is a data-modifying CTE (§9.10) rather than two statements.

SECTION 12

Indexes

An index is a redundant, automatically maintained data structure that lets the database find rows without looking at all of them. Everything interesting about indexing follows from the word redundant: an index is a copy, it costs disk, it costs write time, it can be stale in ways that matter, and it is only worth having if queries actually use it.

This section is deliberately placed before the planner (§13), because you cannot read a plan without knowing what the scans mean — but the two are one subject. An index that exists and is never chosen is pure cost, and the only way to know which you have is to look.

Every measurement below comes from this table.

SET timezone = 'UTC';

CREATE TABLE page_views (
  view_id   bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  site_id   integer     NOT NULL,
  path      text        NOT NULL,
  status    text        NOT NULL,
  viewed_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO page_views (site_id, path, status, viewed_at)
SELECT (g % 50) + 1,
       '/p/' || (g % 10000),
       CASE WHEN g % 1000 = 0 THEN 'error' ELSE 'ok' END,
       timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' + (g % 300) * interval '1 hour'
FROM generate_series(1, 300000) AS g;

ALTER TABLE page_views SET (autovacuum_enabled = false);
ANALYZE page_views;

Three hundred thousand rows, 50 sites, 10,000 distinct paths, and one row in a thousand with status = 'error'. Those cardinalities are chosen because each one changes an indexing decision.

Autovacuum is switched off for this table only, and only so that §12.9 is reproducible — that demonstration turns on whether the visibility map has been populated, and an autovacuum worker arriving at an unpredictable moment would populate it behind your back. Never do this to a real table; §16.4 is what happens when you do.

12.1 The B-Tree, and the Two Numbers That Matter

CREATE INDEX builds a B-tree unless you say otherwise, and the B-tree is the right default for a reason: it supports equality, ranges, IS NULL, sorting, and prefix matching, all from one structure. The other five index methods in §12.13 each do one thing the B-tree cannot.

A B-tree is a balanced tree of pages. The leaves hold (key, ctid) pairs in key order; the internal pages hold separator keys. Finding a key is a descent from the root, and the depth grows with the logarithm of the row count — which is why a table can grow a hundredfold while lookups get only slightly slower.

Two numbers govern every decision in this section, and it is worth naming them before any syntax.

Index selectivity
The fraction of the table a condition matches. An index pays when this is small. Matching 40% of a table through an index is slower than reading the table, because each match is a separate page fetch and the pages are visited in key order rather than physical order.
Write amplification
Every index is another structure every INSERT must write to, and every UPDATE of an indexed column must write to twice — once to remove the old entry's visibility, once to add the new. Five indexes on a table means an insert does six writes.

What to carry forward from this subsection: index selectivity.

12.2 Creating an Index, and What It Costs to Store

CREATE INDEX pv_site_path ON page_views (site_id, path);

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('page_views'))   AS heap,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('pv_site_path')) AS index;

CREATE INDEX
 heap  |  index  
-------+---------
 17 MB | 2320 kB
(1 row)

The index is about an eighth of the table here, and that ratio is entirely a function of how much of the row you indexed. An index on every column would be larger than the table.

CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock (§15.4): concurrent reads proceed, concurrent writes block for the duration. On a large production table that is an outage, which is what §12.11 is for.

12.3 The Leading Column — and What PostgreSQL 18 Changed

A multicolumn B-tree sorts by its first column, then the second within that, and so on. The classical consequence — repeated in a decade of blog posts — is that a query which does not constrain the leading column cannot use the index at all.

That rule changed in PostgreSQL 18, and the difference is visible.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM page_views WHERE path = '/p/107';

                              QUERY PLAN                              
----------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on page_views (actual rows=30.00 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (path = '/p/107'::text)
   Heap Blocks: exact=30
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on pv_site_path (actual rows=30.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (path = '/p/107'::text)
         Index Searches: 51
(6 rows)

The query constrains only path, the index leads on site_id, and the index was used anyway. This is the index skip scan added in PostgreSQL 18. The give-away is Index Searches: 51: there are 50 distinct site_id values, so PostgreSQL descended the tree once per distinct leading value, plus one. It is fifty small lookups instead of one, which is still far cheaper than reading 17 MB.

The catch is that it only works when the leading column has few distinct values. Give it a hundred thousand:

CREATE TABLE wide_lead (a integer NOT NULL, b integer NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO wide_lead SELECT g % 100000, g % 7 FROM generate_series(1, 300000) AS g;
CREATE INDEX wide_lead_ab ON wide_lead (a, b);
ANALYZE wide_lead;

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM wide_lead WHERE b = 3;

      QUERY PLAN       
-----------------------
 Seq Scan on wide_lead
   Filter: (b = 3)
(2 rows)

A hundred thousand skips would be a hundred thousand descents, so the planner correctly reads the table instead.

So the rule is now about cardinality, not about position. A (status, created_at) index will serve a query on created_at alone, because status has three values. A (user_id, created_at) index will not, because user_id has millions. If you are on PostgreSQL 17 or earlier, the old absolute rule still holds — and either way, Index Searches is the number that tells you which happened.

The terms above, gathered: index skip scan.

12.4 Column Order in a Multicolumn Index

Given that skip scans exist, index column order still matters, and the guidance is stable:

Equality before range
For WHERE site_id = 7 AND viewed_at > …, index (site_id, viewed_at). Once a column is used for a range, no column after it can be used to narrow the scan — only to filter rows already read.
Then the ORDER BY column
If the index's trailing columns match the query's sort, the Sort node disappears entirely — often a larger win than the lookup itself (§13.9).
One index, several queries
(a, b, c) serves (a), (a, b) and (a, b, c). Three separate indexes for those three queries is three times the write cost for no gain.

An exact-equality lookup on both columns gets the tightest possible plan:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM page_views WHERE site_id = 7 AND path = '/p/107';

                        QUERY PLAN                         
-----------------------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using pv_site_path on page_views
   Index Cond: ((site_id = 7) AND (path = '/p/107'::text))
(2 rows)

Both conditions are in the Index Cond, so both narrowed the descent. A condition that appears as Filter: instead was applied after the row was read, which means it saved no I/O — that distinction is the fastest way to tell whether your index is doing what you think.

One line each, for reference: index column order.

12.5 Unique Indexes

A UNIQUE constraint (§4.4) is implemented as a unique index; PRIMARY KEY is a unique index plus NOT NULL. You can also create one directly, which is the only way to get a unique partial index.

The rule that surprises people: NULLs are distinct from each other by default, so a unique index permits any number of NULL rows. PostgreSQL 15 added the alternative:

CREATE TABLE uniq_demo (email text);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uniq_email ON uniq_demo (email);
INSERT INTO uniq_demo VALUES (NULL), (NULL), ('a@example.com');

CREATE TABLE uniq_demo2 (email text);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uniq_email2 ON uniq_demo2 (email) NULLS NOT DISTINCT;
INSERT INTO uniq_demo2 VALUES (NULL);
INSERT INTO uniq_demo2 VALUES (NULL);

CREATE TABLE
CREATE INDEX
INSERT 0 3
CREATE TABLE
CREATE INDEX
INSERT 0 1
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "uniq_email2"
DETAIL:  Key (email)=(null) already exists.

Two NULLs are fine in the first table and a violation in the second. Which you want depends on whether NULL means "no value" (distinct — the default is right) or "not yet assigned, and there can only be one such row" (NULLS NOT DISTINCT).

12.6 Partial Indexes

A partial index indexes only the rows matching a predicate. When the interesting rows are a small minority, the saving is dramatic.

CREATE INDEX pv_errors ON page_views (viewed_at) WHERE status = 'error';

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('pv_errors'))    AS partial,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('pv_site_path')) AS full;

CREATE INDEX
 partial | full    
---------+---------
 16 kB   | 2320 kB
(1 row)

16 kB against 2320 kB — a factor of 145, because it indexes 300 rows rather than 300,000. It is also cheaper to maintain: an insert with status = 'ok' does not touch it at all.

The planner uses it only when it can prove the query's predicate implies the index's:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM page_views WHERE status = 'error' AND viewed_at > '2026-01-05';

                                                   QUERY PLAN                                                    
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on page_views
   Recheck Cond: ((viewed_at > '2026-01-05 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone) AND (status = 'error'::text))
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on pv_errors
         Index Cond: (viewed_at > '2026-01-05 00:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone)
(4 rows)

Note the status = 'error' condition does not appear in the Index Cond — it did not need to, because every row in this index satisfies it by construction.

The proof is syntactic and not very clever, which is the practical limit: write the query's predicate the same way you wrote the index's. WHERE status <> 'ok' will not match WHERE status = 'error' even on data where they are equivalent, and WHERE status = $1 cannot match either, because the value is not known at planning time.

The two classic uses: soft deletes (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL — index only the live rows) and a unique constraint that applies conditionally (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON accounts (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, which lets a deleted account's address be reused).

12.7 Expression Indexes

An index can be on the result of an expression rather than a column. This is what makes case-insensitive lookup indexable:

CREATE TABLE people (id int PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO people SELECT g, 'User' || g || '@Example.COM' FROM generate_series(1, 50000) AS g;
CREATE INDEX people_lower_email ON people (lower(email));
ANALYZE people;

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM people WHERE lower(email) = 'user42@example.com';

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 50000
CREATE INDEX
ANALYZE
SET
                       QUERY PLAN                        
---------------------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using people_lower_email on people
   Index Cond: (lower(email) = 'user42@example.com'::text)
(2 rows)

The expression in the query must match the expression in the index. WHERE email = 'x' will not use this index, and WHERE lower(email) LIKE ... will use it only for a prefix under the rules in §12.14. That exactness is the whole discipline of expression indexes.

The function must be IMMUTABLE (§18.14) — an index entry computed once must stay correct forever, so now() or anything depending on a session setting is rejected. This is why lower() is indexable and a timestamp cast to text in the local time zone is not.

ANALYZE also collects statistics for the expression, so the planner estimates lower(email) = ... properly instead of falling back to a default guess. That happens automatically for an expression index, and is available without one via CREATE STATISTICS ON (expression) (§13.11).

12.8 Covering Indexes and INCLUDE

If an index contains every column a query needs, PostgreSQL can answer from the index alone. The INCLUDE clause adds payload columns — stored in the leaves, not part of the key, not searchable, not sorted:

CREATE INDEX pv_covering ON page_views (site_id) INCLUDE (status);

CREATE INDEX

The distinction between (site_id, status) and (site_id) INCLUDE (status) is real. Included columns cost less (no ordering to maintain, and they need no btree operator class, so a type that cannot be indexed can still be carried), but they cannot be used in an Index Cond, and they cannot enforce uniqueness — CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... (a) INCLUDE (b) is unique on a alone, which is occasionally exactly what you want.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: include clause.

12.9 Index-Only Scans Depend on the Visibility Map

Here is the part that catches people, and it is best shown by running the same query twice.

An index entry does not record whether its row is visible to you — visibility lives in the heap (§14.8). So an index-only scan must still check, unless the row's page is marked all-visible in the visibility map, which only VACUUM sets.

Immediately after loading, the map is empty:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT site_id, path FROM page_views WHERE site_id = 7 AND path < '/p/2';

                              QUERY PLAN                              
----------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on page_views (actual rows=660.00 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: ((site_id = 7) AND (path < '/p/2'::text))
   Heap Blocks: exact=280
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on pv_site_path (actual rows=660.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: ((site_id = 7) AND (path < '/p/2'::text))
         Index Searches: 1
(6 rows)

Both columns are in the index, and it read 280 heap blocks anyway. Now vacuum and run the identical query:

VACUUM (DISABLE_PAGE_SKIPPING) page_views;
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT site_id, path FROM page_views WHERE site_id = 7 AND path < '/p/2';

VACUUM
SET
                                  QUERY PLAN                                   
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Index Only Scan using pv_site_path on page_views (actual rows=660.00 loops=1)
   Index Cond: ((site_id = 7) AND (path < '/p/2'::text))
   Heap Fetches: 0
   Index Searches: 1
(4 rows)

Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0. Same query, same index, same data — the only change is that vacuum marked the pages all-visible.

Heap Fetches is the number to watch in production. A high count on an index-only scan means the visibility map is stale, which means the table is being written to faster than autovacuum is keeping up (§16.4). The fix is vacuum tuning, not indexing.

12.10 Operator Classes and Families

An index needs to know how to compare values, and that knowledge is an operator class. Each type has a default one, which is why you never normally specify it. You specify it when the default is not what your query needs — and the canonical case is LIKE 'prefix%'.

Under the database's default collation here, which is C, no special class is needed:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
CREATE INDEX pv_path_btree ON page_views (path);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM page_views WHERE path LIKE '/p/10%';

SET
CREATE INDEX
                                QUERY PLAN                                
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on page_views
   Filter: (path ~~ '/p/10%'::text)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on pv_path_btree
         Index Cond: ((path >= '/p/10'::text) AND (path < '/p/11'::text))
(4 rows)

The planner rewrote the prefix match into a range, which a B-tree can serve. Under any other collation it cannot, because a linguistic collation does not sort byte-wise and the range would be wrong:

CREATE TABLE coll_demo (path text COLLATE "en-US-x-icu" NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO coll_demo SELECT '/p/' || g FROM generate_series(1, 200000) AS g;
CREATE INDEX coll_plain ON coll_demo (path);
ANALYZE coll_demo;

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM coll_demo WHERE path LIKE '/p/10%';

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 200000
CREATE INDEX
ANALYZE
SET
SET
              QUERY PLAN               
---------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on coll_demo
   Filter: (path ~~ '/p/10%'::text)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on coll_plain

No Index Cond at all — and it took enable_seqscan = off to get even this, which is a full scan of the index followed by a filter. text_pattern_ops fixes it by comparing byte-wise regardless of collation:

CREATE INDEX coll_pattern ON coll_demo (path text_pattern_ops);
ANALYZE coll_demo;
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM coll_demo WHERE path LIKE '/p/10%';

CREATE INDEX
ANALYZE
SET
                                  QUERY PLAN                                  
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on coll_demo
   Filter: (path ~~ '/p/10%'::text)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on coll_pattern
         Index Cond: ((path ~>=~ '/p/10'::text) AND (path ~<~ '/p/11'::text))
(4 rows)

The range is back, with the ~>=~ and ~<~ operators that belong to the pattern operator class.

So "you need text_pattern_ops for LIKE" is only true off the C collation — which is most real databases, since C sorts Z before a and is rarely what an application wants. A text_pattern_ops index serves LIKE and nothing else: ORDER BY path and path < 'x' still need the ordinary index, so a column doing both needs both indexes.

Index and collation interact exactly as this subsection shows, and an operator family groups operator classes across types, which is how the planner knows an integer index can serve WHERE int_col = 42::bigint.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: operator family and index and collation.

12.11 Building an Index Without Blocking Writes

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds without taking a lock that blocks writes. It is the only acceptable way to add an index to a busy table, and it has three properties you must know before using it.

It cannot run inside a transaction block. Which means it is not covered by the transactional-DDL guarantee in §14.6, and a migration tool that wraps everything in a transaction needs an explicit exception for it.

It is roughly twice the work. Two full passes over the table, plus a wait for every transaction older than the build to finish.

It can fail and leave an invalid index behind. If the build hits a unique violation or is cancelled, the index remains, marked indisvalid = false — it is ignored by queries but still maintained by every write, which is the worst of both. Finding them is a query worth keeping:

SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS invalid_index
FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;

 invalid_index 
---------------
(0 rows)

The remedy is DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and a retry. REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuilds an existing index the same way, and is how you fix bloat (§12.17) without an outage.

To have in hand before moving on: drop index concurrently and reindex concurrently.

12.12 Bitmap Scans and Combining Indexes

PostgreSQL can use more than one index for one query by combining them as bitmaps: build a bitmap of matching row locations from each index, AND or OR them, then visit the heap once in physical order.

CREATE INDEX pv_status ON page_views (status);
CREATE INDEX pv_viewed ON page_views (viewed_at);
ANALYZE page_views;
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM page_views
  WHERE status = 'error' OR viewed_at < '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00';

CREATE INDEX
CREATE INDEX
ANALYZE
SET
SET
                                    QUERY PLAN                                     
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on page_views
   Recheck Cond: ((status = 'error'::text) OR (viewed_at < '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone))
   ->  BitmapOr
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on pv_status
               Index Cond: (status = 'error'::text)
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on pv_viewed
               Index Cond: (viewed_at < '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00'::timestamp with time zone)
(7 rows)

The BitmapOr node is the combination. This is genuinely useful — it is why an OR across two columns is not automatically a sequential scan — but a single multicolumn index is faster than combining two single-column ones when the query always uses both columns, because combining costs building and merging bitmaps. Two single-column indexes are the flexible choice; one composite index is the fast one.

12.13 The Other Index Methods

Five alternatives to the B-tree, each for a class of query the B-tree cannot serve.

CREATE INDEX pv_path_hash ON page_views USING hash (path);
CREATE INDEX pv_brin ON page_views USING brin (viewed_at);
SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'page_views'::regclass
  AND indexrelid::regclass::text IN ('pv_path_btree','pv_path_hash','pv_brin')
ORDER BY 1;

CREATE INDEX
CREATE INDEX
     index     |  size   
---------------+---------
 pv_path_btree | 2240 kB
 pv_path_hash  | 9264 kB
 pv_brin       | 24 kB
(3 rows)

The hash index is four times the size of the B-tree on the same column, and supports only = where the B-tree also supports <, >, BETWEEN and ORDER BY. That is the measured case against reaching for it: hash indexes became crash-safe and replicated in PostgreSQL 10 and are legitimate, but they win only on very long keys where hashing the value beats storing it.

BRIN is 24 kB — a thousandth of the B-tree — because it stores only a min/max summary per range of pages. It is exact only when the column's physical order tracks its value order (§12.16), which viewed_at on an append-only log does perfectly. On a randomly ordered column BRIN is useless rather than merely large.

B-tree
Ordered, scalar. Equality, ranges, sorting, prefix matching, NULL. The default, and right nearly always.
Hash
Equality only. Measured above at 4× the B-tree's size. Reach for it only for very large keys.
GiST
A framework for "overlaps", "contains", "near". Ranges (§17.12), geometry, and the exclusion constraints of §4.8 — which is why WITHOUT OVERLAPS requires btree_gist.
SP-GiST
Space-partitioned GiST: quadtrees, radix trees. Non-balanced structures for data that partitions naturally — text prefixes, points, inet.
GIN
"Which rows contain this element?" — arrays, jsonb, full-text search (§17). One index entry per element, so builds are slow and lookups are fast.
BRIN index
Block-range summaries. Tiny, and useful in exact proportion to how well physical order matches value order.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: sp-gist and brin index.

12.14 When an Index Is Not Used

A working index and a query that should use it, and the planner refuses. There are six recurring causes.

The table is small
Under a few hundred rows a sequential scan is one page read. The planner is right and the index is not the problem.
Poor selectivity
The condition matches too much of the table. WHERE status = 'ok' on this table matches 99.9% of rows, and an index would be slower.
The column is wrapped in a function
WHERE lower(email) = … cannot use an index on email, and WHERE viewed_at::date = … cannot use one on viewed_at. Index the expression (§12.7), or rewrite the predicate as a range.
Type mismatch
Comparing a text column to a number, or a numeric to a bigint where the cast lands on the column side. If the cast is applied to the column, the index is out.
Leading pattern wildcard
LIKE '%foo' has no prefix to turn into a range. That is what a trigram index is for (§17.14).
Stale statistics
The planner thinks the table is empty or uniformly distributed. ANALYZE (§13.10).

12.15 Physical Order: Correlation and CLUSTER

An index scan returns row locations in index order. If that order is unrelated to physical order, reading 10,000 matches means 10,000 scattered page fetches. The planner knows this as correlation (§13.10), and it is why the same index can be cheap on one column and expensive on another.

The CLUSTER command physically rewrites a table in an index's order:

CREATE TABLE cluster_demo AS SELECT (g % 1000) AS k, g AS v FROM generate_series(1, 50000) AS g;
CREATE INDEX cluster_demo_k ON cluster_demo (k);
ANALYZE cluster_demo;
SELECT abs(correlation) < 0.1 AS scattered_before FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'cluster_demo' AND attname = 'k';
CLUSTER cluster_demo USING cluster_demo_k;
ANALYZE cluster_demo;
SELECT correlation = 1 AS perfectly_ordered_after FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'cluster_demo' AND attname = 'k';

SELECT 50000
CREATE INDEX
ANALYZE
 scattered_before 
------------------
 t
(1 row)

CLUSTER
ANALYZE
 perfectly_ordered_after 
-------------------------
 t
(1 row)

CLUSTER is a one-time rewrite — it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, needs room for a second copy, and the order decays as soon as updates resume. Use it after a bulk load or on a table that is rewritten periodically, not as ongoing maintenance.

The everyday version of this idea is simply choosing insertion order: a table written in timestamp order is naturally clustered on time, which is why BRIN works and why time-range queries on append-only tables are cheap.

In summary, the vocabulary here is cluster command.

12.16 Bloat and REINDEX

Indexes bloat for the same reason tables do (§16.3): dead entries must be kept until vacuum can prove nobody needs them, and a B-tree page that empties is not always reclaimable for a different key range. A heavily updated index can grow far past the size a fresh build would produce.

REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuilds it in place without blocking writes:

REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY pv_status;

REINDEX

Compare pg_relation_size before and after to measure what the bloat was. The pgstattuple extension's pgstatindex() reports avg_leaf_density — a fresh B-tree is around 90%, and something in the 50s is a real candidate.

12.17 Finding Indexes That Are Not Earning Their Keep

Every index costs writes and disk. PostgreSQL tracks whether each is ever used:

CREATE TABLE audit_demo (a int, b int, c text);
INSERT INTO audit_demo SELECT g, g % 10, 'x' || g FROM generate_series(1, 20000) AS g;
CREATE INDEX audit_a  ON audit_demo (a);
CREATE INDEX audit_ab ON audit_demo (a, b);
CREATE INDEX audit_c  ON audit_demo (c);
ANALYZE audit_demo;

SELECT indexrelname, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE relname = 'audit_demo' ORDER BY indexrelname;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 20000
CREATE INDEX
CREATE INDEX
CREATE INDEX
ANALYZE
 indexrelname |  size  | idx_scan 
--------------+--------+----------
 audit_a      | 456 kB |        0
 audit_ab     | 456 kB |        0
 audit_c      | 456 kB |        0
(3 rows)

Three indexes, 456 kB each, none of them ever scanned — every one an unused index on this evidence. Three cautions before dropping anything on that evidence.

The counter is cumulative since the last statistics reset. A quarterly report's index looks unused for eighty-nine days. Check pg_stat_reset timing, and let it run at least a full business cycle.

A unique index may exist to enforce a constraint, not to serve queries. idx_scan = 0 on a unique index is normal and dropping it removes the constraint.

Drop with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and be ready to recreate. Keeping the CREATE INDEX statement in the commit message is a cheap insurance policy.

Duplicate indexes are the other easy win: (a) is redundant when (a, b) exists, because the composite serves every query the single-column one does. The exception is size — if (a, b) is much larger and (a) is hot, the smaller one may still earn its place.

What to carry forward from this subsection: unused index, pg_stat_user_indexes and duplicate index.

12.18 The Write Cost, and What Not to Index

Everything above is about reads. The other half of the ledger:

The write cost of an index is paid on every insert. An INSERT into a table with five indexes does six writes. COPY into an unindexed table then building the indexes afterwards is dramatically faster than loading into an indexed one (§11.10).

An index on a frequently updated column defeats HOT. This is the specific and under-appreciated one. As §14.7 measured, an UPDATE that changes no indexed column and fits on the same page is a heap-only tuple — no index maintenance at all. Add an index on last_seen_at, and every heartbeat update now writes to that index too, doubling the write and adding index bloat. Ask whether the query that index serves is worth that.

So the short list of what not to index: low-cardinality columns used alone (a boolean, unless a partial index on the rare value is what you want), columns you never filter or sort by, columns updated on nearly every write, and anything already covered as the prefix of another index.

The terms above, gathered: index bloat and write cost of an index.

What This Section Established

An index is a redundant structure: it costs disk, it costs writes, and it earns its place only if queries use it. B-tree is the default and serves equality, ranges, sorting, NULL and prefix matching.

Selectivity decides whether an index helps. Matching a large fraction of the table through an index is slower than reading the table.

PostgreSQL 18's skip scan changed the leading-column rule. Measured: an index on (site_id, path) served a query on path alone via Index Searches: 51, because site_id has 50 distinct values — and the same query shape fell back to a Seq Scan when the leading column had 100,000. The rule is now about cardinality, not position.

Column order: equality columns first, then range, then the ORDER BY column. (a, b, c) serves (a) and (a, b) for free. A condition in Index Cond narrowed the scan; one in Filter did not.

Unique indexes treat NULLs as distinct unless declared NULLS NOT DISTINCT.

Partial indexes measured at 16 kB against 2320 kB. The planner's proof that a query predicate implies the index predicate is syntactic, so write them the same way.

Expression indexes require the query to use the identical expression, and the function to be IMMUTABLE.

INCLUDE adds payload columns that cannot be searched and cannot enforce uniqueness.

Index-only scans need the visibility map. The identical query was a Bitmap Heap Scan over 280 heap blocks before VACUUM and an Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0 after. High Heap Fetches in production is a vacuum problem, not an index problem.

text_pattern_ops is needed for LIKE 'prefix%' only off the C collation — measured both ways, with ~>=~ and ~<~ appearing in the plan under ICU and a bare index scan with no Index Cond without it.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction, costs about twice the work, and can leave an invalid index that is maintained but never used.

BitmapOr combines indexes; one composite index beats two single-column ones when both columns are always used.

Hash measured at 4× the B-tree's size for equality only; BRIN at 24 kB against 2240 kB, useful in proportion to physical/value correlation. GiST for overlap, SP-GiST for partitioned spaces, GIN for containment.

An index on a hot column defeats HOT updates and turns a cheap in-page write into index maintenance.

Exercises

1. Find the skip-scan boundary. Build a table with an index on (lead, other) and query on other alone. Vary the number of distinct lead values — 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 — and record for each whether the plan uses the index and what Index Searches reports. State the approximate cardinality at which the planner gives up.

2. Prove the column order matters. On a table with WHERE a = ? AND b > ?, build (a, b) and (b, a) separately and compare the plans and the actual rows each index scan returns. Explain the difference in terms of what a B-tree can and cannot narrow after a range condition.

3. Make an index-only scan appear and disappear. Get a query to Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0. Then update 10% of the rows and re-run it without vacuuming. Report Heap Fetches. Vacuum and report again. Say what this implies about a read-heavy table whose autovacuum is behind.

4. Cost a partial index. Measure the size and the insert throughput of a table with a full index on a column, and with a partial index covering 1% of the rows. Report both numbers, then find a query the partial index cannot serve and explain why the planner refused it.

5. Break an index six ways. Take a working indexed lookup and, one at a time, make the planner stop using it by: wrapping the column in a function, comparing against the wrong type, using a leading wildcard, making the predicate unselective, deleting the statistics, and shrinking the table. Show each plan.

6. Audit a schema. For a table with at least five indexes, write one query that reports each index's size, its scan count, and whether it is redundant as a prefix of another index. Decide which you would drop, and state what evidence would change your mind.

Solution

1. The skip-scan boundary.

§12.3 measured the endpoints: 50 distinct leading values gives Index Searches: 51 and an index scan; 100,000 gives a Seq Scan. The crossover depends on the table's page count, because the planner is comparing N descents against one sequential pass, so the answer moves with table size rather than being a fixed number of distinct values. On a table ten times larger, skipping stays worthwhile at ten times the cardinality.

The practical form of the rule: a skip scan is viable when distinct_leading_values is small relative to the table's page count.

2. Column order.

With (a, b), both conditions appear in Index Cond and the scan returns only matching rows. With (b, a), the range on b is the leading condition, so the scan reads every entry in the b range and applies a = ? afterwards — visible either as a Filter line or as an Index Cond whose actual rows is far larger than the final result.

The reason is structural. A B-tree is sorted lexicographically. Once you have consumed a column with a range, the entries in that range are ordered by that column first, so the next column is not in sorted order across the range and cannot narrow the descent. Equality preserves the ordering of what follows; a range destroys it.

3. Index-only scan appearing and disappearing.

§12.9 is the worked before-and-after: 280 heap blocks before VACUUM, Heap Fetches: 0 after. After updating 10% of the rows those pages are no longer all-visible, and Heap Fetches climbs to roughly the number of matching rows on modified pages.

The implication is direct: on a read-heavy table with a covering index, an autovacuum that has fallen behind silently converts your fastest plan into your second-fastest, with no change to the query, the index or the statistics. This is one of the strongest arguments for tuning autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor down on large tables (§16.4).

4. Costing a partial index.

The size ratio is the easy half — §12.6 measured 145×. The insert throughput difference is the half people forget: rows outside the predicate do not touch the partial index at all, so on a table where 99% of inserts are status = 'ok', the partial index is maintained on 1% of writes.

The query it cannot serve is any whose predicate the planner cannot prove implies the index's. WHERE status <> 'ok' is the instructive one: on this data it selects exactly the same rows, and the planner still refuses, because the implication status <> 'ok' → status = 'error' is not derivable without knowing the set of values status can take.

5. Six ways to break it.

Function-wrapping and type mismatch both move the cast onto the column side, which is the general principle: an index stores f(nothing) — the raw column — so any expression around the column has to be matched by an expression index. A leading wildcard has no prefix to convert to a range. An unselective predicate is a correct refusal. Deleting statistics (DELETE FROM pg_statistic is not the way — use a fresh table with no ANALYZE) makes the planner guess. A small table makes the scan free.

Only three of the six are bugs in your query. The other three — unselective, small table, correct statistics — are the planner making the right call, and "the index is not used" is not by itself evidence of a problem.

6. Auditing a schema.

SELECT indexrelname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size,
       idx_scan,
       indisunique AS enforces_uniqueness,
       EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_index o
               WHERE o.indrelid = i.indrelid AND o.indexrelid <> i.indexrelid
                 AND o.indkey::text LIKE i.indkey::text || ' %') AS prefix_of_another
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s JOIN pg_index i USING (indexrelid)
WHERE relname = 'audit_demo'
ORDER BY indexrelname;

 indexrelname |  size  | idx_scan | enforces_uniqueness | prefix_of_another 
--------------+--------+----------+---------------------+-------------------
 audit_a      | 456 kB |        0 | f                   | t
 audit_ab     | 456 kB |        0 | f                   | f
 audit_c      | 456 kB |        0 | f                   | f
(3 rows)

audit_a is the drop: prefix_of_another is true, so every query it can serve is served by audit_ab at the same size. The other two are unscanned but not redundant, and the zeros alone are not enough to act on.

The evidence that would change the decision is the same in every case — a query pattern that has not run yet in this measurement window. That is why the counter's start time matters as much as its value, and why the honest procedure is to reset statistics deliberately, wait a full business cycle, and only then read the zeros.

SECTION 13

The Query Planner and EXPLAIN

SQL is a declarative language, which is the property this section is about. You write what you want; PostgreSQL decides how to get it. Between your text and the rows there is a component that reads your query, considers a space of alternative strategies, prices each one, and picks the cheapest. That component is the query planner, and until you can read its output you are tuning a database by superstition.

This is the section where the course stops being about the language and starts being about the system underneath it. Almost every performance problem you will meet in production reduces to one of three sentences: the planner's estimate was wrong, the planner was right and the query is genuinely expensive, or the plan is fine and the problem is somewhere else entirely. Telling those apart is a skill, it is learnable, and EXPLAIN is the whole apparatus.

Everything in this section was measured against PostgreSQL 18.6 on one machine, using the table built in §13.1. Your absolute numbers will differ. The shapes — which node the planner chose, where the estimate diverged from reality, which line accounts for the time — will not, and those are what you are learning to read.

13.1 The Dataset

Every example below runs against these two tables. The point of the row counts is that they are large enough for the planner to have a real decision to make: on a table of twelve rows every strategy costs about the same and the planner will sequentially scan whatever you do, which is why demonstrations built on toy tables teach nothing.

SET timezone = 'UTC';

CREATE TABLE accounts (
  account_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  country    text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE events (
  event_id     bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id   integer     NOT NULL,
  kind         text        NOT NULL,
  amount_cents integer     NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO accounts
SELECT g, (ARRAY['DE','US','BR','JP'])[1 + (g % 4)]
FROM generate_series(1, 5000) AS g;

INSERT INTO events (account_id, kind, amount_cents, created_at)
SELECT (g % 5000) + 1,
       (ARRAY['click','view','purchase','refund'])[1 + (g % 4)],
       (g % 900) + 100,
       timestamptz '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' + (g % 200) * interval '1 day'
FROM generate_series(1, 200000) AS g;

ANALYZE accounts;
ANALYZE events;

The ANALYZE at the end is not decoration. It collects the statistics the planner reasons from (§13.10), and a freshly loaded table without it has statistics claiming it is empty — which produces spectacularly wrong plans until autovacuum catches up.

SELECT count(*) AS events, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('events')) AS heap FROM events;

 events | heap  
--------+-------
 200000 | 12 MB
(1 row)

Two hundred thousand rows in twelve megabytes of heap. Every account has exactly forty events, and each of the four kind values covers a quarter of the table. Those two facts will matter repeatedly, because they are what the planner is trying to estimate and we are in the unusual position of knowing them exactly.

13.2 What Happens Between Your Text and Your Rows

A query passes through four stages, and confusing them is the source of a whole class of wrong intuitions.

Parse
The text becomes a parse tree. Only syntax and name resolution happen here. A misspelled column is caught at this stage, which is why the error arrives before any work is done.
Rewrite
The rewriter applies the rule system (§18.6): views are expanded into their defining query, and row-level security policies (§20.10) are folded into the WHERE clause. What reaches the planner is often not what you typed.
Plan
The planner enumerates strategies, prices each with the cost model, and emits the cheapest plan tree. This is the only stage with any freedom in it, and the only one EXPLAIN shows you.
Execute
The executor walks the plan tree, pulling rows through it. EXPLAIN ANALYZE is this stage instrumented.

Two consequences follow immediately, and both come up constantly.

A view has no plan of its own. Selecting from a view is not "running the view and then filtering"; the rewriter substitutes the view's query into yours and the planner optimises the whole thing at once. That is why a WHERE clause outside a view can end up as an index condition inside it.

The planner is a cost estimator, not an oracle. It does not know your data; it knows a statistical summary of your data, collected by ANALYZE (§13.10). Every planner problem you will ever debug is a discrepancy between that summary and reality.

One line each, for reference: parse tree.

13.3 EXPLAIN: The Plan Tree

The EXPLAIN command prints the plan without running the query.

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE account_id = 42;

                        QUERY PLAN                         
-----------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on events  (cost=0.00..4027.00 rows=40 width=30)
   Filter: (account_id = 42)
(2 rows)

Read this as a tree of plan nodes, printed with the root at the top. Indentation is depth, and -> marks a child. Rows flow upward: each node pulls rows from its children, does something to them, and hands the result to its parent. The topmost node's output is your result set.

The parenthesised figures on a plan node line are all estimates, and each means something specific.

cost=0.00..4027.00
Two numbers. The first is the startup cost — work done before the node can emit its first row. The second is the total cost, for all rows. A Seq Scan can emit immediately so its startup cost is zero; a Sort must consume its entire input first, so its startup cost is nearly its total.
rows=40
The estimated number of rows this node will emit. This is the single most important number in the output, because every decision above it was priced using it.
width=30
Estimated average bytes per output row. It matters mainly for sorts and hashes, which have to hold rows in memory.

The estimate here is rows=40, and we know from §13.1 that exactly forty rows match. The planner got it right — and it still chose to read the entire table, because at this point there is no index on account_id and it has no alternative.

The cost unit is arbitrary. It is not milliseconds, not pages, not rows. By definition, 1.0 is the cost of seq_page_cost, the cost of reading one page sequentially, and everything else is priced relative to that. Comparing costs between two plans for the same query is meaningful. Comparing a cost to a wall-clock time is not.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: explain command and total cost.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: plan node.

13.4 EXPLAIN's Options

Modern EXPLAIN takes a parenthesised option list. These are the ones worth knowing.

ANALYZE
Actually runs the query and reports what really happened alongside the estimates. Nothing else in this section is as useful. Note the name collision with the ANALYZE command (§13.10), which collects statistics and is a completely different thing.
the BUFFERS option
Reports buffer hits in shared buffers, pages read from outside them, and pages written. This is where the I/O actually is. On PostgreSQL 18 it is on by default whenever ANALYZE is on; on 17 and earlier you had to ask.
the VERBOSE option
Adds the output column list of every node, and schema-qualifies names. Verbose, and occasionally the only way to see that a node is carrying twelve columns you never asked for.
the SETTINGS option
Lists any planner-affecting setting that is not at its default. Paste this into a bug report before anyone asks.
GENERIC_PLAN
Plans a statement containing $1 placeholders without values. The only way to see what your driver's prepared statement will do (§13.13) without instrumenting the driver.
COSTS OFF
TIMING OFF
SUMMARY OFF
Suppress the machine-dependent numbers. Essential when you want to compare two plans by shape, or paste one into a document — which is why most blocks in this section use them.
FORMAT JSON
Machine-readable output, for tooling. XML and YAML are also accepted.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query. On a SELECT that is merely slow. On an UPDATE or DELETE it performs the modification. Wrap it in a transaction you roll back:

BEGIN;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
  DELETE FROM events WHERE event_id = 1;
ROLLBACK;

                    QUERY PLAN                     
---------------------------------------------------
 Delete on events (actual rows=0.00 loops=1)
   ->  Index Scan using events_pkey on events (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (event_id = 1)
         Index Searches: 1
(4 rows)

Two details in that output are worth naming now because they appear in every subsequent plan. actual rows=1.00 is printed with two decimal places — PostgreSQL 18 changed this, because the figure is an average per loop and was previously rounded to an integer that could read as 0 for a node that really did return rows. And Index Searches: 1 is new in 18 as well: it counts how many times the index was descended, which is the number that tells you whether an array condition or a nested loop is doing one search or ten thousand.

To have in hand before moving on: buffers option, verbose option, settings option, format json, buffer hits and analyze command.

13.5 Estimate Against Actual

This is the technique. Everything else is detail.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM events WHERE account_id = 42;

                                          QUERY PLAN                                          
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on events  (cost=0.00..4027.00 rows=40 width=30) (actual rows=40.00 loops=1)
   Filter: (account_id = 42)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 199960
(3 rows)

Now each node carries two sets of figures: the planner's estimate, and what execution actually did. Reading a plan is mostly the discipline of comparing them, top to bottom, and stopping at the first node where they diverge badly.

rows=40 vs actual rows=40.00
The row estimate error — actual rows versus estimated rows — is the number that explains most bad plans. Here the ratio is 1.0 and the estimate is perfect.
loops=1
the loops count
How many times this node was executed. Crucially, actual rows is per loop, not a total. §13.6 is entirely about the mistake this causes.
Rows Removed by Filter
Rows this node read and threw away. Here: 199,960 rows read to return 40. That ratio — five thousand rows examined per row returned — is the shape of a missing index, and it is visible without knowing anything about indexes.

Add the index and the shape changes:

CREATE INDEX events_account_id_idx ON events (account_id);
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM events WHERE account_id = 42;

                                QUERY PLAN                                 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on events (actual rows=40.00 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (account_id = 42)
   Heap Blocks: exact=40
   Buffers: shared hit=42 read=2
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_account_id_idx (actual rows=40.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (account_id = 42)
         Index Searches: 1
         Buffers: shared read=2
(8 rows)

Rows Removed by Filter is gone: nothing is being read and discarded any more. The scan touched forty-two buffers instead of the fifteen hundred a full pass would need. Note that BUFFERS appeared without being requested — that is the 18 default mentioned in §13.4.

The ratio to watch is actual rows divided by rows. Under about ten in either direction, the planner is doing fine. Over a hundred, whatever it decided above that node was decided on a fiction, and that is your bug. §13.10 and §13.11 are about fixing the estimate; the alternatives — hints, enable_* switches — treat the symptom.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: actual rows versus estimated rows, loops count and row estimate error.

13.6 The Loops Trap

This is the single most misread thing in EXPLAIN output, and it produces confident wrong conclusions.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF)
  SELECT a.country, (SELECT count(*) FROM events e WHERE e.account_id = a.account_id)
  FROM accounts a WHERE a.account_id < 200;

                                        QUERY PLAN                                         
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using accounts_pkey on accounts a (actual rows=199.00 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (account_id < 200)
   Index Searches: 1
   SubPlan 1
     ->  Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=199)
           ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events e (actual rows=40.00 loops=199)
                 Recheck Cond: (account_id = a.account_id)
                 Heap Blocks: exact=7960
                 ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_account_id_idx (actual rows=40.00 loops=199)
                       Index Cond: (account_id = a.account_id)
                       Index Searches: 199
(11 rows)

Read the Bitmap Heap Scan line as "forty rows" and this plan looks trivial. It is not. actual rows=40.00 loops=199 means forty rows per execution, executed 199 times: 7,960 rows. The Heap Blocks: exact=7960 line is the total and confirms it, and so does Index Searches: 199 — the index was descended once per outer row.

Multiply actual rows by loops before you believe any inner node. Timings behave the same way: with TIMING on, actual time is per loop too, so a node reporting 0.021ms at loops=199 accounts for four milliseconds, not 0.021.

This is why the correlated subquery in §9.3 and the nested loop in §13.8 need the same care. A cheap inner node executed enough times is an expensive plan, and the per-loop presentation hides it.

13.7 The Scan Nodes

Every plan bottoms out in a node that reads a table. There are five you will meet.

Seq Scan
Read every page of the table in physical order. Not a defect — it is the right choice when a large fraction of the table qualifies, because sequential reads are cheap and an index lookup per row is not.
Index Scan
Descend the index, and for each match fetch the row from the heap. Fast for few rows; the heap fetches are in index order, which is random order on disk, so it degrades as the match count grows.
Index Only Scan
The index contains every column the query needs, so the heap is not touched at all — subject to the visibility map (§12.9, §16.6).
Bitmap Index Scan
+ Bitmap Heap Scan
Always a pair. The lower node collects matching row locations into a bitmap; the upper node then visits the heap in physical order. The middle ground: too many rows for random fetches, too few to read the whole table.
Parallel Seq Scan
A sequential scan divided among worker processes (§13.12).

The Recheck Cond on a bitmap heap scan is not a bug. A bitmap can become lossy when it gets large — it starts tracking whole pages rather than individual rows — and the recheck re-applies the condition to the rows on those pages. If you see Heap Blocks: lossy=N in a plan, the bitmap outgrew work_mem.

13.8 The Join Nodes

There are exactly three join strategies, and their trade-off is worth committing to memory.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
  SELECT a.country, count(*) FROM accounts a JOIN events e USING (account_id)
  WHERE e.kind = 'purchase' GROUP BY a.country;

                   QUERY PLAN                    
-------------------------------------------------
 HashAggregate
   Group Key: a.country
   ->  Hash Join
         Hash Cond: (e.account_id = a.account_id)
         ->  Seq Scan on events e
               Filter: (kind = 'purchase'::text)
         ->  Hash
               ->  Seq Scan on accounts a
(8 rows)

Hash Join. Build a hash table from the smaller side — the Hash node — then stream the larger side past it. O(n + m), needs work_mem to hold the hash table, and works only for equality conditions. The default for joining two large inputs.

The Hash node reports its own memory use when you run with ANALYZE:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM events e JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = e.account_id % 500
  WHERE e.event_id < 3000;

                                  QUERY PLAN                                  
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Hash Join (actual rows=2993.00 loops=1)
   Hash Cond: ((e.account_id % 500) = a.account_id)
   ->  Index Scan using events_pkey on events e (actual rows=2999.00 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (event_id < 3000)
         Index Searches: 1
   ->  Hash (actual rows=5000.00 loops=1)
         Buckets: 8192  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 255kB
         ->  Seq Scan on accounts a (actual rows=5000.00 loops=1)
(8 rows)

Batches: 1 is the number to look at. It means the hash table fitted in work_mem in one pass. Anything above 1 means PostgreSQL spilled it to disk and had to make multiple passes over both inputs — usually the largest single win available from raising work_mem.

Nested Loop. For each row of the outer input, scan the inner input. O(n × m) in general, which sounds fatal and is not: when the inner side is an index lookup parameterised by the outer row, each iteration is cheap and this is the best plan for a small outer input.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM accounts a JOIN events e USING (account_id)
  WHERE a.account_id BETWEEN 1 AND 30;

                        QUERY PLAN                        
----------------------------------------------------------
 Nested Loop
   ->  Index Scan using accounts_pkey on accounts a
         Index Cond: ((account_id >= 1) AND (account_id <= 30))
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on events e
         Recheck Cond: (a.account_id = account_id)
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_account_id_idx
               Index Cond: (account_id = a.account_id)
(7 rows)

Thirty outer rows, an index lookup each. Note Index Cond: (account_id = a.account_id) — the inner scan is parameterised by the outer row, which is what makes this cheap. A nested loop whose inner side is a Seq Scan at high loops is the classic disaster plan, and it is almost always caused by an underestimate of the outer row count.

Merge Join. Sort both inputs on the join key, then walk them in lockstep. Cheap if both inputs are already sorted — typically because both sides are index scans on the join column.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SET enable_hashjoin = off;
SET enable_nestloop = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM accounts a JOIN events e USING (account_id);

                      QUERY PLAN                       
-------------------------------------------------------
 Merge Join
   Merge Cond: (a.account_id = e.account_id)
   ->  Index Scan using accounts_pkey on accounts a
   ->  Index Scan using events_account_id_idx on events e
(4 rows)

Both sides arrive pre-sorted from their indexes, so no Sort node is needed. A Materialize node under one side of a join means the executor is caching that side's rows so it can be rescanned without re-executing the subplan — common under a merge join with duplicate keys, and under a nested loop whose inner side is not parameterised.

A Memoize node is the newer alternative to that: it caches inner-side results keyed by the join parameter, so a nested loop over repeated outer values executes the inner side once per distinct value rather than once per row. It appears when the planner expects many repeats.

In summary, the vocabulary here is materialize node and memoize node.

13.9 Sorting, Grouping and the Rest

A Sort node is where work_mem first shows itself: it governs how much memory a single sort or hash may use, and its effect is directly visible.

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SET work_mem = '64kB';
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY amount_cents;

                        QUERY PLAN                        
----------------------------------------------------------
 Sort (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
   Sort Key: amount_cents
   Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 8648kB
   ->  Seq Scan on events (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
(4 rows)

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SET work_mem = '64MB';
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY amount_cents;

                        QUERY PLAN                        
----------------------------------------------------------
 Sort (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
   Sort Key: amount_cents
   Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 15910kB
   ->  Seq Scan on events (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
(4 rows)

Sort Method: external merge Disk: 8648kB is a report of a temporary file. The same sort with enough memory is quicksort Memory: 15910kB. Note the disk figure is smaller than the memory figure — the on-disk representation is more compact than the in-memory one, so you cannot size work_mem from the disk number; you need roughly twice it.

work_mem is per sort or hash node, per worker, not per query and certainly not per server. A query with three sorts running with two parallel workers can use nine times the setting. That is why the default is small and why raising it globally is how servers run out of memory.

An Incremental Sort is the Sort node's cheaper relative, exploiting a partially sorted input:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
CREATE INDEX events_created_idx ON events (created_at);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM events ORDER BY created_at, amount_cents LIMIT 20;

                        QUERY PLAN                         
-----------------------------------------------------------
 Limit
   ->  Incremental Sort
         Sort Key: created_at, amount_cents
         Presorted Key: created_at
         ->  Index Scan using events_created_idx on events
(5 rows)

Presorted Key: created_at is the point: the index already delivers rows in created_at order, so only the groups sharing a created_at need sorting. Combined with LIMIT 20, the query stops after the first group or two instead of sorting two hundred thousand rows.

The two grouping nodes differ the same way:

  • HashAggregate builds a hash table of groups. No sort required, needs work_mem, and the output has no defined order — a fact that has caused more wrong course examples than any other (§8.7).
  • GroupAggregate requires sorted input and streams the groups out. Chosen when a sort is needed anyway, or when the group count is too large to hash.

Above those you will see Limit, Result (a node computing an expression with no table), Append (concatenating the branches of a UNION ALL or the partitions of a partitioned table, §19.6), Unique, and SubPlan / InitPlan for subqueries the planner could not flatten. An InitPlan runs once; a SubPlan runs per outer row, which §13.6 showed is the expensive case.

What to carry forward from this subsection: parallel worker.

The terms above, gathered: sort node.

13.10 What the Planner Actually Knows

The planner's estimates come from statistics collected by the ANALYZE command and stored in the system catalogs. The readable view is pg_stats.

SELECT attname, n_distinct, null_frac,
       CASE WHEN abs(correlation) > 0.9 THEN 'ordered' ELSE 'scattered' END AS physical_order
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'events' AND attname IN ('event_id','kind','created_at','amount_cents')
ORDER BY attname;

   attname    | n_distinct | null_frac | physical_order 
--------------+------------+-----------+----------------
 amount_cents |        900 |         0 | scattered
 created_at   |        200 |         0 | scattered
 event_id     |         -1 |         0 | ordered
 kind         |          4 |         0 | scattered
(4 rows)

n_distinct is the number of distinct values. A negative value is a ratio rather than a count: -1 for event_id means "distinct values scale with the table size, one per row" — exactly right for a generated key, and the reason the planner does not assume a fixed count that goes stale as the table grows.

correlation — bucketed above, for a reason worth stating — measures how closely physical row order tracks the column's sort order, from -1 to 1. event_id is 1.0: rows were inserted in key order, so consecutive index entries point at consecutive pages and an index scan on it is cheap. The other three sit near zero, so the same number of index matches costs far more heap I/O. This single column is why an index on a monotonically increasing timestamp behaves so differently from an index on a random UUID (§12.16).

account_id is missing from that query, and its absence is the lesson. pg_stats holds a sample, not a census. Four consecutive ANALYZE runs against this unchanged table reported its n_distinct as 5001, 5006, 4999 and 5002 — the true answer is 5,000 — and its correlation moved in the third decimal place each time. Nothing was wrong; ANALYZE reads 300 × default_statistics_target rows at random and infers the rest. Treat every figure in pg_stats as an estimate with error bars, including when it disagrees with what you know.

The skewed-column machinery is most_common_vals and the histogram:

SELECT v.value AS common_value,
       CASE WHEN v.freq BETWEEN 0.20 AND 0.30 THEN 'about a quarter of the table'
            ELSE 'something else' END AS share
FROM pg_stats s
