CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(s.most_common_vals::text::text[], s.most_common_freqs)
                     AS v(value, freq)
WHERE s.tablename = 'events' AND s.attname = 'kind'
ORDER BY v.value;

 common_value |            share             
--------------+------------------------------
 click        | about a quarter of the table
 purchase     | about a quarter of the table
 refund       | about a quarter of the table
 view         | about a quarter of the table
(4 rows)

All four values are most common values, stored with their measured frequencies, so estimating WHERE kind = 'purchase' is a lookup rather than a guess. That is what makes a skewed column safe: status = 'archived' matching 99% of rows and status = 'pending' matching 0.1% get different plans, because the MCV list knows the difference.

Values too rare for the MCV list are covered by the histogram bounds in histogram_bounds, an equi-depth histogram — each bucket holds roughly the same number of rows, so the bucket widths encode the distribution.

SELECT array_length(histogram_bounds::text::text[], 1) AS boundaries
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'events' AND attname = 'amount_cents';

 boundaries 
------------
        101
(1 row)

101 boundaries is 100 buckets, which is default_statistics_target — 100 MCV entries, 100 histogram buckets, sampled from 300 × 100 = 30,000 rows. Raising it — globally, or per column with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS — buys better estimates for skewed columns at the cost of slower ANALYZE and slightly slower planning. Raise it on the column that is actually mis-estimating, not everywhere.

ANALYZE runs automatically via autovacuum (§16.4). It runs manually after a bulk load, because a table you just loaded a million rows into has statistics that say it is empty, and every plan against it will be wrong until the daemon catches up.

One line each, for reference: most common values and histogram bounds.

13.11 Extended Statistics: When Columns Are Not Independent

Per-column statistics assume columns are independent. Real schemas are full of columns that are not, and the resulting underestimate is one of the most common causes of a bad plan.

CREATE TABLE geo AS
SELECT g AS id,
       (ARRAY['DE','US','BR'])[1 + (g % 3)] AS country,
       (ARRAY['Berlin','NYC','Rio'])[1 + (g % 3)] AS city
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) AS g;
ANALYZE geo;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM geo WHERE country = 'DE' AND city = 'Berlin';

                                        QUERY PLAN                                        
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on geo  (cost=0.00..2076.00 rows=11267 width=12) (actual rows=33333.00 loops=1)
   Filter: ((country = 'DE'::text) AND (city = 'Berlin'::text))
   Rows Removed by Filter: 66667
(3 rows)

Every row in Berlin is in Germany, so the two conditions select exactly the same third of the table. The planner estimated 11,267 against an actual 33,333 — it multiplied the two selectivities as if they were independent, and landed at a third of a third. On a scan that error is harmless. Feed rows=11267 into a join above it and the planner will pick a nested loop for a workload three times larger than it expects.

CREATE STATISTICS tells the planner about the relationship.

CREATE STATISTICS geo_stx (dependencies, ndistinct) ON country, city FROM geo;
ANALYZE geo;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
  SELECT * FROM geo WHERE country = 'DE' AND city = 'Berlin';

                                        QUERY PLAN                                        
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on geo  (cost=0.00..2076.00 rows=33600 width=12) (actual rows=33333.00 loops=1)
   Filter: ((country = 'DE'::text) AND (city = 'Berlin'::text))
   Rows Removed by Filter: 66667
(3 rows)

11,267 became 33,600 against an actual 33,333 — an error of 3× reduced to an error of 0.8%. Nothing about the query, the data or the indexes changed; the planner was simply told that the columns are related.

The three kinds of extended statistics answer different questions.

dependencies
Functional dependency statistics. "Knowing city tells you country." Fixes the multiplied-selectivity underestimate above, which is the common case.
ndistinct
ndistinct statistics. How many distinct combinations the columns take. Fixes group-count estimates for GROUP BY country, city, which otherwise multiplies out to nine when the truth is three.
mcv
Most-common combinations, with frequencies. The most precise and the most expensive; use it when the dependency is not uniform across values.

Statistics can also be built on expressions: CREATE STATISTICS ON (lower(email)) FROM users gives the planner a distribution for an expression it would otherwise have to guess at with a hardcoded default. That is the same problem an expression index solves (§12.7), without the index.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: functional dependency statistics and ndistinct statistics.

13.12 Parallel Query

For a large scan the planner may divide the work among parallel workers.

EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE kind = 'purchase';

                      QUERY PLAN                       
-------------------------------------------------------
 Finalize Aggregate
   ->  Gather
         Workers Planned: 1
         ->  Partial Aggregate
               ->  Parallel Seq Scan on events
                     Filter: (kind = 'purchase'::text)
(6 rows)

Read it from the bottom. Each worker runs a Parallel Seq Scan over its share of the pages and a Partial Aggregate over what it finds. The Gather node collects the partial results into the leader process, and Finalize Aggregate combines them into one. That two-stage shape is parallel aggregation, and it is why count(*), sum() and avg() parallelise while an arbitrary user-defined aggregate may not.

Gather does not preserve order. When ordered output is needed the planner uses Gather Merge, which merges pre-sorted worker streams and keeps the sort.

The settings that govern this:

max_parallel_workers_per_gather
Workers per Gather, default 2. Setting it to 0 disables parallelism for the session — which is exactly what most blocks in this section do, so that the plans printed here are stable and comparable.
min_parallel_table_scan_size
8 MB by default. Below it, no parallel scan is considered at all — which is why parallelism never appears in small demonstrations.
parallel_setup_cost
1000 by default. Starting workers is not free, and this constant is what stops the planner parallelising a query that would finish first without them.

Workers Planned and Workers Launched can differ. The planner asks for workers; the executor gets what the server's global pool has left. A plan that was fast in testing and slow in production, with the same shape, is often this: Workers Launched: 0 because max_parallel_workers was already exhausted.

A function must be marked parallel-safe to run inside a worker. Anything that writes to the database, reads session state, or is marked PARALLEL UNSAFE (the default for a user-defined function, §18.13) forces the whole query to run serially — a mislabelled function is a common and invisible reason a query refuses to parallelise.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: gather node, gather merge, parallel-safe and parallel aggregation.

13.13 Generic Plans and Custom Plans

A prepared statement — PREPARE, or a parameterised query from any driver — plans once and executes many times. But planning with the actual parameter is better, so PostgreSQL does both, and the switchover is observable.

PREPARE p(int) AS SELECT * FROM events WHERE account_id = $1;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE p(42);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE p(42);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE p(42);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE p(42);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE p(42);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) EXECUTE p(42);

                    QUERY PLAN                    
--------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on events
   Recheck Cond: (account_id = 42)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_account_id_idx
         Index Cond: (account_id = 42)
(4 rows)

... four more plans, identical to the first ...

                    QUERY PLAN                    
--------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on events
   Recheck Cond: (account_id = $1)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_account_id_idx
         Index Cond: (account_id = $1)
(4 rows)

The first five executions show account_id = 42; the sixth shows account_id = $1. Those first five are custom plans, planned afresh with the real value. On the sixth, PostgreSQL compares the average custom-plan cost against the generic plan it built, finds the generic one no more expensive, and switches to it permanently — saving the planning work on every subsequent call. This is prepared statement plan caching, and the "five, then decide" rule is exactly what you just watched happen.

It is the right default and it has one sharp failure mode: a skewed parameter. If account_id = 42 matches forty rows but account_id = 7 matches four hundred thousand, the generic plan is a compromise that suits neither, and the query mysteriously slows down on its sixth call. plan_cache_mode forces the issue — force_custom_plan when parameter values genuinely change the right strategy, force_generic_plan when planning cost dominates.

GENERIC_PLAN lets you see the generic plan without executing anything, which is how you check what your driver will actually run:

EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN, COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM events WHERE account_id = $1;

                    QUERY PLAN                    
--------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on events
   Recheck Cond: (account_id = $1)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on events_account_id_idx
         Index Cond: (account_id = $1)
(4 rows)

To have in hand before moving on: prepared statement plan caching.

13.14 The Cost Model and Its Constants

The planner cost model prices every plan from a handful of settings.

SELECT name, setting, unit FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('seq_page_cost','random_page_cost','cpu_tuple_cost',
               'cpu_index_tuple_cost','cpu_operator_cost','effective_cache_size')
ORDER BY name;

         name         | setting | unit 
----------------------+---------+------
 cpu_index_tuple_cost | 0.005   | 
 cpu_operator_cost    | 0.0025  | 
 cpu_tuple_cost       | 0.01    | 
 effective_cache_size | 524288  | 8kB
 random_page_cost     | 4       | 
 seq_page_cost        | 1       | 
(6 rows)

Read these as ratios against seq_page_cost = 1. Processing one row costs a hundredth of a page read; evaluating one operator costs a four-hundredth.

random_page_cost = 4 is the one that is usually wrong. It encodes the assumption that a random read costs four times a sequential one — true of a spinning disk, and roughly four times too pessimistic on SSDs. On flash storage, 1.1 is the usual recommendation, and lowering it is the single most effective way to stop the planner preferring sequential scans over index scans on a machine where the difference barely exists.

effective_cache_size is not an allocation. It tells the planner how much memory it should assume is available for caching across PostgreSQL and the operating system together, and it is used only to decide how likely an index page is to already be in cache. Setting it to about half to three-quarters of system RAM is the convention. It costs nothing to be generous with, because nothing is reserved.

jit is on by default, and compiles expressions to machine code once a plan's estimated cost exceeds jit_above_cost (500,000). It is a large win on genuinely analytical queries and a measurable loss on a cheap query whose estimate was inflated — compilation time is spent before the query starts. A query whose plan shows a JIT section and finishes in two milliseconds of execution after twenty of compilation is a real pattern, and the fix is fixing the estimate.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: planner cost model.

13.15 Nudging the Planner, and Why You Usually Should Not

PostgreSQL has no query hints, deliberately. What it has instead are session settings.

The enable_* family — enable_seqscan, enable_indexscan, enable_nestloop, enable_hashjoin, enable_hashagg and about twenty more — are diagnostic tools, not configuration. And they do not do what their names suggest:

CREATE TABLE tiny_unindexed AS SELECT g AS n FROM generate_series(1, 1000) AS g;
ANALYZE tiny_unindexed;
SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM tiny_unindexed;

            QUERY PLAN            
----------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Seq Scan on tiny_unindexed
         Disabled: true
(3 rows)

The table has no index, enable_seqscan is off, and the planner sequentially scanned it anyway. These settings add an enormous cost penalty; they do not remove the option, because a query with no usable index must still be answerable. PostgreSQL 18 says so out loud with the Disabled: true annotation — before 18 the only clue was an absurd cost figure around 1e10, which is easy to miss and easier to misread.

Use these switches to ask "what would the second-best plan have been, and what did it cost?", then fix the underlying estimate. Shipping enable_nestloop = off in application code is how a system acquires a setting nobody can remove five years later.

join_collapse_limit (default 8) is different in kind. Above that many tables in a FROM clause, the planner stops considering all join orders — the search space is factorial — and geqo_threshold (12) switches it to a genetic algorithm that samples rather than enumerates. A twelve-table join that plans slowly and executes badly is often this, and explicit JOIN syntax constrains the order in a way comma-separated tables do not.

PostgreSQL 18 adds two optimisations with their own switches, both on by default: enable_self_join_elimination removes a self-join on a unique key that could not change the result, and enable_distinct_reordering lets SELECT DISTINCT reorder its keys to avoid a sort.

In summary, the vocabulary here is from clause.

13.16 Finding the Queries Worth Looking At

Everything above assumes you already know which query is slow. Three tools tell you that.

pg_stat_statements is the one that matters. It is an extension, enabled by adding it to shared_preload_libraries and restarting, then:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

CREATE EXTENSION

It aggregates every executed statement by normalised text — constants replaced by placeholders, so a million single-row lookups appear as one row — with total and mean execution time, call count, rows returned and buffer counts. Sort by total_exec_time, not mean_exec_time. The query worth fixing is usually not the slow one; it is the two-millisecond query called four hundred thousand times an hour.

auto_explain logs the plan of any statement exceeding a duration threshold, so you get the plan for the slow production execution rather than the fast one you can reproduce. It is a loadable module rather than a CREATE EXTENSION extension — it is loaded through shared_preload_libraries or session_preload_libraries and configured with auto_explain.log_min_duration. Enable auto_explain.log_analyze with care: it instruments every statement, and on a busy server the timing overhead is real.

log_min_duration_statement is the slow query log, built in and requiring nothing. Set it to a threshold you actually care about and the statement text lands in the server log. It is the crudest of the three and the first one to turn on.

The pg_stat_activity view (§1.9) covers the other half of the question — not "what was slow" but "what is running right now, and what is it waiting for".

What to carry forward from this subsection: slow query log.

What This Section Established

The planner turns a declarative query into a plan tree by pricing alternatives with a cost model fed by sampled statistics. Every performance investigation is an attempt to find where that pricing went wrong.

EXPLAIN prints the tree, root at the top, rows flowing upward; cost=startup..total, rows and width are estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and adds what actually happened.

The core technique is comparing rows against actual rows from the top down and stopping at the first large divergence. Under 10× is fine; over 100× means everything decided above that node was decided on a fiction.

actual rows and actual time are per loop. Multiply by loops before drawing a conclusion — a node reporting 40 rows at 199 loops moved 7,960 rows.

Scans: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, and the Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan pair for the middle ground. Joins: Hash Join for two large inputs, Nested Loop for a small outer input with a parameterised inner index scan, Merge Join for two pre-sorted inputs. Materialize and Memoize cache an inner side for rescanning.

work_mem is per node per worker. Sort Method: quicksort versus external merge, and Batches: 1 versus more, are the two lines that say whether it was enough.

Statistics live in pg_stats: n_distinct (negative means a ratio), correlation (why an index on a sequential key behaves unlike one on a UUID), most_common_vals and the histogram. Per-column statistics assume independence; CREATE STATISTICS fixes the resulting underestimate, measured here as 11,267 against 33,333 becoming 33,600.

Parallel plans read bottom-up as worker scan → partial aggregate → Gather → finalize. Workers Planned is a request, Workers Launched is what arrived.

A prepared statement plans a custom plan five times, then switches to a generic plan — watched happen in §13.13 — which is the right default and a trap for skewed parameters.

random_page_cost = 4 assumes a spinning disk. enable_* settings are diagnostics, and they penalise rather than prohibit. pg_stat_statements sorted by total time is how you find the query that matters.

Exercises

1. Read a plan cold. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF) on SELECT count(*) FROM events e JOIN accounts a USING (account_id) WHERE a.country = 'DE' AND e.kind = 'purchase'. For each node, state its job, its estimated rows, its actual rows, and the ratio. Identify the node where the estimate is worst and explain what it caused above it.

2. Multiply the loops. Take the correlated-subquery plan from §13.6 and compute, from the plan alone, the total number of heap rows visited by the inner bitmap heap scan. Verify against Heap Blocks and Index Searches. Then rewrite the query as a GROUP BY join and compare both the plan shape and the total work.

3. Make the estimate wrong on purpose. Build a two-column table where the columns are perfectly correlated, query both columns with equality, and record the estimate and the actual. Add CREATE STATISTICS with dependencies, re-ANALYZE, and record both again. Then delete the statistics object and instead raise default_statistics_target — report whether it helps, and explain why.

4. Find the memory cliff. Sort events by amount_cents at work_mem values of 64kB, 1MB, 4MB and 64MB. Record Sort Method and the reported disk or memory figure at each. State the smallest work_mem at which the sort stays in memory, and explain why the disk figure is smaller than the memory figure.

5. Watch the plan freeze. PREPARE a statement whose parameter is heavily skewed — build a table where one value appears in 90% of rows and the rest are rare. Execute it six times with a rare value, printing the plan each time, and identify the execution at which the plan becomes generic. Then execute with the common value and explain what the generic plan costs you. Fix it with plan_cache_mode.

6. Price the disk. Find a query on events that the planner answers with a Seq Scan. Lower random_page_cost step by step and find the value at which it switches to an index scan. State what that value implies about the storage the default is written for, and whether the switch made the query faster on your machine.

Solution

1. Reading a plan cold.

The plan is a Hash Join with a filtered Seq Scan on events and a filtered Seq Scan on accounts under a Hash, with an Aggregate on top.

The method, not the specific numbers, is the answer. Work top-down. The Aggregate emits one row, always, so its estimate is uninteresting. The join's estimate is the product of its inputs' estimates and its selectivity — if it is wrong, look at the inputs before blaming the join. kind = 'purchase' is estimated from the MCV list in §13.10 and should be within a percent. country = 'DE' likewise.

The instructive part is that both filters are accurate and the join estimate can still drift, because the join selectivity is computed from n_distinct on both sides. That is why n_distinct being 5002 rather than 5000 matters more at a join than at a scan.

2. Multiplying the loops.

40.00 × 199 = 7,960 heap rows, which is exactly the Heap Blocks: exact=7960 figure, and Index Searches: 199 confirms 199 separate descents of the index.

Rewritten as a join:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF, BUFFERS OFF)
SELECT a.country, count(e.event_id)
FROM accounts a LEFT JOIN events e USING (account_id)
WHERE a.account_id < 200
GROUP BY a.account_id, a.country;

                                         QUERY PLAN                                          
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 HashAggregate (actual rows=199.00 loops=1)
   Group Key: a.account_id
   Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 32kB
   ->  Hash Right Join (actual rows=7960.00 loops=1)
         Hash Cond: (e.account_id = a.account_id)
         ->  Seq Scan on events e (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
         ->  Hash (actual rows=199.00 loops=1)
               Buckets: 1024  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 16kB
               ->  Index Scan using accounts_pkey on accounts a (actual rows=199.00 loops=1)
                     Index Cond: (account_id < 200)
                     Index Searches: 1
(11 rows)

The same 7,960 result rows, reached a completely different way. The subquery form did 199 index searches and touched 7,960 heap blocks; the join form does one sequential pass over all 200,000 rows and hashes 199 accounts against it — Index Searches does not appear at all, because the events table is never indexed into.

Which is better depends entirely on the outer row count, and that is the real lesson. At 199 accounts out of 5,000 the planner judged one full scan cheaper than 199 index descents. Narrow the WHERE to account_id < 5 and it will switch back to a nested loop. The rewrite did not make the query faster by itself; it made a second strategy available, and the planner picked between them. A correlated subquery of this shape can only ever be executed one way.

3. Making the estimate wrong on purpose.

§13.11 is the worked version: 11,267 estimated against 33,333 actual, becoming 33,600 after CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies).

Raising default_statistics_target does not help, and understanding why is the point of the exercise. The per-column statistics were never wrong — country = 'DE' really is a third of the table and city = 'Berlin' really is a third. More samples make both more precise and leave their product exactly as wrong. The error is in the independence assumption, not in the sampling, and only extended statistics address it.

4. The memory cliff.

64kB gives external merge Disk: 8648kB; 64MB gives quicksort Memory: 15910kB. The crossover on this dataset is between 4 MB and 64 MB, and the exact point depends on the row width.

The disk figure is smaller because the on-disk tuple format for a sort run is packed, while the in-memory representation carries per-tuple pointers and alignment padding (§3.14). So sizing work_mem from the Disk: figure systematically under-provisions; roughly double it is the working rule.

5. Watching the plan freeze.

The switch happens on the sixth EXECUTE, as measured in §13.13: five custom plans showing the literal value, then one showing $1.

With a skewed column, the five rare-value executions produce a cheap index plan, and their average cost is what the generic plan is compared against. The generic plan is built from the average selectivity across all values, which for a 90/10 skew is dominated by the common value — so the generic plan is a sequential scan, and every subsequent rare-value lookup pays for a full table read.

SET plan_cache_mode = 'force_custom_plan';

Re-plans every time. The cost is planning work on every execution; the benefit is that the plan always matches the parameter. Use it on a statement with a known-skewed parameter, not globally.

6. Pricing the disk.

The switch point depends on the fraction of the table selected. The general result: the planner compares random_page_cost × pages_fetched_randomly against seq_page_cost × total_pages, so as random_page_cost falls toward seq_page_cost the index becomes attractive for larger and larger result fractions.

4 encodes a seek-dominated device: a spinning disk, where a random read really is several milliseconds and a sequential read is nearly free. An SSD has no seek, so the honest ratio is close to 1.0; 1.1 is the common recommendation, leaving a small margin so the planner still prefers sequential access all else being equal.

Whether the switch made it faster is the second half, and the honest answer is often "no" — on a table already in shared buffers, both plans read from memory and the cost model's distinction is invisible. That is what effective_cache_size exists to express, and it is why measuring beats tuning constants from a blog post.

SECTION 14

Transactions, MVCC and Isolation

A transaction is the unit in which a database keeps its promises. Everything you have written so far has been running inside one — PostgreSQL wraps every bare statement in an implicit transaction — and this section is about taking control of that boundary, and about what happens when two of them run at the same time.

The second half is the part that matters and the part most often taught badly. Concurrency bugs in databases are not crashes. They are quietly wrong answers: a balance that lost a deposit, two doctors who both went off call, a booking counted twice. They pass tests, because tests run one thing at a time. They appear in production, because production does not.

Every concurrency example in this section actually runs two sessions. That is unusual — most treatments print a two-column table of "session 1 / session 2" and ask you to believe it — and it matters, because several of the results below are not what the folklore says.

14.1 The Two-Session Harness

To make interleaved transactions runnable in a single script, this section opens a second connection to the same database with the dblink extension and sends statements down it. In real work you would use two psql windows; the mechanism differs, the semantics do not.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS dblink;

CREATE FUNCTION other(sql text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$
  SELECT dblink_exec('host=127.0.0.1 port=' || current_setting('port')
                     || ' dbname=' || current_database()
                     || ' user=' || current_user, sql)
$$;

CREATE EXTENSION
CREATE FUNCTION

other('...') runs its argument in a separate backend, with its own transaction, and returns when that finished. Because it is a separate connection, its work is invisible to our transaction until it commits — which is the whole subject of this section.

The connection string is built from current_setting('port') and current_database() rather than hardcoded, so it works on any server without editing. Note that dblink sends its own transaction: unless the string you pass contains BEGIN, each statement commits immediately.

14.2 ACID, and What Each Letter Costs

Atomicity
All of the transaction happens, or none of it. Implemented by writing new row versions and deciding at commit whether they are visible — which is why a rollback in PostgreSQL is nearly free and a commit is the expensive one.
Consistency
ACID consistency is the weakest letter: it means only that constraints hold at the end. It is your schema's job, not the database's — a CHECK nobody wrote is a rule nobody enforces.
Isolation
ACID isolation is the letter with a dial on it (§14.9). "As if run one at a time" is only what the strongest setting gives you, and it is not the default.
Durability
Once committed, it survives a crash. Bought by the write-ahead log (§16.9), and negotiable — synchronous_commit = off trades a window of recent commits for throughput.

The terms above, gathered: atomicity, acid consistency and acid isolation.

14.3 The Boundary: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK

Outside an explicit block, each statement runs in an implicit transaction of its own. That is autocommit, and it is a client-side convention rather than a server mode: the server wraps any statement not already in a block. A BEGIN statement (or the spelling START TRANSACTION) opens a block; a COMMIT statement (or END) makes it durable; a ROLLBACK statement (or ABORT) discards it.

CREATE TABLE ledger (id int PRIMARY KEY, holder text, amount int);
INSERT INTO ledger VALUES (1, 'ada', 100), (2, 'lin', 100);

BEGIN;
UPDATE ledger SET amount = amount - 30 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE ledger SET amount = amount + 30 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

SELECT holder, amount FROM ledger ORDER BY holder;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
BEGIN
UPDATE 1
UPDATE 1
COMMIT
 holder | amount 
--------+--------
 ada    |     70
 lin    |    130
(2 rows)

The transfer is atomic: no other session ever observes a moment where the thirty exists in neither account or in both. That is the entire reason the boundary exists.

One line each, for reference: begin statement, commit statement, rollback statement, start transaction and autocommit.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: implicit transaction.

14.4 A Failed Statement Poisons the Block

This behaviour surprises people arriving from other databases, and it is deliberate.

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
CREATE TABLE poison (v int);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO poison VALUES (1);
SELECT 1/0;
SELECT 'can I still run?';
ROLLBACK;
SELECT count(*) AS rows_kept FROM poison;

CREATE TABLE
BEGIN
INSERT 0 1
ERROR:  division by zero
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
ROLLBACK
 rows_kept 
-----------
         0
(1 row)

The first line of that block is a psql meta-command: \set ON_ERROR_STOP off tells psql to keep going after an error rather than exiting, which is what an interactive session does by default and what a script needs to be told. Every other block in this course runs with it on.

After any error the transaction enters an aborted state and refuses everything until you end the block. The successful INSERT is discarded too, because it was part of a transaction that did not commit — ROLLBACK here is not undoing your choice, it is the only exit.

That is safe by construction, and occasionally too blunt. §14.5 is the escape hatch.

14.5 Savepoints and Subtransactions

A savepoint marks a point you can return to without abandoning the whole transaction.

CREATE TABLE steps (v int);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO steps VALUES (1);
SAVEPOINT before_risky;
INSERT INTO steps VALUES (2);
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_risky;
INSERT INTO steps VALUES (3);
RELEASE SAVEPOINT before_risky;
COMMIT;
SELECT v FROM steps ORDER BY v;

CREATE TABLE
BEGIN
INSERT 0 1
SAVEPOINT
INSERT 0 1
ROLLBACK
INSERT 0 1
RELEASE
COMMIT
 v 
---
 1
 3
(2 rows)

Row 2 is gone, rows 1 and 3 survived. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT also clears the aborted state from §14.4, which is what makes "try this, and carry on if it fails" possible inside one transaction. RELEASE SAVEPOINT discards the marker without undoing anything.

Each savepoint opens a subtransaction with its own transaction id, and they are not free. A loop that opens one per iteration — which in PL/pgSQL means a BEGIN ... EXCEPTION block per iteration (§18.20), because an exception handler is an implicit savepoint — can allocate tens of thousands of subtransaction ids, overflow the per-backend cache of 64, and force other sessions into slow visibility checks. "Catch the exception inside the loop" is a well-known way to make a fast function slow at scale.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: exception block.

14.6 Transactional DDL

PostgreSQL's CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP INDEX and almost every other schema change are transactional — a property MySQL and Oracle do not share, and one that changes how you write migrations (§20.5).

BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE ghost (x int);
INSERT INTO ghost VALUES (1);
ROLLBACK;
SELECT to_regclass('ghost') IS NULL AS table_is_gone;

BEGIN
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
ROLLBACK
 table_is_gone 
---------------
 t
(1 row)

A migration that adds three columns, backfills them and adds a constraint either happens entirely or leaves no trace. The exceptions are few and each has a reason: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (§12.11), CREATE DATABASE, VACUUM, and ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE before PostgreSQL 12 all need to be outside a transaction block.

14.7 MVCC: What an UPDATE Physically Does

Multiversion Concurrency Control is the mechanism underneath everything else in this section, and the fastest way to understand it is to look at the page.

An UPDATE in PostgreSQL does not overwrite a row. It writes a new row version and marks the old one as expired. ctid — the physical (page, item) address — shows it moving:

CREATE TABLE mvcc_demo (id int PRIMARY KEY, v text);
INSERT INTO mvcc_demo VALUES (1, 'first');
UPDATE mvcc_demo SET v = 'second' WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE mvcc_demo SET v = 'third'  WHERE id = 1;
SELECT ctid, id, v FROM mvcc_demo;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
UPDATE 1
UPDATE 1
 ctid  | id |   v   
-------+----+-------
 (0,3) |  1 | third
(1 row)

One logical row, and it is now the third item on page zero. The first two versions are still physically present, and pageinspect will show them:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
CREATE TABLE mvcc_page (id int PRIMARY KEY, v text);
INSERT INTO mvcc_page VALUES (1, 'first');
UPDATE mvcc_page SET v = 'second' WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE mvcc_page SET v = 'third'  WHERE id = 1;
SELECT lp, t_ctid, f.raw_flags
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('mvcc_page', 0)) hpi,
     LATERAL (SELECT (heap_tuple_infomask_flags(hpi.t_infomask, hpi.t_infomask2)).raw_flags) AS f
ORDER BY lp;

CREATE EXTENSION
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
UPDATE 1
UPDATE 1
 lp | t_ctid |                             raw_flags                             
----+--------+-------------------------------------------------------------------
  1 | (0,2)  | {HEAP_HASVARWIDTH,HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED,HEAP_HOT_UPDATED}
  2 | (0,3)  | {HEAP_HASVARWIDTH,HEAP_UPDATED,HEAP_HOT_UPDATED,HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE}
  3 | (0,3)  | {HEAP_HASVARWIDTH,HEAP_XMAX_INVALID,HEAP_UPDATED,HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE}
(3 rows)

Three physical rows for one logical row, chained by t_ctid: version 1 points at version 2, which points at version 3, which points at itself because it is current. HEAP_XMAX_INVALID on the last one means nothing has expired it.

Four consequences follow from this single design, and they explain most of PostgreSQL's operational character.

Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers
A reader looking for an older version finds it still there. This is the payoff, and it is why PostgreSQL needs no read locks at all.
Updates create garbage
Every update leaves a dead tuple behind. Someone has to collect them, which is VACUUM (§16.1), and failing to is table bloat (§16.3).
Rollback is cheap, commit is the work
Aborting means marking a transaction id as never-committed. Nothing is undone; the versions it wrote simply never become visible.
count(*) must count
There is no single true row count, because the answer depends on who is asking. That is why PostgreSQL cannot keep a counter the way MyISAM could.

The HEAP_HOT_UPDATED and HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE flags above mark a HOT update — heap-only tuple. When an update changes no indexed column and the new version fits on the same page, PostgreSQL skips creating index entries entirely and chains the versions within the page. That is a large win, and it is the concrete reason for the advice in §12.18 not to index a column your workload updates constantly: an index on last_seen_at turns every heartbeat write from a HOT update into an index write.

To have in hand before moving on: table bloat.

14.8 xmin, xmax and Visibility

Every row carries two hidden system columns (§4.11) that decide who can see it.

CREATE TABLE visibility_demo (id int PRIMARY KEY, v text);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO visibility_demo VALUES (1, 'first');
SELECT xmin = pg_current_xact_id()::text::xid AS written_by_this_transaction,
       xmax = '0'::xid                        AS not_yet_expired,
       v
FROM visibility_demo;
COMMIT;

CREATE TABLE
BEGIN
INSERT 0 1
 written_by_this_transaction | not_yet_expired |   v   
-----------------------------+-----------------+-------
 t                           | t               | first
(1 row)

COMMIT

The BEGIN is load-bearing, and getting it wrong is instructive. Without it the INSERT and the SELECT are two separate transactions, so pg_current_xact_id() in the second one reports a different id and the comparison comes back f — which looks like evidence that xmin is not what this section says it is, and is really evidence that you changed transactions between the two statements.

That comparison is the whole of tuple visibility. xmin is the transaction that created this version; xmax is the transaction that expired it, or 0 if it is still current. A row is visible to you if xmin committed before your MVCC snapshot was taken and xmax is either zero or belongs to a transaction that had not committed by then. That is the whole rule.

The actual xid values are not printed here on purpose — they differ on every run — but the comparison is the point. And one detail of the mechanism is worth knowing because it explains a real operational fact:

SELECT pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned() IS NULL AS read_only_session_has_no_xid;

 read_only_session_has_no_xid 
------------------------------
 t
(1 row)

A transaction that has not written anything is assigned no transaction id at all. Ids are handed out lazily, on the first write. This is why a reporting workload of pure SELECTs consumes no xids and contributes nothing to wraparound (§16.7) — though, as §14.17 covers, a long read-only transaction still holds back vacuum by keeping an old snapshot alive.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: mvcc snapshot and tuple visibility.

14.9 The Four Isolation Levels

The transaction isolation level is set per transaction, and the SQL standard defines four of them by which anomalies they forbid. PostgreSQL implements three of them; READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted for compatibility and behaves exactly like READ COMMITTED, because MVCC gives no way to read uncommitted data even if you asked.

Level
Non-repeatable read
Phantom read
Write skew
Read Committed
the default
possible
possible
possible
Repeatable Read
prevented
prevented
possible
Serializable
prevented
prevented
prevented

Two entries in that table are worth flagging before the demonstrations.

PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevents phantom reads, which the SQL standard permits it to allow. The standard's table was written for a lock-based implementation; a snapshot-based one gets phantom prevention for free. So advice ported from other databases about "use Serializable to avoid phantoms" does not apply here.

Write skew is the anomaly the standard's table does not mention, and it is the one that bites real applications. §14.13 is entirely about it.

The default is set by default_transaction_isolation and is read committed; a single transaction overrides it with BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL ... or SET TRANSACTION.

In summary, the vocabulary here is transaction isolation level and non-repeatable read.

14.10 Read Committed: Each Statement Gets a Fresh Snapshot

At READ COMMITTED, every statement takes a new snapshot. So within one transaction, two identical queries can return different answers.

CREATE TABLE rc_demo (id int PRIMARY KEY, amount int);
INSERT INTO rc_demo VALUES (1, 100);

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
SELECT amount AS first_read FROM rc_demo WHERE id = 1;
SELECT other('UPDATE rc_demo SET amount = 999 WHERE id = 1') AS meanwhile;
SELECT amount AS second_read FROM rc_demo WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
BEGIN
 first_read 
------------
        100
(1 row)

 meanwhile 
-----------
 UPDATE 1
(1 row)

 second_read 
-------------
         999
(1 row)

COMMIT

100, then 999, inside one transaction. That is a non-repeatable read, and it is not a bug — it is what READ COMMITTED is defined to allow. The 999 is committed data, so nothing was dirty; it simply arrived between the two statements.

A phantom read is the same thing at the level of row membership:

CREATE TABLE phantom_demo (id int PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO phantom_demo VALUES (1), (2);

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
SELECT count(*) AS first_count FROM phantom_demo;
SELECT other('INSERT INTO phantom_demo VALUES (3)') AS meanwhile;
SELECT count(*) AS second_count FROM phantom_demo;
COMMIT;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
BEGIN
 first_count 
-------------
           2
(1 row)

 meanwhile  
------------
 INSERT 0 1
(1 row)

 second_count 
--------------
            3
(1 row)

COMMIT

A read skew is the related shape where two reads inside one transaction see a mutually inconsistent picture of related rows, and it follows from the same snapshot rule.

A dirty read — seeing another transaction's uncommitted work — is the one anomaly PostgreSQL cannot produce at any level. Uncommitted row versions have an xmin belonging to an in-progress transaction, and the visibility rule in §14.8 excludes them.

There is one subtlety in READ COMMITTED that catches people, and it is not a snapshot rule. When an UPDATE finds a row that another transaction has concurrently modified and committed, it does not use its own snapshot's version — it waits for the other transaction, then re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the new version and proceeds if it still matches. That is why UPDATE ledger SET amount = amount - 30 is safe under concurrency while a read-then-write in application code is not, which is §14.11.

What to carry forward from this subsection: dirty read and read skew.

14.11 The Lost Update

This is the most common real concurrency bug, and it needs no exotic isolation level to produce.

CREATE TABLE lost_demo (id int PRIMARY KEY, amount int);
INSERT INTO lost_demo VALUES (1, 100);

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
SELECT amount AS i_read FROM lost_demo WHERE id = 1;
SELECT other('UPDATE lost_demo SET amount = amount + 50 WHERE id = 1') AS meanwhile;
UPDATE lost_demo SET amount = 100 - 30 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;
SELECT amount AS final FROM lost_demo WHERE id = 1;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
BEGIN
 i_read 
--------
    100
(1 row)

 meanwhile 
-----------
 UPDATE 1
(1 row)

UPDATE 1
COMMIT
 final 
-------
    70
(1 row)

The deposit of 50 vanished. We read 100, the other session added 50 to make 150, and then we wrote back 100 - 30 = 70 — a value computed from a number that was no longer true. Nothing errored. The balance is simply wrong.

This is exactly the shape of balance = fetch(); balance -= 30; save(balance) in application code, and it is why that shape is a bug. There are three fixes, in increasing order of scope.

Compute in SQL
UPDATE ... SET amount = amount - 30. The re-evaluation rule from §14.10 makes this correct with no locking, no retry and no extra round trip. Prefer it whenever the new value is a function of the old.
Lock the row you read
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (§15.6). The other session blocks until you commit. Necessary when the new value depends on something SQL cannot compute — a decision made in application code, or a call to another service.
Detect and retry
REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE turn this into an error you must handle (§14.15), or an explicit version column (§11.12).

14.12 Repeatable Read: One Snapshot for the Whole Transaction

At REPEATABLE READ isolation, the snapshot is taken once, at the first statement, and every subsequent statement in the transaction sees exactly that.

CREATE TABLE rr_demo (id int PRIMARY KEY, amount int);
INSERT INTO rr_demo VALUES (1, 100);

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT amount AS first_read FROM rr_demo WHERE id = 1;
SELECT other('UPDATE rr_demo SET amount = 999 WHERE id = 1') AS meanwhile;
SELECT amount AS second_read FROM rr_demo WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;
SELECT amount AS after_commit FROM rr_demo WHERE id = 1;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
BEGIN
 first_read 
------------
        100
(1 row)

 meanwhile 
-----------
 UPDATE 1
(1 row)

 second_read 
-------------
         100
(1 row)

COMMIT
 after_commit 
--------------
          999
(1 row)

100 and 100, where READ COMMITTED gave 100 and 999 — and 999 the moment the transaction ends. This is what you want for a report that runs twenty queries and must have them agree with each other.

The cost is that writing becomes fallible. If a REPEATABLE READ transaction tries to update a row that changed after its snapshot, it cannot silently use the newer version — that would break the illusion — so it aborts with ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update, SQLSTATE 40001. Your application must be prepared to retry (§14.15).

The terms above, gathered: repeatable read isolation and sqlstate 40001.

14.13 Write Skew: The Anomaly Repeatable Read Allows

Repeatable Read prevents your reads from changing. It does not prevent two transactions from making decisions on overlapping data and writing conclusions that are jointly wrong. The canonical case is an on-call rota with a rule: at least one doctor must remain on call.

CREATE TABLE oncall (doctor text PRIMARY KEY, on_call boolean NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO oncall VALUES ('ada', true), ('lin', true);

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT count(*) AS others_on_call FROM oncall WHERE on_call AND doctor <> 'ada';
SELECT other($x$ BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
                 SELECT count(*) FROM oncall WHERE on_call AND doctor <> 'lin';
                 UPDATE oncall SET on_call = false WHERE doctor = 'lin';
                 COMMIT; $x$) AS lin_went_off_call;
UPDATE oncall SET on_call = false WHERE doctor = 'ada';
COMMIT;
SELECT count(*) AS still_on_call FROM oncall WHERE on_call;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
BEGIN
 others_on_call 
----------------
              1
(1 row)

 lin_went_off_call 
-------------------
 COMMIT
(1 row)

UPDATE 1
COMMIT
 still_on_call 
---------------
             0
(1 row)

Both transactions checked the rule, both saw one other doctor on call, both committed, and nobody is on call. No error, no conflict, no lost update — the two transactions wrote different rows, so nothing collided. Each was individually correct against the state it saw. Their combination is not.

That is write skew — a serialization anomaly, meaning an outcome no serial order could have produced — and it is the reason Repeatable Read is not enough for an invariant that spans rows. Notice what would not have caught it: a CHECK constraint cannot see other rows; a unique index has nothing to be unique on; SELECT FOR UPDATE on the rows you read would have worked but requires knowing in advance that this is the hazard.

One line each, for reference: serialization anomaly.

14.14 Serializable: Refusing the Combination

SERIALIZABLE guarantees that any set of concurrent transactions that commit produce a result achievable by running them one at a time, in some order. PostgreSQL implements it with Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): it runs at Repeatable Read speed with no extra blocking, tracks the read/write dependencies between transactions with predicate locks, and aborts one when the pattern it detects could not have arisen serially.

The same rota, one word changed:

CREATE TABLE oncall_ssi (doctor text PRIMARY KEY, on_call boolean NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO oncall_ssi VALUES ('ada', true), ('lin', true);

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT count(*) AS others_on_call FROM oncall_ssi WHERE on_call AND doctor <> 'ada';
SELECT other($x$ BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
                 SELECT count(*) FROM oncall_ssi WHERE on_call AND doctor <> 'lin';
                 UPDATE oncall_ssi SET on_call = false WHERE doctor = 'lin';
                 COMMIT; $x$) AS lin_went_off_call;
UPDATE oncall_ssi SET on_call = false WHERE doctor = 'ada';
COMMIT;

BEGIN
 others_on_call 
----------------
              1
(1 row)

 lin_went_off_call 
-------------------
 COMMIT
(1 row)

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during write.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.
ROLLBACK

The second transaction was refused. Two details in that output are worth reading precisely, because both are commonly stated wrongly.

It failed at the UPDATE, not at COMMIT. SSI detects the dangerous structure as soon as this transaction becomes the pivot — the one with both an incoming and an outgoing read/write dependency — which here is at the write. Serialization failures at commit time do also happen; the point is that you cannot assume the failure arrives only there, so your error handling has to wrap the whole transaction.

The HINT is part of the contract. "The transaction might succeed if retried" is not consolation; retrying is the documented way to use this isolation level. A SERIALIZABLE application without a retry loop is an application that will fail under load.

SSI's costs are real and worth stating: it tracks predicate locks in a fixed-size shared structure, and when that fills, locks are escalated from row to page to relation, which increases false positives — aborts of transactions that would in fact have been fine. max_pred_locks_per_transaction governs the budget. And read-only transactions can be declared DEFERRABLE (§14.16) to get a snapshot that is guaranteed conflict-free.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: serializable snapshot isolation.

14.15 The Retry Loop

At REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, 40001 is a normal outcome, not an exception. The transaction did nothing wrong; it was chosen as the one to sacrifice.

The rules for handling it are short and each has a failure mode attached.

Retry the whole transaction
From BEGIN, re-reading everything. The old snapshot is what was wrong; reusing any value read under it reintroduces the bug you were paying to avoid.
Match on SQLSTATE, not the message
40001 serialization_failure, and its neighbour 40P01 deadlock_detected (§15.6), which is retryable for exactly the same reason. Message text is localised and it changes between releases.
Back off, and cap the attempts
Immediate retries of a contended transaction reproduce the conflict. Exponential backoff with jitter, and a limit — an unbounded retry loop against a genuinely conflicting workload is a busy-wait.
Retry must be safe to repeat
The database rolled its work back; anything outside the database — an email, a payment call, a queue message — did not. Keep external effects out of a retryable transaction (§20.3).

The rate of 40001 is a tuning signal. A few per thousand transactions is the cost of the guarantee. A steady stream means genuine contention on the same rows, and the fix is in the data model — sharding a hot counter, or queueing the updates — not in the isolation level.

14.16 READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE

A READ ONLY transaction, declared with SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY, is an intent the server enforces:

BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY;
CREATE TABLE nope (x int);
ROLLBACK;

BEGIN
SET
ERROR:  cannot execute CREATE TABLE in a read-only transaction
ROLLBACK

It blocks INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and DDL on non-temporary objects. Two reasons to use it beyond safety: a read-only transaction is never chosen as the victim of a serialization failure, and on a hot standby (§16.16) it is the only kind permitted.

A DEFERRABLE transaction — SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE — is the specialist tool. The transaction waits until it can obtain a snapshot guaranteed to be free of serialization conflicts, and then runs with no predicate-lock overhead and no possibility of 40001. For a long analytical query that must see a consistent state and must not fail, that trade — an unpredictable wait at the start, in exchange for never aborting — is usually the right one.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: read only transaction, deferrable transaction and hot standby.

14.17 Long Transactions Are an Operational Hazard

MVCC's price is that no dead row version can be removed while any snapshot might still need it. An open transaction pins a snapshot. Therefore:

One idle transaction can bloat the entire database. Not just the tables it touched — vacuum cannot clean any row version newer than the oldest snapshot in the system (§16.5). A session that ran one SELECT, held the transaction open and went to lunch will stop vacuum making progress on every table for an hour.

The state to look for is idle in transaction:

SELECT state, backend_type FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' ORDER BY state;

 state  |  backend_type  
--------+----------------
 active | client backend
(1 row)

active means running a statement. idle in transaction means inside BEGIN and running nothing — waiting on the application, which is the dangerous one. idle with no transaction is harmless.

The defences are settings, and they should be on in production:

  • idle_in_transaction_session_timeout terminates a session that sits in an open transaction too long. Minutes, not hours.
  • statement_timeout caps any single statement.
  • transaction_timeout (new in PostgreSQL 17) caps the whole transaction regardless of how it splits into statements.

The application-side cause is nearly always the same: a connection pool or ORM that opens a transaction at the start of a web request and holds it across an HTTP call to another service. Open the transaction as late as you can, and close it before doing anything slow that is not the database's business.

To have in hand before moving on: statement_timeout.

What This Section Established

A transaction is the unit of atomicity. BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK set the boundary; outside one, every statement is its own transaction.

An error aborts the whole block and every subsequent statement is refused until you end it. SAVEPOINT is the escape hatch, and it opens a real subtransaction with a real cost — one per loop iteration is a known way to make a function slow.

DDL is transactional, which is why migrations can be all-or-nothing.

MVCC means an UPDATE writes a new row version rather than overwriting. Measured with pageinspect: one logical row, three physical versions on one page, chained by t_ctid, flagged as HOT updates because no indexed column changed. Readers never block writers; the price is dead tuples, vacuum and bloat.

xmin is the creating transaction, xmax the expiring one. A transaction that has not written is assigned no xid at all.

Three usable isolation levels. READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot per statement — demonstrated: 100 then 999 in one transaction. REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot for the transaction — 100 then 100. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevents phantoms, which the standard permits it to allow.

The lost update needs no exotic level: read 100, another session adds 50, we write 70, and the 50 is gone with no error. Fix it by computing in SQL, by SELECT FOR UPDATE, or by an isolation level that turns it into a retryable error.

Write skew is the anomaly Repeatable Read allows: both doctors checked the rule, both saw a colleague on call, both went off call, and zero remained. SERIALIZABLE refuses it — and the refusal arrived at the UPDATE, not at COMMIT, with Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during write.

40001 is a normal outcome at those levels. Retry the whole transaction, match on SQLSTATE rather than message text, back off with a cap, and keep external side effects out of anything retryable.

READ ONLY is enforced and is never chosen as a serialization victim; SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE waits for a safe snapshot and then cannot fail.

Long transactions block vacuum globally. Watch for idle in transaction, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout and transaction_timeout.

Exercises

1. Poison and recover. Inside one transaction, run a statement that errors, then prove that a subsequent valid statement is refused. Repeat with a SAVEPOINT before the failing statement and a ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after it, and show that the transaction continues and commits. State which of the two behaviours you would want in a batch importer and why.

2. Watch the row move. Create a one-row table and record its ctid. Update it five times, recording ctid each time. Then run VACUUM and update it once more. Explain the sequence of addresses, and say what changed after the vacuum.

3. Produce a lost update, then three fixes. Reproduce §14.11. Then fix it three ways — computing the new value in SQL, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and REPEATABLE READ with a retry — and for each, state what it costs and when it is the right choice.

4. Prove Repeatable Read prevents phantoms. Run the §14.10 phantom experiment at REPEATABLE READ instead. Report the two counts. Then explain why the SQL standard lists phantom reads as permitted at this level, and why PostgreSQL does not exhibit them.

5. Skew, then serialize. Build an invariant that spans two rows — a rota, or "the sum of these balances must stay non-negative". Break it with two concurrent REPEATABLE READ transactions. Then run the identical experiment at SERIALIZABLE, and report the exact error, the statement it arrived at, and the reason code.

6. Cost the guarantee. Write a retry loop around a SERIALIZABLE transaction. Run a contended workload through it and count retries per successful commit. Then change the workload so the transactions touch disjoint rows, and count again. Explain what the difference tells you about where serialization failures come from.

7. Block a vacuum. In one session, open a transaction, run a single SELECT and leave it open. In another, update and delete rows in an unrelated table repeatedly and run VACUUM (VERBOSE). Report what the vacuum says about removable rows. Close the first transaction and vacuum again. State the setting that would have prevented this.

Solution

1. Poison and recover.

Without a savepoint, ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block, and the earlier successful insert is lost as well. With a savepoint:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
CREATE TABLE importer (v int);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO importer VALUES (1);
SAVEPOINT row2;
INSERT INTO importer VALUES (1/0);
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT row2;
INSERT INTO importer VALUES (3);
COMMIT;
SELECT v FROM importer ORDER BY v;

CREATE TABLE
BEGIN
INSERT 0 1
SAVEPOINT
ERROR:  division by zero
ROLLBACK
INSERT 0 1
COMMIT
 v 
---
 1
 3
(2 rows)

For a batch importer that must skip bad rows, the savepoint version is what you want — but per §14.5 it allocates a subtransaction per row, and at a million rows that is a real cost. The usual production answer is neither: validate in a staging table, or use COPY ... ON_ERROR ignore with REJECT_LIMIT (§11.9), which does the skipping without a subtransaction per row.

2. Watching the row move.

ctid advances (0,1), (0,2), (0,3), … as each update writes a new version onto the same page, exactly as §14.7 measured. After VACUUM reclaims the dead versions, the next update can reuse a freed line pointer, so the address may go backwards rather than continuing to climb. That is the whole point of vacuum: without it the page fills and the table grows (§16.3).

ctid is therefore not an identifier. It changes on every update and is reused after vacuum, so storing one is a bug.

3. Lost update, three fixes.

Computing in SQL:

CREATE TABLE fix_sql (id int PRIMARY KEY, amount int);
INSERT INTO fix_sql VALUES (1, 100);
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
SELECT other('UPDATE fix_sql SET amount = amount + 50 WHERE id = 1') AS meanwhile;
UPDATE fix_sql SET amount = amount - 30 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;
SELECT amount AS final FROM fix_sql WHERE id = 1;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
BEGIN
 meanwhile 
-----------
 UPDATE 1
(1 row)

UPDATE 1
COMMIT
 final 
-------
   120
(1 row)

120, not 70. Both changes survived: 100 + 50 − 30. No locking, no retry, one statement. This is the right fix whenever the new value is a function of the old.

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE costs a blocked writer for the duration of your transaction, and is what you need when the new value comes from outside SQL. REPEATABLE READ costs a retry loop and is what you need when the decision spans several rows or several statements.

4. Repeatable Read and phantoms.

Both counts are 2. The insert commits, and our snapshot predates it, so the row is invisible for the life of the transaction.

The standard's table describes a lock-based implementation, where preventing phantoms requires range locks that two-phase locking at "repeatable read" does not take. A snapshot-based implementation has no such gap: the snapshot excludes every transaction that had not committed when it was taken, whether that transaction updated a row or inserted one. PostgreSQL gets phantom prevention as a side effect of the mechanism, not as an extra guarantee it chose to buy.

5. Skew, then serialize.

§14.13 and §14.14 are the worked answers: still_on_call = 0 at REPEATABLE READ, and at SERIALIZABLE:

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during write.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.

Arriving at the UPDATE. "Pivot" is the SSI term: the transaction sitting in the middle of a dangerous structure, with a read/write dependency in and another out. Aborting the pivot is sufficient to break the cycle, which is why one of the two transactions succeeds rather than both failing.

6. Costing the guarantee.

On the same rows, retries scale with concurrency — every transaction reads what another is about to write, so the dangerous structure forms constantly. On disjoint rows the rate falls to approximately zero.

The lesson is that serialization failures are a property of the access pattern, not of the isolation level. SERIALIZABLE did not create the contention; it made a pre-existing correctness problem visible as an error instead of as a wrong number. Raising the isolation level of a workload that hammers one counter row converts silent corruption into a retry storm, and neither is the fix — the data model is.

7. Blocking a vacuum.

VACUUM (VERBOSE) reports dead tuples that it cannot remove, in the form N dead row versions cannot be removed yet, oldest xmin: NNN. That oldest xmin is the open transaction's snapshot.

The critical observation is that the open transaction touched an unrelated table. Vacuum's horizon is global: it cannot remove any version that any snapshot in the system might still need, and it has no way to know that this snapshot will never look at this table.

idle_in_transaction_session_timeout would have terminated the idle session. In PostgreSQL 17 and later transaction_timeout also covers the case where the session is not idle but merely slow.

SECTION 15

Locking, Concurrency Patterns and Deadlocks

§14 was about what a transaction sees. This section is about what a transaction stops other transactions from doing, which is a separate mechanism with separate rules.

MVCC means PostgreSQL takes no locks for reading. Everything below is therefore about writes, about schema changes, and about the cases where you deliberately want to make a reader block — because sometimes "read the current value and act on it" is a claim you need to enforce rather than a hope.

The two-session harness from §14.1 is reused throughout, with two additions so that a second session can run a query and return a value.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION conn() RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$
  SELECT 'host=127.0.0.1 port=' || current_setting('port')
         || ' dbname=' || current_database() || ' user=' || current_user
$$;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION other(sql text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql AS $$
  SELECT dblink_exec(conn(), sql)
$$;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION other_bool(sql text) RETURNS boolean LANGUAGE sql AS $$
  SELECT r FROM dblink(conn(), sql) AS t(r boolean)
$$;

CREATE TABLE seats (seat_id int PRIMARY KEY, taken_by text);
INSERT INTO seats SELECT g, NULL FROM generate_series(1, 5) AS g;

CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 5

15.1 Two Lock Systems

PostgreSQL has two independent locking systems, and confusing them makes lock diagnosis impossible.

Table-level locks
Eight named modes on a whole relation, taken automatically by every statement and held to the end of the transaction. Visible in pg_locks. This is what makes ALTER TABLE dangerous and SELECT harmless.
Row-level locks
Four strengths on individual rows, stored in the row itself — in xmax and the infomask (§14.8), not in shared memory. There is therefore no limit on how many you can hold, and no lock-escalation behaviour of the kind SQL Server has.

That second point deserves emphasis, because it is a real architectural difference. PostgreSQL never escalates row locks to a table lock. Locking ten million rows costs ten million row headers, not a table lock — the memory cost is paid in the heap, which is already being written. (The exception is predicate locks under SERIALIZABLE, §14.14, which do live in shared memory and do escalate.)

15.2 The Eight Table-Level Lock Modes

Every statement takes a table-level lock, whether or not you asked. You can watch it:

BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM seats;
SELECT mode, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE relation = 'seats'::regclass;
COMMIT;

BEGIN
 count 
-------
     5
(1 row)

      mode       | granted 
-----------------+---------
 AccessShareLock | t
(1 row)

COMMIT

BEGIN;
UPDATE seats SET taken_by = 'ada' WHERE seat_id = 1;
SELECT mode, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE relation = 'seats'::regclass ORDER BY mode;
COMMIT;

BEGIN
UPDATE 1
       mode       | granted 
------------------+---------
 RowExclusiveLock | t
(1 row)

COMMIT

A SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE; an UPDATE takes ROW EXCLUSIVE. The names are historical and slightly misleading — ROW EXCLUSIVE is a table-level mode despite the word "row"; it means "this transaction is modifying rows in this table".

The eight modes, weakest first, with what takes each:

ACCESS SHARE
SELECT. Conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.
ROW SHARE
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE.
ROW EXCLUSIVE
INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE. Several transactions hold it at once — this is the normal write mode.
SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE
VACUUM, ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and the cheap forms of ALTER TABLE. Allows reads and writes; blocks schema changes and itself.
SHARE
CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY. Reads proceed; writes block.
SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE
CREATE TRIGGER, and some ALTER TABLE forms. Blocks writes and itself.
EXCLUSIVE
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY. Only plain SELECT is still allowed.
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
Most ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, REINDEX, CLUSTER, VACUUM FULL. Blocks everything, including SELECT.
BEGIN;
LOCK TABLE seats IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE;
SELECT mode, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE relation = 'seats'::regclass ORDER BY mode;
COMMIT;

BEGIN
LOCK TABLE
        mode         | granted 
---------------------+---------
 AccessExclusiveLock | t
(1 row)

COMMIT

Two rules follow, and between them they cause most production lock incidents.

A lock is held until the transaction ends, not until the statement ends. An ALTER TABLE inside a long transaction holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole transaction, not for the millisecond the alter took.

A blocked ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request blocks everything queued behind it. Lock requests are served in order, so the lock queue is first-in, first-out. So an ALTER TABLE waiting behind one long-running SELECT will stall every subsequent SELECT too — the table appears completely frozen, and the cause is a statement that is merely slow rather than one that is blocking. This is why every migration should set lock_timeout (§15.8).

Named once more, since each is referred to later: share row exclusive and lock queue.

In summary, the vocabulary here is SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE.

15.3 Row-Level Locks: Four Strengths

BEGIN;
SELECT seat_id FROM seats WHERE seat_id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT other($x$ SELECT seat_id FROM seats WHERE seat_id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT; $x$);
COMMIT;

BEGIN
 seat_id 
---------
       1
(1 row)

ERROR:  could not obtain lock on row in relation "seats"
CONTEXT:  while executing command on unnamed dblink connection
ROLLBACK

The second session was refused because the first holds the row. The four strengths, strongest first:

FOR UPDATE
"I intend to change or delete this row." Blocks every other row lock, and — see §15.4 — blocks inserts into referencing tables.
FOR NO KEY UPDATE
"I intend to change a non-key column." What a plain UPDATE takes when it does not touch a unique key. Weaker in exactly one way, and that way matters.
FOR SHARE
"Nobody may change this row while I look at it." Several sessions may hold it together.
FOR KEY SHARE
"Nobody may change this row's key." What a foreign-key check takes on the parent row.

15.4 The Foreign-Key Trap

This one costs people real outages, and it is invisible until you look.

CREATE TABLE parent (id int PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE child (id int PRIMARY KEY, parent_id int REFERENCES parent);
INSERT INTO parent VALUES (1);

BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM parent WHERE id = 1 FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
SELECT other('INSERT INTO child VALUES (1, 1)') AS child_insert;
COMMIT;

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
BEGIN
 id 
----
  1
(1 row)

 child_insert 
--------------
 INSERT 0 1
(1 row)

COMMIT

The child insert succeeded while the parent row was locked. Now the same thing with FOR UPDATE:

BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM parent WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT other($x$ SET lock_timeout = '150ms'; INSERT INTO child VALUES (2, 1); $x$) AS child_insert;
COMMIT;

BEGIN
 id 
----
  1
(1 row)

ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
CONTEXT:  while locking tuple (0,1) in relation "parent"
SQL statement "SELECT 1 FROM ONLY "public"."parent" x WHERE "id" OPERATOR(pg_catalog.=) $1 FOR KEY SHARE OF x"
while executing command on unnamed dblink connection
ROLLBACK

The error message shows PostgreSQL's own foreign-key check, and it is a FOR KEY SHARE on the parent — which FOR UPDATE blocks and FOR NO KEY UPDATE does not.

So: locking a row in a table that other tables reference will block inserts into all of them, if you use FOR UPDATE. On a "tenants" or "organisations" table this is catastrophic and mystifying: a background job locks one organisation row, and every write anywhere in the application for that customer stops.

Use FOR NO KEY UPDATE unless you are actually going to change the key or delete the row. That is the whole rule, and it is the reason the mode exists.

15.5 NOWAIT, SKIP LOCKED, and the Queue Pattern

The default when a row lock conflicts is to wait. Two modifiers change that.

NOWAIT raises an error immediately, as §15.3 showed. Use it when waiting is worse than failing — an interactive request that should say "someone else is editing this" rather than hang.

SKIP LOCKED silently omits locked rows. That one word makes a correct work queue possible:

BEGIN;
SELECT seat_id AS i_locked FROM seats ORDER BY seat_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT other($x$ CREATE TABLE claimed AS
                 SELECT seat_id FROM seats ORDER BY seat_id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; $x$);
COMMIT;
SELECT seat_id AS other_session_got FROM claimed;

BEGIN
 i_locked 
----------
        1
(1 row)

  other   
----------
 SELECT 1
(1 row)

COMMIT
 other_session_got 
-------------------
                 2
(1 row)

Session one took seat 1; session two asked for "the first seat" and got seat 2. No blocking, no conflict, no duplicate. That queue table pattern is the entire mechanism behind every "just use your database as a job queue" article, and it is genuinely sound:

CREATE TABLE jobs (job_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
                   payload text NOT NULL, state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ready');
INSERT INTO jobs (payload) SELECT 'job ' || g FROM generate_series(1, 3) AS g;

UPDATE jobs SET state = 'running'
WHERE job_id = (SELECT job_id FROM jobs WHERE state = 'ready'
                ORDER BY job_id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1)
RETURNING job_id, payload;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 job_id | payload 
--------+---------
      1 | job 1   
(1 row)
UPDATE 1

Two properties make this correct where a naive SELECT then UPDATE is not. The subquery locks the row it picks, so no two workers can select the same job; and SKIP LOCKED means the second worker moves to the next row rather than waiting for the first. Add a partial index on (job_id) WHERE state = 'ready' (§12.6) and the scan stays cheap as completed jobs accumulate.

The honest limits: this queue has no delivery guarantee beyond the transaction, no cross-database fan-out, and a worker that crashes leaves a row in running until something times it out. For many systems that is entirely acceptable and one less service to operate.

What to carry forward from this subsection: lock conflict and queue table pattern.

15.6 Deadlocks

A deadlock is a cycle: A holds what B wants, B holds what A wants. PostgreSQL detects it and kills one of them.

Two sessions, each updating two rows in the opposite order, is the minimal case. Running it requires genuine concurrency — two asynchronous connections — and the exception handler is there because the whole point is that one of them fails:

CREATE TABLE dl (id int PRIMARY KEY, v int);
INSERT INTO dl VALUES (1, 0), (2, 0);

DO $$
BEGIN
  PERFORM dblink_connect('a', conn()), dblink_connect('b', conn());
  PERFORM dblink_exec('a', 'BEGIN'), dblink_exec('b', 'BEGIN');
  PERFORM dblink_exec('a', 'UPDATE dl SET v = 1 WHERE id = 1');       -- a holds row 1
  PERFORM dblink_exec('b', 'UPDATE dl SET v = 1 WHERE id = 2');       -- b holds row 2
  PERFORM dblink_send_query('a', 'UPDATE dl SET v = 2 WHERE id = 2'); -- a now wants row 2
  PERFORM dblink_send_query('b', 'UPDATE dl SET v = 2 WHERE id = 1'); -- b now wants row 1
  PERFORM * FROM dblink_get_result('b') AS r(x text);
  PERFORM * FROM dblink_get_result('a') AS r(x text);
  RAISE NOTICE 'no deadlock was detected';
EXCEPTION WHEN deadlock_detected THEN
  RAISE NOTICE 'SQLSTATE % (%)', SQLSTATE, 'deadlock_detected';
END $$;
SELECT dblink_disconnect('a'), dblink_disconnect('b');

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
NOTICE:  SQLSTATE 40P01 (deadlock_detected)
DO
 dblink_disconnect | dblink_disconnect 
-------------------+-------------------
 OK                | OK
(1 row)

40P01, deadlock_detected. The full message a client would see names both processes and the tuple involved:

ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 64242 waits for ShareLock on transaction 2239; blocked by process 64243.
Process 64243 waits for ShareLock on transaction 2238; blocked by process 64242.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,2) in relation "dl"

Four things worth knowing about that:

Deadlock detection is not instant. PostgreSQL waits deadlock_timeout — one second by default — before it even looks for a cycle, because building the wait-for graph is expensive and almost every wait resolves on its own. So a deadlock costs at least a second before anyone is released. Lowering deadlock_timeout makes detection faster and the check more frequent; it is rarely the right knob.

One transaction is killed, the other proceeds. You cannot choose which.

40P01 is retryable, exactly like 40001 (§14.15). Same handler, same backoff.

The fix is lock ordering. If every transaction that touches several rows takes them in a consistent order — ascending primary key is the usual choice — a cycle cannot form. That is a code discipline, not a setting, and it is the only real prevention. ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE in the statement that acquires the locks is often all it takes.

The terms above, gathered: deadlock detection and lock ordering.

15.7 Seeing What Is Blocked

When something is stuck, three views answer three different questions.

BEGIN;
UPDATE seats SET taken_by = 'ada' WHERE seat_id = 1;
SELECT dblink_connect('waiter', conn());
SELECT dblink_exec('waiter', 'BEGIN');
SELECT dblink_send_query('waiter', 'UPDATE seats SET taken_by = ''lin'' WHERE seat_id = 1');
SELECT pg_sleep(0.4);
SELECT count(*) > 0 AS a_lock_request_is_waiting FROM pg_locks WHERE NOT granted;
SELECT count(*) > 0 AS something_is_blocked
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
COMMIT;
SELECT * FROM dblink_get_result('waiter') AS r(x text);
SELECT * FROM dblink_get_result('waiter') AS r(x text);
SELECT dblink_disconnect('waiter');

pg_locks
Every lock held or requested. WHERE NOT granted is the whole diagnostic — those rows are the waiters.
pg_blocking_pids(pid)
The array of backends blocking this one. Far easier than joining pg_locks to itself, which is what everyone did before it existed.
pg_stat_activity
The blocking query's text, the state, and wait_event_type/wait_event. Join it to the pids to get from "something is blocked" to "this statement, run by this application, is the culprit".

The blocker is often not the waiter's neighbour. Follow pg_blocking_pids transitively to the root — a backend that is blocked by nobody but is holding a lock everything else is queued behind. Nine times in ten it is idle in transaction (§14.17).

pg_terminate_backend(pid) ends a session; pg_cancel_backend(pid) cancels its current statement and leaves the session alive. Prefer cancel first.

One line each, for reference: blocking query.

15.8 Timeouts

Waiting forever is never the behaviour you want in production.

the lock_timeout setting
Caps time spent waiting for a lock, not time executing. Set it before every migration: a low value makes the ALTER TABLE fail fast instead of queueing behind a slow query and freezing the table (§15.2).
statement_timeout
Caps total statement time. The blunt instrument, and the right default for anything driven by a web request.
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
Kills a session sitting in an open transaction. The single most valuable of the four, per §14.17.
deadlock_timeout
How long to wait before checking for a cycle. Not a timeout on anything you own.

The migration idiom is worth memorising:

SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE seats ADD COLUMN row_label text;

SET
ALTER TABLE

If the lock cannot be had in three seconds, the migration fails and you retry it — instead of holding a queue of blocked application queries for the length of whatever was running.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: lock_timeout setting.

15.9 Advisory Locks

Advisory locks are named locks with no attachment to any row or table. PostgreSQL only counts them; the meaning is yours.

SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42) AS i_took_it,
       pg_try_advisory_lock(42) AS and_again_in_the_same_session;
SELECT other_bool('SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42)') AS other_session_got_it;
