SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42), pg_advisory_unlock(42);
SELECT other_bool('SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42)') AS other_session_after_release;

 i_took_it | and_again_in_the_same_session 
-----------+-------------------------------
 t         | t
(1 row)

 other_session_got_it 
----------------------
 f
(1 row)

 pg_advisory_unlock | pg_advisory_unlock 
--------------------+--------------------
 t                  | t
(1 row)

 other_session_after_release 
-----------------------------
 t
(1 row)

Three behaviours are visible there. The other session was refused. The holding session could take it twice — advisory locks are re-entrant, and each acquisition needs its own unlock, which is why there are two pg_advisory_unlock calls. And once released, the other session got it.

Two families, and picking the wrong one is the usual mistake:

  • pg_advisory_lock(key) is session-scoped. It survives commit and rollback, and is released by pg_advisory_unlock, pg_advisory_unlock_all, or disconnection. Under a transaction-pooling connection pooler (§20.3) this is a bug: your next transaction may run on a different backend, and the lock is stranded on the old one.
  • pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) is transaction-scoped and released automatically at commit or rollback. It cannot be unlocked early, and it is the safe default.

pg_try_advisory_lock returns false instead of waiting — the non-blocking form, and what you want for "am I the leader?" checks.

The keys are one bigint or two ints, in a single global namespace with no schema and no ownership. Two features that both hash a string to a key will silently collide, so use a documented constant or a shared helper, and keep a list.

What they are genuinely good for: making a job run in only one place (a cron task on three application servers), serialising a migration so two deploys cannot run it at once, and rate-limiting an expensive operation to one at a time. What they are not good for: anything that should be a row lock, because an advisory lock has no relationship to the data and nothing stops a different code path from ignoring it.

15.10 Patterns That Get Concurrency Right

Four recurring problems, and the shape of each solution.

A counter that many sessions increment. UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = 1 is correct (§14.11) but serialises every writer on one row — throughput collapses, and under SERIALIZABLE it becomes a retry storm. The fix is not a lock; it is more rows. Insert a row per event and aggregate on read, or keep N shards and sum them. That is counter contention, and it is a data-modelling problem wearing a locking costume.

Read, decide, write. SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE, then decide, then write, all in one transaction. Not FOR UPDATE, per §15.4. And keep it short — no HTTP calls between the lock and the commit.

Two writers must not create the same thing. Not "check then insert", which has a race. Use a unique constraint plus ON CONFLICT (§11.7): the database arbitrates, at no cost when there is no conflict. A unique index is the cheapest concurrency control available, because it is one you were probably going to have anyway.

An invariant across rows. Either a serializable retry pattern (§14.15), or materializing the conflict: create a row that both transactions must update — a rota_version row, an exclusion constraint (§4.8) — so that a genuine conflict becomes an ordinary lock conflict on one row. The second is more code and more predictable, and it works at any isolation level.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: counter contention, serializable retry pattern and materializing the conflict.

What This Section Established

Two independent systems: table-level locks in shared memory, and row-level locks stored in the rows themselves. PostgreSQL never escalates row locks to table locks.

Eight table modes. SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE, UPDATE takes ROW EXCLUSIVE, most ALTER TABLE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and blocks even readers. Locks are held to the end of the transaction, and a blocked ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request blocks everything queued behind it — which is how one slow SELECT freezes a table during a migration.

Four row-lock strengths. FOR UPDATE blocks inserts into referencing tables, because a foreign-key check takes FOR KEY SHARE on the parent — measured, with PostgreSQL's own internal check query visible in the error. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is the right default.

NOWAIT fails instead of waiting. SKIP LOCKED skips instead of waiting, which is what makes a correct database-backed job queue possible — measured: one session took seat 1, the other asked for "the first seat" and got seat 2.

Deadlocks are cycles, detected after deadlock_timeout (one second by default), reported as 40P01, retryable exactly like 40001. The prevention is consistent lock ordering, which is code discipline rather than configuration.

pg_locks WHERE NOT granted finds the waiters; pg_blocking_pids() finds who is blocking them; pg_stat_activity says what they are running. Follow the chain to the root, which is usually idle in transaction.

lock_timeout before every migration. statement_timeout for request-driven work. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout always.

Advisory locks are re-entrant, live in one global namespace, and come in session-scoped and transaction-scoped families — use the transaction-scoped one unless you have a specific reason, and never the session-scoped one behind a transaction pooler.

Counter contention is a data-modelling problem. Uniqueness races are solved by a unique constraint and ON CONFLICT, not by locking. Cross-row invariants need SERIALIZABLE or a materialised conflict row.

Exercises

1. Map the conflict matrix by experiment. For four of the eight table-level modes, open a transaction that takes it and, from a second session with a short lock_timeout, attempt a SELECT, an INSERT and an ALTER TABLE. Build the table of which combinations conflict, and compare it to the documentation.

2. Reproduce the foreign-key trap. Build a parent table with two child tables referencing it. Lock a parent row FOR UPDATE and show that inserts into both children block. Switch to FOR NO KEY UPDATE and show they do not. Then explain what would have happened to an application whose background job held that lock for thirty seconds.

3. Build a work queue. Implement claim, complete and fail with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Run three concurrent workers against a hundred jobs and prove no job is processed twice and none is missed. Then kill a worker mid-job and describe what happens to its row — and add whatever you need to recover it.

4. Cause a deadlock, then prevent it. Write two transactions that update the same two rows in opposite orders and produce 40P01. Then change only the order in which they take the rows and show the deadlock is gone. Explain why this is a property of the code and not of the isolation level.

5. Find the root blocker. Create a chain: session A idle in transaction holding a lock, session B blocked behind it, session C blocked behind B. Write one query that reports, for every blocked backend, the pid at the root of its wait chain. Then say which session you would terminate and why.

6. Choose the right advisory lock. Implement "only one instance of this job runs at a time" with pg_advisory_lock and again with pg_advisory_xact_lock. Describe a concrete failure of each: one where the session-scoped lock leaks, and one where the transaction-scoped lock is released too early.

7. Fix a hot counter. Build a table with one counter row and measure the throughput of many concurrent increments. Then shard it across sixteen rows and measure again. Report both, and state what you gave up.

Solution

1. The conflict matrix.

The pattern that emerges: ACCESS SHARE (a plain SELECT) conflicts with exactly one mode, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Everything else in the middle of the table is about writes and schema changes conflicting with each other. That asymmetry is the practical content of the matrix — reads are almost never blocked, and the exception is the mode most ALTER TABLE forms take.

The instructive discovery is that SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (VACUUM, ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) conflicts with itself. Two concurrent CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY statements on one table serialise, which is why building six indexes concurrently takes six times as long as one.

2. The foreign-key trap.

§15.4 is the worked version. With two children, both inserts block under FOR UPDATE and both succeed under FOR NO KEY UPDATE.

The thirty-second version is the point. On a tenants table with twenty referencing tables, a job that does SELECT ... FROM tenants WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE and then calls an external API stops every write for that tenant, in every table, for the duration of the call. The symptom is "the application is down for one customer", and nothing in the application logs points at a SELECT.

3. The work queue.

The claim statement from §15.5, plus:

UPDATE jobs SET state = 'done'  WHERE job_id = <job_id>;
UPDATE jobs SET state = 'ready' WHERE job_id = <job_id>;   -- fail: hand it back

No job is processed twice because the claim locks the row inside the same transaction that flips its state, and SKIP LOCKED guarantees two workers never select the same row. None is missed because a worker that finds nothing simply retries.

The killed worker is the interesting case: its transaction rolls back, so its row returns to ready if the claim and the work share a transaction — and stays running forever if they do not, which is the design most people actually want, because you do not hold a transaction open for the length of the work. The recovery is a claimed_at timestamp and a sweeper that returns rows stuck in running past a threshold. At-least-once delivery, which means the work must be idempotent.

4. Deadlock, then prevention.

§15.6 produces 40P01. The fix:

SELECT id FROM dl WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR NO KEY UPDATE;

Both transactions now request both rows in ascending id order, in one statement. Whichever gets row 1 also gets row 2; the other waits and then proceeds. No cycle can form because a cycle requires two transactions to disagree about the order.

It is a property of the code because the database has no way to know, when transaction A locks row 1, that it will later want row 2. Only the application knows the full set in advance, so only the application can sort it. No isolation level helps — at SERIALIZABLE you get 40001 instead of 40P01, which is a different error for the same avoidable cycle.

5. The root blocker.

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT pid, unnest(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) AS blocker, 1 AS depth
  FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.pid, unnest(pg_blocking_pids(c.blocker)), c.depth + 1
  FROM chain c WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(c.blocker)) > 0
)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (pid) pid, blocker AS root_blocker, depth
FROM chain ORDER BY pid, depth DESC;

A recursive CTE (§9.11) over the blocking graph, taking the deepest hop for each blocked pid.

Terminate the root, not the visible victim. Killing B frees nothing, because A still holds the lock and C is still queued. And check state first: if the root is idle in transaction, terminating it is safe and the real fix is idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. If it is active and running a legitimate long query, terminating it may be the wrong call — the honest answer is often to let it finish and fix the migration's lock_timeout instead.

6. Advisory lock scope.

pg_advisory_lock leaks when the code path that unlocks is skipped — an exception, an early return, or a connection returned to a pool without a reset. Behind a transaction pooler it leaks by design: the lock is on a backend you no longer own, and the next attempt from your own application blocks against yourself.

pg_advisory_xact_lock is released too early whenever the work outlives the transaction. A job that takes the lock, commits its first batch, and then continues has lost the lock at that commit — and a second instance can start. If the work must span several transactions, you need the session-scoped lock plus a dedicated connection, or a claim row with a heartbeat.

7. The hot counter.

One row serialises every writer: throughput is bounded by one transaction's round trip, and it does not improve with concurrency. Sixteen shards divide contention by sixteen and throughput scales until the next bottleneck.

What you gave up is a cheap exact read. SELECT n FROM counter becomes SELECT sum(n) FROM counter_shards, which is sixteen rows instead of one — negligible — but it also means the count is only exact as of one snapshot, and any code that read the single row is now reading an aggregate. On a counter read far more often than written, the single row was the right design and the contention was never the problem; measure before sharding.

SECTION 16

Vacuum, Bloat, WAL and Durability

§14.7 established that PostgreSQL never overwrites a row: an UPDATE writes a new version and leaves the old one behind. This section is the bill for that decision, and the mechanism that pays it.

It is the most operational section in the course, and the one whose absence causes the most production incidents. A database that is slow for no apparent reason, whose queries have not changed and whose plans look fine, is very often a database whose autovacuum has fallen behind. The symptoms do not point at the cause, which is why the cause is worth knowing before you meet it.

The second half is the other side of the same page: the write-ahead log, which is how PostgreSQL keeps a commit through a power cut, and the settings that let you trade some of that guarantee for speed.

16.1 Why Vacuum Exists

Three jobs, and only the first is obvious.

Reclaim dead tuples
Row versions no snapshot can still need are removed and their space made reusable. Without this a table grows forever.
Update the visibility map
Mark pages where every row is visible to everyone — which is what makes index-only scans possible (§12.9) and lets later vacuums skip work.
Freeze old rows
Mark rows as older than every possible transaction, which is what prevents transaction id wraparound (§16.7). This one is not optional and not deferrable.

ANALYZE — collecting planner statistics (§13.10) — is a fourth job, run by the same daemon and frequently confused with the first three. It is a separate operation with separate thresholds, and a table can be badly in need of one and perfectly vacuumed, or the reverse.

The three jobs fail in different ways, and it is worth knowing which symptom points where. Unreclaimed dead tuples show up as a table and its indexes growing while the row count does not, and as sequential scans that read three times the pages they need (§16.2). A stale visibility map shows up as an index-only scan quietly becoming a heap scan (§12.9) — no error, no plan change you would notice, simply a slower query that used to be fast. And unfrozen rows show up as nothing at all, for months, and then as an anti-wraparound vacuum that will not yield a lock, or in the worst case as a cluster refusing to accept transactions.

That asymmetry is the reason transaction id wraparound is treated separately from the other two throughout this section. Bloat is a cost you can measure, budget for and live with; a stale visibility map is a performance regression you can find with EXPLAIN. Transaction id wraparound is neither — it is a hard limit with a fixed deadline, and the database will stop rather than cross it. §16.7 is that story in full, and the one alert every deployment needs comes from it.

16.2 Watching Bloat Happen

CREATE TABLE churn (id int PRIMARY KEY, pad text);
ALTER TABLE churn SET (autovacuum_enabled = false);
INSERT INTO churn SELECT g, repeat('x', 200) FROM generate_series(1, 50000) AS g;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('churn')) AS after_load;

CREATE TABLE
ALTER TABLE
INSERT 0 50000
 after_load 
------------
 11 MB
(1 row)

Autovacuum is disabled here so the demonstration is reproducible; do not do this to a real table. Now update every row, twice:

UPDATE churn SET pad = repeat('y', 200);
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('churn')) AS after_one_update;
UPDATE churn SET pad = repeat('z', 200);
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('churn')) AS after_two_updates;

UPDATE 50000
 after_one_update 
------------------
 23 MB
(1 row)

UPDATE 50000
 after_two_updates 
-------------------
 34 MB
(1 row)

Eleven megabytes of data occupying thirty-four megabytes of disk. Nothing was inserted. Two full-table updates tripled the file, because each one wrote fifty thousand new row versions and left fifty thousand dead ones behind.

That is table bloat, and it is not merely wasted disk. Every sequential scan now reads three times as many pages; the shared buffer cache holds a third as much useful data; every backup is three times the size. A bloated table is slow in a way no index can fix.

16.3 VACUUM Does Not Shrink the File

This is the part that surprises people.

VACUUM churn;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('churn')) AS after_vacuum;
VACUUM FULL churn;
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('churn')) AS after_vacuum_full;

VACUUM
 after_vacuum 
--------------
 34 MB
(1 row)

VACUUM
 after_vacuum_full 
-------------------
 11 MB
(1 row)

After a plain VACUUM command the file is still 34 MB. The dead space inside it was marked reusable, so the next fifty thousand updates will fit without growing the file — but the space was not returned to the operating system. That is the design, and it is right: returning it would mean rewriting the table, and the space is about to be used again.

VACUUM FULL does rewrite the table, and gets you back to 11 MB. Its cost is severe and worth stating in full: it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole rewrite, so nothing can read or write the table, and it needs enough free disk for a second copy — which is exactly what you may not have on the disk that filled up. It is a recovery tool, not maintenance. pg_repack (an extension) does the same job without the exclusive lock and is what production systems use.

The right steady state is bloat that stops growing, not bloat that is zero. A table under constant update settles at some equilibrium where vacuum reclaims space as fast as updates create it, and that equilibrium is fine. The problem is when it does not settle.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the exclusive lock and vacuum command.

16.4 Reading VACUUM VERBOSE

VACUUM (VERBOSE) explains itself, and the lines are worth being able to read. This is a trimmed version of a real run against the table above — the exact numbers differ on every run:

INFO:  vacuuming "course_main.public.churn"
INFO:  finished vacuuming "course_main.public.churn": index scans: 1
pages: 0 removed, 4412 remain, 4412 scanned (100.00% of total), 0 eagerly scanned
tuples: 50000 removed, 50000 remain, 0 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 5181, which was 0 XIDs old when operation ended
new relfrozenxid: 5180, which is 4 XIDs ahead of previous value
visibility map: 2942 pages set all-visible, 2940 pages set all-frozen
index scan needed: 2942 pages from table (66.68% of total) had 99986 dead item identifiers removed
index "churn_pkey": pages: 276 in total, 0 newly deleted, 0 currently deleted, 0 reusable
WAL usage: 7634 records, 0 full page images, 928521 bytes, 0 buffers full
are dead but not yet removable
The single most important number. Anything above zero means an old snapshot is holding rows back, and the vacuum accomplished less than it appeared to. §16.5.
pages: N removed
Pages returned to the operating system — only ever trailing empty pages, which is why it is zero here despite 50,000 tuples being removed.
removable cutoff
The horizon: no version newer than this transaction id can be removed. "0 XIDs old" means nothing was holding it back.
visibility map: N pages set all-visible
The index-only-scan enabler of §12.9, being populated.
index scans: N
How many passes over the indexes were needed. More than one means maintenance_work_mem was too small to hold all the dead item pointers at once, and every index was scanned again. Raising it is often the cheapest vacuum tuning available.

16.5 What Stops Vacuum

Vacuum cannot remove a row version that any snapshot in the system might still need. Four things hold that horizon back, and they are the complete list.

A long-running transaction, as §14.17 measured — and its effect is global, not limited to the tables it touched.

A long-running query on a hot standby, when hot_standby_feedback = on. The primary respects the standby's oldest snapshot, so a report running on a replica bloats the primary. That is a genuinely surprising causal chain and a common one.

An abandoned replication slot. A slot retains WAL and holds a horizon; a slot for a subscriber that has been switched off retains them forever, and this is the classic way a disk fills up with nobody having written anything.

A prepared transaction left behind by two-phase commit that nothing ever committed or rolled back.

The one query that finds all four:

SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity
        WHERE state <> 'idle' AND backend_type = 'client backend') AS active_backends,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE NOT active)  AS inactive_slots,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_prepared_xacts)                      AS prepared_xacts;

 active_backends | inactive_slots | prepared_xacts 
-----------------+----------------+----------------
               1 |              0 |              0
(1 row)

In production the version to run adds xact_start and state from pg_stat_activity and sorts by age — the oldest transaction is the one holding the horizon, and it is usually one session, not many.

In summary, the vocabulary here is long-running transaction and replication slot.

16.6 The Visibility Map

Two bits per page: all-visible (every row on this page is visible to every transaction) and all-frozen (every row is frozen).

All-visible is what §12.9 measured: it lets an index-only scan skip the heap entirely, and it lets the next vacuum skip the page. All-frozen lets an aggressive vacuum skip the page too, which is what keeps freezing affordable on a large mostly-static table.

The map is tiny — one page covers about 32,000 heap pages — and it is set only by vacuum. It is also why a read-heavy table with an idle autovacuum quietly loses its fastest plan (§12.9), with no change to any query.

PostgreSQL 18 added eager freezing: a normal vacuum will now freeze some all-visible pages rather than leaving every one to an aggressive vacuum later, which spreads the cost instead of concentrating it. The eagerly scanned line in §16.4's output is that at work.

16.7 Freezing and Wraparound

Transaction ids are 32 bits, so they wrap. PostgreSQL treats the id space as circular: two billion ids are "in the past" and two billion "in the future". A row whose xmin fell more than two billion transactions behind would appear to be in the future and become invisible — which would be silent, catastrophic data loss.

Freezing prevents it. A row old enough to be visible to every possible transaction is marked frozen, and a frozen tuple is visible regardless of ids. vacuum_freeze_min_age (50 million by default) decides when a vacuum bothers.

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('autovacuum','autovacuum_vacuum_threshold','autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor',
               'autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor','autovacuum_naptime',
               'autovacuum_max_workers','vacuum_freeze_min_age','autovacuum_freeze_max_age',
               'vacuum_cost_limit')
ORDER BY name;

                 name                  |  setting  
---------------------------------------+-----------
 autovacuum                            | on
 autovacuum_freeze_max_age             | 200000000
 autovacuum_max_workers                | 3
 autovacuum_naptime                    | 60
 autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor | 0.2
 autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor        | 0.2
 autovacuum_vacuum_threshold           | 50
 vacuum_cost_limit                     | 200
 vacuum_freeze_min_age                 | 50000000
(9 rows)

autovacuum_freeze_max_age is 200 million: once a table's oldest unfrozen id is that far behind, autovacuum starts an anti-wraparound vacuum on it whether or not anything changed, and — unlike an ordinary autovacuum — it will not yield to a conflicting lock request. A migration that blocks behind one is a common and confusing incident.

The escalation, and the reason this section exists:

200M behind
Anti-wraparound autovacuum starts, and does not step aside.
~40M remaining
Warnings in the log on every commit.
~3M remaining
The database refuses all new transactions and must be recovered in single-user mode. This is an outage of the whole cluster, and it is entirely preventable.

The one alert every PostgreSQL deployment should have:

SELECT max(age(datfrozenxid)) < 150000000 AS wraparound_headroom_ok FROM pg_database;

 wraparound_headroom_ok 
------------------------
 t
(1 row)

Alert well below autovacuum_freeze_max_age, and investigate rather than raising the threshold — the answer is always a table autovacuum cannot finish, or one of §16.5's four blockers.

What to carry forward from this subsection: frozen tuple.

16.8 Autovacuum's Thresholds

Autovacuum wakes every autovacuum_naptime (60s) and vacuums any table where

dead tuples > autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor × reltuples

With the defaults — 50 and 0.2 — that is 20% of the table, and the scale factor is the problem. On a thousand-row table, 20% is 200 dead rows and vacuum runs constantly. On a hundred-million-row table, 20% is twenty million dead rows before anything happens at all, by which time the bloat is enormous and the vacuum is a huge job.

Lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor on large tables. Per table, which is the right granularity:

ALTER TABLE churn SET (autovacuum_enabled = true,
                       autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,
                       autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000,
                       autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.01);
SELECT reloptions FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'churn';

ALTER TABLE
                                                            reloptions                                                            
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 {autovacuum_enabled=true,autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.02,autovacuum_vacuum_threshold=1000,autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor=0.01}
(1 row)

autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor (PostgreSQL 13 and later) is the counterpart for insert-only tables, which under the old rules were never vacuumed at all — no dead tuples, no trigger — and therefore never got their visibility map populated or their rows frozen, until an anti-wraparound vacuum arrived to do all of it at once.

Two more knobs matter when vacuum is too slow. autovacuum_max_workers (3) caps concurrency, and a cluster with thousands of tables can starve. autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay and vacuum_cost_limit throttle vacuum's I/O deliberately; on modern storage the defaults are conservative, and raising vacuum_cost_limit is usually the fix for "autovacuum never catches up".

16.9 Monitoring

SELECT relname,
       n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       last_autovacuum IS NOT NULL AS ever_autovacuumed
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'churn';

 relname | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup | ever_autovacuumed 
---------+------------+------------+-------------------
 churn   |      50000 |          0 | f
(1 row)

pg_stat_user_tables carries n_dead_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum, last_analyze and vacuum_count. The two things to watch: dead tuples as a fraction of live tuples, trending rather than absolute, and last_autovacuum falling behind on a table you know is being written.

pg_stat_progress_vacuum shows a running vacuum's phase and progress, which answers "is it stuck or just slow". PostgreSQL 18 added time spent in vacuum and analyze to pg_stat_all_tables, so the cost is now attributable per table.

Two refinements make the difference between a dashboard and a diagnosis.

n_dead_tup is only meaningful against n_live_tup. A hundred thousand dead rows on a table of ten million is a healthy steady state; the same hundred thousand on a table of two hundred thousand is a table that has doubled in size. Alert on the ratio, and only above a size floor, or a small busy table will page you every night for nothing.

last_autovacuum is more useful than any count. A NULL there on a table you know is written to means autovacuum has never completed on it — which is the signal that matters, because every count-based metric is downstream of that one fact. The query worth keeping is a join of pg_stat_user_tables to pg_class that lists tables above some size where last_autovacuum is null or older than a threshold, ordered by size: it finds the tables where the problem is expensive, rather than the ones where it is merely present.

Note also that these counters are cumulative since the last statistics reset, and pg_stat_reset() zeroes them for the whole database. A dashboard showing suspiciously healthy numbers immediately after a maintenance window is usually showing you a reset, not an improvement — stats_reset in pg_stat_database is the column that tells you which.

16.10 The Write-Ahead Log

Durability's mechanism is one rule: the WAL record describing a change reaches stable storage before the changed data page does. After a crash, replay the log from the last checkpoint and the data pages are correct again.

That inversion is what makes commits fast. A commit does not write your table's pages; it writes a small sequential log record and flushes that. Random writes to data pages happen later, in bulk, by the background writer and the checkpointer.

A position in the log is a log sequence number, a monotonically increasing byte offset:

SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() IS NOT NULL      AS have_an_lsn,
       pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()) IS NOT NULL AS have_a_segment_name;

 have_an_lsn | have_a_segment_name 
-------------+---------------------
 t           | t
(1 row)

Every page carries the LSN of the last change to it, which is how recovery knows what to replay. The LSN is also the unit of replication lag (§16.16) — "the standby is 4 MB behind" is a difference of LSNs.

wal_level decides how much is logged: minimal (crash recovery only), replica (the default — enough for streaming replication and archiving), logical (enough to decode into row changes, §16.16).

One line each, for reference: wal record, log sequence number, crash recovery, streaming replication and replication lag.

16.11 Checkpoints

A checkpoint flushes all dirty shared buffers to disk and records that everything up to this LSN is safely in the data files, so recovery need never look further back.

SELECT name, setting, unit FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('checkpoint_timeout','checkpoint_completion_target','max_wal_size','wal_level')
ORDER BY name;

             name             | setting | unit 
------------------------------+---------+------
 checkpoint_completion_target | 0.9     | 
 checkpoint_timeout           | 300     | s
 max_wal_size                 | 1024    | MB
 wal_level                    | replica | 
(4 rows)

Checkpoints happen every checkpoint_timeout (5 minutes) or when max_wal_size of log has accumulated, whichever comes first — and the second is the one that hurts. A write-heavy system hitting 1 GB of WAL every thirty seconds is checkpointing every thirty seconds, and every checkpoint means a burst of page writes and, because of §16.12, a burst of full page images in the WAL that follows.

The tuning is counter-intuitive and worth stating plainly: raising max_wal_size makes a busy system faster, because fewer checkpoints mean fewer full-page writes and less repeated flushing of the same hot pages. The cost is a longer crash recovery and more disk for the log. checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9 spreads each checkpoint's writes over 90% of the interval rather than issuing them in a spike.

log_checkpoints is on by default and its log lines say whether checkpoints were triggered by time or by size — which is the measurement that tells you whether to raise max_wal_size.

16.12 The Durability Dial

Three settings trade durability for speed, and they trade different amounts.

synchronous_commit
default on
Turning it off gives an asynchronous commit: commit returns before the WAL is flushed. A crash loses at most wal_writer_delay × 3 of recent commits — typically under a second — and the database is still consistent. No corruption, no torn transactions, just a few lost commits. This is a legitimate trade, and it can double throughput on a commit-heavy workload.
fsync
default on
Turning it off means the WAL itself is never forced to disk. A crash can leave the data files inconsistent and unrecoverable. This is not the same trade at all.
a full_page_writes full page write
default on
Writes a complete image of each page the first time it changes after a checkpoint, so a torn page — half old, half new, from a crash mid-write — can be reconstructed. Off, a torn page is unrecoverable corruption.

The distinction between the first and the other two is the thing to take away. synchronous_commit = off risks losing recent commits; fsync = off risks losing the database. They are frequently discussed as if they were the same dial, and they are not.

synchronous_commit can also be set per transaction, which is the best of both: leave it on globally and turn it off for the one bulk-import job where a lost batch can simply be re-run.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: full page write and asynchronous commit.

16.13 Checksums, and Non-Durable Settings

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'data_checksums';

      name      | setting 
----------------+---------
 data_checksums | on
(1 row)

PostgreSQL 18 enables data checksums by default for new clusters, which 17 and earlier did not. Every data page carries a checksum verified on read, so silent corruption from failing storage is detected rather than served. The cost is a few percent of CPU, and it is worth it — on an older cluster, pg_checksums can enable them offline.

The server these examples ran on has fsync, full_page_writes and synchronous_commit all switched off, because it is a disposable test cluster created and destroyed for each run. That is exactly the case the PostgreSQL documentation calls non-durable settings, and it is legitimate for one purpose: a database whose entire contents can be recreated from a script. A test suite, a CI run, a bulk-load staging cluster you will back up afterwards. UNLOGGED tables (§4.4) are the finer-grained version of the same idea — no WAL at all for that table, and it is emptied after a crash.

Anywhere data matters, all three stay on.

16.14 Backups

Two families, and they answer different questions.

Logical backup
pg_dump
SQL or an archive format that reproduces the schema and data. Portable across versions and architectures, restorable table by table, and internally consistent because it runs in one REPEATABLE READ transaction (§14.12). Slow to restore — everything is re-inserted and every index rebuilt.
Physical backup
pg_basebackup
A byte copy of the data directory plus the WAL generated during the copy. Fast to take and to restore, restores the whole cluster or nothing, and is tied to the same major version and architecture. The basis of PITR and of replication.

pg_dump -Fc (custom format) is the one to use: compressed, and pg_restore can then select individual tables, reorder, run in parallel with -j, or emit the SQL for inspection. pg_dumpall adds the cluster-wide objects — roles and tablespaces — that pg_dump omits, and forgetting it is how a restore comes up with no users.

Because pg_dump holds one long transaction, it is also one of §16.5's vacuum blockers for its whole duration. Dumping a large database is not free of side effects.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: pg_basebackup and logical backup.

To have in hand before moving on: physical backup.

16.15 Point-in-Time Recovery

A base backup plus every WAL segment since gives you any moment in between.

The pieces are WAL archiving — archive_mode = on and an archive_command (or archive_library) that copies each completed WAL segment somewhere durable; a pg_basebackup taken while archiving runs; and, to restore, the base backup plus a restore_command and a recovery_target_time.

This is what makes "someone ran DELETE without a WHERE clause at 14:32" a recoverable event rather than a data-loss event, and it is the reason a nightly pg_dump alone is not a backup strategy — it can only take you back to midnight.

Three cautions from practice. An archive that is not restored is not a backup; rehearse it. A failing archive_command fills the disk, because PostgreSQL retains every segment it could not archive. And timelines exist so that recovering to a point in the past and then continuing does not overwrite the history you branched from — recovering twice to two different times gives two timelines, and pg_rewind is what puts a diverged server back on one.

pg_verifybackup checks a base backup against its manifest, and PostgreSQL 17 added incremental base backups via pg_combinebackup.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: wal archiving.

16.16 Replication

Physical (streaming) replication ships WAL to a standby that replays it. The standby is byte-identical, can serve read-only queries as a hot standby, and is the basis of high availability. It replicates everything — all databases, all tables, no filtering — and both servers must run the same major version.

A replication slot makes the primary retain WAL until the standby has consumed it. That guarantees the standby can always catch up, and it is the mechanism behind two of the most common production incidents: a slot for a standby that is gone retains WAL forever until the disk fills, and an active slot with hot_standby_feedback = on holds back vacuum on the primary (§16.5).

Logical replication decodes WAL into row changes and applies them by SQL, using a PUBLICATION on the source and a logical replication subscription on the target. It replicates selected tables, works between major versions — which makes it the standard tool for a near-zero-downtime upgrade — and, unlike physical replication, the target is writable. It requires wal_level = logical, and it needs every replicated table to have a primary key or a REPLICA IDENTITY, without which an UPDATE cannot be matched to a row on the target.

Replication is asynchronous by default: a commit returns before the standby has it, so a failover can lose recent transactions. synchronous_standby_names makes commits wait for a standby, trading latency for that guarantee — the same shape of trade as §16.12, one level up.

In summary, the vocabulary here is publication and logical replication subscription.

What This Section Established

Vacuum does three jobs: reclaim dead tuples, populate the visibility map, and freeze old rows. The third is not optional.

Measured bloat: 11 MB of data became 23 MB after one full-table update and 34 MB after two. Nothing was inserted.

VACUUM does not shrink the file — still 34 MB — it makes the space reusable. VACUUM FULL rewrites to 11 MB and takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE plus room for a second copy; pg_repack is the production alternative. Steady-state bloat is fine; growing bloat is not.

In VACUUM VERBOSE, dead but not yet removable above zero means a snapshot is holding the horizon, and index scans above one means maintenance_work_mem was too small.

Four things block vacuum, all global in effect: a long transaction, a standby query under hot_standby_feedback, an inactive replication slot, and an orphaned prepared transaction.

The visibility map's all-visible bit is what index-only scans need and only vacuum sets. PostgreSQL 18 freezes eagerly to spread that cost.

Wraparound: freeze or lose data. Anti-wraparound vacuum starts at 200M and does not yield to lock requests; at ~3M remaining the cluster refuses transactions. Alert on max(age(datfrozenxid)).

The default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor of 0.2 means 20% of the table, which is far too much on a large one. Set it per table. autovacuum_vacuum_insert_scale_factor covers insert-only tables, which under the old rules were never vacuumed at all.

WAL: the log record reaches disk before the data page. That is why commits are fast. LSNs order everything and measure replication lag.

Checkpoints fire on time or on max_wal_size, and raising max_wal_size makes a busy system faster by reducing full-page writes.

synchronous_commit = off risks a second of commits and keeps the database consistent; fsync = off risks the database. They are not the same dial. synchronous_commit can be set per transaction.

PostgreSQL 18 turns on data checksums by default. Non-durable settings are legitimate only where the contents can be recreated from a script — which is exactly what the server behind this course is.

pg_dump is portable, consistent, slow to restore, and holds a long transaction; pg_basebackup is fast, whole-cluster and version-locked. pg_dumpall for roles.

PITR is a base backup plus archived WAL. Rehearse the restore, watch for a failing archive_command filling the disk, and understand timelines before recovering twice.

Physical replication ships WAL and replicates everything; logical replication decodes it, replicates selected tables, crosses major versions, and needs a replica identity. Both are asynchronous unless you ask otherwise.

Exercises

1. Measure bloat and reclaim it. Reproduce §16.2. Then, instead of VACUUM FULL, run a plain VACUUM and re-run the two updates. Report the file size after the second round and explain why it did not triple again.

2. Block a vacuum and see it. Hold a transaction open in one session. In another, delete rows and run VACUUM (VERBOSE). Find the dead but not yet removable line and the removable cutoff age. Close the transaction, vacuum again, and report the difference.

3. Tune a table's autovacuum. For a table of ten million rows, compute how many dead tuples the defaults require before autovacuum triggers. Choose a scale factor and threshold that trigger at roughly one percent, apply them, and state what you traded.

4. Find the wraparound headroom. Write the alert query for age(datfrozenxid) across all databases and for the oldest table. Say what value you would alert at and why it is well below autovacuum_freeze_max_age.

5. Watch checkpoints. Enable log_checkpoints, run a sustained write workload, and record how many checkpoints were triggered by time versus by max_wal_size. Raise max_wal_size, repeat, and report the change in WAL volume.

6. Prove the durability distinction. Explain, without running it, exactly what a reader would lose under a power cut with synchronous_commit = off, and what they would lose with fsync = off. Then state which of the two you would ever set in production, on what workload, and what you would do to make the loss acceptable.

7. Restore something. Take a pg_dump -Fc of a database, drop a table, and restore only that table with pg_restore -t. Then take a pg_basebackup and describe precisely what you would have to do differently to recover the same single table from it.

Solution

1. Measuring and reclaiming.

After a plain VACUUM, the file stays at 34 MB but the dead space inside it is on the free space map. The second round of two updates therefore fits in the existing file — it grows only slightly, if at all, rather than reaching 68 MB.

That is the whole design in one measurement: vacuum's job is not to give space back, it is to stop the file growing. A table at steady state under constant update reaches a size and stays there, and that size is larger than the data. Chasing it to zero with VACUUM FULL on a schedule buys nothing and costs an exclusive lock.

2. Blocking a vacuum.

With a transaction open, tuples: N removed drops and M are dead but not yet removable becomes non-zero. The removable cutoff ... which was N XIDs old line reports how far behind the horizon was dragged.

Close the transaction, vacuum again, and the same rows are removed with 0 are dead but not yet removable. Nothing about the table changed between the two runs; the only difference was a snapshot in an unrelated session.

3. Tuning autovacuum.

Defaults: 50 + 0.2 × 10,000,000 = 2,000,050 dead tuples before autovacuum triggers. At an average row of 200 bytes that is roughly 400 MB of dead space accumulated before anything happens, and then one very large vacuum.

For about one percent: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 1000 triggers at about 101,000 dead tuples.

The trade is more frequent vacuums — more I/O, more CPU, more WAL, and a worker occupied more often out of only three. On a large busy table that is the right trade, because the alternative is not "no vacuum" but "one enormous vacuum at an unpredictable moment". Pair it with a raised vacuum_cost_limit so each run actually finishes.

4. Wraparound headroom.

SELECT max(age(datfrozenxid)) < 150000000 AS headroom_ok FROM pg_database;

 headroom_ok 
-------------
 t
(1 row)

Print the age itself when you run it — it is omitted here only because it differs on every server. The per-table version reads age(relfrozenxid) from pg_class where relkind IN ('r','m','t'), ordered descending — because one stuck table is what drags the database value up.

Alert at 150M against a 200M autovacuum_freeze_max_age, so that there is time to investigate before anti-wraparound vacuums begin taking non-yielding locks. Alerting at 190M leaves no room, and raising autovacuum_freeze_max_age in response to an alert removes the warning without removing the problem.

5. Watching checkpoints.

log_checkpoints output distinguishes checkpoint starting: time from checkpoint starting: wal. A healthy system shows mostly time; a system checkpointing on wal is one where max_wal_size is too small for the write rate.

Raising it reduces checkpoint frequency, and total WAL volume falls — which is the counter-intuitive part. Fewer checkpoints mean fewer first modifications of a page after a checkpoint, and it is those that emit a full page image. A hot page modified a hundred times between two checkpoints emits one full image; the same page across ten checkpoints emits ten.

6. The durability distinction.

With synchronous_commit = off: a power cut loses commits acknowledged within roughly the last 3 × wal_writer_delay — under a second by default. Recovery replays what did reach disk and produces a consistent database at some slightly earlier point. No corruption, no partial transactions.

With fsync = off: the WAL was never forced to disk, so recovery cannot trust it. The data files may be a mixture of pages from before and after a checkpoint with no reliable log to reconcile them. The database may not start, and if it does it may be quietly wrong.

synchronous_commit = off is defensible in production on a workload where a second of lost writes is recoverable by other means — ingesting events that the producer will retry, or a queue that redelivers. Make the loss acceptable by making the writes idempotent and replayable, not by hoping.

fsync = off is never defensible on data you cannot regenerate from a script.

7. Restoring.

pg_dump -Fc -d mydb -f mydb.dump
pg_restore -d mydb -t orders --data-only mydb.dump

From a physical base backup there is no -t equivalent, and that is the fundamental difference. A base backup is a byte image of the whole cluster: to get one table out of it you restore the entire cluster somewhere else — a scratch server, or a temporary data directory on the same machine — start it, and then pg_dump -t the table from there.

So the two are not substitutes. Physical backups give you fast whole-cluster recovery and point-in-time; logical dumps give you selective, cross-version restore. Production systems that care keep both, and the reason is precisely this exercise.

SECTION 17

JSON, Arrays, Ranges and Full-Text Search

Everything so far has treated a column as holding one scalar. This section is about the four PostgreSQL type families that do not: jsonb for documents, arrays for lists, ranges for intervals, and tsvector for searchable text.

They share a design idea worth naming up front. Each is a composite value in one column, and each comes with an operator set and a GIN or GiST index method that makes those operators fast. Without the index they are conveniences; with it they are the reason you do not need a second datastore for documents or for search.

They also share a hazard: it is easy to reach for them where a normalised table would be better, and the resulting schema is harder to query, harder to constrain and harder to index than the one you avoided. §17.10 makes that judgement explicit.

17.1 json and jsonb Are Different Types

PostgreSQL has two JSON types — the json type and the jsonb type — and the difference between json versus jsonb is not cosmetic.

SELECT '{"b":1,"a":2,"a":3}'::json  AS as_json,
       '{"b":1,"a":2,"a":3}'::jsonb AS as_jsonb;

       as_json       |     as_jsonb     
---------------------+------------------
 {"b":1,"a":2,"a":3} | {"a": 3, "b": 1}
(1 row)

json stores the text you gave it, verbatim: key order preserved, whitespace preserved, duplicate keys preserved. jsonb stores a parsed binary structure: jsonb key order is normalised to sorted, whitespace is gone, and on a duplicate key in jsonb the last one wins — "a":2 was silently discarded in favour of "a":3.

json
jsonb
Stored as
the original text
a decomposed binary tree
Write cost
cheap — validate only
parse on input
Read cost
re-parse on every access
no parsing
Indexable
no (except on an expression)
yes, with GIN
Equality
none defined
structural

Use jsonb. The only reason to choose json is a requirement to reproduce the input byte for byte — an audit log of payloads received, or a signature computed over the exact text. Everything else in this section is jsonb, and everything else in this section is why.

What to carry forward from this subsection: jsonb type, json versus jsonb, jsonb key order and duplicate key in jsonb.

17.2 Getting Values Out

Four extraction operators, and the distinction between two of them accounts for most confusion. Each is a jsonb operator taking a document on the left.

CREATE TABLE docs (id int PRIMARY KEY, body jsonb);
INSERT INTO docs VALUES
 (1,'{"name":"Ada","tags":["db","sql"],"meta":{"active":true,"score":9}}'),
 (2,'{"name":"Lin","tags":["ui"],"meta":{"active":false,"score":4}}'),
 (3,'{"name":"Kai","tags":["db","perf","sql"],"meta":{"active":true,"score":7}}');

SELECT id,
       body ->  'name'           AS arrow,
       body ->> 'name'           AS double_arrow,
       body -> 'meta' -> 'score' AS chained,
       body #>  '{meta,score}'   AS path_op,
       body #>> '{meta,score}'   AS path_text
FROM docs ORDER BY id;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
 id | arrow | double_arrow | chained | path_op | path_text 
----+-------+--------------+---------+---------+-----------
  1 | "Ada" | Ada          | 9       | 9       | 9
  2 | "Lin" | Lin          | 4       | 4       | 4
  3 | "Kai" | Kai          | 7       | 7       | 7
(3 rows)

-> returns jsonb; the ->> operator returns text. Look at the first two columns: "Ada" with quotes, and Ada without. The quoted one is a JSON string value, and it is not equal to the SQL string 'Ada'.

That is the rule to internalise: use -> to keep navigating, ->> at the last step to get a SQL value. body -> 'meta' ->> 'score' is right; body ->> 'meta' -> 'score' is a type error, because ->> already left JSON.

The #> path operator and #>> take a path as a text array and do the same job in one operator, which is more readable once the path is more than two levels deep. Both accept integers for array positions: '{tags,0}'.

Integer subscripts on -> index into arrays, and negative indexes count from the end: body -> 'tags' -> -1 is the last tag.

The terms above, gathered: jsonb operator, ->> operator and #> path operator.

17.3 Subscripting

Since PostgreSQL 14, jsonb supports array-style subscripting on a column or variable:

SELECT id, body['meta']['score'] AS subscripted FROM docs ORDER BY id;

 id | subscripted 
----+-------------
  1 | 9
  2 | 4
  3 | 7
(3 rows)

jsonb subscripting is equivalent to chained ->, returns jsonb, and reads better for deep paths. Two limits worth knowing: it does not work directly on a literal — '{"a":1}'::jsonb['a'] is a syntax error, because the parser wants a column or variable — and there is no subscripting equivalent of ->>, so you still cast or use #>> for text.

Subscripting also works on the left of an assignment, which is the concise way to update a nested value (§17.5).

One line each, for reference: jsonb subscripting.

17.4 Containment and Existence

These are the operators GIN can index, which makes them the ones your WHERE clauses should be built from.

SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @> '{"meta":{"active":true}}' ORDER BY id;

 id 
----
  1
  3
(2 rows)

The @> operator is containment, and jsonb containment is the single most useful jsonb predicate: "does the left document contain the right one as a sub-structure?" It is recursive and partial — you give a skeleton, and it matches any document with at least that shape. <@ is the same test reversed.

Containment for arrays means "contains these elements", in any order and regardless of extras:

SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body -> 'tags' @> '["sql"]' ORDER BY id;

 id 
----
  1
  3
(2 rows)

The jsonb existence operators ask about keys — or, for an array, about string elements:

SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM docs WHERE body -> 'tags' ?  'perf')            AS has_perf,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM docs WHERE body -> 'tags' ?| array['ui','perf']) AS has_either,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM docs WHERE body -> 'tags' ?& array['db','sql'])  AS has_both;

 has_perf | has_either | has_both 
----------+------------+----------
        1 |          2 |        2
(1 row)

The ? operator is "has this key or string element", ?| is "any of these", ?& is "all of these".

A trap worth stating plainly: ? is also the placeholder character in JDBC and several other drivers, so body ? 'key' may be mangled before it reaches the server. The workaround is the function form — jsonb_exists(body, 'key') — or your driver's escaping rule.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: jsonb containment, @> operator, jsonb existence and ? operator.

17.5 Building and Modifying

jsonb values are immutable like every other SQL value; "modifying" means computing a new one.

SELECT jsonb_set('{"a":{"b":1}}', '{a,b}', '42')                    AS after_set,
       jsonb_set('{"a":1}', '{b}', '2', true)                       AS created_missing,
       '{"a":1}'::jsonb || '{"b":2}'::jsonb                          AS concatenated,
       '{"a":1,"b":2}'::jsonb - 'a'                                  AS key_removed,
       jsonb_strip_nulls('{"a":1,"b":null,"c":{"d":null}}')          AS stripped;

      after_set      | created_missing | concatenated  | key_removed |     stripped      
---------------------+-----------------+---------------+-------------+-------------------
 {"a": {"b": 42}}    | {"a": 1, "b": 2} | {"a": 1, "b": 2} | {"b": 2}    | {"a": 1, "c": {}}
(1 row)

Four things there are worth noticing. jsonb_set's fourth argument decides whether a missing key is created (default true). || merges at the top level only — it is not a deep merge, and a nested object on the right replaces rather than merges. - removes a key, or an array element by integer. And jsonb_strip_nulls( left "c": {} behind: it removes null members, not the now-empty objects containing them.

Building from SQL values goes the other way:

SELECT jsonb_build_object('k', 1, 'arr', jsonb_build_array(1, 2, 3)) AS built,
       to_jsonb('a string'::text)                                     AS scalar,
       row_to_json(ROW(1, 'x'))                                       AS from_a_row;

           built            |  scalar    | from_a_row        
----------------------------+------------+-------------------
 {"k": 1, "arr": [1, 2, 3]} | "a string" | {"f1":1,"f2":"x"} 
(1 row)

Never build JSON by concatenating strings. jsonb_build_object( escapes correctly; '{"name":"' || name || '"}' produces invalid JSON the first time a name contains a quote, and is an injection vector besides.

The aggregate forms — jsonb_agg() and jsonb_object_agg() — turn a result set into one document, which is how you return a nested API response in a single round trip:

SELECT jsonb_agg(id ORDER BY id) AS ids,
       jsonb_object_agg(id, body ->> 'name') AS names
FROM docs;

    ids    |                names                 
-----------+--------------------------------------
 [1, 2, 3] | {"1": "Ada", "2": "Lin", "3": "Kai"}
(1 row)

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: jsonb_agg(.

17.6 Expanding JSON Into Rows

The reverse direction: a set-returning function in FROM turns a document into rows you can join and aggregate.

SELECT id, t.tag
FROM docs, jsonb_array_elements_text(body -> 'tags') AS t(tag)
ORDER BY id, tag;

 id | tag  
----+------
  1 | db
  1 | sql
  2 | ui
  3 | db
  3 | perf
  3 | sql
(6 rows)

Six rows from three documents. This is an implicit LATERAL join (§6.11) — the function is evaluated per row of docs, and may reference its columns.

jsonb_array_elements( returns jsonb where ..._text returns text; jsonb_each( and jsonb_each_text do the same for object members. jsonb_to_record projects a document onto a column list, which is the cleanest way to get typed columns out:

SELECT * FROM jsonb_to_record('{"a":1,"b":"x"}') AS t(a int, b text);

 a | b 
---+---
 1 | x
(1 row)

The column definition list is required, because the function's return type cannot be known until you say what you want.

To have in hand before moving on: jsonb_array_elements( and jsonb_each(.

17.7 jsonpath

jsonpath is a query language for JSON, standardised in SQL:2016 and available in PostgreSQL 12 and later. It expresses navigation, wildcards and filters in one string.

SELECT id, jsonb_path_query(body, '$.meta.score') AS score FROM docs ORDER BY id;

 id | score 
----+-------
  1 | 9
  2 | 4
  3 | 7
(3 rows)

$ is the document root, .key navigates, [*] is every array element, ** is any depth. The filter expression is what the operators cannot do:

SELECT jsonb_path_query_array('{"a":[1,2,3,4]}', '$.a[*] ? (@ > 2)') AS filtered;

 filtered 
----------
 [3, 4]
(1 row)

? (...) is a filter and @ is the current element. The whole notation is the SQL/JSON path language standardised in SQL:2016. So $.a[*] ? (@ > 2) reads "every element of a that is greater than 2".

The function family divides on two axes — whether you want the values or a boolean, and whether you want one row or an array:

jsonb_path_query
jsonb_path_query( is set-returning: one row per match. Belongs in FROM, or in the select list at the cost of a set-returning expression.
jsonb_path_query_array
All matches as one jsonb array. One row, always.
jsonb_path_exists
Boolean. jsonb_path_exists( is the one for a WHERE clause, and the one the @? operator wraps.
jsonb_path_match
For a path that is itself a predicate, returning its truth value rather than whether it matched. The @@ operator.
SELECT id FROM docs WHERE jsonb_path_exists(body, '$.meta.score ? (@ > 5)') ORDER BY id;

 id 
----
  1
  3
(2 rows)

Each function has a _tz variant for date/time comparisons that need a time zone, and each takes an optional vars argument — a jsonb object whose members are referenced as $name in the path. Use vars rather than string-concatenating a value into the path, for the same reason you use bind parameters in SQL.

By default jsonpath is in lax mode, which silently unwraps arrays and ignores structural errors. strict $.a.b raises an error instead when the structure is not as described — worth using when a missing key is a bug rather than a normal case.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: sql/json path language.

17.8 The SQL/JSON Standard Functions

PostgreSQL 17 added the SQL:2023 constructs, and they are worth preferring in new code when they fit, because they are portable.

SELECT JSON_VALUE('{"a":{"b":7}}'::jsonb, '$.a.b' RETURNING int) AS json_value,
       JSON_QUERY('{"a":{"b":7}}'::jsonb, '$.a')                 AS json_query,
       JSON_EXISTS('{"a":{"b":7}}'::jsonb, '$.a.c')              AS json_exists,
       '{"a":1}'::jsonb IS JSON OBJECT                           AS is_json_object;

 json_value | json_query | json_exists | is_json_object 
------------+------------+-------------+----------------
          7 | {"b": 7}   | f           | t
(1 row)

JSON_VALUE extracts a scalar and casts it with RETURNING; JSON_QUERY extracts a structure; asking JSON_VALUE for an object is an error rather than a surprise, which is the point of having two. Both take ON EMPTY and ON ERROR clauses (NULL, ERROR, DEFAULT expr) so that the failure behaviour is explicit.

The IS JSON predicate comes with variants — IS JSON OBJECT, ARRAY, SCALAR, VALUE, and WITH UNIQUE KEYS — which is how you validate a text column before casting it.

JSON_TABLE is the largest of them: it turns a document into a relation, in FROM.

SELECT * FROM JSON_TABLE(
  '{"items":[{"sku":"A","qty":2},{"sku":"B","qty":5}]}'::jsonb,
  '$.items[*]' COLUMNS (sku text PATH '$.sku', qty int PATH '$.qty')
) ORDER BY sku;

 sku | qty 
-----+-----
 A   |   2
 B   |   5
(2 rows)

One row per array element, typed columns, no manual unnesting. It also supports FOR ORDINALITY for a row number, NESTED PATH for arrays inside arrays, and EXISTS columns. For anything beyond a single flat array it is dramatically clearer than a stack of jsonb_array_elements calls.

In summary, the vocabulary here is is json predicate.

17.9 Indexing jsonb

Without an index, every @> is a sequential scan that deserialises every document. A GIN index on jsonb fixes that, and there are two operator classes.

CREATE INDEX docs_gin ON docs USING gin (body);
SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @> '{"meta":{"active":true}}';

CREATE INDEX
SET
                          QUERY PLAN                          
--------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on docs
   Recheck Cond: (body @> '{"meta": {"active": true}}'::jsonb)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on docs_gin
         Index Cond: (body @> '{"meta": {"active": true}}'::jsonb)
(4 rows)
default (jsonb_ops)
Indexes every key and every value separately. Supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&, @? and @@. Larger, and slower to build.
jsonb_path_ops
Indexes a hash of each root-to-leaf path. Smaller and faster, but supports only @>, @? and @@ — no key-existence operators.

Choose jsonb_path_ops when every query is a containment query, which is common. Choose the default when you also ask "does this key exist".

The third option is often the best and is the one people forget: index the expression. If the only thing you filter on is one scalar, a B-tree on that expression is far smaller and supports ranges and sorting, which GIN does not:

CREATE INDEX docs_score ON docs (((body #>> '{meta,score}')::int));
SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
  SELECT id FROM docs WHERE (body #>> '{meta,score}')::int > 5;

CREATE INDEX
SET
                            QUERY PLAN                            
------------------------------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using docs_score on docs
   Index Cond: (((body #>> '{meta,score}'::text[]))::integer > 5)
(2 rows)

The cast must be IMMUTABLE and the query must use the identical expression (§12.7). A GIN index could not serve > 5 at all.

What to carry forward from this subsection: gin index on jsonb.

17.10 When jsonb Is the Wrong Choice

jsonb is genuinely good, which is why it gets over-used. The honest guidance:

Good fit
A schema-on-read shape: payloads you receive and must keep whole; sparse or per-tenant custom attributes; configuration blobs; an event's variable detail alongside fixed columns; a cached denormalised projection.
Bad fit
Anything you join on, anything you need a foreign key for, anything with a fixed known shape, and anything you frequently update one field of.

Four costs are worth naming because they are invisible until they bite. You lose constraints — no NOT NULL, no CHECK, no foreign key on a value inside a document, so nothing stops a typo'd key appearing in 3% of rows. You lose statistics — the planner has no per-key histogram, so estimates for a @> filter come from a fixed default and every plan above them is guesswork (§13.10). Updates rewrite the whole document, because a row version is written whole (§14.7), so touching one field of a 40 kB document writes 40 kB. And a large document is TOASTed (§3.13) — compressed and stored out of line, so reading one field decompresses the whole thing.

The middle path is usually right: fixed, queried, constrained fields as real columns; the variable remainder in one jsonb column beside them.

The terms above, gathered: schema-on-read.

17.11 Arrays

Any type can be an array type, written type[], and PostgreSQL arrays are ordinary values — stored in the row, compared, indexed.

SELECT array_length(ARRAY[3,1,2], 1)     AS len,
       array_position(ARRAY[3,1,2], 2)   AS pos_of_2,
       array_remove(ARRAY[3,1,2], 1)     AS removed,
       ARRAY[1,2] <@ ARRAY[1,2,3]        AS contained,
       ARRAY[1,2,3] && ARRAY[3,4]        AS overlaps,
       2 = ANY(ARRAY[1,2,3])             AS any_match,
       ARRAY[1,2,3] || 4                 AS appended;

 len | pos_of_2 | removed | contained | overlaps | any_match | appended 
-----+----------+---------+-----------+----------+-----------+----------
   3 |        3 | {3,2}   | t         | t        | t         | {1,2,3,4}
(1 row)

Arrays are 1-based, and array_length takes a dimension argument because arrays can be multidimensional — and in PostgreSQL a multidimensional array must be rectangular, which is a real constraint people meet unexpectedly.

Each of those is an array operator, and ANY on an array — = ANY(array) — is the idiom that replaces a long IN list, and it is what most drivers generate for a parameterised list — one placeholder instead of N, so the query text is stable and the plan is cached.

array_position( finds an element's index and array_remove( returns a copy without it, while unnest() turns an array into rows and is the bridge back to ordinary relational work:

SELECT u FROM unnest(ARRAY['b','a','c']) AS u ORDER BY u;

 u 
---
 a
 b
 c
(3 rows)

WITH ORDINALITY adds the original position, which is how you preserve order through an unnest. array_agg() is the inverse, and takes ORDER BY inside it (§7.5).

A GIN index supports array containment with @> and <@, and overlap with &&, so "rows whose tag array contains 'sql'" is indexable exactly as the jsonb case is.

When is an array right? When the elements have no identity of their own, are always read together, and are never joined to — a list of tags, a set of flags, a fixed-length vector. When any of those fails, a junction table (§5.6) is better, and the tell is when you find yourself writing unnest in order to join.

One line each, for reference: array type, array_agg(, array operator, any on an array, unnest( and array containment.

17.12 Ranges and Multiranges

A range type is one value holding an interval, with bound inclusivity as part of the value.

SELECT int4range(1,10)                      AS r,
       int4range(1,10) @> 5                 AS contains,
       int4range(1,10) && int4range(5,20)   AS overlaps,
       upper(int4range(1,10))               AS upper_bound,
       int4range(1,10) = int4range(1,9,'[]') AS canonicalised,
       numrange(1,10,'[]')                  AS inclusive,
       int4multirange(int4range(1,5), int4range(10,15)) AS multi;

   r    | contains | overlaps | upper_bound | canonicalised | inclusive |      multi      
--------+----------+----------+-------------+---------------+-----------+-----------------
 [1,10) | t        | t        |          10 | t             | [1,10]    | {[1,5),[10,15)}
(1 row)

Three things there. A range bound may be inclusive or exclusive, and an unbounded range — one with NULL for a bound — runs forever in that direction, and the default bounds are [) — inclusive lower, exclusive upper — which is the convention that makes adjacent ranges tile without gaps or overlaps, and is why [1,10) prints that way.

int4range(1,10) = int4range(1,9,'[]') is true: for a discrete type PostgreSQL canonicalises to [), so those are the same value. For numrange there is no canonical form, because there is no "next" real number, and [1,10) and [1,10] are genuinely different.

A multirange type holds a set of disjoint ranges, and every range type has one automatically. It is what union and difference return when the answer is not contiguous.

The built-ins are int4range, int8range, numrange, tsrange, tstzrange and daterange; CREATE TYPE ... AS RANGE makes more. Each of those is a range operator: range containment with @> and <@, range overlap with &&, then <<, >>, -|- (adjacent), +, * and -. All are indexable with GiST.

The payoff is the exclusion constraint (§4.8): EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&) makes double-booking impossible at the database level, which no CHECK constraint can express. A tstzrange column plus that constraint replaces a page of application code and is correct under concurrency, which the application code was not.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: multirange type, unbounded range, range operator, range containment and range overlap.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: range bound.

17.13 Pattern Matching

Three levels, in increasing power and cost.

SELECT 'postgresql' LIKE 'postgres%'         AS like_prefix,
       'postgresql' LIKE '%gres%'            AS like_infix,
       'PostgreSQL' ILIKE 'postgres%'        AS case_insensitive,
       'abc123'  SIMILAR TO '[a-z]+[0-9]+'   AS similar_to,
       'abc123' ~  '^[a-z]+[0-9]+$'          AS posix_regex,
       'ABC123' ~* '^[a-z]+'                 AS posix_ci,
       regexp_replace('a1b2c3', '[0-9]', '#', 'g') AS replaced;

 like_prefix | like_infix | case_insensitive | similar_to | posix_regex | posix_ci | replaced 
-------------+------------+------------------+------------+-------------+----------+----------
 t           | t          | t                | t          | t           | t        | a#b#c#
(1 row)

LIKE has two wildcards, % and _, and is the only one of the three that a B-tree can accelerate — for a prefix pattern only, and subject to the collation rules in §12.10. ILIKE is the case-insensitive form and is PostgreSQL-specific.

SIMILAR TO is the SQL standard's regular expressions, and is a strange hybrid: % and _ as in LIKE, plus |, *, +, () and [] from regex. It is implemented by translating to a POSIX regex. There is essentially no reason to use it — learn one regex dialect, not one and a half.

POSIX regular expressions are the real tool: ~ matches, ~* matches case-insensitively, !~ and !~* negate. regexp_match(, regexp_replace(, regexp_split_to_array, regexp_split_to_table, and — from PostgreSQL 15 — regexp_count, regexp_instr, regexp_like and regexp_substr round it out. The g flag replaces globally; without it regexp_replace changes only the first match, which is a common surprise.

None of %foo, SIMILAR TO or ~ can use a B-tree index. That is what §17.14 is for.

To have in hand before moving on: b-tree index, posix regular expression, regexp_match( and regexp_replace(.

17.14 Trigram Similarity

pg_trgm breaks strings into three-character sequences and compares the sets, which gives fuzzy matching and an index for leading-wildcard patterns.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
SELECT round(similarity('postgresql','postgres')::numeric, 3) AS sim,
       'postgresql' % 'postgres'                              AS above_threshold,
       show_limit()                                           AS threshold;

CREATE EXTENSION
  sim  | above_threshold | threshold 
-------+-----------------+-----------
 0.667 | t               |       0.3
(1 row)

similarity() is a number from 0 to 1; % is true when it exceeds pg_trgm.similarity_threshold, which defaults to 0.3. <-> is the distance — 1 - similarity — and is what you ORDER BY for "closest match first".

A trigram index — CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (col gin_trgm_ops) — accelerates %, <->, LIKE '%anything%' and ~. That last is the important one: it is the only way to make a leading-wildcard search fast, and it is why "search as you type" over a name column does not need a search engine.

It also handles typos, which full-text search does not: to_tsquery will not match postgersql to postgresql, and a trigram index will.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: similarity(.

17.15 Full-Text Search: The Two Types

Full-text search is a different problem from pattern matching. It cares about words, their variants, their importance and their proximity — not about substrings.

Two types carry it. tsvector is a processed document: a sorted list of normalised words with positions. tsquery is a processed search expression.

SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The quick brown foxes were jumping over the lazy dogs') AS tsv;

                          tsv                           
--------------------------------------------------------
 'brown':3 'dog':10 'fox':4 'jump':6 'lazi':9 'quick':2
(1 row)

Read what happened to those eleven words. the, were and over are gone — stop words, too common to discriminate. foxes became fox, jumping became jump, dogs became dog, lazy became lazi — stemming reduced each to a root by the english configuration, which is why searching for jump finds jumping. The stems are not always real words (lazi), and that is fine: they are only ever compared to other stems. The numbers are positions, which is what makes phrase search possible.

to_tsvector must be given a configuration — 'english' here. Omit it and it uses default_text_search_config, which is a server setting and may not be what you assumed. A tsvector built with one configuration and a tsquery built with another will simply not match, silently.

In summary, the vocabulary here is stop word and stemming.

17.16 The Four Query Parsers

SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'fox & dog')                          AS to_tsquery,
       plainto_tsquery('english', 'jumping foxes')                 AS plainto,
       phraseto_tsquery('english', 'brown fox')                    AS phraseto,
       websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"brown fox" -lazy or dogs') AS websearch;

  to_tsquery   |    plainto     |     phraseto      |              websearch              
---------------+----------------+-------------------+-------------------------------------
 'fox' & 'dog' | 'jump' & 'fox' | 'brown' <-> 'fox' | 'brown' <-> 'fox' & !'lazi' | 'dog'
(1 row)
to_tsquery
Full operator syntax — &, |, !, <->, parentheses. Raises a syntax error on malformed input, so never hand it raw user text.
plainto_tsquery
plainto_tsquery( ANDs every word. Safe with any input, and offers the user no control at all.
phraseto_tsquery
phraseto_tsquery( puts words in sequence, using the <-> "followed by" operator.
websearch_to_tsquery
The syntax users already know from web search: quotes for a phrase, - for exclusion, or for alternatives. Never errors. This is the one to expose to users.

The <-> operator is genuinely positional, not just an ordered AND:

SELECT to_tsvector('english','the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog')
       @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english','"brown fox"') AS phrase_matches,
       to_tsvector('english','the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog')
       @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english','"fox brown"') AS reversed_matches;

 phrase_matches | reversed_matches 
----------------+------------------
 t              | f
(1 row)

@@ is the @@ match operator, and it is what a GIN index accelerates.

What to carry forward from this subsection: -> operator and @@ match operator.

17.17 A Searchable Table, End to End

The modern way to store a searchable document is a generated column (§4.10) plus a GIN index. Before PostgreSQL 12 this needed a trigger; it no longer does.

CREATE TABLE articles (id int PRIMARY KEY, title text, body text);
INSERT INTO articles VALUES
 (1,'Indexing strategies','B-tree indexes speed up range queries on ordered data.'),
 (2,'Vacuum and bloat','Dead tuples accumulate; autovacuum removes them from tables.'),
 (3,'Query planning','The planner estimates rows and chooses between index and sequential scans.');

ALTER TABLE articles ADD COLUMN tsv tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title,'')), 'A') ||
                       setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body ,'')), 'B')) STORED;

CREATE INDEX articles_tsv ON articles USING gin (tsv);

SELECT id, title,
       round(ts_rank(tsv, websearch_to_tsquery('english','index'))::numeric, 4) AS rank
FROM articles
WHERE tsv @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english','index')
ORDER BY rank DESC, id;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
ALTER TABLE
CREATE INDEX
 id |        title        |  rank  
----+---------------------+--------
  1 | Indexing strategies | 0.6687
  3 | Query planning      | 0.2432
(2 rows)

Five decisions are packed into that, and each is deliberate.

STORED, not virtual. A generated column defaults to VIRTUAL in PostgreSQL 18 (§4.10), and virtual generated columns cannot be indexed — so a search column must say STORED.

coalesce on every input, because NULL || anything is NULL and one missing subtitle would erase the whole document.

setweight tags each part with a weight label from A to D. ts_rank( weights them by default {0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0} for D, C, B, A, so a match in the title outranks one in the body — which is exactly what the result shows: article 1 has "Indexing" in its title and scores 0.6687; article 3 has "index" only in its body and scores 0.2432.

The expression must be IMMUTABLE, which is why the configuration is spelled 'english' rather than left to the server default: to_tsvector(text) with one argument depends on a session setting and is only STABLE.

GIN, not GiST — §17.19.

The terms above, gathered: column default, to_tsvector( and weight label.

17.18 Ranking and Highlighting

ts_rank scores by term frequency and weight; ts_rank_cd — cover density — also accounts for how close the terms are to each other, and is better for phrase-like queries. Both take an optional normalisation flag to divide by document length, without which long documents win by accumulating matches.

Ranking is not free and it is not indexed. The GIN index finds the matching rows; the rank is then computed for every one of them, and ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT 10 sorts them all. On a query matching a million rows that is a million rank computations. The usual mitigation is to narrow the match first — with other WHERE conditions, or a two-stage query that limits candidates before ranking.

ts_headline( returns the matching text with the terms marked:

SELECT ts_headline('english',
  'The planner estimates rows and chooses between index and sequential scans.',
  websearch_to_tsquery('english','planner scans')) AS headline;

                                        headline
