------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 The <b>planner</b> estimates rows and chooses between index and sequential <b>scans</b>.
(1 row)

ts_headline( works on the original text, not on the tsvector — the vector has no original words in it. So it must re-parse the document, which makes it expensive: apply it after LIMIT, never to every match. Its options — StartSel, StopSel, MaxWords, MinWords, MaxFragments — are passed as a comma-separated string.

17.19 Configurations, Dictionaries, and Choosing an Index

A text search configuration is a pipeline: a parser splits text into tokens with types (word, number, email, URL, host), and each token type is passed through a list of dictionaries until one recognises it. Each entry in that list is a text search dictionary.

A dictionary either returns replacement lexemes, returns an empty result (a stop word — the token is dropped), or passes the token to the next one. The built-in kinds are simple (lowercase, check a stop list), synonym (a flat mapping), thesaurus (multi-word phrases), ispell (a real morphological dictionary, more accurate than a stemmer) and snowball (the stemmer behind the english configuration).

\dF lists the configurations, and ts_debug() shows exactly what happened to each token — which is the tool to reach for when a search does not match what you expected. Building a custom configuration is CREATE TEXT SEARCH CONFIGURATION plus ALTER ... ADD MAPPING, and the most common reason is adding an unaccent dictionary so that café and cafe are the same word.

GIN versus GiST for text is the last decision:

GIN
Exact, and roughly three times faster to search. Slower to build and to update. The default choice for a document table that is read far more than written.
GiST
Lossy — it produces candidates that must be rechecked against the heap, so it is slower and its cost grows with document count. Cheaper to update. Worth it only for a heavily written table.

GIN buffers updates in a pending list to keep insertion cheap; fastupdate controls it, and gin_pending_list_limit its size. A search must scan that pending list linearly, so a burst of writes can make searches temporarily slower until vacuum merges it in — a real and confusing symptom worth recognising.

One line each, for reference: text search dictionary, lexeme and gin versus gist for text.

17.20 Collation and Case-Insensitive Text

A collation decides how text sorts and compares. It is a property of a column, an expression or a database, and it changes results rather than just performance.

SELECT 'a' < 'B' COLLATE "C"          AS in_c_collation,
       'a' < 'B' COLLATE "en-US-x-icu" AS in_icu_collation;

 in_c_collation | in_icu_collation 
----------------+------------------
 f              | t
(1 row)

The same comparison gives opposite answers. C sorts by byte value, so every uppercase letter precedes every lowercase one; a linguistic collation sorts as a dictionary does. This is not a corner case — it changes ORDER BY, <, BETWEEN, and which index a LIKE can use (§12.10).

PostgreSQL supports two providers: libc (the operating system's, so results can change when the OS is upgraded — a genuine hazard, because an index built under the old rules is then subtly corrupt) and ICU (versioned with the database, more predictable, and the better default). PostgreSQL 17 added a built-in provider offering C.UTF-8, which gives byte ordering with correct Unicode case handling.

For case-insensitive comparison there are three options, in increasing order of correctness:

lower() on both sides, with an expression index (§12.7). Explicit, portable, and easy to forget in one query out of thirty.

citext, an extension type that compares case-insensitively by itself. Convenient, and it folds case using lower(), so its notion of "same" is only as good as that.

A nondeterministic ICU collation — CREATE COLLATION ... (provider = icu, locale = 'und-u-ks-level2', deterministic = false) — which makes the column case-insensitive at the collation level, so unique indexes and joins respect it too. It is the correct answer, and its cost is that some optimisations are unavailable on such a column, notably the pattern-range trick from §12.10 — though PostgreSQL 18 did add LIKE support for nondeterministic collations, which was previously an outright error.

PostgreSQL 18 also added casefold(), a Unicode-correct alternative to lower() for case-insensitive matching: it implements full case folding, which handles cases lower() gets wrong.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: case folding, nondeterministic collation, icu collation, casefold( and citext.

What This Section Established

json keeps the input text; jsonb parses it, sorts keys, drops whitespace and keeps the last of duplicate keys — measured. Use jsonb unless you must reproduce bytes.

-> returns jsonb, ->> returns text: navigate with the first, finish with the second. #>/#>> take a path. Subscripting works on columns, not literals.

@> containment and ?/?|/?& existence are the GIN-indexable operators, so build WHERE clauses from them. ? collides with the placeholder character in some drivers.

jsonb_set, || (top level only, not a deep merge), -, and jsonb_strip_nulls (which leaves empty objects behind). Build with jsonb_build_object, never string concatenation.

jsonb_array_elements, jsonb_each, jsonb_to_record expand documents into rows — an implicit LATERAL.

jsonpath: $, .key, [*], **, and ? (@ ...) filters. jsonb_path_exists for WHERE; pass values through vars, not concatenation; strict mode when a missing key is a bug.

SQL/JSON: JSON_VALUE for scalars with RETURNING, JSON_QUERY for structures, IS JSON for validation, and JSON_TABLE to turn a document into a relation in FROM.

Index jsonb with GIN — jsonb_path_ops when every query is containment, default when you also test key existence — or with a B-tree on an expression when you filter one scalar, which is smaller and supports ranges.

jsonb costs you constraints, planner statistics, whole-document rewrites on update, and TOAST decompression. Fixed queried fields belong in columns.

Arrays are 1-based, must be rectangular if multidimensional, support @>/&&/= ANY with a GIN index, and are the wrong choice the moment you need to join to the elements.

Ranges default to [); discrete types canonicalise, so int4range(1,10) = int4range(1,9,'[]') is true. Multiranges hold disjoint sets. The payoff is the exclusion constraint.

LIKE is prefix-indexable; SIMILAR TO is a hybrid with no reason to exist; POSIX regex is the real tool and needs the g flag to replace globally. Only a trigram index makes %foo% and ~ fast, and only trigrams tolerate typos.

to_tsvector stems, removes stop words and records positions — foxes/jumping/lazy became fox/jump/lazi, and the/were/over vanished. Always pass the configuration explicitly.

Four query parsers. websearch_to_tsquery is the one to expose to users: it never errors and speaks the syntax they already know. <-> is positional — "brown fox" matched and "fox brown" did not.

A searchable table is a STORED generated tsvector (virtual cannot be indexed) with coalesce on every input and setweight per part, plus a GIN index. Weighting made a title match score 0.6687 against a body match's 0.2432.

Ranking is computed per matching row and is not indexed. ts_headline re-parses the original text — apply it after LIMIT.

GIN is the default for search; GiST only for write-heavy tables. GIN's pending list can make searches temporarily slow after a write burst.

Collation changes results, not only order: 'a' < 'B' is false under C and true under ICU. Prefer ICU over libc. For case-insensitivity: lower() plus an expression index, citext, or a nondeterministic collation — and PostgreSQL 18's casefold() where lower() is not Unicode-correct.

Exercises

1. Prove the two JSON types differ. Insert the same document with a duplicate key, extra whitespace and unsorted keys into a json column and a jsonb column. Show all three differences. Then try to create a GIN index on each and report what happens.

2. Extract three ways. Get the same nested value from a document using ->/->>, #>>, and jsonb_path_query. Then produce a type error by using ->> too early, and explain the message.

3. Index a document filter and prove it. Load ten thousand documents. Write a containment query and record the plan. Add a jsonb_path_ops GIN index and record it again. Then write a range query on a numeric field inside the document and show the GIN index does not help — and what does.

4. Choose between array and table. Model "an article has tags" both as a text[] column and as a junction table. Write, for each: find articles with a given tag; count articles per tag; rename a tag everywhere. Say which model won each time and why.

5. Prevent a double booking. Build a bookings table with a tstzrange and an exclusion constraint that forbids two overlapping bookings for the same room. Prove it rejects an overlap, accepts an adjacent booking, and — using two sessions — that it holds under concurrency where an application-level check would not.

6. Build a search that behaves. Create a table with title and body, a STORED weighted tsvector, and a GIN index. Search it with all four query parsers for the same user input, including input containing a bare &. Report which ones error. Then add ranking and highlighting, and say where in the query each belongs relative to LIMIT.

7. Break a search silently. Build a tsvector with one configuration and query it with another, and show that a document which obviously matches does not. Then show the same failure caused by omitting coalesce around a NULL column. State what you would add to a test suite to catch both.

Solution

1. The two types.

§17.1 shows key sorting, whitespace removal and last-duplicate-wins in one query.

The index attempt is the instructive half:

CREATE TABLE two_types (j json, b jsonb);
CREATE INDEX ON two_types USING gin (b);

CREATE TABLE
CREATE INDEX

A GIN index on the jsonb column succeeds. On the json column it fails, because no GIN operator class exists for json — there is nothing to index without parsing, and the type's whole promise is that it does not parse. The only way to index a json column is on an expression that extracts a scalar.

2. Extract three ways.

All three are in §17.2 and §17.7. The type error:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT (body ->> 'meta') -> 'score' FROM docs;

ERROR:  operator does not exist: text -> unknown
LINE 1: SELECT (body ->> 'meta') -> 'score' FROM docs;
                                 ^
HINT:  No operator matches the given name and argument types. You might need to add explicit type casts.

The message is precise once you know the rule: ->> returned text, and there is no -> operator taking text on the left. The hint about casts is a red herring here — the fix is to use -> for the intermediate step, not to cast.

3. Indexing a document filter.

§17.9 has the containment plan with and without the index.

The range query is the point. WHERE (body #>> '{meta,score}')::int > 5 cannot use a GIN index at all: GIN indexes elements, and answering "greater than 5" would require enumerating every value above 5 and looking each one up. Only a B-tree on the extracted expression answers it, which is the third index shown in §17.9. The general rule: GIN for "contains", B-tree on an expression for "compares".

4. Array against junction table.

Find articles with a tag: both work, both indexable — array with tags @> ARRAY['sql'] and a GIN index, junction table with a join and a B-tree.

Count articles per tag: the array needs unnest then GROUP BY, which reads every row; the junction table is a GROUP BY on an indexed column. Junction table wins clearly.

Rename a tag everywhere: the array needs array_replace over every affected row, rewriting each one; the junction table needs a single-row update if tags are their own entity, or one indexed UPDATE if not. Junction table wins decisively.

The pattern: arrays win when elements have no identity and are only ever read with their parent. The moment you aggregate by element or update elements independently, they have identity, and the relational model already has a name for that.

5. Preventing a double booking.

CREATE TABLE bookings (
  room text NOT NULL,
  during tstzrange NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES ('A', tstzrange('2026-03-01 09:00+00','2026-03-01 10:00+00'));
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES ('A', tstzrange('2026-03-01 10:00+00','2026-03-01 11:00+00'));
SELECT count(*) AS adjacent_bookings_accepted FROM bookings;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 1
INSERT 0 1
 adjacent_bookings_accepted 
----------------------------
                          2
(1 row)

Adjacent is fine, because the default [) bounds mean 10:00 belongs to the second booking only. Now the overlap:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES ('A', tstzrange('2026-03-01 09:30+00','2026-03-01 10:30+00'));

ERROR:  conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "bookings_room_during_excl"
DETAIL:  Key (room, during)=(A, ["2026-03-01 09:30:00+00","2026-03-01 10:30:00+00")) conflicts with existing key (room, during)=(A, ["2026-03-01 09:00:00+00","2026-03-01 10:00:00+00")).

btree_gist — installed in §4.8 — is needed because the constraint mixes an equality test on text with an overlap test on a range, and plain GiST has no operator class for text equality.

The concurrency argument is the real one. An application that runs SELECT ... WHERE during && $1 and then inserts if it finds nothing has a race: two requests can both find nothing and both insert. Under READ COMMITTED nothing prevents it — this is the write skew of §14.13. The exclusion constraint is enforced by the index at insert time, so one of the two fails with the error above regardless of isolation level.

6. A search that behaves.

§17.17 is the table and index. The parser comparison:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'index & ');

ERROR:  no operand in tsquery: "index & "

to_tsquery errors. plainto_tsquery, phraseto_tsquery and websearch_to_tsquery all accept it and return a usable query. That is the whole argument for never putting to_tsquery in front of a user.

Placement relative to LIMIT: the @@ match belongs in WHERE so the index does the filtering; ts_rank belongs in ORDER BY, and is computed for every matching row; ts_headline belongs outside a subquery that has already applied LIMIT, because it re-parses the original document and you want to pay for ten of those, not ten thousand.

SELECT id, title, ts_headline('english', body, q) AS snippet
FROM (SELECT id, title, body, websearch_to_tsquery('english','index') AS q
      FROM articles
      WHERE tsv @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english','index')
      ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, websearch_to_tsquery('english','index')) DESC, id
      LIMIT 1) t;

 id |        title        |                       snippet                       
----+---------------------+-----------------------------------------------------
  1 | Indexing strategies | B-tree <b>indexes</b> speed up range queries on ordered data.
(1 row)

7. Breaking a search silently.

SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'running quickly') @@ to_tsquery('english', 'run') AS same_config,
       to_tsvector('simple',  'running quickly') @@ to_tsquery('english', 'run') AS mismatched,
       to_tsvector('english', 'title') || to_tsvector('english', NULL) IS NULL AS null_erases;

 same_config | mismatched | null_erases 
-------------+------------+-------------
 t           | f          | t
(1 row)

The simple configuration does not stem, so the document holds running and the query holds run, and they never meet. No error, no warning — the row simply never appears.

The NULL case is worse, because it silently erases the whole vector: one missing subtitle and the document becomes unsearchable by any term, including the ones in its title.

Two tests catch both. Assert a round trip: for each searchable table, take a known row, extract a word from its indexed text, search for it, and assert the row comes back. That catches the configuration mismatch, the missing coalesce, and a generated column someone changed. And assert no row has an empty vector — SELECT count(*) FROM articles WHERE tsv = ''::tsvector should be zero, or should equal a number you can explain.

SECTION 18

Views, Functions, Procedures and Triggers

Everything so far has been things you send to the database. This section is about things you store in it: named queries, callable code, and code the database runs on your behalf when data changes.

That last category deserves a warning at the top rather than the bottom. A trigger is invisible from the statement that fires it, so business logic in a trigger is logic that does not appear in any code review of the query that triggered it. There are cases where that is exactly right — auditing, denormalisation, enforcing an invariant nothing else can — and cases where it produces a system nobody can reason about. §18.20 draws the line explicitly.

CREATE TABLE staff (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text, dept text, active boolean);
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (1,'Ada','eng',true), (2,'Lin','eng',false), (3,'Kai','ops',true);

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3

18.1 A View Is a Saved Query

CREATE VIEW active_staff AS SELECT id, name, dept FROM staff WHERE active;
SELECT * FROM active_staff ORDER BY id;

CREATE VIEW
 id | name | dept 
----+------+------
  1 | Ada  | eng
  3 | Kai  | ops
(2 rows)

A view stores no data. As §13.2 established, the rewriter substitutes the view's definition into your query and the planner optimises the whole thing at once — so a WHERE clause applied outside a view can become an index condition inside it. There is no "run the view then filter" step to worry about.

That also means a view costs nothing to have and does not go stale. What it buys is a name for a query, a stable interface over a schema you may want to change, and a place to put a filter you want applied consistently.

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW redefines one in place, but only if the new definition produces the same column names and types in the same order, and only if it adds columns at the end rather than removing or reordering. Anything more is DROP and recreate, which fails on a view dependency — another view built on this one — PostgreSQL tracks the dependency and refuses. That is a real friction in migrations and the reason CASCADE exists, and using CASCADE on views is how a dependent view silently disappears.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: view dependency and create or replace view.

18.2 Views You Can Write Through

A view is auto-updatable if it selects from exactly one table, with no aggregation, no DISTINCT, no GROUP BY, no set operation, no window function, and only simple column references in its select list. active_staff qualifies:

UPDATE active_staff SET dept = 'platform' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT id, dept FROM staff ORDER BY id;

UPDATE 1
 id |   dept   
----+----------
  1 | platform
  2 | eng
  3 | ops
(3 rows)

The update went through to the base table. Now the hazard:

INSERT INTO active_staff (id, name, dept) VALUES (4, 'Mo', 'ops');
SELECT count(*) AS rows_in_table FROM staff;
SELECT count(*) AS rows_in_view  FROM active_staff;

INSERT 0 1
 rows_in_table 
---------------
             4
(1 row)

 rows_in_view 
--------------
            2
(1 row)

The insert succeeded and the row is invisible through the view it was inserted into. active was not in the view's column list, so it defaulted to NULL, and WHERE active excludes it. The application inserted a row and then could not find it.

18.3 WITH CHECK OPTION

That is what WITH CHECK OPTION is for: it requires every row written through the view to satisfy the view's own condition.

CREATE VIEW checked_staff AS
  SELECT id, name, dept FROM staff WHERE active WITH CHECK OPTION;
\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
INSERT INTO checked_staff (id, name, dept) VALUES (5, 'Rae', 'ops');

CREATE VIEW
ERROR:  new row violates check option for view "checked_staff"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (5, Rae, ops, null).

LOCAL checks only this view's condition; CASCADED — the default — also checks every view underneath. Put it on every updatable view you expose, unless you have a specific reason to allow writes you cannot read back.

For anything the auto-updatable rules exclude — a view over a join, an aggregate, a union — an INSTEAD OF trigger (§18.17) makes it writable with logic you supply.

To have in hand before moving on: instead of trigger.

18.4 Views and Security

A view runs with the privileges of its owner, not its caller. That is the mechanism behind using views as an access-control layer: grant SELECT on a view exposing four columns, grant nothing on the ten-column table underneath.

Two options modify it, and both matter.

A security_invoker view — security_invoker = true, PostgreSQL 15 and later — reverses it: the view is executed with the caller's privileges, so the caller must have access to the base table. That is what you want when the view is a convenience rather than a privilege boundary — and it is what makes row-level security (§20.10) apply to the person querying rather than the view's owner.

security_barrier = true closes a leak. Without it, the planner may push a user-supplied WHERE clause below the view's own filter — so a function in the caller's predicate can be evaluated on rows the view was meant to hide, and a RAISE NOTICE inside that function leaks their contents. The barrier forbids that reordering for any function that is not marked LEAKPROOF. Set it on any view whose filter is a security boundary; expect it to cost you some plans.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: security_barrier and security_invoker view.

18.5 Materialized Views

A materialized view does store its result. It is a table that remembers the query that filled it.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW dept_counts AS
  SELECT dept, count(*) AS n FROM staff GROUP BY dept;
SELECT dept, n FROM dept_counts ORDER BY dept;

SELECT 3
   dept   | n 
----------+---
 eng      | 1
 ops      | 2
 platform | 1
(3 rows)

It does not track changes:

INSERT INTO staff VALUES (9, 'Zed', 'eng', true);
SELECT dept, n FROM dept_counts ORDER BY dept;
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW dept_counts;
SELECT dept, n FROM dept_counts ORDER BY dept;

INSERT 0 1
   dept   | n 
----------+---
 eng      | 1
 ops      | 2
 platform | 1
(3 rows)

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
   dept   | n 
----------+---
 eng      | 2
 ops      | 2
 platform | 1
(3 rows)

Stale until refreshed, and nothing warns you. That is the whole trade: you pay for the query once per refresh instead of once per read, and in exchange the data is as old as your last refresh.

A plain REFRESH takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — the view is unreadable while it rebuilds. REFRESH CONCURRENTLY avoids that, and has one prerequisite:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY dept_counts;

ERROR:  cannot refresh materialized view "public.dept_counts" concurrently
HINT:  Create a unique index with no WHERE clause on one or more columns of the materialized view.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX dept_counts_dept ON dept_counts (dept);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY dept_counts;

CREATE INDEX
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW

The unique index is how PostgreSQL identifies rows in order to compute a diff rather than replacing the whole relation. CONCURRENTLY is slower in total work — it builds the new result and then merges — and it does not block readers, which is usually the trade you want.

A materialized view can have its own indexes, and usually should; it is a table. It cannot be refreshed inside a transaction that also queries it, and it has no incremental refresh — a change to one source row rebuilds everything.

In summary, the vocabulary here is refresh concurrently.

18.6 The Rule System

Underneath views is the rule system, which rewrites query trees before planning. CREATE VIEW is implemented as an ON SELECT DO INSTEAD rule, and the auto-updatable behaviour of §18.2 is implemented by the rewriter too.

You can write rules directly with CREATE RULE, and you should not. Rules operate on the query tree rather than on rows, which means a rule containing a volatile function can evaluate it a different number of times than you expect, and a rule that references NEW more than once evaluates the source expression more than once. The failure modes are subtle and the diagnostics are poor. Triggers do the same jobs with per-row semantics you can reason about, and the only remaining reason to know rules exist is that views are built on them.

18.7 Functions

A function takes arguments, returns a value, and can be called anywhere an expression can. PostgreSQL ships four procedural languages — sql, plpgsql, plpython3u and pltcl — plus C, and extensions add more.

The two you will use are sql and plpgsql, and the choice is simple: sql when the body is one query, plpgsql when you need variables, branching or loops.

CREATE FUNCTION add_tax(cents int, rate numeric) RETURNS int
LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE
BEGIN ATOMIC
  SELECT (cents * (1 + rate))::int;
END;
SELECT add_tax(10000, 0.19) AS with_tax;

CREATE FUNCTION
 with_tax 
----------
    11900
(1 row)

BEGIN ATOMIC is the modern body syntax (PostgreSQL 14 and later) and it is a real improvement over the traditional string body. A string body is parsed only when the function first runs, so a typo or a reference to a dropped table is discovered in production; BEGIN ATOMIC is parsed at creation time, and the dependency on staff is recorded, so dropping a table a function depends on is refused rather than silently breaking it.

18.8 Returning Sets

RETURNS TABLE (...) declares a function that produces rows, callable in FROM:

CREATE FUNCTION dept_members(p_dept text) RETURNS TABLE (id int, name text)
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY SELECT s.id, s.name FROM staff s WHERE s.dept = p_dept ORDER BY s.id;
END $$;
SELECT * FROM dept_members('eng') ORDER BY id;

CREATE FUNCTION
 id | name 
----+------
  2 | Lin
  9 | Zed
(2 rows)

Note s.id rather than id in the body: RETURNS TABLE puts id and name in scope as output variables, and an unqualified reference is ambiguous. PostgreSQL raises an error rather than guessing, and qualifying the table is the fix. The common convention — prefixing parameters with p_, as here — exists for the same reason.

RETURNS SETOF type is the alternative when the shape is an existing composite type or a single column. RETURN NEXT emits rows one at a time; RETURN QUERY emits a whole result set and is faster.

A set-returning function in FROM is opaque to the planner. It has no statistics, so PostgreSQL estimates 1000 rows by default (ROWS on the function declaration overrides that), and it cannot push your outer WHERE clause inside. A function wrapping a query is often slower than the query, and always harder to plan.

What to carry forward from this subsection: setof.

18.9 Arguments, Defaults and Overloading

A default argument makes a trailing parameter optional. Arguments are positional by default and can be passed by name — add_tax(cents => 10000, rate => 0.19) — which is worth using for anything with more than two.

The DEFAULT keyword in a parameter list is what creates a default argument. Function overloading works on argument types, which means the identity of a function is its name plus its argument types: DROP FUNCTION add_tax is ambiguous if two exist, and DROP FUNCTION add_tax(int, numeric) is not.

Overloading plus defaults is a trap: f(int) and f(int, int DEFAULT 0) makes f(1) ambiguous, and PostgreSQL will tell you so at call time rather than at creation. OUT and INOUT parameters are the alternative to a composite return type, and a function with several OUT parameters and no RETURNS clause returns a record.

The terms above, gathered: function overloading.

One line each, for reference: default argument.

18.10 Volatility, and Why It Is Not Optional

Function volatility declares how much the planner may assume. Every function has one, and the default is the most pessimistic. The default is the most pessimistic, and leaving it there is the most common performance mistake with functions.

IMMUTABLE volatility
Same arguments always give the same result, forever. No database access at all. Can be folded to a constant at planning time, and is the only kind usable in an index expression (§12.7).
STABLE volatility
Constant within one statement. May read the database and session settings. Can be used in an index scan condition — which is why WHERE ts < now() uses an index and WHERE ts < clock_timestamp() does not.
VOLATILE
The default. May return anything, may have side effects. Re-evaluated for every row, never folded, never inlined, and forces a re-plan of anything depending on it.
CREATE FUNCTION unmarked() RETURNS int LANGUAGE sql AS 'SELECT 1';
SELECT proname, provolatile, proparallel
FROM pg_proc WHERE proname IN ('add_tax','unmarked') ORDER BY proname;

CREATE FUNCTION
 proname  | provolatile | proparallel 
----------+-------------+-------------
 add_tax  | i           | u
 unmarked | v           | u
(2 rows)

unmarked is v — volatile — despite returning a constant, because nothing was declared. And note proparallel is u for both: a user-defined function is PARALLEL UNSAFE by default, which as §13.12 warned forces the entire query containing it to run serially. Two words on the declaration — IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE — are frequently the difference between a parallel plan and a serial one.

Declaring a function IMMUTABLE when it is not is not caught and not safe: PostgreSQL will cache its result and use it in an index, and the index will silently disagree with the data.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: function volatility, immutable volatility and stable volatility.

18.11 Function Inlining

A SQL function that is a single SELECT, is not VOLATILE, is not SECURITY DEFINER, and has no SET clauses can be inlined — its body is substituted into the calling query and optimised as part of it. The function disappears from the plan entirely and costs nothing.

A PL/pgSQL function is never inlined. It is a black box with a function-call boundary, its own snapshot handling, and no visibility for the planner.

That single difference is the practical argument for writing simple helpers in LANGUAGE sql. A LANGUAGE sql scalar helper used in a WHERE clause can become an index condition; the same helper in PL/pgSQL becomes a per-row function call that defeats the index.

18.12 PL/pgSQL

PL/pgSQL adds variables, control flow and exception handling around SQL. Its structure is a block:

DO $$
DECLARE
  n int;
  rows_affected int;
BEGIN
  SELECT count(*) INTO n FROM staff;
  RAISE NOTICE 'staff rows: %', n;
  UPDATE staff SET active = true WHERE NOT active;
  GET DIAGNOSTICS rows_affected = ROW_COUNT;
  RAISE NOTICE 'updated %, FOUND is %', rows_affected, FOUND;
END $$;

NOTICE:  staff rows: 5
NOTICE:  updated 1, FOUND is t
DO

A DO block is an anonymous function: it runs once, takes no arguments and returns nothing. It is the right tool for a one-off migration step that needs a loop.

A plpgsql variable is declared in DECLARE and assigned with := or with SELECT ... INTO. SELECT ... INTO var assigns a single row; it does not error if the query returns no rows — the variable is set to NULL — nor if it returns several, in which case you get the first. SELECT ... INTO STRICT errors on anything but exactly one row, and is what you usually want.

The FOUND variable is a boolean set by the last SELECT INTO, UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE or FOR loop. GET DIAGNOSTICS ... = ROW_COUNT gives the actual number. A RAISE statement prints — RAISE NOTICE — and % is its placeholder and there is no positional numbering, so the arguments are consumed in order.

Control flow is IF/ELSIF/ELSE and CASE, plus the plpgsql loop forms: LOOP, WHILE, FOR i IN 1..10, FOREACH x IN ARRAY, and — the one that matters most — FOR IN SELECT, written FOR rec IN SELECT ..., which iterates a query without a cursor.

The most important thing to know about PL/pgSQL is when not to use it. A loop that runs one UPDATE per row is between ten and a thousand times slower than the single set-based UPDATE that does the same thing. If you find yourself writing FOR rec IN SELECT ... LOOP UPDATE ... END LOOP, the answer is almost always one statement.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: set-based, do block, plpgsql variable, raise statement, found variable, plpgsql loop and for in select.

18.13 Exceptions

CREATE FUNCTION safe_div(a numeric, b numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN a / b;
EXCEPTION
  WHEN division_by_zero THEN
    RAISE NOTICE 'caught % (%)', SQLSTATE, SQLERRM;
    RETURN NULL;
END $$;
SELECT safe_div(10, 2) AS ok, safe_div(10, 0) AS caught;

CREATE FUNCTION
NOTICE:  caught 22012 (division by zero)
         ok         | caught 
--------------------+--------
 5.0000000000000000 |       
(1 row)

Handlers name a condition (division_by_zero, unique_violation, foreign_key_violation) or a SQLSTATE (SQLSTATE '22012'), and OTHERS catches everything except query cancellation. Inside a handler, SQLSTATE and SQLERRM describe the error, and GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS retrieves more — PG_EXCEPTION_DETAIL, PG_EXCEPTION_HINT, PG_EXCEPTION_CONTEXT, CONSTRAINT_NAME.

Every EXCEPTION block is an implicit savepoint, with the cost §14.5 described. A block with a handler is measurably more expensive than one without, and a handler inside a loop over a million rows creates a million subtransactions. Where a handler exists only to ignore a duplicate, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (§11.7) does the same job with no subtransaction at all.

RAISE EXCEPTION throws: RAISE EXCEPTION 'bad state for %', id USING ERRCODE = 'check_violation', HINT = 'call support'. Choose a real SQLSTATE, or use the P0001 default and accept that callers cannot distinguish your errors from each other.

18.14 Cursors

A FOR ... IN SELECT loop is a cursor with the bookkeeping hidden, and covers nearly every case. An explicit cursor — DECLARE cursor, then OPEN, then FETCH from a cursor — is for the rest:

DO $$
DECLARE
  c CURSOR FOR SELECT id, name FROM staff ORDER BY id;
  r record;
BEGIN
  OPEN c;
  FETCH c INTO r;
  RAISE NOTICE 'first row: % %', r.id, r.name;
  MOVE FORWARD 1 IN c;
  FETCH c INTO r;
  RAISE NOTICE 'third row: % %', r.id, r.name;
  CLOSE c;
END $$;

NOTICE:  first row: 1 Ada
NOTICE:  third row: 3 Kai
DO

The two real reasons to use one: processing a result too large to hold in memory, and returning a cursor to the client as a refcursor, so the application pages through a result set the server holds open. That second use is far less common than it was — LIMIT/OFFSET and keyset pagination (§8.9) are usually better, because a held cursor pins a transaction open, which §14.17 explains is expensive.

To have in hand before moving on: declare cursor and fetch from a cursor.

18.15 Dynamic SQL

When the table or column name is not known until runtime, EXECUTE builds and runs the statement:

CREATE FUNCTION count_rows(tbl text) RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE n bigint;
BEGIN
  EXECUTE format('SELECT count(*) FROM %I', tbl) INTO n;
  RETURN n;
END $$;
SELECT count_rows('staff') AS rows;

CREATE FUNCTION
 rows 
------
    5
(1 row)

format() is not optional, and its three specifiers are the whole discipline:

SELECT format('%I %L %s', 'my table', E'O\'Brien', 42) AS formatted;

        formatted         
--------------------------
 "my table" 'O''Brien' 42
(1 row)

%I — equivalently quote_ident( — quotes as an identifier, and note it added the double quotes that my table needs. Reserve quote_ident( for the cases where format is not convenient. %L quotes as a literal, doubling the embedded apostrophe. %s inserts raw text and is the one that is an injection vector (§20.5).

Better still: pass values as parameters, not as text. EXECUTE 'SELECT ... WHERE id = $1' USING p_id sends the value out of band, and it also allows plan caching in plpgsql: a static statement is prepared once per session while a dynamic one is re-planned on every call, so no quoting question arises. Reserve %L for cases where the value must be part of the statement text, and %I for identifiers, which cannot be parameters.

Dynamic SQL is re-planned on every call, so a function that could have been static is slower as well as riskier.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: plan caching in plpgsql.

18.16 Procedures and Transaction Control

A procedure is invoked by a CALL statement, returns nothing by default, and — the reason it exists — can commit and start new transactions.

CREATE PROCEDURE reset_dept() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE staff SET dept = 'eng';
  COMMIT;
  UPDATE staff SET dept = 'ops' WHERE id = 3;
  COMMIT;
END $$;
CALL reset_dept();
SELECT id, dept FROM staff ORDER BY id;

CREATE PROCEDURE
CALL
 id | dept 
----+------
  1 | eng
  2 | eng
  3 | ops
  4 | eng
  9 | eng
(5 rows)

Transaction control in a procedure is the whole reason procedures exist. A function cannot do it: a function runs inside the caller's transaction and has no boundary to commit. That makes procedures the right tool for batch jobs that must not hold one enormous transaction — process ten thousand rows, commit, repeat — which is precisely the shape that keeps vacuum working (§14.17).

The restriction: a procedure can only commit when it was invoked by a top-level CALL, not from inside a function or a query. And OUT parameters make a procedure return values, which is how you get a result out of one.

In summary, the vocabulary here is call statement and transaction control in a procedure.

18.17 Triggers: The Matrix

A trigger binds a function to a table and an event. Four axes, and the combination decides what the trigger can do.

BEFORE
Runs before the row is written. Can modify NEW, and can cancel the operation for that row by returning NULL. Constraints have not been checked yet.
AFTER trigger
Runs after the write and after constraint checks. Cannot change the row. The right place for auditing and for anything that must see the final state.
INSTEAD OF
Views only. Replaces the operation entirely — the mechanism for writable non-updatable views (§18.3).
FOR EACH ROW
Once per affected row, with NEW and OLD available.
FOR EACH STATEMENT
Once per statement, even when it affected zero rows. No NEW/OLD — use transition tables (§18.19).

TG_OP tells the function which event fired it, TG_TABLE_NAME which table, and TG_ARGV carries arguments given in the CREATE TRIGGER. A WHEN condition on a trigger avoids calling the function at all — WHEN (OLD.dept IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.dept) is much cheaper than the same test inside the function.

Triggers on one table fire in name order, which is the only control you have over sequencing. Naming them 01_validate, 02_audit is a real technique rather than a joke.

What to carry forward from this subsection: tg_op and when condition on a trigger.

The terms above, gathered: after trigger.

18.18 Writing a Trigger Function

A trigger function takes no arguments, returns trigger, and reads the NEW record and the OLD record from scope.

CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  entry_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  op text, who text, old_dept text, new_dept text);

CREATE FUNCTION staff_audit() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO audit_log (op, who, old_dept, new_dept)
  VALUES (TG_OP, coalesce(NEW.name, OLD.name), OLD.dept, NEW.dept);
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;

CREATE TRIGGER staff_audit_trg AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON staff
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION staff_audit();

UPDATE staff SET dept = 'platform' WHERE id = 1;
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (7, 'Sam', 'ops', true);
SELECT op, who, old_dept, new_dept FROM audit_log ORDER BY entry_id;

CREATE TABLE
CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE TRIGGER
UPDATE 1
INSERT 0 1
   op   | who | old_dept | new_dept 
--------+-----+----------+----------
 UPDATE | Ada | eng      | platform
 INSERT | Sam |          | ops
(2 rows)

OLD is NULL on an insert and NEW is NULL on a delete, which is why the function uses coalesce. The return value matters, and only for BEFORE ... FOR EACH ROW triggers: returning NEW proceeds, returning a modified NEW writes the modification, and returning NULL silently skips the row. For AFTER and statement-level triggers the return value is ignored, and RETURN NULL is the conventional thing to write.

A BEFORE trigger really does change the stored row:

CREATE FUNCTION upper_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN NEW.name := upper(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER upper_name_trg BEFORE INSERT ON staff
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION upper_name();
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (8, 'quiet', 'ops', true);
SELECT name FROM staff WHERE id = 8;

CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE TRIGGER
INSERT 0 1
 name  
-------
 QUIET
(1 row)

The application inserted quiet and the table holds QUIET. That is a BEFORE trigger's power and precisely its danger — a RETURNING clause would have reported the modified value, and an application that logs what it sent now disagrees with the database.

One line each, for reference: returning clause, returning new, statement-level trigger, new record and old record.

18.19 Statement Triggers and Transition Tables

A row-level trigger on a statement affecting a million rows runs a million times. A statement-level trigger runs once, and transition tables give it the whole set:

CREATE FUNCTION count_changes() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE n int;
BEGIN
  SELECT count(*) INTO n FROM changed;
  RAISE NOTICE 'statement changed % rows', n;
  RETURN NULL;
END $$;

CREATE TRIGGER count_changes_trg AFTER UPDATE ON staff
  REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS changed
  FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION count_changes();

UPDATE staff SET active = true;

CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE TRIGGER
NOTICE:  statement changed 7 rows
UPDATE 7

REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS ... NEW TABLE AS ... makes the before and after images available as ordinary relations you can join, aggregate and insert from. One INSERT INTO audit SELECT ... FROM changed replaces a million per-row inserts, and that is usually a large enough difference to be the reason to restructure an audit trigger.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: row-level trigger and audit trigger.

18.20 Event Triggers, and When Not to Use a Trigger

Event triggers fire on DDL rather than on data: ddl_command_start, ddl_command_end, table_rewrite and sql_drop. pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands() reports what was executed. They are how you log every schema change, or forbid DROP TABLE in production, and they are the only trigger that can see DDL.

The judgement, promised at the start:

Good uses
Auditing that must not be bypassable. Maintaining a denormalised column or a search vector. Enforcing an invariant no constraint can express. INSTEAD OF on a view. Anything that must hold no matter which application wrote the row.
Bad uses
Business rules the application should own. Anything reaching outside the database — a notification, an HTTP call — since it runs inside the caller's transaction and a rollback cannot recall it. Cascading chains where one trigger fires another.

Four costs are worth stating explicitly. A trigger is invisible at the call site — nothing in INSERT INTO staff ... says that four other tables will change. It runs inside the caller's transaction, so its work is part of their latency and its locks are part of their lock set. A row trigger is per row, so a bulk load with a trigger is a different operation from a bulk load without one. And triggers compose badly: two independently reasonable triggers on one table can be a recursion, and PostgreSQL will not stop you.

Prefer, in order: a constraint (declarative, planner-visible, cheap), a generated column (§4.10, for derived values), and only then a trigger. When you do write one, keep it small, make it idempotent, and give it a WHEN clause so it does not run when nothing relevant changed.

What This Section Established

A view stores no data; the rewriter inlines it, so an outer WHERE can become an inner index condition. CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW may only add columns at the end.

An auto-updatable view is one table, no aggregation, simple columns. An insert through a view can produce a row the view cannot see — measured, 4 rows in the table and 2 in the view. WITH CHECK OPTION prevents it and belongs on every updatable view.

A view runs as its owner. security_invoker reverses that; security_barrier stops the planner pushing a caller's predicate below the view's filter.

A materialized view stores its result and is stale until refreshed, with nothing to warn you. REFRESH CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index and does not block readers.

Rules underlie views and should not be written directly; triggers do the same jobs with per-row semantics.

LANGUAGE sql for one query, plpgsql for logic. BEGIN ATOMIC is parsed at creation time and records dependencies, unlike a string body.

RETURNS TABLE needs qualified column references. A set-returning function is opaque to the planner and estimated at 1000 rows.

Volatility is not optional: the default is VOLATILE, measured as provolatile = 'v' on an unmarked constant function, and PARALLEL UNSAFE is also the default — which forces the whole query serial. Only IMMUTABLE may be used in an index expression.

SQL functions inline; PL/pgSQL functions never do. That is the argument for writing scalar helpers in LANGUAGE sql.

SELECT INTO does not error on zero or many rows; INTO STRICT does. FOUND and GET DIAGNOSTICS ROW_COUNT report what happened. A per-row loop is between ten and a thousand times slower than the set-based statement it replaces.

Every EXCEPTION block is an implicit savepoint with a real cost; ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is cheaper than catching unique_violation.

Dynamic SQL: %I for identifiers, %L for literals, %s is the injection vector — and passing values with USING is better than any of them.

A procedure can COMMIT, which is why batch jobs are procedures and not functions.

Triggers: BEFORE can modify NEW and cancel the row by returning NULL; AFTER sees the final state; INSTEAD OF is views only. Statement triggers fire even for zero rows, and transition tables give them the whole change set as a relation — measured at one notice for a six-row update.

A BEFORE trigger changed quiet into QUIET between the application's INSERT and the stored row.

Prefer a constraint, then a generated column, then a trigger. Never put an external side effect in one.

Exercises

1. Break a view three ways. Build an updatable view with a filter. Insert a row through it that it cannot see. Add WITH CHECK OPTION and show the insert now fails. Then make the view non-updatable (add a join) and report the error from an UPDATE, and fix it with an INSTEAD OF trigger.

2. Measure the staleness window. Create a materialized view over a table you then modify. Show it stale. Add the unique index, refresh concurrently, and time both refresh forms on a table of a hundred thousand rows. Report both numbers and say which you would schedule.

3. Prove inlining. Write the same scalar helper twice — once in LANGUAGE sql, once in plpgsql — and use each in a WHERE clause against an indexed column. Compare the plans. Report which one produced an index condition and explain why.

4. Cost the default volatility. Declare a function that returns a constant with no volatility marker. Use it in a query over a large table and record the plan and timing. Add IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE and record both again.

5. Replace a loop. Write a PL/pgSQL function that loops over ten thousand rows issuing one UPDATE each, and time it. Write the equivalent single UPDATE and time that. Report the ratio, and state the one case where the loop is still the right answer.

6. Audit two ways. Implement an audit trail with a row-level AFTER trigger, then with a statement-level trigger and a transition table. Update ten thousand rows in one statement under each. Compare the number of trigger invocations and the elapsed time.

7. Build a trigger you would defend. Choose one invariant that no constraint can express, implement it as a trigger, and write the three-sentence justification you would put in the code review — including what would break if someone dropped it.

Solution

1. Breaking a view.

The first two are §18.2 and §18.3. The third:

CREATE VIEW staff_with_audit AS
  SELECT s.id, s.name, a.op FROM staff s LEFT JOIN audit_log a ON a.who = s.name;
\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
UPDATE staff_with_audit SET name = 'x' WHERE id = 1;

CREATE VIEW
ERROR:  cannot update view "staff_with_audit"
DETAIL:  Views that do not select from a single table or view are not automatically updatable.
HINT:  To enable updating the view, provide an INSTEAD OF UPDATE trigger or an unconditional ON UPDATE DO INSTEAD rule.

The DETAIL names the rule that was violated, and the HINT names both remedies. An INSTEAD OF UPDATE trigger makes it work by deciding, in code you write, which base table a given update applies to — which is the honest reason the automatic rules stop at one table: with a join there is no single right answer.

2. The staleness window.

The functional half is §18.5. On a large table the timing result is consistent: plain REFRESH is faster in wall-clock time, and CONCURRENTLY is the one you schedule, because plain refresh holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for its whole duration and every reader is blocked for exactly that long.

The decision is therefore not about which is faster but about who waits. A nightly refresh of a reporting view with no readers at 03:00 should be plain. Anything refreshed while the application is serving should be CONCURRENTLY, and the extra total work is the price of not blocking.

3. Proving inlining.

CREATE TABLE big (id int PRIMARY KEY, v int);
INSERT INTO big SELECT g, g FROM generate_series(1, 50000) g;
ANALYZE big;
CREATE FUNCTION sq_sql(x int) RETURNS int LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS 'SELECT x * 2';
CREATE FUNCTION sq_plpgsql(x int) RETURNS int LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$
BEGIN RETURN x * 2; END $$;
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM big WHERE id = sq_sql(21);
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT * FROM big WHERE id = sq_plpgsql(21);

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 50000
ANALYZE
CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE FUNCTION
SET
                QUERY PLAN                
------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using big_pkey on big
   Index Cond: (id = 42)
(2 rows)

                QUERY PLAN                 
-------------------------------------------
 Index Scan using big_pkey on big
   Index Cond: (id = sq_plpgsql(21))
(2 rows)

Both use the index here, and the difference is visible in the Index Cond: the SQL function was folded to the constant 42 at planning time, while the PL/pgSQL one remains a call the executor must make. With an IMMUTABLE constant argument that costs one call; with the function applied to a column the SQL version can become an index condition on an expression index and the PL/pgSQL version cannot.

4. The cost of the default.

An unmarked function is VOLATILE (§18.10), so it is re-evaluated per row rather than once, and it cannot be folded into a constant. Marking it IMMUTABLE moves the evaluation to planning time.

PARALLEL SAFE is the larger effect on a big table: with the default PARALLEL UNSAFE, no plan containing the function may use a Gather node at all, so a query that would have used four workers runs on one. The plan difference is visible without timing anything.

5. Replacing a loop.

The ratio is typically between 10× and 1000×, and the reason is that each iteration is a separate statement with its own planning, execution and row-level bookkeeping, while the single UPDATE plans once and streams.

The one case where the loop is still right: when the work genuinely cannot be expressed as one statement and must be committed in batches — a backfill over ten million rows that would otherwise be one transaction holding back vacuum for an hour (§14.17). Then the loop belongs in a procedure with a COMMIT per batch (§18.16), and each batch is still a set-based UPDATE over a range of keys, not a row at a time.

6. Auditing two ways.

The row trigger fires once per row: ten thousand invocations, ten thousand inserts into the audit table. The statement trigger fires once and does a single INSERT INTO audit_log SELECT ... FROM changed.

The difference is not marginal, and it is not only the function-call overhead — it is ten thousand single-row inserts against one ten-thousand-row insert, which is the same comparison as §11.10's bulk-load advice.

The row trigger keeps one advantage worth naming: it can veto or modify per row, and it sees each row in isolation, which makes it simpler to write correctly. Use the statement form when the volume justifies the extra care.

7. A trigger worth defending.

A defensible example: an order may not be marked shipped unless every one of its items has a non-null dispatch reference. No CHECK constraint can express it, because a check sees one row and this spans two tables. A foreign key cannot express it either. It must hold regardless of which service writes the row.

The three sentences: what it enforces ("an order cannot reach shipped while any of its items lacks a dispatch reference"), why it is here rather than in the application ("three services write this table and one of them is a vendor integration we do not control"), and what breaks without it ("orders reach customers' shipping notifications with items that were never dispatched, and we find out from support tickets").

If any of those three sentences is hard to write, the logic probably belongs in the application.

SECTION 19

Partitioning, Sharding and Scale

Everything so far has assumed one table on one server. This section is about what changes when that stops being enough: splitting a table into pieces the database manages, splitting a database across machines, sharing a limited pool of connections, and changing a schema that is being written to while you change it.

The honest framing first. PostgreSQL scales vertically further than most people expect, and the first answer to "we need to shard" is almost always an index, a query rewrite, or a bigger machine. The techniques below solve real problems and each one costs you something — usually a constraint you can no longer enforce, or an operation that used to be one statement and is now three.

19.1 Declarative Partitioning

A partitioned table is a logical table whose rows live in child tables. You query the parent; PostgreSQL routes writes and directs reads.

SET timezone = 'UTC';
CREATE TABLE ev (at date NOT NULL, v int) PARTITION BY RANGE (at);
CREATE TABLE ev_jan PARTITION OF ev FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-02-01');
CREATE TABLE ev_feb PARTITION OF ev FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-02-01') TO ('2026-03-01');
CREATE TABLE ev_default PARTITION OF ev DEFAULT;
INSERT INTO ev SELECT date '2026-01-01' + (g % 75), g FROM generate_series(1, 7500) AS g;
ANALYZE ev;
SELECT tableoid::regclass AS partition, count(*) FROM ev GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

SET
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 7500
ANALYZE
 partition  | count 
------------+-------
 ev_jan     |  3100
 ev_feb     |  2800
 ev_default |  1600
(3 rows)

One INSERT into the parent, three partitions filled. tableoid (§4.11) is how you see which one a row landed in.

The DEFAULT partition catches rows matching no bound. Without it, an out-of-range insert fails — which is a genuine choice: the default partition prevents errors and quietly accumulates rows that should have had a partition, and its presence also makes attaching a new partition more expensive, because PostgreSQL must scan the default to prove none of its rows belong in the newcomer.

19.2 The Three Strategies

RANGE partitioning
Bounds are [from, to) — inclusive lower, exclusive upper, so consecutive months tile exactly. The common case, almost always on time.
LIST partitioning
Explicit values per partition. For a small closed set — region, tenant tier, country group.
HASH
Modulus and remainder. Even distribution with no natural boundary — and no pruning for range queries, because the hash destroys ordering.
CREATE TABLE hash_demo (id int, v text) PARTITION BY HASH (id);
CREATE TABLE hash_demo_0 PARTITION OF hash_demo FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE hash_demo_1 PARTITION OF hash_demo FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 1);
CREATE TABLE hash_demo_2 PARTITION OF hash_demo FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 2);
CREATE TABLE hash_demo_3 PARTITION OF hash_demo FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 3);
INSERT INTO hash_demo SELECT g, 'x' FROM generate_series(1, 4000) AS g;
SELECT tableoid::regclass AS part, count(*) FROM hash_demo GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 4000
    part     | count 
-------------+-------
 hash_demo_0 |   984
 hash_demo_1 |  1007
 hash_demo_2 |  1018
 hash_demo_3 |   991
(4 rows)

Even to within 2%. Changing the modulus later means rewriting everything, which is the main argument against hash partitioning: range and list partitions can be added and removed, and a hash scheme's partition count is effectively fixed at design time.

LIST with a DEFAULT is the flexible middle:

CREATE TABLE list_demo (region text, v int) PARTITION BY LIST (region);
CREATE TABLE list_demo_eu    PARTITION OF list_demo FOR VALUES IN ('DE','FR','ES');
CREATE TABLE list_demo_other PARTITION OF list_demo DEFAULT;
INSERT INTO list_demo VALUES ('DE',1), ('FR',2), ('JP',3);
SELECT tableoid::regclass AS part, region FROM list_demo ORDER BY region;

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
      part       | region 
-----------------+--------
 list_demo_eu    | DE
 list_demo_eu    | FR
 list_demo_other | JP
(3 rows)

Partitions may themselves be partitioned — sub-partitioning, for example by month and then by region. It works, and it multiplies the number of tables, so the planning cost of §19.5 arrives sooner.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: range partitioning, list partitioning and hash partitioning.

19.3 Partition Pruning

The payoff. A query whose WHERE clause constrains the partition key touches only the relevant partitions:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM ev WHERE at >= '2026-02-01' AND at < '2026-03-01';

SET
                                 QUERY PLAN                                 
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Seq Scan on ev_feb ev
         Filter: ((at >= '2026-02-01'::date) AND (at < '2026-03-01'::date))
(3 rows)

One partition in the plan. The other two are not scanned, not opened, and not planned. Without the predicate, all three appear under an Append:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM ev;

SET
             QUERY PLAN              
-------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Append
         ->  Seq Scan on ev_jan ev_1
         ->  Seq Scan on ev_feb ev_2
         ->  Seq Scan on ev_default ev_3
(5 rows)

Pruning happens at two times, and the difference matters. Plan-time pruning uses constant predicates, as above. Runtime partition pruning handles values not known at planning — a parameter in a prepared statement, or a value produced by the other side of a nested loop — and shows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE as Subplans Removed: N.

Constraint exclusion — the constraint_exclusion setting — is the older mechanism, used with inheritance-based partitioning and with CHECK constraints; declarative partitioning uses the newer pruning code and does not need it.

To have in hand before moving on: runtime partition pruning and constraint exclusion.

19.4 Attaching and Detaching

The operational payoff is that a partition is a table, so bulk operations become metadata changes.

A second parent, with no DEFAULT partition, so that a newcomer has somewhere to go:

CREATE TABLE evx (at date NOT NULL, v int) PARTITION BY RANGE (at);
CREATE TABLE evx_jan PARTITION OF evx FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-01-01') TO ('2026-02-01');
INSERT INTO evx SELECT date '2026-01-01' + (g % 31), g FROM generate_series(1, 310) AS g;

CREATE TABLE evx_feb (LIKE evx INCLUDING ALL);
INSERT INTO evx_feb VALUES ('2026-02-05', 1), ('2026-02-06', 2);
ALTER TABLE evx_feb ADD CONSTRAINT evx_feb_range CHECK (at >= '2026-02-01' AND at < '2026-03-01');
ALTER TABLE evx ATTACH PARTITION evx_feb FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-02-01') TO ('2026-03-01');
SELECT tableoid::regclass AS part, count(*) FROM evx GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 310
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 2
ALTER TABLE
ALTER TABLE
  part   | count 
---------+-------
 evx_jan |   310
 evx_feb |     2
(2 rows)

A DEFAULT partition would have blocked that attach. The default is defined as "everything not matched by another partition", so adding a February partition to a parent whose default already holds February rows requires PostgreSQL to scan the default and prove none of them belong to the newcomer — and if any do, it refuses. That is the hidden cost of a default partition mentioned in §19.1.

The CHECK constraint before the ATTACH is the important part. Attaching normally scans the whole table to verify every row is in range, holding a lock while it does. With a matching validated constraint already present, PostgreSQL skips the scan — so a table you load offline over hours becomes visible in milliseconds.

Two restrictions catch people. A partition may not contain an identity column — ALTER TABLE ... ATTACH refuses with "The new partition may not contain an identity column", so LIKE ... INCLUDING ALL on a parent with an identity column produces a table that cannot be attached. And the attached table's columns must match the parent exactly in name, type and order.

Detaching is the reverse, and is how you expire old data:

ALTER TABLE evx DETACH PARTITION evx_feb;
SELECT count(*) AS still_in_parent FROM evx WHERE at >= '2026-02-01';
SELECT count(*) AS still_in_evx_feb FROM evx_feb;

ALTER TABLE
 still_in_parent 
-----------------
               0
(1 row)

 still_in_evx_feb 
------------------
                2
(1 row)

Detaching is instant and destroys nothing — the rows are still there, in a table that is now independent. DROP TABLE evx_feb after that frees the space immediately, where DELETE FROM evx WHERE at >= '2026-02-01' would have written a dead version per row and left the work to vacuum (§16.2).

That is the single strongest argument for time-partitioning a large log or event table: retention becomes DETACH and DROP instead of a mass delete.

DETACH CONCURRENTLY avoids the brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, at the cost of not being runnable inside a transaction block.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: attach partition, detach partition and detach concurrently.

19.5 What Partitioning Costs

Four costs, and each is a rule you can no longer enforce or an operation that got harder.

Unique keys must include the partition key
A global unique index across partitions does not exist, so UNIQUE (email) on a table partitioned by month is impossible. This is frequently the fact that decides against partitioning.
Foreign keys to a partitioned table
Supported since PostgreSQL 12, and only against a key that includes the partition column — which follows from the point above.
Planning cost
Grows with the partition count. Hundreds are fine; thousands make planning itself the bottleneck, especially for queries that cannot prune.
An update that moves a row
Changing the partition key is implemented as a delete plus an insert into another partition. It works (since PostgreSQL 11) and it is not cheap.

Partition on the column your queries filter on, not on the one that divides most evenly — pruning is the whole point, and a partition key nothing filters by gives you every cost and no benefit.

Partitionwise join (enable_partitionwise_join) joins matching partitions pairwise rather than appending everything first, and partitionwise aggregate does the same for GROUP BY. Both are off by default, because they increase planning time and memory, and both are large wins when two tables are partitioned identically.

In summary, the vocabulary here is partitionwise join.

19.6 The Time-Series Pattern

Time-series partitioning is the shape worth memorising, because it is what most partitioning is:

Range on time
One partition per day, week or month, sized so that the active partition fits comfortably in cache.
Create ahead
A scheduled job creates next month's partition before it is needed. Relying on a DEFAULT partition to catch the overflow works and puts the rows in the wrong place.
Partition maintenance
DETACH then DROP, or DETACH and archive. Constant time, no bloat.
Index per partition
An index on the parent is created on every partition. Old, cold partitions can have fewer indexes than the hot one — a real saving that a single table cannot offer.

pg_partman automates creation and retention, and TimescaleDB goes further with automatic chunking and compression. Both are worth considering before writing the maintenance job yourself.

What to carry forward from this subsection: partition maintenance and time-series partitioning.

19.7 Sharding

Partitioning splits a table within one server. Sharding splits data across servers, and PostgreSQL has no built-in transparent sharding.

The available routes, in ascending order of complexity:

Application-level routing. The application knows which server holds which tenant and connects accordingly. Simple, explicit, and it gives up cross-shard queries and cross-shard transactions entirely — which for a multi-tenant system where tenants never interact is not a loss.

postgres_fdw with partitions on foreign tables. A partitioned table whose partitions are foreign tables on other servers. Queries work, pruning works, and joins that cannot be pushed down pull rows across the network. Transactions across shards are not atomic without two-phase commit, which brings its own operational burden.

Citus, an extension that distributes tables across a cluster with a coordinator, handling routing, distributed joins and distributed transactions. The most complete answer and the largest commitment.

Before any of them, exhaust the alternatives: read replicas for read scaling (§16.16), partitioning for table size, connection pooling for connection count, and a bigger machine — which today can mean hundreds of cores and terabytes of RAM. Sharding permanently costs you cross-shard queries, cross-shard uniqueness and cross-shard transactions, and there is no undo.

19.8 Connection Pooling

PostgreSQL forks a process per connection (§1.3). Each costs memory and a share of every internal scan of the process array, so max_connections in the low hundreds is normal and raising it to thousands degrades the whole server.

Applications want more connections than that, and a pooler is the answer.

session pooling
A client keeps a server connection for its whole session. Safe for everything, and saves only the cost of connecting.
transaction pooling
A server connection is assigned per transaction. Thousands of clients over dozens of connections. The mode people actually want, and the one with rules.
statement pooling
Per statement. Breaks multi-statement transactions outright; essentially unusable.

What transaction pooling breaks, and this list is the whole of it:

Session-scoped state does not survive. SET outside a transaction, SET ROLE, temporary tables, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and session-level advisory locks (§15.9) may all end up on a different backend next transaction. Use SET LOCAL inside the transaction, and pg_advisory_xact_lock.

A prepared statement in a pool is per-connection. A driver that prepares once and executes many times will find its statement missing, or — worse — will silently re-prepare on every new backend and lose the benefit. PgBouncer 1.21 and later can track them; before that, the fix was to disable server-side prepares in the driver, which also gives up the plan caching of §13.13.

PgBouncer is the standard choice — small, single-process, mature. pgcat and Odyssey are multi-threaded alternatives. And several drivers pool in-process, which is enough when the application has a fixed small number of instances and unnecessary complexity to duplicate if a pooler is already there.

The terms above, gathered: prepared statement in a pool.

19.9 Migrations That Do Not Take the Site Down

A schema migration on a live database is a lock problem before it is anything else (§15.2). Three rules cover most of it.

Set the lock_timeout in a migration, before every one.

SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE ev ADD COLUMN note text;

SET
ALTER TABLE

Without it, an ALTER TABLE that cannot get its lock waits — and everything behind it waits too, because lock requests queue in order. A three-second timeout turns "the site is down" into "the migration failed, retry it".

Know which forms rewrite (§4.12). Catalogue-only changes are instant at any size; a rewrite is an outage proportional to the table.

Split anything that cannot be done atomically into expand and contract. The pattern is four deployments, every step is a backward-compatible migration, and together they are the whole of zero-downtime migration:

1. Expand
Add the new column, table or index. Additive only, so the running application is unaffected.
2. Write both
Deploy code that writes old and new, and reads old. Backfill the new column in committed batches (§11.7).
3. Read new
Deploy code that reads the new column. Still writing both, so a rollback is safe.
4. Contract
Stop writing the old, then drop it — after you are sure no rollback will need it.

Renaming a column is the canonical example: ALTER TABLE ... RENAME is instant and breaks every running instance of the old code at once. The four-step version never has a moment where deployed code disagrees with the schema.

Three specific rules that fall out of it: add a column nullable or with a constant default (instant since 11, §4.2); create indexes CONCURRENTLY (§12.11), which means outside a transaction, which means your migration tool needs an escape hatch; and add constraints NOT VALID then VALIDATE (§4.9).

A migration tool's job is to record which migrations have run, in order, exactly once — and to do that transactionally, which PostgreSQL's transactional DDL (§14.6) makes possible and most other databases do not. The two features worth requiring of one: it can run a migration outside a transaction (for CONCURRENTLY), and it can express a lock timeout.

One line each, for reference: schema migration, backward-compatible migration, expand and contract, zero-downtime migration and lock_timeout in a migration.

What This Section Established

Partitioning splits a table within one server; sharding splits across servers; PostgreSQL has the first built in and not the second.

Rows route on insert and tableoid shows where they landed. A DEFAULT partition prevents out-of-range errors, accumulates misfiled rows, and makes later ATTACHes more expensive.

RANGE bounds are [from, to) and tile exactly. HASH distributes evenly — measured within 2% over four partitions — and its modulus cannot be changed without rewriting everything. LIST plus DEFAULT is the flexible middle.

Pruning is the payoff: one partition in the plan with a constraining predicate, all three under an Append without. Plan-time pruning uses constants; run-time pruning reports Subplans Removed.

ATTACH with a matching validated CHECK already in place skips the verification scan. A partition may not contain an identity column. DETACH is instant and destroys nothing, which makes retention a DETACH plus a DROP rather than a mass delete.

The costs: a unique constraint must include the partition key, so global uniqueness is impossible; foreign keys to a partitioned table must target such a key; planning cost grows with partition count; and an update that moves a row is a delete plus an insert. Partition on the column you filter by.

Partitionwise join and aggregate are off by default and are large wins on identically partitioned tables.

Sharding: application routing, postgres_fdw partitions, or Citus — and none of them is atomic across shards without two-phase commit. Exhaust replicas, partitioning, pooling and a bigger machine first, because sharding has no undo.

A process per connection means max_connections in the hundreds. Transaction pooling breaks session state: SET outside a transaction, SET ROLE, temp tables, LISTEN, session advisory locks and server-side prepared statements. Use SET LOCAL and pg_advisory_xact_lock.

Migrations: lock_timeout before every one, because a blocked ALTER TABLE blocks everything behind it. Know which ALTER forms rewrite. Expand and contract in four deployments for anything not atomically safe. Indexes CONCURRENTLY, constraints NOT VALID then VALIDATE.

Exercises

1. Build a time-partitioned table. Range-partition by month, load a year of data, and verify pruning with EXPLAIN for a single-month query and a full-table query. Then add next month's partition and expire the oldest with DETACH and DROP, timing both against the equivalent DELETE.

2. Attach without a scan. Load a table offline, attach it as a partition with and without a pre-existing matching CHECK constraint, and compare the duration and the lock taken. Report both.

3. Hit the unique-constraint limit. Try to add UNIQUE (email) to a table partitioned by month. Report the error. Then design two ways around it and say what each gives up.

4. Find the partition-count cliff. Create a partitioned table with 10, 100, 1,000 and 5,000 partitions. Time planning for a query that prunes to one and for a query that cannot prune. Report where planning time becomes the dominant cost.

5. Break transaction pooling. With a pooler in transaction mode — or by simulating one with two connections — demonstrate a session-level advisory lock being stranded, and a SET not surviving. Then fix each and state the rule.

6. Migrate a column rename with no downtime. Take a column two application versions depend on, and perform the four-step expand-and-contract. Write out the exact SQL and the deployment order, and state at which points a rollback is safe.

7. Time a blocked migration. Start a long SELECT, then run an ALTER TABLE in another session, then a third SELECT. Show the third one blocked behind the second. Add lock_timeout and show the difference.

Solution

1. A time-partitioned table.

§19.3 measures pruning. The retention comparison is the interesting half: DETACH plus DROP is two catalogue operations and an unlink — effectively constant time regardless of the partition's size. DELETE FROM ev WHERE at < '2026-02-01' writes a dead row version for every row (§14.7), generates WAL proportional to the data, leaves the space to vacuum, and bloats the table until it runs.

On a month of a large event table the difference is between milliseconds and hours, and the bloat afterwards is the part that keeps costing.

2. Attaching without a scan.

Without a matching constraint, ATTACH scans the whole table to verify every row is within the bounds, holding a lock on the parent while it does. With a validated CHECK that implies the bounds, PostgreSQL proves it from the catalogue and skips the scan entirely.

The practical procedure that follows: build the new partition as an ordinary table, load it at whatever pace you like, add the CHECK, then attach. The visible operation is then milliseconds regardless of how long the load took.

3. The unique-constraint limit.

CREATE TABLE up (id int, email text, at date NOT NULL) PARTITION BY RANGE (at);
\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
ALTER TABLE up ADD CONSTRAINT up_email UNIQUE (email);

CREATE TABLE
ERROR:  unique constraint on partitioned table must include all partitioning columns
DETAIL:  UNIQUE constraint on table "up" lacks column "at" which is part of the partition key.

The message states the rule exactly. Two ways around it:

Do not partition that table. Uniqueness on a non-partition-key column is a strong signal that the table is an entity table rather than an event log, and entity tables are usually the wrong thing to partition.

Keep a separate unpartitioned table holding just the unique column and a reference, with the unique constraint on it, written in the same transaction. That gives up nothing except an extra insert and a join — and it gives up atomicity if the two writes are ever separated, so they must not be.

A third option people reach for and should not: enforcing uniqueness in the application. That is §14.13's write skew with a longer fuse.

4. The partition-count cliff.

Planning time grows with the number of partitions the planner must consider, which pruning reduces. A query that prunes to one partition stays fast well past a thousand; a query that cannot prune degrades roughly linearly, and somewhere in the low thousands the planning cost exceeds the execution cost for short queries.

The practical rule: a few hundred partitions is comfortable, a few thousand needs every query to prune, and tens of thousands needs a different design. Sub-partitioning multiplies the count and reaches the cliff faster than people expect.

5. Breaking transaction pooling.

The stranded lock: session A takes pg_advisory_lock(1) and its transaction ends; the pooler returns the connection to the pool. Session A's next transaction lands on a different backend, and its attempt to unlock finds nothing — while the original backend still holds the lock, and will until it is reused by someone who happens to unlock it or the connection closes.

SET app.tenant = 'x' outside a transaction has the mirror-image problem: the next transaction may not see it, so a row-level security policy reading it (§20.10) silently returns nothing.

The rules are one line each: SET LOCAL inside the transaction, and pg_advisory_xact_lock. Both tie the state to the transaction, which is exactly the unit the pooler preserves.

6. Renaming with no downtime.

1. ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN new_name text;              -- instant
2. deploy: write both columns, read old
   backfill in batches: UPDATE t SET new_name = old_name WHERE new_name IS NULL ...
3. deploy: read new_name, still writing both
4. deploy: write only new_name
5. ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN old_name;                  -- instant

Rollback is safe at every point between 2 and 4, because both columns are populated and either version of the code works. It stops being safe after step 4's deployment has been running long enough for new rows to exist with only new_name — which is why step 5 waits, and why the wait is measured in days rather than minutes.

The single ALTER TABLE ... RENAME alternative is instant and correct at the database level, and breaks every running instance of the old code in the moment between the rename and the deployment finishing. That gap is the outage.

7. A blocked migration.

The third SELECT blocks, and that is the result worth seeing: it conflicts with nothing that is running — it is queued behind the ALTER TABLE's pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request, which is itself queued behind a SELECT that is merely slow.

SET lock_timeout = '3s' on the migration session changes the outcome entirely: the ALTER TABLE fails after three seconds, releases its place in the queue, and the third SELECT runs immediately. The migration is retried, perhaps several times, and at no point is the table unavailable.
