That is the whole argument, and it is why lock_timeout belongs in the migration tool's configuration rather than in a runbook.

SECTION 20

Security, Operations and the Application Boundary

The last content section is about the database as something other people can reach: who may do what, how an application should talk to it, and what to watch once it is running.

The security half rests on a single observation. Your database is not protected by your application. It is reached by a connection string, and anything holding one — a compromised service, a leaked backup, an engineer with psql, a second application written by another team — has exactly the privileges that connection's role was granted. Every rule that matters must be enforced by the database, which is the same argument §4 made about constraints, applied to access.

20.1 Roles

PostgreSQL has one concept where other systems have two: a role is both a user and a group, and the difference is only whether it has LOGIN.

DROP ROLE IF EXISTS app_reader, app_writer;
CREATE ROLE app_reader NOLOGIN;
CREATE ROLE app_writer NOLOGIN;
SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcanlogin, rolbypassrls, rolinherit
FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname LIKE 'app_%' ORDER BY rolname;

NOTICE:  role "app_reader" does not exist, skipping
NOTICE:  role "app_writer" does not exist, skipping
DROP ROLE
CREATE ROLE
CREATE ROLE
  rolname   | rolsuper | rolcanlogin | rolbypassrls | rolinherit 
------------+----------+-------------+--------------+------------
 app_reader | f        | f           | f            | t
 app_writer | f        | f           | f            | t
(2 rows)

On a fresh server DROP ROLE IF EXISTS finds nothing, says so in a NOTICE per role, and still reports DROP ROLE — that is the output above. Run the block a second time and the notices disappear, because the roles now exist. That difference is itself the point: the DROP ROLE IF EXISTS is there for a reason worth stating: roles belong to the cluster, not to a database. Dropping and recreating the database leaves them behind, which is why a setup script that only creates roles is not re-runnable and why a role cannot be dropped while it still owns an object in any database of the cluster.

A role attribute is set at CREATE ROLE or altered later, and the ones that matter are: the LOGIN privilege (may connect), SUPERUSER (bypasses every permission check, including row-level security), CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLS, and INHERIT — which decides whether membership in a group grants its privileges automatically or requires SET ROLE.

Role membership is the mechanism: the pattern worth adopting is group roles for privileges and login roles for identities. An INHERIT role attribute on the member decides whether the group's privileges apply automatically. Grant SELECT to app_reader; make each service's login role a member. A new service is one GRANT ... TO, and revoking is one statement rather than an audit of every table.

PostgreSQL ships predefined roles for common needs, so that "read everything" no longer requires superuser: pg_read_all_data, pg_write_all_data, pg_monitor, pg_signal_backend, pg_read_server_files, and — new in 18 — pg_signal_autovacuum_worker. pg_monitor in particular is what a metrics exporter should have, and handing one superuser is a common and unnecessary risk.

Nothing routine should run as a superuser. Not the application, not migrations, not the monitoring agent. A superuser ignores every mechanism in this section.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: login privilege, role membership, inherit role attribute and predefined role.

20.2 GRANT and REVOKE

CREATE TABLE secrets (id int PRIMARY KEY, tenant text, body text);
INSERT INTO secrets VALUES (1,'ada','a'), (2,'lin','b'), (3,'ada','c');
GRANT SELECT ON secrets TO app_reader;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON secrets TO app_writer;
SELECT grantee, string_agg(privilege_type, ',' ORDER BY privilege_type) AS privileges
FROM information_schema.role_table_grants
WHERE table_name = 'secrets' AND grantee LIKE 'app_%'
GROUP BY grantee ORDER BY grantee;

CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
GRANT
GRANT
  grantee   |      privileges      
------------+----------------------
 app_reader | SELECT
 app_writer | INSERT,SELECT,UPDATE
(2 rows)

A GRANT statement adds a privilege and a REVOKE statement removes one. Privileges exist on tables (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER), as a column-level privilege (GRANT SELECT (id, tenant) ON secrets TO ...), on schemas (USAGE, CREATE), on databases, functions, sequences and types.

Two facts about the model catch people.

USAGE on a schema is required as well. A GRANT SELECT on a table in a schema the role cannot USAGE is useless, and the resulting "permission denied for schema" points at the wrong object.

Object ownership carries everything implicitly and cannot be revoked from without changing the owner. Owner privileges do not appear in role_table_grants for that role, which is why an audit that lists grants can miss the account with the most power.

ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES is the fix for the commonest operational failure in this area — a table created next month having none of the grants you set up today:

ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO app_reader;
CREATE TABLE created_later (id int);
SELECT has_table_privilege('app_reader', 'created_later', 'SELECT') AS granted_automatically;

ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES
CREATE TABLE
 granted_automatically 
-----------------------
 t
(1 row)

It applies to objects created by a particular role — the role running it, unless FOR ROLE names another — which is the detail people miss: default privileges set up for your own account do nothing for tables a migration tool creates as a different role.

has_table_privilege() is the right way to check, rather than reading catalogues:

SELECT has_table_privilege('app_reader','secrets','SELECT') AS can_select,
       has_table_privilege('app_reader','secrets','INSERT') AS can_insert;

 can_select | can_insert 
------------+------------
 t          | f
(1 row)

Note also that the PUBLIC role — the pseudo-role meaning everyone — used to have CREATE on the public schema**, so any user could create objects there. PostgreSQL 15 changed that default. On a database created before 15, REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC is worth running.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: public schema, grant statement, revoke statement, object ownership, column-level privilege, usage on a schema and public role.

20.3 Row-Level Security

Table privileges are all-or-nothing per table. Row-level security filters at the row.

ALTER TABLE secrets ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON secrets USING (tenant = current_setting('app.tenant', true));
SET app.tenant = 'ada';
SET ROLE app_reader;
SELECT id, tenant FROM secrets ORDER BY id;
RESET ROLE;

ALTER TABLE
CREATE POLICY
SET
SET
 id | tenant 
----+--------
  1 | ada
  3 | ada
(2 rows)

RESET

SET app.tenant = 'lin';
SET ROLE app_reader;
SELECT id, tenant FROM secrets ORDER BY id;
RESET ROLE;

SET
SET
 id | tenant 
----+--------
  2 | lin
(1 row)

RESET

The same query, the same role, different rows — decided by a session variable the policy reads. That is multi-tenant isolation enforced by the database rather than by every WHERE clause in the application, and it holds for a query written by someone who has never heard of the tenant column.

A policy has two expressions: a USING expression filters what is visible to SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE, and a WITH CHECK expression validates what may be written by INSERT and UPDATE. Omitting WITH CHECK on a writable table lets a tenant insert a row belonging to another tenant that they then cannot see — which is a real and easily-missed hole.

The unset variable behaves correctly, which is worth confirming rather than assuming:

RESET app.tenant;
SET ROLE app_reader;
SELECT count(*) AS with_no_tenant_set FROM secrets;
RESET ROLE;

RESET
SET
 with_no_tenant_set 
--------------------
                  0
(1 row)

RESET

Zero — current_setting('app.tenant', true) returns NULL, tenant = NULL is unknown, and no row qualifies. Failing closed is the behaviour you want, and note that the second argument to current_setting is what makes it return NULL instead of raising.

Now the part that must be understood before relying on any of it:

SET app.tenant = 'ada';
SELECT count(*) AS as_table_owner FROM secrets;
ALTER TABLE secrets FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
SELECT count(*) AS after_force FROM secrets;

SET
 as_table_owner 
----------------
              3
(1 row)

ALTER TABLE
 after_force 
-------------
           3
(1 row)

Three rows both times, with app.tenant set to ada. The policy did not apply, and FORCE did not change that — because this session is a superuser, and a superuser bypasses row-level security unconditionally. So does a role with BYPASSRLS, and by default so does the table's owner, which is what FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY exists to change.

The rules to take away: RLS does not apply to superusers, to BYPASSRLS roles, or (without FORCE) to the table owner. An application connecting as the owner of its tables gets no isolation at all — which is exactly how a multi-tenant system ships with RLS configured and not working. The application's role must not own the tables.

Views interact too: a view runs as its owner (§18.4), so RLS on the base table is evaluated against the view owner unless the view is declared security_invoker.

To have in hand before moving on: using expression and with check expression.

20.4 SECURITY DEFINER

A function normally runs with the caller's privileges. SECURITY DEFINER makes it run with its owner's — the mechanism for "let this role do exactly this one privileged thing".

CREATE FUNCTION whoami() RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER
  SET search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp
  AS $$ SELECT current_user::text $$;
SET ROLE app_reader;
SELECT whoami() AS runs_as;
RESET ROLE;
SELECT proname, prosecdef, proconfig FROM pg_proc WHERE proname = 'whoami';

CREATE FUNCTION
SET
 runs_as 
---------
 course
(1 row)

RESET
 proname | prosecdef |              proconfig              
---------+-----------+-------------------------------------
 whoami  | t         | {"search_path=pg_catalog, pg_temp"}
(1 row)

Called by app_reader, it ran as course. That is the whole feature, and it is also the whole risk: the function is a hole in the privilege system, deliberately made, and everything inside it runs with elevated rights.

Four rules, and the first two are not optional:

Pin the search_path
SET search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp, or the function is open to a search_path attack. Otherwise the caller controls which schema an unqualified name resolves in, and can supply their own lower() or their own table (§4.14). pg_temp must be last, or a temporary object can shadow a real one.
Revoke from PUBLIC
A new function is executable by everyone by default. REVOKE EXECUTE ... FROM PUBLIC then grant to the role that should have it.
Validate everything
Arguments are attacker-controlled. A definer function that builds dynamic SQL from one is a privilege escalation (§20.5).
Keep it small
One operation, narrowly defined. A definer function that does five things is five holes.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: search_path attack.

20.5 SQL Injection

The mechanism is string concatenation: a value becomes part of the statement text rather than a value in it.

PREPARE lookup(text) AS SELECT id, tenant FROM secrets WHERE tenant = $1;
EXECUTE lookup('ada'' OR ''1''=''1');
DEALLOCATE lookup;

PREPARE
 id | tenant 
----+--------
(0 rows)

DEALLOCATE

Zero rows. The attack string was compared as a literal tenant name, found no match, and did nothing — because the statement was parsed before the value existed. Concatenated into the text, the same string would have made the condition always true.

That is the fix, and it is one rule: a parameterized query sends values as parameters, never as text. A PREPARE statement plans it once and an EXECUTE statement supplies the values. Every driver supports it; the syntax differs ($1, ?, :name) and the mechanism is identical — the SQL is planned first, and the value can never become syntax.

Where a parameter is impossible, the escapes are the second line:

SELECT quote_literal('x'' OR ''1''=''1') AS quoted,
       format('%L', 'x'' OR ''1''=''1')  AS formatted,
       format('%I', 'my table')          AS identifier;

       quoted       |     formatted      | identifier  
--------------------+--------------------+-------------
 'x'' OR ''1''=''1' | 'x'' OR ''1''=''1' | "my table"
(1 row)

Identifiers cannot be parameters. A table or column name chosen at run time must be interpolated, and %I (or quote_ident) is how — never %s. The stronger form is not to interpolate at all: validate the name against a fixed allowlist, or look it up in pg_class, so that only names that already exist can reach the statement.

Two more shapes worth naming. ORDER BY is not parameterisable, so a sortable column supplied by the client is an allowlist, not an escape. And LIKE patterns need % and _ escaped in the value, or a user searching for 100% matches everything.

The defence in depth beyond that is the rest of this section: a least privilege role means a successful injection reads what that role could read; RLS means it reads one tenant's rows; statement_timeout means it cannot run for an hour.

In summary, the vocabulary here is like pattern, parameterized query, prepare statement, execute statement and least privilege.

20.6 Encryption and Secrets

In transit, sslmode in the connection string is the setting, and its values are not equally safe. require encrypts and does not verify the certificate, so it stops passive eavesdropping and not an active attacker. verify-ca checks the certificate chain; verify-full also checks the hostname and is the only value that is actually secure. The default is prefer, which silently falls back to no encryption at all.

At rest, PostgreSQL has no built-in table encryption. Full-disk encryption is the usual answer and protects against a stolen disk, not against anyone with a connection. pgcrypto encrypts individual columns and moves the problem to key management — and a column encrypted in the database cannot be indexed, sorted or searched, which is usually what makes the design impractical.

Passwords use scram-sha-256; the older md5 method is deprecated and should be migrated. Nothing sensitive belongs in a connection string in source control, and pg_hba.conf decides which methods are even offered.

Logging leaks. log_statement = 'all' writes every statement including its literals, and an error message quotes the offending value — §1.13's DETAIL: Key (email)=(...) already exists is a real address in a log file. Treat the server log as containing production data.

20.7 Auditing

Three levels, in ascending order of cost and fidelity.

log_statement and its relatives are built in and free. ddl logs schema changes and is a reasonable permanent setting; all logs everything and is a performance and privacy cost.

Trigger-based auditing (§18.18) writes a row per change to an audit table, with the old and new values — and PostgreSQL 18's RETURNING old.*, new.* (§11.2) makes the statement-level version cheaper than it was. It captures what changed, and not who read what.

pgaudit is the extension for compliance work: it can log by object and by class, including SELECTs, in a parseable format. It is what you reach for when an auditor asks the question rather than when you do.

An audit trail the audited role can modify is not an audit trail. The audit table should be writable only by a role the application does not have, which in practice means a SECURITY DEFINER trigger function owned by someone else.

20.8 What to Monitor

Database monitoring rests on five views, and they answer different questions.

pg_stat_activity
What is running now, what it is waiting on, and how long it has been in idle in transaction (§14.17).
pg_stat_statements
Which queries consume the time, aggregated by normalised text. Sort by total, not mean (§13.16).
pg_stat_user_tables
Dead tuples, last autovacuum, sequential versus index scans per table (§16.9).
pg_stat_database
Cache hit ratio, deadlocks, conflicts, transaction rate, and — added in 18 — parallel worker activity.
pg_stat_io
Reads, writes, hits and evictions by backend type and context. In 18 it reports bytes as well as block counts, and includes WAL activity.
SELECT count(*) > 0 AS pg_stat_io_exists FROM pg_stat_io;
SELECT count(*) >= 0 AS pg_aios_exists FROM pg_aios;

 pg_stat_io_exists 
-------------------
 t
(1 row)

 pg_aios_exists 
----------------
 t
(1 row)

pg_aios is new in PostgreSQL 18 and shows in-flight asynchronous I/O — the subsystem behind the new io_method setting, which on this server is worker and can also be io_uring on Linux.

The alerts worth having, drawn from the rest of the course: transaction id age (§16.7, the one that ends in an outage), replication lag and inactive slots (§16.16, the one that fills the disk), connection count against max_connections, idle in transaction duration, and dead tuples on the largest tables. Cache hit ratio is the metric most often watched and least often actionable — a 99% ratio on a badly-indexed query is 99% of far too many reads.

What to carry forward from this subsection: io_method, asynchronous i/o and database monitoring.

20.9 Extensions

SELECT extname FROM pg_extension ORDER BY extname;

      extname       
--------------------
 btree_gist

 pageinspect
 pg_stat_statements
 pg_trgm

(7 rows)

Those are the ones this course installed. The ones worth knowing exist:

pg_stat_statements
Query statistics. Install it on every server; needs a restart, so do it before you need it.
pg_trgm
Fuzzy matching and leading-wildcard indexes (§17.14).
btree_gist / btree_gin
Mixed-operator exclusion constraints (§4.8) and composite GIN indexes.
pgcrypto
Hashing and column encryption.
postgres_fdw / dblink
Reaching other servers (§4.15). dblink is what made §14's two-session experiments runnable.
PostGIS / pgvector / TimescaleDB
Geospatial, vector similarity, and time-series — three cases where an extension replaces a separate datastore.

Installing a PostgreSQL extension with CREATE EXTENSION runs arbitrary code as its author intended, so it requires appropriate privileges and the list of installed extensions is part of your security posture. PostgreSQL 18's extension_control_path makes it easier to install extensions outside the system directory, which is convenient and widens that surface.

The terms above, gathered: postgresql extension.

20.10 The Application Boundary

Where should logic live? The answer is not "always the database" or "always the application", and the dividing line is stable:

In the database
Anything that must be true of the data regardless of who wrote it. Types, constraints, foreign keys, uniqueness, tenant isolation. These are properties of the data, and the database outlives the application.
In the application
Workflow, presentation, orchestration, anything calling other services, anything that changes weekly. These are properties of a process, not of the data.

The test that resolves most arguments: "if a second application were written against this database tomorrow, would this rule still have to hold?" If yes, it belongs in the database. Almost every "the ORM should own this" disagreement dissolves once that question is asked, because the honest answer for a uniqueness rule or a foreign key is always yes.

Three practical corollaries.

An ORM is a mapping layer, not a schema authority. Letting it generate migrations is convenient and produces schemas with no check constraints, nullable columns everywhere, and indexes only where a query was slow. Read what it generates, and add what it omits.

N+1 is the dominant performance bug in application data access, and it is §1.2's "think in sets" failing in practice: a loop that issues one query per row. pg_stat_statements finds it immediately — a query with an enormous call count and a tiny mean time.

Keep transactions short and free of external calls (§14.17). A transaction that spans an HTTP request holds its snapshot, blocks vacuum globally, and holds every lock it has taken while waiting for a network it does not control.

20.11 A Checklist Worth Keeping

Drawn from the whole course, in the order things go wrong:

Before launch
Not superuser. statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout set. pg_stat_statements installed. sslmode=verify-full. A restore rehearsed, not just a backup taken.
Weekly
Top queries by total time. Unused and duplicate indexes. Tables with growing dead tuples. Transaction id age.
Per migration
lock_timeout set. Rewrite forms identified. Indexes CONCURRENTLY. Constraints NOT VALID then VALIDATE. Expand-and-contract for anything not additive.
Per query written
Parameters not concatenation. ORDER BY if order matters, and total. EXPLAIN before shipping anything that scans a large table.

What This Section Established

Your database is reached by a connection string, so every rule that matters must be enforced by the database.

A role is a user and a group; LOGIN is the only difference. Group roles carry privileges, login roles carry identity. Predefined roles like pg_monitor exist so that monitoring need not be superuser. Nothing routine should be superuser.

GRANT needs USAGE on the schema too. The owner has everything implicitly and does not appear in a grants audit. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES covers objects created later — by the role that runs it, which is the detail that makes it silently not work.

Row-level security filters rows by a policy — measured: the same query and role returned Ada's two rows and then Lin's one, and zero with no tenant set, because NULL fails closed. USING governs reads, WITH CHECK governs writes, and omitting the latter lets a tenant write rows they cannot see.

RLS does not apply to superusers, BYPASSRLS roles, or the table owner without FORCE — measured, three rows returned with a tenant set and FORCE on, because the session was superuser. The application's role must not own its tables.

SECURITY DEFINER runs as the owner — measured. Pin search_path with pg_temp last, revoke from PUBLIC, validate every argument, keep it small.

Injection is fixed by parameters — measured, 'ada'' OR ''1''=''1' matched nothing. Identifiers cannot be parameters, so %I or an allowlist; ORDER BY is an allowlist; LIKE patterns need % escaped in the value.

sslmode=verify-full is the only setting that verifies the host; the default prefer silently falls back to plaintext. There is no built-in encryption at rest, and an encrypted column cannot be indexed. Server logs contain production data.

Monitor pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements (by total time), pg_stat_user_tables, pg_stat_database and pg_stat_io. Alert on transaction id age, replication lag and inactive slots, connections, idle in transaction, and dead tuples.

The boundary: if a second application would still need the rule, it belongs in the database. An ORM is a mapping layer, not a schema authority. N+1 is the dominant application data bug. Transactions stay short and contain no external calls.

Exercises

1. Build a least-privilege role set. For an application with a web tier and a background worker, define group roles and login roles so that the web tier cannot run the worker's writes. Prove each restriction with has_table_privilege, and show a table created afterwards inheriting the grants.

2. Make RLS not work. Configure tenant isolation, then connect as the table's owner and show it returning every row. Add FORCE, and show it still failing if the role is superuser. Then fix it properly and state the two rules.

3. Close the WITH CHECK hole. Write an RLS policy with only USING, and demonstrate a tenant inserting a row they cannot then read. Add WITH CHECK and show the insert refused.

4. Escalate through a definer function. Write a SECURITY DEFINER function with no pinned search_path that calls an unqualified function, and show a low-privilege role redirecting it. Fix it, and explain why pg_temp must be last.

5. Inject three ways, defend three ways. Demonstrate injection through a value, through an identifier and through an ORDER BY clause. Defend each — parameter, %I, allowlist — and say why the second and third cannot use the first.

6. Find your own N+1. Enable pg_stat_statements, exercise an application path, and find the query with the highest call count. Rewrite it as a single set-based query and compare total time.

7. Write the alert queries. Produce runnable SQL for the five alerts in §20.8, each returning a single boolean or a number you would threshold. Say what value you would alert at and why.

Solution

1. A least-privilege role set.

DROP ROLE IF EXISTS web_role, worker_role;
CREATE ROLE web_role NOLOGIN;
CREATE ROLE worker_role NOLOGIN;
CREATE TABLE jobs_q (id int PRIMARY KEY, state text);
GRANT SELECT ON jobs_q TO web_role;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON jobs_q TO worker_role;
SELECT has_table_privilege('web_role','jobs_q','UPDATE')    AS web_can_update,
       has_table_privilege('worker_role','jobs_q','UPDATE') AS worker_can_update;

NOTICE:  role "web_role" does not exist, skipping
NOTICE:  role "worker_role" does not exist, skipping
DROP ROLE
CREATE ROLE
CREATE ROLE
CREATE TABLE
GRANT
GRANT
 web_can_update | worker_can_update 
----------------+-------------------
 f              | t
(1 row)

The login roles are then members: CREATE ROLE web_svc LOGIN IN ROLE web_role. Adding a second web instance is one statement, and revoking is one statement.

The part that fails in practice is the next table. ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO web_role fixes it — and only for tables created by the role that ran it, which is why it must be run FOR ROLE <migration_role> when a migration tool owns the DDL.

2. Making RLS not work.

§20.3 measures it: three rows as the table owner, three rows still after FORCE, because the session is superuser.

The two rules: the application must not connect as a superuser, and the application must not own the tables it queries — or, if it must, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is mandatory. The usual arrangement is a separate migration role that owns the schema and an app role that has only the grants it needs, which satisfies both without FORCE.

Worth noting how this fails: it fails open, silently, with the policies visibly configured. \d shows the policies, the tests written by a developer connecting as the app role pass, and production connects as the owner. Verify by querying as the actual production role.

3. The WITH CHECK hole.

With only USING, an INSERT is not filtered — USING governs which existing rows are visible, and an inserted row is not an existing row. So a tenant can insert tenant = 'someone_else', the row is stored, and the same session cannot read it back.

That is worse than it sounds: the write succeeded, so the application reports success; the data is in another tenant's view; and no error was raised anywhere. WITH CHECK (tenant = current_setting('app.tenant', true)) refuses it at insert time.

The rule: a policy on a writable table needs both clauses. USING alone is complete only for a read-only table.

4. Escalating through a definer function.

Without a pinned path, the caller's search_path applies inside the definer function. A role that can create objects in any schema on that path supplies its own function or table, and it runs with the definer's privileges.

pg_temp must be last because every session can create temporary objects and the temporary schema is searched implicitly. If it is not named explicitly at the end, PostgreSQL searches it first — so a caller creates pg_temp.some_table, and a definer function referring to some_table reads the attacker's table instead of the real one. Naming it last is what pushes it behind pg_catalog.

5. Three injections.

Value: fixed by a parameter, as §20.5 measures.

Identifier: cannot be a parameter, because the statement cannot be planned without knowing which table it reads. format('%I') quotes it safely; an allowlist is better still, because it also prevents reading a table the query was never meant to touch.

ORDER BY: cannot be a parameter for the same reason, and %I alone is insufficient — a valid column name can still be one the user should not be able to sort by, and sort order can leak the contents of a column they cannot select. An explicit map from client-visible sort keys to column expressions is the only correct defence.

The general principle: parameters protect the places where a value goes; everything that is part of the statement's structure needs an allowlist.

6. Finding an N+1.

SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 3) AS mean_ms, query
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY calls DESC LIMIT <n>;

The signature is a very high calls with a very low mean_exec_time and a total_exec_time near the top of the list. The query text is usually a single-row primary-key lookup — which looks perfectly efficient in isolation, and is the point: each execution is fine and the aggregate is the problem.

The rewrite is a join, or WHERE id = ANY($1) with an array of the ids (§17.11) — one statement instead of a thousand, one round trip instead of a thousand. The saving is usually dominated by network round trips rather than by database time, which is why it does not show up in a profile of the database alone.

7. The alert queries.

SELECT max(age(datfrozenxid)) < 150000000                          AS wraparound_ok FROM pg_database;
SELECT count(*) = 0                                                AS no_inactive_slots FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE NOT active;
SELECT count(*)::float / current_setting('max_connections')::float < 0.8 AS connections_ok FROM pg_stat_activity;
SELECT count(*) = 0                                                AS no_long_idle_txn FROM pg_stat_activity
  WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' AND xact_start < now() - interval '5 minutes';
SELECT coalesce(max(n_dead_tup), 0) < 1000000                      AS dead_tuples_ok FROM pg_stat_user_tables;

 wraparound_ok 
---------------
 t
(1 row)

 no_inactive_slots 
-------------------
 t
(1 row)

 connections_ok 
----------------
 t
(1 row)

 no_long_idle_txn 
------------------
 t
(1 row)

 dead_tuples_ok 
----------------
 t
(1 row)

The thresholds and their reasons: 150 million against a 200-million autovacuum_freeze_max_age, leaving time to investigate rather than to react (§16.7). Any inactive slot, because a single one fills the disk eventually and there is no benign case. 80% of max_connections, because the last 20% is what an incident needs. Five minutes idle in transaction, because anything longer is a bug and it blocks vacuum globally (§14.17). Dead tuples is the one that needs a per-table threshold rather than a global one — the useful form is dead as a fraction of live, on tables above some size, and trending rather than absolute.

SECTION 21

Capstone: Building a System That Holds Up

Everything in this course has been one idea at a time. This section is one system, built end to end, where the ideas have to work together — and where several of them constrain each other in ways that only appear when you build.

The brief: a multi-tenant ticketing service. Organisers create events; each event has seats; customers book seats. It must be impossible to double-book a seat, impossible for one organiser to see another's data, and possible to answer "how are sales going" without a table scan. It has a background worker, it retains a year of activity logs, and it is deployed continuously.

That brief is chosen because it forces every hard decision in this course: an invariant no CHECK can express (§4.8), a race no application code can win (§15.5), tenant isolation (§20.3), a retention policy (§19.4), and a report that must be fast (§13).

Work through each stage before reading its solution.

21.1 Stage 1 — The Schema

Task. Design tables for organisers, events, seats, bookings and an activity log. Decide every type, every key, every constraint. State for each nullable column why it is nullable.

The constraints to satisfy, in words:

  • A seat belongs to exactly one event; a seat's label is unique within its event.
  • A booking is for one seat, by one customer, at one time.
  • Money is exact.
  • Every row is attributable to an organiser.
  • An event's activity log will grow to hundreds of millions of rows and is queried only by recent time ranges.
Solution — Stage 1 
CREATE TABLE tix_organiser (
  organiser_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  slug         text        NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (slug ~ '^[a-z0-9-]{2,40}$'),
  name         text        NOT NULL,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE tix_event (
  event_id     bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  organiser_id bigint      NOT NULL REFERENCES tix_organiser,
  title        text        NOT NULL CHECK (length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),
  starts_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  ends_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
  status       text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft'
                           CHECK (status IN ('draft','on_sale','closed','cancelled')),
  CONSTRAINT tix_event_times CHECK (ends_at > starts_at)
);

CREATE TABLE tix_seat (
  seat_id     bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id    bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES tix_event ON DELETE CASCADE,
  label       text    NOT NULL,
  price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0),
  UNIQUE (event_id, label)
);

CREATE TABLE tix_booking (
  booking_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  seat_id     bigint      NOT NULL REFERENCES tix_seat,
  customer_ref text       NOT NULL,
  booked_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  state       text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'held'
                          CHECK (state IN ('held','paid','released')),
  paid_cents  integer     CHECK (paid_cents IS NULL OR paid_cents >= 0),
  CONSTRAINT tix_booking_paid_when_paid
    CHECK ((state = 'paid') = (paid_cents IS NOT NULL))
);

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE

Six decisions worth defending.

bigint identity keys everywhere (§3.1). The conversion later is an outage, and four bytes is nothing.

price_cents integer, not numeric and never float (§3.3). Integer minor units are exact, compare at hardware speed, and force display formatting to be explicit.

timestamptz, never timestamp (§3.6). An event's start is an instant; a naive timestamp cannot be compared across time zones and this system has organisers in several.

Every CHECK is paired with NOT NULL where it matters (§4.4), because a NULL satisfies every check. The one deliberate exception is paid_cents, which is nullable — and its nullability is tied to state by CHECK ((state = 'paid') = (paid_cents IS NOT NULL)), so the two cannot disagree (§5.9).

slug has a format check. It appears in URLs, so the constraint that keeps it URL-safe belongs in the database rather than in whichever service happens to insert next.

UNIQUE (event_id, label) rather than a global unique on label — seat "A1" exists at every event, and the uniqueness is per event.

21.2 Stage 2 — The Invariant No CHECK Can Express

Task. A seat must not be double-booked. A released booking must not block a new one. Enforce this so that it holds under concurrency, and prove it holds by attempting the race from two sessions.

Think about why a UNIQUE (seat_id) is not enough before reading on.

Solution — Stage 2

UNIQUE (seat_id) is wrong because a released booking would permanently block the seat. The rule is "at most one active booking per seat", which is a partial unique index (§12.6):

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX tix_one_active_booking
  ON tix_booking (seat_id) WHERE state IN ('held','paid');

CREATE INDEX

Now the race. Two sessions try to book the same seat at the same moment, using the harness from §14.1:

INSERT INTO tix_organiser (slug, name) VALUES ('acme','Acme Events');
INSERT INTO tix_event (organiser_id, title, starts_at, ends_at, status)
VALUES (1, 'Opening Night', '2026-06-01 19:00+00', '2026-06-01 22:00+00', 'on_sale');
INSERT INTO tix_seat (event_id, label, price_cents)
SELECT 1, 'A' || g, 4500 FROM generate_series(1, 20) AS g;

SELECT other($x$ INSERT INTO tix_booking (seat_id, customer_ref) VALUES (1, 'first') $x$)
       AS other_session_booked;
\set ON_ERROR_STOP off
INSERT INTO tix_booking (seat_id, customer_ref) VALUES (1, 'second');

INSERT 0 1
INSERT 0 1
INSERT 0 20
 other_session_booked 
----------------------
 INSERT 0 1
(1 row)

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "tix_one_active_booking"
DETAIL:  Key (seat_id)=(1) already exists.

The second booking was refused by the index, not by any code. That is the property that matters: it holds for a booking made by the web tier, by the worker, by a support engineer at a psql prompt, and by a service written next year by another team.

Releasing the seat frees it, which is what the partial predicate buys:

UPDATE tix_booking SET state = 'released' WHERE seat_id = 1;
INSERT INTO tix_booking (seat_id, customer_ref, booked_at)
VALUES (1, 'third', '2026-05-01 10:00+00')
RETURNING booking_id, seat_id;

UPDATE 1
 booking_id | seat_id 
------------+---------
          3 |       1
(1 row)

INSERT 0 1

Note booking_id is 3, not 2: the refused insert above consumed a sequence value and did not give it back. Gaps are normal (§3.4), and a system that needs a gapless series cannot use a sequence.

The alternatives and why they lose. Check-then-insert in the application is the write skew of §14.13 — two sessions both find the seat free. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the seat row works but serialises every booking attempt for that seat and, per §15.4, would block inserts into any table referencing tix_seat. SERIALIZABLE works and costs a retry loop everywhere. The partial unique index costs nothing and is checked by the storage engine.

For a seat range rather than a single seat — a table at a dinner, a time slot in a studio — the same reasoning leads to an exclusion constraint (§4.8) instead, and the argument is identical.

21.3 Stage 3 — The Booking Transaction

Task. Write the statement a worker runs to convert a held booking to paid, given a booking id and an amount. It must be safe to run twice — the worker may be killed after committing and before acknowledging — and it must report whether it did anything.

Solution — Stage 3 
UPDATE tix_booking
SET state = 'paid', paid_cents = 4500
WHERE booking_id = 3 AND state = 'held'
RETURNING booking_id, old.state AS was, new.state AS now;

 booking_id |  was  | now  
------------+-------+------
          3 | held  | paid
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

Run it again:

UPDATE tix_booking
SET state = 'paid', paid_cents = 4500
WHERE booking_id = 3 AND state = 'held'
RETURNING booking_id, old.state AS was, new.state AS now;

 booking_id | was | now 
------------+-----+-----
(0 rows)

UPDATE 0

Zero rows the second time. Three techniques are doing the work.

The AND state = 'held' in the WHERE clause is optimistic concurrency (§11.12): the update succeeds exactly once, and a second attempt matches nothing. No lock, no retry, no version column.

RETURNING reports which happened — a row means this call made the transition, no rows means someone else already did. The worker acknowledges either way, and neither outcome is an error.

old. and new. qualifiers (§11.2, PostgreSQL 18) let one statement report both sides, so the audit record needs no prior read and therefore has no race between the read and the write.

Note what is not here: no BEGIN, because one statement is already atomic; no SELECT first, because that would introduce the gap the WHERE clause closes; and no external call, because §14.17 says a transaction that waits on a network holds its snapshot while it waits.

21.4 Stage 4 — The Worker Queue

Task. The worker processes bookings that have been held too long and releases them. Several workers run at once. Write the claim query so that no two workers take the same booking and no worker waits for another.

Solution — Stage 4 
CREATE INDEX tix_booking_held ON tix_booking (booked_at) WHERE state = 'held';
INSERT INTO tix_booking (seat_id, customer_ref, booked_at)
VALUES (2, 'stale-hold', '2026-05-01 09:00+00');

UPDATE tix_booking SET state = 'released'
WHERE booking_id = (
  SELECT booking_id FROM tix_booking
  WHERE state = 'held'
  ORDER BY booked_at
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 1)
RETURNING booking_id, seat_id;

CREATE INDEX
INSERT 0 1
 booking_id | seat_id 
------------+---------
          4 |       2
(1 row)

UPDATE 1

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (§15.5) is the whole mechanism: the subquery locks the row it picks, so two workers cannot select the same one, and SKIP LOCKED means the second worker moves to the next candidate rather than blocking.

The partial index on (booked_at) WHERE state = 'held' is what keeps this cheap as the table grows: the queue is a small minority of a large table, and without the partial predicate the scan would grow with the history rather than with the backlog (§12.6).

Two properties to state plainly rather than assume. The delivery guarantee is at-least-once — a worker that dies after committing but before acknowledging leaves work that looks done and may be retried, which is why Stage 3's statement is idempotent. And a worker that dies mid-transaction rolls back, so its row returns to the queue automatically; a worker that dies after committing a claim but before finishing needs a claimed_at column and a sweeper.

21.5 Stage 5 — Sales Reporting

Task. For one organiser, produce: total revenue per event, each event's share of the organiser's total, the running revenue by day, and the three best-selling events. One pass over the data where possible.

Solution — Stage 5 
INSERT INTO tix_booking (seat_id, customer_ref, state, paid_cents, booked_at)
SELECT s.seat_id, 'c' || s.seat_id, 'paid', s.price_cents,
       timestamptz '2026-05-01 00:00+00' + (s.seat_id % 5) * interval '1 day'
FROM tix_seat s WHERE s.seat_id BETWEEN 5 AND 18;

SELECT e.title,
       sum(b.paid_cents)                                      AS revenue_cents,
       round(100.0 * sum(b.paid_cents)
             / sum(sum(b.paid_cents)) OVER (), 1)             AS pct_of_organiser
FROM tix_event e
JOIN tix_seat s    ON s.event_id = e.event_id
JOIN tix_booking b ON b.seat_id = s.seat_id AND b.state = 'paid'
WHERE e.organiser_id = 1
GROUP BY e.event_id, e.title
ORDER BY revenue_cents DESC;

INSERT 0 14
     title     | revenue_cents | pct_of_organiser 
---------------+---------------+------------------
 Opening Night |         67500 |            100.0
(1 row)

sum(sum(...)) OVER () — a window over aggregated rows (§10.7) — gives each event's share of the total without a second query or a self-join.

The running total by day:

SELECT b.booked_at::date AS day,
       sum(b.paid_cents) AS day_cents,
       sum(sum(b.paid_cents)) OVER (ORDER BY b.booked_at::date
                                    ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_cents
FROM tix_booking b
JOIN tix_seat s ON s.seat_id = b.seat_id
JOIN tix_event e ON e.event_id = s.event_id AND e.organiser_id = 1
WHERE b.state = 'paid'
GROUP BY b.booked_at::date
ORDER BY day;

    day     | day_cents | running_cents 
------------+-----------+---------------
 2026-05-01 |     18000 |         18000
 2026-05-02 |     13500 |         31500
 2026-05-03 |     13500 |         45000
 2026-05-04 |     13500 |         58500
 2026-05-05 |      9000 |         67500
(5 rows)

ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, not the default frame — §10.4 measured what the default does to a running total when the ordering column has duplicates. Here the GROUP BY makes days unique so both would agree, and writing ROWS states the intent and survives someone removing the grouping.

Top three per organiser is §10.8's pattern, and note it needs a subquery because a window function cannot be filtered in WHERE:

SELECT title, revenue_cents FROM (
  SELECT e.title, sum(b.paid_cents) AS revenue_cents,
         row_number() OVER (ORDER BY sum(b.paid_cents) DESC, e.event_id) AS rn
  FROM tix_event e
  JOIN tix_seat s    ON s.event_id = e.event_id
  JOIN tix_booking b ON b.seat_id = s.seat_id AND b.state = 'paid'
  WHERE e.organiser_id = 1
  GROUP BY e.event_id, e.title) t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY rn;

     title     | revenue_cents 
---------------+---------------
 Opening Night |         67500
(1 row)

The tiebreak , e.event_id in the window's ORDER BY is not decoration (§10.3): without it, two events with equal revenue get an arbitrary and possibly unstable ordering.

21.6 Stage 6 — Indexing, and Reading the Plan

Task. The sales report above is run constantly. Decide which indexes it needs, add them, and verify from the plan that they are used. Then find one index you should not add and say why.

Solution — Stage 6

The join path is tix_event → tix_seat → tix_booking, filtered by organiser and by booking state.

CREATE INDEX tix_event_organiser ON tix_event (organiser_id);
CREATE INDEX tix_seat_event      ON tix_seat (event_id);
CREATE INDEX tix_booking_paid    ON tix_booking (seat_id) INCLUDE (paid_cents)
  WHERE state = 'paid';
ANALYZE tix_event; ANALYZE tix_seat; ANALYZE tix_booking;
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT sum(b.paid_cents) FROM tix_event e
JOIN tix_seat s ON s.event_id = e.event_id
JOIN tix_booking b ON b.seat_id = s.seat_id AND b.state = 'paid'
WHERE e.organiser_id = 1;

CREATE INDEX
CREATE INDEX
CREATE INDEX
ANALYZE
ANALYZE
ANALYZE
SET
SET
                            QUERY PLAN                            
------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Nested Loop
         ->  Nested Loop
               ->  Index Scan using tix_event_organiser on tix_event e
                     Index Cond: (organiser_id = 1)
               ->  Index Scan using tix_seat_event on tix_seat s
                     Index Cond: (event_id = e.event_id)
         ->  Index Scan using tix_booking_paid on tix_booking b
               Index Cond: (seat_id = s.seat_id)
(9 rows)

Three index scans, each serving one step of the join. Note that enable_seqscan = off was needed to force this shape on twenty rows — on a toy table a sequential scan really is cheaper, and §13.15 explains why that switch is a diagnostic rather than a setting.

The three decisions:

tix_seat_event is an index on a foreign key. PostgreSQL does not create it (§4.5), and without it a cascade delete of an event scans the whole seat table.

tix_booking_paid is partial and covering. Partial because only paid bookings are summed, so it indexes a fraction of the rows (§12.6); INCLUDE (paid_cents) so the sum can come from the index without a heap fetch (§12.8) — subject to the visibility map (§12.9), which means it only pays off on a table autovacuum is keeping up with.

The index not to add: tix_booking (state). Low cardinality — three values — so it is unselective for the common value and useless for the rare one that a partial index already covers. Worse, state is updated on every booking transition, so an index on it turns every HOT update into index maintenance (§11.11, §14.7). It costs writes on the hottest path in the system to serve a query that would rather have the partial index.

One line each, for reference: index on a foreign key.

21.7 Stage 7 — The Activity Log

Task. Activity rows arrive continuously, are queried only for the last few days, and must be kept for a year. Design the table so that retention is cheap and recent queries are fast.

Solution — Stage 7 
CREATE TABLE tix_activity (
  at           timestamptz NOT NULL,
  organiser_id bigint      NOT NULL,
  kind         text        NOT NULL,
  detail       jsonb
) PARTITION BY RANGE (at);

CREATE TABLE tix_activity_2026_05 PARTITION OF tix_activity
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-01') TO ('2026-06-01');
CREATE TABLE tix_activity_2026_06 PARTITION OF tix_activity
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-06-01') TO ('2026-07-01');

INSERT INTO tix_activity (at, organiser_id, kind, detail)
SELECT timestamptz '2026-05-01 00:00+00' + (g % 45) * interval '1 day',
       1, 'booking_created', jsonb_build_object('seat', g)
FROM generate_series(1, 4500) AS g;
ANALYZE tix_activity;

SELECT tableoid::regclass AS partition, count(*) FROM tix_activity GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 4500
ANALYZE
      partition       | count 
----------------------+-------
 tix_activity_2026_05 |  3100
 tix_activity_2026_06 |  1400
(2 rows)

A recent-window query touches one partition:

SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
SELECT count(*) FROM tix_activity WHERE at >= '2026-06-01' AND at < '2026-06-15';

SET
                                 QUERY PLAN                                 
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate
   ->  Seq Scan on tix_activity_2026_06 tix_activity
         Filter: ((at >= '2026-06-01'::timestamp with time zone) AND (at < '2026-06-15'::timestamp with time zone))
(3 rows)

Pruning to one partition (§19.3). And retention is a metadata operation:

ALTER TABLE tix_activity DETACH PARTITION tix_activity_2026_05;
DROP TABLE tix_activity_2026_05;
SELECT count(*) AS rows_remaining FROM tix_activity;

ALTER TABLE
DROP TABLE
 rows_remaining 
----------------
           1400
(1 row)

Three thousand one hundred rows expired in two instant statements. DELETE FROM tix_activity WHERE at < '2026-06-01' would have written a dead version per row, generated WAL proportional to the data, and left the space for vacuum (§16.2) — the difference is the entire argument for partitioning a log table.

Two design notes. No primary key, because a unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key (§19.5) and there is nothing here that needs one — the log is append-only and identified by nothing. And detail jsonb is the right use of §17.10's guidance: the shape varies by kind, it is never joined on, and the fields that are queried — at, organiser_id, kind — are real columns.

21.8 Stage 8 — Tenant Isolation

Task. One organiser must never see another's events, regardless of the query. Enforce it in the database, prove it works, and identify the configuration mistake that would silently disable it.

Solution — Stage 8 
DROP ROLE IF EXISTS tix_app;
CREATE ROLE tix_app NOLOGIN;
GRANT SELECT ON tix_event TO tix_app;

INSERT INTO tix_organiser (slug, name) VALUES ('other','Other Events');
INSERT INTO tix_event (organiser_id, title, starts_at, ends_at, status)
VALUES (2, 'Rival Gig', '2026-07-01 19:00+00', '2026-07-01 22:00+00', 'on_sale');

ALTER TABLE tix_event ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tix_event_tenant ON tix_event
  USING (organiser_id = current_setting('app.organiser', true)::bigint)
  WITH CHECK (organiser_id = current_setting('app.organiser', true)::bigint);

SET app.organiser = '1';
SET ROLE tix_app;
SELECT event_id, title FROM tix_event ORDER BY event_id;
RESET ROLE;

NOTICE:  role "tix_app" does not exist, skipping
DROP ROLE
CREATE ROLE
GRANT
INSERT 0 1
INSERT 0 1
ALTER TABLE
CREATE POLICY
SET
SET
 event_id |     title     
----------+---------------
        1 | Opening Night
(1 row)

RESET

SET app.organiser = '2';
SET ROLE tix_app;
SELECT event_id, title FROM tix_event ORDER BY event_id;
RESET ROLE;

SET
SET
 event_id | title     
----------+-----------
        2 | Rival Gig
(1 row)

RESET

One row each, decided entirely by the session variable. No WHERE organiser_id = ... appears in either query, and none needs to — a developer who has never heard of the policy cannot write a query that crosses tenants.

Three details that make it correct rather than nearly correct.

WITH CHECK as well as USING (§20.3). Without it, tix_app could insert an event belonging to organiser 2 while unable to read it back.

current_setting(..., true) — the second argument returns NULL instead of raising when unset, and organiser_id = NULL is unknown, so an unconfigured session sees nothing. Failing closed.

SET LOCAL app.organiser in production, not SET. Behind a transaction pooler (§19.8) a plain SET may not survive to the next transaction, and the session that inherits the connection would run with the previous tenant's setting — which is the worst possible failure of this mechanism.

The configuration mistake that silently disables all of it: connecting as the table's owner, or as a superuser. §20.3 measured it — three rows returned with a policy in force, because RLS does not apply to the owner without FORCE and never applies to a superuser. The application's role must own nothing, and the check is to run the isolation test as the production role, not as yourself.

21.9 Stage 9 — Operations

Task. List what must be configured before this system takes traffic, and write the queries that would have caught each of the failures this course has described.

Solution — Stage 9 
SELECT current_setting('idle_in_transaction_session_timeout')  <> '0'  AS idle_txn_timeout_set,
       current_setting('lock_timeout')                         <> '0'  AS lock_timeout_set,
       (SELECT max(age(datfrozenxid)) FROM pg_database) < 150000000    AS wraparound_ok,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE NOT active) = 0 AS no_dead_slots;

 idle_txn_timeout_set | lock_timeout_set | wraparound_ok | no_dead_slots 
----------------------+------------------+---------------+---------------
 f                    | f                | t             | t
(1 row)

Both timeouts are f, which is the honest state of a default installation and exactly the point: neither is on unless you turn it on, and each of them is the difference between an incident and a failed statement.

The pre-launch list, each item traceable to a failure in this course:

Not superuser, not owner
Or Stage 8's isolation does not apply at all (§20.3).
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
One forgotten transaction blocks vacuum on every table (§14.17, §16.5).
statement_timeout, lock_timeout
A blocked ALTER TABLE blocks every query behind it (§15.2).
pg_stat_statements
Needs a restart, so install it before you need it (§13.16).
autovacuum tuned per table
The 20% default is far too lax for tix_booking (§16.8), which is updated on every state change.
A rehearsed restore
A backup nobody has restored is a hypothesis (§16.15).

And the diagnostic query for the failure most likely to happen first — a blocked migration:

SELECT count(*) AS waiting_lock_requests FROM pg_locks WHERE NOT granted;

 waiting_lock_requests 
-----------------------
                     0
(1 row)

Zero is what you want. Anything else, follow pg_blocking_pids() to the root (§15.7) — which will usually be idle in transaction, which is why that timeout is first on the list.

21.10 What This System Demonstrates

Read back over the nine stages and notice what carried the weight. Almost nothing was application code.

Types and constraints
Made most invalid states unrepresentable before a single query was written.
A partial unique index
Made double-booking impossible under concurrency, in one line, at no runtime cost.
One conditional UPDATE
Replaced a read, a decision, a write and a lock — and is idempotent by construction.
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Made a correct multi-worker queue out of a table.
Window functions
Answered three reporting questions in one pass each, where each would otherwise be a self-join.
Partitioning
Turned a year's retention from a mass delete into two metadata statements.
Row-level security
Made a cross-tenant query unwritable rather than merely discouraged.

The through-line is that each of those pushes a rule from a place where it can be forgotten to a place where it cannot. That is the argument this course has been making since §1, and the reason to learn the database rather than only the query language: the alternatives all work, right up until the second code path.

Exercises

1. Extend the invariant. Add a rule that an event cannot move to on_sale unless it has at least one seat. Decide where it belongs — a CHECK, a trigger, or the application — and defend the choice in the three sentences §18.20 asks for.

2. Add a seat-range booking. Some events sell tables of six rather than single seats. Add a during-style range or a seat range, and enforce non-overlap with an exclusion constraint. Prove it under concurrency.

3. Find the report's real plan. Load a hundred thousand bookings and re-run Stage 5's queries with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Report which index was used, where the estimate diverged from actual, and whether the covering index avoided heap fetches.

4. Break the isolation. Connect as the table owner and show Stage 8's policy not applying. Then fix it two ways — FORCE, and a non-owning role — and say which you would ship and why.

5. Automate retention. Write the procedure that creates next month's activity partition and drops the one from thirteen months ago. Make it idempotent and safe to run twice on the same day.

6. Migrate with traffic. Add a currency column to tix_seat, backfill it, and make it NOT NULL — with no statement holding a lock for more than a second. Write out the exact statements and the deployment order.

7. Cost the wrong choices. For three decisions in Stage 1 — float instead of integer cents, timestamp instead of timestamptz, and a nullable state — describe the specific bug each would eventually produce, and how it would first be noticed.

Solutions

1. Extending the invariant.

A CHECK cannot express it: it spans two tables. So it is a trigger or the application, and the three sentences decide it.

What it enforces: an event may not reach on_sale with no seats. Why in the database: the web tier, the import job and the admin console all change event status, and a customer reaching a purchase page with nothing to buy is a support ticket. What breaks without it: events go on sale empty, and the failure surfaces to customers rather than to us.

All three sentences are easy to write, so a BEFORE UPDATE trigger with a WHEN (NEW.status = 'on_sale' AND OLD.status <> 'on_sale') condition is justified — and the WHEN clause matters, so the check runs on the transition rather than on every update (§18.17).

2. Seat-range booking.

The same shape as §4.8's room bookings: an int4range of seat numbers plus EXCLUDE USING gist (event_id WITH =, seats WITH &&), requiring btree_gist. Under concurrency it holds for the same reason the partial unique index does — it is an index check at insert time, not an application check with a gap.

The design question it raises is worth noticing: with ranges, "seat" stops being a row and becomes a number, which means seat-level attributes (a price per seat, an accessibility flag) have nowhere to live. That is the trade, and it is why most ticketing systems keep seats as rows and accept the partial unique index.

3. The report's real plan.

At a hundred thousand bookings the plan usually becomes a hash join rather than the nested loops of Stage 6 — which is correct, and is §13.8's rule about outer input size doing its work.

The covering index avoids heap fetches only when the visibility map is populated, so a freshly loaded table shows Heap Fetches well above zero until it is vacuumed (§12.9). That is the measurement worth taking, because it is the difference between the index you designed and the index you got.

The estimate to watch is the one on state = 'paid', because it is a skewed low-cardinality column and its selectivity comes from the MCV list (§13.10) — accurate after ANALYZE and badly wrong on a table that has just changed shape.

4. Breaking the isolation.

As the owner, the policy does not apply and every event is returned. ALTER TABLE tix_event FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY fixes it for the owner and still not for a superuser.

Ship the non-owning role. FORCE is a safety net for a case that should not exist, and it does nothing about the superuser case — whereas a role that owns nothing and is not superuser is subject to policies unconditionally. The ownership split also gives you the migration boundary of §19.9 for free: one role owns the schema, another uses it.

5. Automating retention.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE tix_roll_partitions(as_of date) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE nxt date := date_trunc('month', as_of + interval '1 month')::date;
        old date := date_trunc('month', as_of - interval '13 months')::date;
BEGIN
  EXECUTE format(
    'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS %I PARTITION OF tix_activity FOR VALUES FROM (%L) TO (%L)',
    'tix_activity_' || to_char(nxt, 'YYYY_MM'), nxt, nxt + interval '1 month');
  EXECUTE format('DROP TABLE IF EXISTS %I', 'tix_activity_' || to_char(old, 'YYYY_MM'));
END $$;
CALL tix_roll_partitions(DATE '2026-06-15');
SELECT count(*) AS partitions FROM pg_inherits WHERE inhparent = 'tix_activity'::regclass;

CREATE PROCEDURE
NOTICE:  table "tix_activity_2025_05" does not exist, skipping
CALL
 partitions 
------------
          2
(1 row)

IF NOT EXISTS on the create and IF EXISTS on the drop make it idempotent; %I and %L are not optional (§18.15) even though the values are computed rather than supplied, because that is a habit and not a case-by-case judgement.

The production version drops nothing without first checking that the partition is empty of anything still needed, or detaches and archives rather than dropping — because a retention bug that runs on a schedule destroys thirteen months of data before anyone reads the log.

6. Migrating with traffic.

1. ALTER TABLE tix_seat ADD COLUMN currency text;              -- catalogue only
2. deploy: application writes currency on every insert
3. backfill in batches, committing each:
     UPDATE tix_seat SET currency = 'EUR'
     WHERE currency IS NULL AND seat_id BETWEEN <lo> AND <hi>;
4. SET lock_timeout = '1s';
   ALTER TABLE tix_seat ADD CONSTRAINT tix_seat_currency_nn
     CHECK (currency IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;                   -- brief lock
5. ALTER TABLE tix_seat VALIDATE CONSTRAINT tix_seat_currency_nn;  -- weak lock, scans
6. SET lock_timeout = '1s';
   ALTER TABLE tix_seat ALTER COLUMN currency SET NOT NULL;    -- instant, proved by (5)
   ALTER TABLE tix_seat DROP CONSTRAINT tix_seat_currency_nn;

Step 1 is instant because the default is absent (§4.2). Step 5 takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so reads and writes continue while it scans. Step 6 is instant because the validated check proves the condition (§4.12). No step holds a blocking lock for longer than it takes to acquire it, and every step is separately retryable.

Adding NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR' in one statement would also be instant — and would silently label existing rows with a currency that may be wrong, which is why the backfill is explicit.

7. Costing the wrong choices.

float for money. Sums drift (§3.2 measured a thousand additions of one cent coming to 9.999999999999831). First noticed as a reconciliation report that is off by a few cents, months after launch, with no way to identify which transactions contributed — because every one of them is slightly wrong.

timestamp for starts_at. Two organisers in different zones enter "19:00" and the values compare as if they were the same instant. First noticed when a listing sorted by start time puts events in the wrong order for one region, or when a reminder job fires an hour early for half the users — and the data itself does not record enough to repair it, because the zone was never stored.

A nullable state. Every WHERE state = 'held' silently excludes the null rows (§5.7), so a booking with a null state is invisible to the worker, invisible to the report, and holds a seat forever via the partial unique index — which does not exclude it, because state IN ('held','paid') is unknown for a null and the index predicate excludes it, so the seat is bookable twice. First noticed as a double-booked seat that no code path can explain, which is the worst possible way to discover a nullable column.

You started this course able to write queries. You now know what PostgreSQL is doing with them — which is the difference between hoping a query is fast and being able to say why it is not.

What you can now do

  1. Read a plan instead of guessing. EXPLAIN prints a tree, root at the top, rows flowing upward. Compare rows against actual rows from the top down and stop at the first large divergence; under 10× is fine, over 100× means everything above it was decided on a fiction. And multiply by loops before believing any inner node — 40 rows at 199 loops is 7,960 rows.
  2. Choose an index for a reason. Selectivity decides whether one helps at all. Column order is equality, then range, then sort. A condition in Index Cond narrowed the scan; one in Filter did not. And PostgreSQL 18's skip scan changed the leading-column rule from a rule about position into one about cardinality — measured, Index Searches: 51 on an index the query never mentioned the first column of.
  3. Predict what a concurrent write will do. The lost update needs no exotic isolation level: read 100, another session adds 50, write 70, and the 50 is gone with no error. Compute in SQL, or lock the row you read, or accept a retryable failure — but choose, because the default is silent.
  4. Recognise write skew. Both doctors checked the rule, both saw a colleague on call, both went off call, and zero remained. REPEATABLE READ permits it and SERIALIZABLE refuses it — at the UPDATE, not at COMMIT, with Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot.
  5. Put integrity where it cannot be forgotten. A partial unique index made double-booking impossible in one line. An exclusion constraint made overlapping reservations impossible under concurrency, where the application check has a race. Every such rule survives the second code path; none of the application-side versions does.
  6. Handle NULL deliberately. note <> 'set' found one row where IS DISTINCT FROM found two. 3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) returns nothing at all. A NULL satisfies every CHECK. These are not curiosities; they are the shape of the most common silently-wrong query.
  7. Use window functions instead of self-joins. One pass instead of two, and the running-total trap is real: the default RANGE frame includes peers, so a first row reported 300 where 100 was meant. Write ROWS.
  8. Know what vacuum is for and what stops it. Eleven megabytes of data became thirty-four after two updates; VACUUM did not shrink the file and VACUUM FULL did, at the cost of an exclusive lock. One idle transaction holds the horizon for every table in the cluster.
  9. Migrate a live schema. Which ALTER forms rewrite, NOT VALID then VALIDATE, CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction, expand-and-contract in four deployments — and lock_timeout before every one, because a blocked ALTER TABLE blocks everything queued behind it.
  10. Reach for the right storage. jsonb for documents you receive whole, arrays for elements with no identity, ranges plus an exclusion constraint for intervals, tsvector for search — and a normalised table for anything you join on, constrain, or aggregate by.
  11. Enforce tenant isolation in the database. A policy, a session variable, and the same query returning different rows for different tenants — with the caveat that made it worth measuring: it does not apply to a superuser or to the table's owner, which is how a system ships with RLS configured and not working.
  12. Ask the server rather than the internet. Nearly every number in this course came from running something, and several contradicted what is widely repeated.

What was measured rather than repeated

Worth listing, because each one is a claim you will meet stated the other way.

Generated columns default to VIRTUAL in PostgreSQL 18 (attgenerated = 'v'), and virtual columns cannot be indexed — so the new default is the one you cannot search. Every pre-18 source says STORED is mandatory.

NOT VALID still checks new rows; only the existing ones are skipped. NOT ENFORCED — new in 18 — checks nothing at all. The names sound alike and mean opposite things.

A prepared statement switches to a generic plan on the sixth execution, not the first. Five custom plans showing the literal, then one showing $1.

text_pattern_ops is needed for LIKE 'prefix%' only off the C collation. Under ICU the plain index produced no Index Cond at all; the pattern index produced ~>=~ and ~<~.

A hash index is four times the size of a B-tree on the same column and supports only equality. BRIN was 24 kB against 2,240 kB.

An index-only scan needs the visibility map: the identical query was a Bitmap Heap Scan over 280 heap blocks before VACUUM and Heap Fetches: 0 after.

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a parent row blocks inserts into every referencing table, because a foreign-key check takes FOR KEY SHARE — with PostgreSQL's own internal check query visible in the error. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is the fix.

Extended statistics moved an estimate from 11,267 to 33,600 against an actual 33,333. Raising default_statistics_target would not have helped, because the per-column statistics were never wrong.

round(2.5) is 3 on numeric and 2 on double precision. A thousand additions of one cent came to 9.999999999999831.

Column order cost 16% of a table's size — 1,184 kB against 1,024 kB for the same four columns.

json keeps duplicate keys; jsonb keeps the last one and silently discards the rest.

And one that did not reproduce, reported because the absence matters: six variants of a guarded division all evaluated the guard first, despite the documentation declining to promise it. Write the CASE anyway — an observed behaviour that no rule requires is §8.6's lesson in a different costume.

Where to go next

The parts of PostgreSQL this course did not cover are mostly operational: replication topologies, connection routing, high availability tooling (Patroni, pgBackRest), and the extension ecosystem beyond the handful named in §20.9. Each is a deep subject and each becomes urgent at a predictable moment rather than in advance.

PostGIS, pgvector and TimescaleDB are the three extensions that most often replace a second datastore. All three are worth knowing exist before someone proposes adding a service.

The release notes are the highest-value reading. PostgreSQL ships a major version every September, and the notes are specific, honest about what changed under you, and short enough to read in an hour. Several things in this course were true only from 18, and several things widely believed about PostgreSQL stopped being true in 11, 12 or 15.

The two habits that keep this current

Ask the installed server before planning around a feature. Four lines settled a dozen questions here — whether generated columns default to virtual, whether NOT ENFORCED really skips, whether a skip scan happens at this cardinality, whether text_pattern_ops is needed at this collation. Documentation describes what the feature does; the server tells you what your server does.

And measure rather than quote. The single most useful habit in this course was writing the query first and the sentence afterwards. It corrected the plan for the ATTACH demo, the sequence gap in the capstone, the float sum, the extended-statistics estimate, and a claim about evaluation order that turned out to be unreproducible. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), pg_stat_statements ordered by total time, and a scratch database you are willing to break will answer almost any question this course raised — and they will keep answering after the version this was written against has been superseded.
